en: [1] The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara.
The Section on the Householder’s Life;
Auspicious Invocation:
Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of Obstacles, the bestower of the fruit of freedom from obstacles.
The formal proposition (the statement of the subject matter):
His mastery of the Vedic study was for the sake of attaining the reality of the meaning, for the accomplishment of virtuous deeds,
for the destruction of all impurities without remainder, and that [mastery] led, in turn, to liberation.
Having celebrated the festival of the songs sung by the wives of many preeminent brahmins in the cities he bestowed, that Lakṣmīdhara now speaks of the second section: the life of the householder.

In this [section], marriage with its various stages is described, as well as its different forms; furthermore, supersession of a wife, supersession by a younger brother, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the rules for living together are explained.
Next follows the ritual for establishing the sacred fires (agnyādhāna), and thereafter the acts of sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices;
then the means of livelihood for Brahmins, the various occupations of Brahmins, and agriculture.
Trade, usury, and other such occupations are the highest [means of livelihood];
then follow the activities and duties of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, which result in white and black wealth respectively.
The livelihood and duties of a Śūdra, the vows of a Snātaka,
the restraints (yamas) and so forth for families, the causes of family ruin, and the preservation of the family.
Likewise, one must correctly understand what is to be spoken and what is not to be spoken, as well as the rules for entering and departing [the assembly].

One should never, in any circumstance, step upon those things that are not to be stepped upon, nor occupy those places that are not to be occupied, nor gaze upon those things that are not to be looked at.
Now, the wise Lakṣmīdhara declares, in due order, those things not to be given to a Śūdra, the avoidance of anger and the like, and the repayment of debts.
Thus, in this section on the householder, there are twenty-seven festivals.
[3] 1 Now, on the householder's life.
Having thus declared the duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), Saṃvarta says:
"This duty has been fully explained for the twice-born man in the first stage of life (*āśrama*);
hereafter, having returned home (*samāvṛtta*), he should take a wife."
“Samāvṛttaḥ”: having returned from the teacher’s house (gurukula) and performed the sacramental rite known as the ceremonial bath (snāna). Manu says:
“Having studied the Vedas—either all of them, two of them, or even one—in due order...”
Without having violated his vow of celibacy, he may enter the stage of life of a householder.
The options beginning with "one Veda" or "two Vedas" depend upon a person's capacity. "In due order" means according to the prescribed procedure for study and the ritual requirements.
And so Yama says:
"Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, then according to the rule..."
One who knows the Dharma, having not violated his vow of celibacy, should take a wife.
[4] Thus, it is indicated that one whose celibate life has been ruined and who has not performed expiation is ineligible for the subsequent stages of life (*uttarāśrama*).
Likewise:
"Having bathed with the permission of his teacher, he returns home according to the rule."
A twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who is endowed with auspicious marks.
"Lakṣaṇānvitām" means endowed with auspicious indicative marks. Yama says:
"Or, having obtained the permission of the preceptor and having offered the preceptor's fee (guru-dakṣiṇā)..."
Abiding by the will of his mother and father, he should take a wife who is his equal.

The word "vā" (or) is used with reference to the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate). In the phrase "having obtained permission" (*samanujñaya*), the causative sense is implied within the meaning of "having caused [him] to obtain permission.
Nārada states: "[A Brahmin may marry] for the sake of taking wives from among Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras..."
A wife of the same caste is superior for a man, and a husband of the same caste is superior for a woman.
“Of the same caste” means of an identical birth. “Superior” means excellent.
[5] Vasiṣṭha says:

A householder, having subdued anger and joy, being permitted by his teacher, and having performed the ritual bath (*snāna*), shall take a wife who is of the same lineage as the Ṛṣis (*ārṣeyī*), who has not experienced sexual intercourse, who is younger than himself, and who is of equal status.

The term "householder" (*gṛhastha*) is used here figuratively with respect to one who will become so, for the purpose of attaining those duties. Therefore, even one who has not yet taken a wife, provided he possesses the intention to live as a householder and has turned away from other stages of life (*āśrama*), is entitled to the duties of a householder; thus says Bhartṛyajña. Bṛhaspati states:
"One should marry a wife of equal status in terms of family, character, age, and virtues."
Together with her, he should, with a concentrated mind, practice the Dharma according to the Śruti and the Smṛti.

“Of equal status” means one who is suitable in terms of lineage and suitable in terms of age. And that has been stated in such passages as: “A man three times [one’s own age] should marry a wife who is one-tenth his age,” and so forth.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own dharma, who inherits the father's Vedic legacy, and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland. (Manu 3.3)

“Him”—the religious student (*brahmacārin*). “Returning”—having turned back, being intent upon the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*). “By his own duty”—by means of courtesy and so forth. “The receiver of the Veda-inheritance from his father” [6]. The *brahmadāya* (Veda-inheritance) is the inheritance that is the Veda itself. This is a restatement for the sake of emphasizing the primary attainment: that he has acquired the Veda from his father. “One should honor”—one should worship; the words “his father and others” are to be supplied. “With a cow”—this is an elliptical expression for the *madhuparka* offering. Thus says Hārīta.

Permitted by his teacher, he may take ornaments and such; he should wear these only as appropriate. Having formally addressed [his teacher] and taken a wife according to the rules, and having established the sacred fires, he should maintain himself by means of gleaned grain or what is obtained unasked, and for the sake of the ancestors and men, he should provide sustenance from the very food received from virtuous people when they are begging, but not for his own sake.

“Ornaments and so forth” refers to earrings and the like prescribed in one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. By the word “and so forth,” garlands, perfumes, and other items taught in the *Gṛhya* texts are included; their acquisition at the time of the *samāvartana* ceremony is mandatory. Thereafter, they may be worn according to need. “According to need” means that after the *samāvartana*, one should wear them as required by circumstances; however, at the time of the *samāvartana* itself, there is a strict rule (*niyama*). This is the restriction (*yama*).

Having studied one, two, or three Vedas, having satisfied his teacher, and being permitted by him, he should perform the removal of the *muñja* grass, marry a woman of the same caste through a *brāhma* or other approved form of marriage, approach her during her fertile period to procreate sons, establish the domestic sacred fire (*āvasathya*), and honor guests. [7] Kaśyapa says:
"All ritual acts depend upon a wife, especially for Brāhmaṇas."
Then, with every effort, one should marry a wife who is pure.
The worship of the gods, the water-rites for the ancestors, and the taking of a wife proceed from marriage; a wife is the bridge to heaven.
Thus is this the opinion of Kaśyapa and the instruction of Brahmā.
“Pure” means pure by birth and by nature.
Now follows the determination of which girls are suitable for marriage and which are not; regarding this, Manu and Śātātapa state:
She who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the matrimonial rite for sexual union.

“Not a sapinda of her mother” means one other than the daughter of her maternal uncle and so forth. On this point, some say: “In the matter of taking a wife” (*dārakarmaṇi*) refers to the marriage that produces the status of being a wife. [8] “In sexual intercourse” (*maithune*) refers to the act of procreation and so forth, which is accomplished by a male and female denoted by the word *mithuna*, and not merely to acts such as cooking which are accomplished by the woman alone; rather, the meaning is that she would be praiseworthy even in what is accomplished by both. Alternatively, “in sexual intercourse” refers to the production of a righteous son (*dharmyaputra*) and so forth, which is accomplished by the couple. —Gautama.

Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara*. [One may marry] beyond the seventh degree from paternal relatives and beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives on the side of the progenitor.

The state of having the same *pravara* occurs when there is equality in both number and name, as is established by the context. "Paternal kinsmen" (*pitṛbāndhavāḥ*) refers to the sons of the father’s maternal uncle, the father’s mother’s sister, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and [the kinsmen] of the progenitor" (*bījinaś ca*), the expression "beyond the seventh" (*ūrdhvaṃ saptamāt*) is understood to carry over. A "progenitor" (*bījī*) is one who, according to the scriptural injunction, sows the seed in another's field through the mere act of procreation. "Maternal kinsmen" (*mātṛbāndhavāḥ*) refers to the mother’s maternal uncle, the mother’s sister, or the mother’s brother’s wife. Marriage with those beyond the fifth degree from these is permitted. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.

One should choose a maiden who does not share one's *ṛṣi* lineage (*asamānārṣeyī*). One should avoid [marrying her if she is descended from] five generations on the mother’s side and seven on the father’s side; or alternatively, three on the mother’s side and five on the father’s side.
In this regard, there is a fixed option: five generations if she is of the same caste (*samānajātīyā*), and three if she is of a different caste (*asamānajātīyā*). Sumantu says:

Having married the daughter of a paternal aunt, the daughter of a maternal uncle, one who belongs to the same *gotra* as his mother, or one who shares the same *ṛṣi* lineage (*samānārṣeyī*), he shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance; and having abandoned her, he should maintain her [as a dependent].
Furthermore, this prohibition regarding those of the same *gotra* as one's mother refers to the mother’s kinship by birth, provided that there is recognition of both the birth and the name.
Thus says Vyāsa:
"Some do not even permit marriage with a woman of the same lineage as one's mother; however, if her birth or family name is unknown, one may marry her without hesitation. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.

One should choose a bride born of a noble family and endowed with proper conduct. According to the Dharma, one should avoid the daughters of one’s father’s and mother’s sisters, as well as the daughters of one’s maternal uncles; for they are considered sisters. [Thus it is known. Although this prohibition is already established by virtue of their being paternal and maternal relatives, this repeated prohibition is intended to demonstrate the greater gravity of the fault. [10] Manu says:
Having approached the daughter of his father’s sister, his own sister, or the sister of his mother,
as well as the daughter of his mother’s full brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives;
they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by marrying them, he falls.

Because Manu has proclaimed these [relations] as those with whom marriage is prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*), the phrase "the daughter of the mother’s brother" refers to the sister of one's own mother; this is because the prohibition against marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle is stated in other *smṛtis*.

Sumantu says: "Daughters related through the mother or the father are ineligible for marriage up to the seventh degree; for others, up to the fifth degree. All the wives of one's father are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles; their daughters are sisters; and their offspring are sisters' sons. Otherwise, they cause the confusion of castes. This same rule applies to one's own teacher."
The phrase "as far as the seventh degree" (*āsaptamāt*) refers to the maternal *sapinda* lineage, based on the statement of Vyāsa:

"The maternal *sapindas* must be carefully avoided by the twice-born. [11] Regarding the word "otherwise": the meaning is that the daughters of those just mentioned, if married [in such a manner], become performers of unrighteous acts consisting of the nature of mixed castes (*saṅkara*).
Manu says:

One should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has an auspicious name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
“Saumyanāmnīm” means one whose name does not cause agitation. “Tanulomakeśadaśanām” means one whose body hair, hair, and teeth are *tanu*, that is, fine. Śātātapa says:
[One should marry] a girl with the voice of a swan, the complexion of a cloud, and eyes tawny like honey.
Choosing such a maiden as his wife, the householder prospers in happiness.

“Meghavarṇām” means having a glossy, dark complexion like a cloud. “Madhupiṅgalalocanām” means having eyes that are slightly reddish-brown like honey. “Sukham edhate” means she prospers in happiness; that is, she increases in well-being as is fitting. Āśvalāyana says:
One should marry a woman who is endowed with intelligence, beauty, good character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease.
"Lakṣaṇas" are marks indicating auspiciousness. These are described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
[12] "Their soles are well-settled and possess a luster equal to that of a red lotus."

Their soles are well-settled, with the surfaces of their feet firmly attached to the ground. Likewise: "Furthermore, those with hands that are hideous, fleshless, rough, or covered in prominent veins, undoubtedly attain poverty and misfortune."
Karāla means terrifying.
Likewise: the fingers are joined, rounded, straight, and have smooth nails.
They exercise absolute sovereignty and enjoy royal pleasures with women.
“Close-set” means without gaps. “Royal enjoyment” means the full experience of royal pleasures.
Short lines indicate a short life; sparse lines lead to the loss of wealth.
Roots that consume the base (mūlabhuk) signify poverty, while broad roots indicate servitude.
“Root-eaters” are those whose first joints are curved; “broad” means thick. Likewise:
with thin, old joints that are mutually interlocked.
O twice-born ones, even after killing many husbands, she indeed becomes a slave.
[13] However, those with fingers having elevated joints, which are prominent and endowed with softness, lead to the acquisition of jewels and gold; the opposite leads to misfortune.
Good fortune comes from glossy nails, and wealth from those that are slightly coppery;
sons are obtained when these are elevated, and sovereignty when they are very fine.
Through nails that are pale, cracked, rough, dark blue, smoky, or harsh, women suffer from poverty; and through those that are yellow, they consume what is unfit for food.
If they are white, glossy, round, and likewise well-proportioned with their heads elevated,
they would bestow a city upon one's kinsmen and others, and they would attain full success.
Shins that are veinless, resembling the stalks of reeds, well-rounded, and sparsely hairy,
bring about good fortune as well as travel by means of elephants and horses.
A woman with hairy calves suffers; one with high ankle-bones wanders;
one with "crow-feet" (kākajaṅghā) kills her husband; as do one who is talkative and one who is tawny-haired.
And with knees that resemble those of a cat or a lion,
they obtain prosperity, good fortune, and likewise sons.

If the frontal globes are pot-shaped, travelers' wives will be widowed; if they are fleshless, unchaste women will appear; if they are veined, they will be murderous; and if they are split apart, they will be destitute of wealth.
With hairs that are extremely curled, rough, split at the tips, and as dark as molasses,
and with body-hairs likewise produced in great numbers and of the same nature.
A woman who is extremely tawny is certain to be a Piśāca maiden;
within seven days she will kill her husband, of this there is no doubt.
With thighs that resemble the trunks of elephants, rounded like plantain stalks, and tapering like the forearms of an elephant, women constantly experience the bliss born of the god of love.
They say that lack of flesh indicates misfortune, while hairy thighs indicate bondage; thinness indicates poverty, and gaps in the waist indicate lack of sovereignty.
O twice-born ones, a woman’s broad hips, which are level, beautiful, and covered with fine hair, are praised as they bring about the pleasure of sexual union.
She whose vulva has upright hairs, which is even and well-knit,
becomes a queen even if born of a low family.
It resembles the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, has the back of a tortoise, is indeed without foundation,
resembles the orb of the moon, and is likewise shaped like a cart.
The *bhaga* (vulva) that is most highly praised among women is that which increases pleasure and good fortune;
it resembles the flower of the sesame plant, and that which resembles the hoof of a horse.
Both of these act as servants to others and bring about poverty;
they produce grief like mortars and manifest death with gaping mouths.
One who has no secondary sexual characteristics, very little flesh, or body hair identical to that of elephants or horses,
encounters bad character, misfortune, and poverty.
O twice-born ones, the buttocks of women are praised when they resemble the kapittha fruit—plump and free from wrinkles; otherwise, they are censured.
The waist of women, bent by the weight of their breasts, heavy with the three folds of skin like young sprouts,
and adorned with the line of body hair, brings auspiciousness.
Even with drums like paṇavas and mṛdaṅgas, or those shaped like barley grains in the middle, people experience fear and exhaustion; such is the case even with [the results of] immoral conduct.
[16] It has beautiful, broad, and firm backrests, well-constructed and very stable; furnished with various cushions and couches, it provides supreme pleasure and comfort.
If a woman’s back is humpbacked, lacks a central depression, and is hairy,
she possesses no happiness even in her dreams, and she shall kill her husband.
A woman with a broad and very delicate belly gives birth to many children;
a woman whose belly is shaped like a frog gives birth to a king.
If the lines are elevated, there will be wrinkles; if they are closed, the woman will be unchaste. She who is devoted to the acts of a paramour shall not attain authority.
Those with uneven and depressed [lines] are base; those with irregular [lines] have irregular intentions; those with hearts that are level possess longevity and sovereignty, as do women.
A pair of breasts that are well-rounded, elevated, full, not protruding too far, and broad is always praised; anything other than this brings unhappiness.
In the first pregnancy, there is swelling in two places, one of which is more pronounced;
if it occurs on the left, a daughter is born, but if on the right, it shall be a son.
A woman whose nipples are long is cunning and fond of sexual pleasure;
however, she whose nipples are inverted always hates her husband.
Women who adopt the behavior of men attain poverty, possessing breasts shaped like the hoods of serpents and having the form of a dog's tongue.
O twice-born ones, in this world there are likewise those who are like jars made of brass—
smooth, fleshy, beautiful, and devoid of veins and hair.
A woman whose chest is thus shall enjoy her desired pleasures;
however, she becomes predatory by means of a curved [chest], while a hairy one indicates bad character.
If the palm is fleshless, there is widowhood; if it is broad, she is fond of quarreling. Four lines on a woman's hand that are red, deep, and glossy—
If there should be lines starting from the base of the little finger and extending to the forefinger, one who possesses them attains happiness despite being subject to lack of mastery.
Her lifespan would be one hundred years; as it gradually diminished, her joints became well-formed, her tips sharp, and her skin soft.
A woman whose fingers are equal in length increases her enjoyments;
with high nails as red as the bandhujīva flower, she shall attain sovereignty.

O twice-born ones, with nails that are smoke-colored, one lacks mastery; with those that are white or yellow, there is a lack of sovereignty; with those that are red and soft, there is lordship; and with those that have no gaps between the fingers, one attains greatness.
[18] Those women on whose joints of the thumbs and fingers there are seven lines— distinct, continuous, rough, coarse, palm-sized, and harsh— are [unfortunate].
For them there is indeed vast happiness, as well as inexhaustible wealth and grain;
their wrist is unbroken and adorned with three lines.
And after a short time, he establishes [the city] adorned with jewels and gold,
featuring dwellings for elephants and horses marked with the signs of the Śrīvatsa, the lotus, and the conch.
With wheels, svastikas, vajras, swords, full jars, and hooks;
with palaces, parasols, crowns, necklaces, armlets, and earrings.
With conch shells, arches, and gateways held in their hands, the wives of the king [offered them];
on the palms of whose hands there were lines [depicting] a red garland, a water-pot, and a water-jar.
She on whose feet these [marks] are seen becomes a queen;
likewise, women [are distinguished] by their streets, marketplaces, weights and measures, as well as by seals and so forth.
The wives of merchants who abound in jewels and gold become [mere symbols] of the sickle,
the yoke-tie, the pair of oxen, the binding-rope, the plowshare, the mortar, the plow, and the pole.
The wives of the farming folk become rich in wealth and grain;
their heads and joints are not protruding, and they are plump and free from body hair.
The pair of arms of women is auspicious when shaped like a cow's tail;
those whose elbows have hidden joints and are devoid of hair [are likewise auspicious].

The shoulders of women are highly praised when they are many, playful, well-rounded, and soft; likewise, a shoulder that is neither too thick nor hairy, and characterized by a slight elevation and depression, always increases one's good fortune and health.
If the shoulder is thick, one carries a heavy burden; if it is hairy, she becomes diseased. If the shoulder is crooked, she will be barren; if it is both elevated and depressed, she will be unchaste.
She whose neck clearly displays two lines four finger-breadths apart wears ornaments enriched with jewels, gold, and pearls.
A woman with a thin neck is poor; one with a long neck is unchaste;
one with a short neck has stable offspring; and one with a thick neck is miserable.
She whose nape of the neck is not protruding and is even-fleshed and level shall have a very long life, and her husband shall live for a long time.
One who is fleshless, one with excessive flesh, one with prominent veins, one who is hairy, as well as one who is crooked, deformed, or broad— such a woman is not praised.
[20] Neither too thick nor too thin, neither crooked nor hairy—such is the jaw that is most excellent; any other than this is not praised.
A woman with a square face is cunning; one with a circular face is even-tempered. A woman with a horse-like face is childless, and one with a large mouth is unfortunate.
Those women who have the faces of dogs, boars, wolves, owls,
or monkeys are cruel, performers of evil deeds, and devoid of offspring and kinsmen.
Her face possesses the fragrance of jasmine, *vakula*, lotus, and blue water-lily; yet this fragrance is not released from them [the flowers], nor by the consumption of betel.
If the lower lip of women has a copper-like luster, is slightly curved, is free from being too thick or too thin, and is prominent, it always bestows enjoyment.
If the upper lip is thick, she will be quarrelsome; if it is discolored, she will be exceedingly miserable;
and if the upper lip is sharp, the woman will be extremely prone to anger.
The tongue is praised when it is very thin, slightly curved, copper-colored, and long;
it is censured when it is thick, short, discolored at the edges, crooked, or split.
With teeth that are white as a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, glossy, prominent, without gaps, and not protruding, one obtains sweet food and drink.
[21] With hair that is fine, extremely thin, short, cracked, sparse, and rough, one is constantly afflicted by suffering; with such deformed hair, there will be a lack of right understanding.
The auspicious face of excellent women, possessing a luster like that of a well-polished mirror, a lotus, or the full orb of the moon, bestows unseen fruits.
She whose nose is thick, slender, not too curved, not too long, and well-elevated— such a woman is blessed and brings auspiciousness.
For women, lines that are elevated, soft, pure, unconfused, resembling the half-moon, and fine bring happiness.
One with lines equal to a bow brings good fortune; one with long hair will be barren;
and one that is tawny, joined [with another], or short leads to poverty—of this there is no doubt.
With these eyes of women, which resemble the petals of the blue lotus and possess beautiful reddish-brown lashes, one becomes a partaker of enjoyments and good fortune.
A woman with eyes like a hare’s, eyes like a deer’s, or eyes like a boar’s,
even if born in such-and-such [lowly] circumstances, shall obtain great enjoyment.
In this world, the wives of kings possess eyes that are not deep-set, nor too narrow, endowed with many lines, and honey-brown in hue.
The eyes of women that are shaped like crows, with long outer corners,
though clear and beautiful, do not lead to prosperity.
Those with deep and tawny eyes will be afflicted by suffering yet long-lived;
and that woman whose eyes are prominent will lose her life in middle age.
A woman with red eyes, uneven eyes, smoky-colored eyes, or eyes like those of a *preta*, as well as one with eyes like a dog's, should always be avoided from afar.
In this place, the women have eyes as variegated as wandering white lotuses;
they are constantly fond of wine and meat, and are fickle in every respect.
The ears, shaped like the letter *la* and resting upon the tops of their drooping shoulders,
bear ornaments of gold and jewels that radiate a blossoming luster.
Women who have ears like those of a donkey, a camel, a mongoose, an owl,
or a pigeon generally experience great suffering and indeed often go forth as renunciants.
Those that are slightly pale on the cheeks, well-rounded, and possess the luster of the full moon are praiseworthy;
however, those that are small and adorned with pores are censured.
The forehead of excellent women, which has the full expanse of a half-moon, is hairy and well-proportioned; it brings about the happiness of enjoyment and is most auspicious.
A forehead that is twice the width [of the face] and three times its height, and a head [proportionate thereto], are praised for women; those with heads like an elephant's trunk are never barren.
Hair that is fine, black, soft, glossy, and curled at the tips brings prosperity to women; otherwise, it causes distress and sorrow.
Women with voices like those of swans, cuckoos, lutes, bees, peacocks,
and flutes obtain manifold enjoyments and command their servants.
A woman whose voice is like the sound of broken bell-metal, or who has the voice of a donkey or a crow,
encounters danger from disease and affliction, sorrow, and poverty.
A woman who walks with the gait of a swan, a bull, a chakravaka bird, or a rutting elephant,
is worthy of heaven and shall become the queen of a king.
A woman who walks with the gait of a dog or a jackal is censurable; she who moves like a crow becomes a servant girl; and a woman with the gait of a deer will be unfortunate and an unchaste woman.

The colors of women that bring good fortune are those resembling the *phalinī* flower, the *rocanā* pigment, or the luster of gold and saffron; likewise, a color like the sprout of *dūrvā* grass is auspicious.
Those women whose limbs are soft, covered with fine hair, not excessively prone to perspiration, and fragrant are honored.

[24] Āśvalāyana says: Having made eight lumps of earth whose characteristics are difficult to discern, and having consecrated the lumps with the mantra, "In the sacrifice, *ṛta* was first placed in the fire; upon *ṛta* truth is established. Whatever this maiden has been born to, may that be obtained here. Let that which is the truth be seen," he should say to the maiden, "Take one of these."

If he should take [earth] from a field that yields two crops, he should know: "Her offspring will be provided with food. From a cow-pen, she will be rich in cattle; from the soil of the sacrificial altar, she will be a speaker of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinī*). From a non-perishing pool, she will be endowed with everything; from a gambling ground, she will be a gambler; from a crossroads, she will be one who wanders about; from barren saline soil, she will be childless; from a cemetery, she will be a slayer of her husband.

And the preparation of eight lumps (*piṇḍa*) is to be done with earth from the fields and other locations that will be mentioned. "Goṣṭha" is a place where cows stay. "Vedapurīṣa" is the earth from a sacrificial altar (*vedi*). "Devana" is a gambling place, so called because one plays (*dīvyate*) therein. "Vipravrājinī" is a woman who, having abandoned her husband, has the habit of wandering as a renunciant. "Īriṇa" is saline soil (*ūṣara*). Manu: Even if they are prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain... [25]
In matters concerning marriage with a woman, one should avoid these ten families.
Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, those afflicted with hairy hemorrhoids,
as well as families suffering from consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, and leprosy;

“Large” means populous. “Prosperous” means well-endowed with the cattle and other things to be mentioned hereafter. “In connection with women” is the ellipsis for “should be performed. “Devoid of rites” means lacking the prescribed rites such as the *garbhādhāna* (conception ceremony) and so forth. “Lacking male offspring” means having a preponderance of female births. “Lacking Vedic study” means devoid of the practice of the Vedas. “Hairy” means excessively covered in hair. “Afflicted with hemorrhoids” means suffering from the disease of hemorrhoids (*arśas*). “Leucodermic” means afflicted with white leprosy (*śvitra*). Thus says Hārīta.

Those afflicted with vitiligo, leprosy, abdominal dropsy, consumption, epilepsy, those who do not belong to a lineage of seers (*anārṣeya*), and those whose lineage of seers is identical to that of a non-Brahmin (*abrahmasamānārṣeya*)—these families, even if they have not fallen from their status, are to be avoided. For offspring conform to the nature of the family. The first six [categories] are *anārṣeya* because they are unfit for sacrifice; the last is called *samānārṣeya* because it lacks a deity and is not a Brahmin lineage. Therefore, having examined seven generations on the father’s side and five on the mother’s side, one should take as a wife a maiden who is excellent, has brothers, and is still unwedded.

"Afflicted with disease" (*āmayāvin*) here refers to one suffering from other contagious diseases. Regarding the statement that "six families, beginning with those of leprosy (*śvitrin*), are to be avoided," the reason for this is: "Offspring conform to the lineage. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason. "Lacking a *ṛṣi-ancestry*" (*anārṣeya*) means one whose *gotra* and *pravara* are not remembered. The reason for his exclusion is "because he is unfit for sacrifice" (*ayajñiyatvāt*). His unfitness for sacrifice arises because one whose *pravara* is not remembered has no entitlement to participate in sacrifices. "Lacking sacred knowledge" (*abrahman*) means one who does not possess the study of the Vedas. The reason for his exclusion is "because he is not a deity" (*adaivatvāt*), meaning he is devoid of divine rites. A "naked girl" (*nagnikā*) is ten years old, according to the statement in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "A ten-year-old girl is indeed a *nagnikā*."
Furthermore, Hārīta says:

"And truth is indeed the mantra; therefore, one should choose a woman who possesses knowledge of her family and constellations, [extending] to the fifth generation on the mother's side and the seventh on the father's side.
Yama says:

One should specify that these fourteen families are not to be intermarried with; among Brāhmaṇas, one should avoid those who lack a lineage of Vedic seers (anārṣeya) as well as those who serve as officiating priests (ṛtvij).
One should avoid those who are excessively tall or excessively short,
those with an abnormal complexion, those with missing limbs or extra limbs, and families afflicted by disease.
[27] One should indeed practice avoidance of those families afflicted by vitiligo, leprosy, and the like;
the family of lustful persons should always be avoided, as should the family of those with excessive body hair.
"Those belonging to the family of epilepsy" (apasmārikula) and those belonging to the family of jaundice (pāṇḍukula).

Here, "sacrificial priests" (ṛtvijaḥ) refers to censurable officiants. "The family of desire" (kāmakula) is a family in which desire predominates. "Excessive color" (ativarṇa) means either excessively dark or excessively fair. [Thus says] Manu.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.

One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a serpent, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name.
A wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter).

The meaning is that one should not marry a girl who has no brother, for fear of the *putrikā-dharma*. And this *putrikā-dharma* is as follows: by means of a son born of her, the father of the maiden becomes one who possesses a son.
Gautama says:
"According to some, she is a *putrikā* by mere intention alone; fearing that [status], one should not marry a girl who has no brother."

"By mere intention" (*abhisandhimātrāt*) means from the thought, "This one is his offspring. By the word "mere" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of the procedure for an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) as stated by Gautama, such as [the requirement of] fire or Prajāpati and so forth. Kātyāyana says:
"She who is tainted by public scandal is proclaimed to be 'tainted' (*duṣṭā*)."
Any woman whose wealth is attached elsewhere and who has engaged in sexual intercourse [with another]—
“Saṃspṛṣṭamaithunā” means one whose virginity has been violated. Nārada states:
“One who is afflicted by a long-standing or loathsome disease, one who is deformed, or one whose virginity has been violated.”
And having her affections fixed on another man—these are proclaimed as the faults of a maiden.
“Chronic” refers to quartan fever and the like; “loathsome disease” refers to epilepsy and the like. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
“Neither too hairy nor hairless, neither too black nor tawny...”
One should not, by nature, marry a woman who has an extra limb or one who is deficient in a limb.
One should not [marry] a girl who is impure, afflicted by disease, crooked, or excessively ill;
nor one who is wicked, of evil disposition, or defective on account of her father or mother.
One should not [marry] a woman who has a beard or secondary sexual characteristics, nor one with a masculine appearance;
nor one with a gurgling voice, nor one who is emaciated, nor one with a voice like a crow's.
Likewise, one should not marry a woman whose eyes are too wide apart, nor one with round eyes; nor one whose shanks are hairy, nor one whose ankles are prominent.
A wise man, discerning in his duties, should not marry a girl who has dimples appearing on her cheeks when she laughs.
A wise man should not marry a girl whose skin is excessively rough, whose hands and feet are pale, whose eyes are reddish, or whose hands and feet are yellowish.
[30] One should not marry a woman who is too short, nor one who is too tall, nor one with arched eyebrows; likewise, not one with excessively gapped teeth, nor one with a gaping mouth.

"Excessive hair" means having too much hair. "By nature" means by her very constitution she has extra limbs. "Deformed from her father or mother" refers to one whose parents are deformed. "Bearded" means having long hair in the place where a beard grows. "Having secondary sexual characteristics" means being endowed with breasts and so forth. "Emaciated" means thin. "With eyes too tightly closed" means one whose eyes are mostly shut. "Round-eyed" means having circular eyes. "Nail" refers to the fingernail. "Slightly yellowish" (*āpīna*) means somewhat pale-yellow. "With joined eyebrows" means one whose eyebrows meet. "One should not marry a woman with a gaping mouth"—this follows as a recurring injunction in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
"One who is hairless, one with excessive hair, one who is talkative, and one with squinting eyes"—
"squinting-eyed" means having only one eye. Kaśyapa says:
These seven types of girls who are destined for rebirth are the lowest of their families and should be avoided.
She who has been given by word, she who has been given in thought, she for whom the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony has been performed,
she who has been touched by water, and she whose hand has been taken in marriage.
"She who has been superseded by another husband, and she who gives birth to a child out of wedlock— these, as declared by Kaśyapa, burn the family like fire."

“Having performed the auspicious rites of kautuka,” meaning she has had the marriage bracelet bound upon her. “Touched with water,” meaning she has been given away with the preceding libation of water. [31] Smṛti states:

“One who has been verbally betrothed, one to whom the mind has been given, one who has circumambulated the fire, one who has been led to the seventh step, one who has been enjoyed, one who has conceived a fetus, and one who has given birth—these are the seven types of women; by taking any of them, one becomes a womanizer and shall find neither offspring nor merit.”

“*Prajām*” (offspring) refers to those possessing the characteristics of one’s own caste; this is the implied meaning. “*Dharmam*” (duty) refers to rites such as the *agnihotra* that are to be accomplished by means of a wife. Furthermore, within this context, regarding those injunctions and prohibitions for which there is no connection to visible benefits or defects—such as “she who is not a *sapinda* of the mother,” and so forth—if these are transgressed, she does not even attain the status of a wife (*bhāryā*). This is because the word *bhāryā*, like the words *āhavanīya* and others, is a term denoting a sacramental consecration (*saṃskāra-śabda*). However, regarding those injunctions and prohibitions where they are based on the observation of visible benefits or defects—for example:
“Not even from a prosperous man, if he is afflicted with the defect of a contagious disease.”

In such cases as these, there is no loss of the status of wife (*bhāryātva*) upon transgression; rather, due solely to the violation of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is merely the necessity of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, in the case of women named after constellations (*ṛkṣa*), trees (*vṛkṣa*), and so forth, because they fall within the scope of injunctions and prohibitions that follow from perceived merits and defects, and because Manu has separately prescribed prohibitions regarding *sapiṇḍas* and others, a transcendental defect (*adṛṣṭa-doṣa*) must be inferred. Furthermore, abandonment (*parityāga*) is ordained for one who has taken a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*), according to the statement of Baudhāyana: "If one should marry a *sagotra* even unintentionally, he should maintain her like a mother. This is not the case for those named after the river Kapilā and the like. The same principle applies to the groom as well, in the case of a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*), and so forth.
[32] Now follows the determination of the bridegroom by Nārada.
One who is insane, fallen from caste, impotent, unfortunate, or abandoned by kinsmen,
as well as those two defects previously mentioned regarding a maiden— these are the defects and virtues in a groom.

“Unfortunate” means one who is hated by women. “Abandoned by kinsmen” means one who conducts affairs independently, having left behind blameless relatives. Regarding the phrase “and the two defects of a maiden which were mentioned before”: a maiden afflicted by long-standing loathsome diseases, one who is deformed, one who has already had sexual intercourse, and one whose affection is fixed on another—these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden.
In that verse, the two "former" ones—the first two consisting of being long-sickly and having a deformed limb—are indeed those mentioned by Nārada. Kātyāyana says:
"One who has departed from him, one who is hated by him, and likewise one who has been abandoned by his own kinsmen..."
If she is of another caste, subject to decay, a slave, a eunuch, or has a distended belly;
One who is insane, fallen [from caste], afflicted with leprosy, likewise a eunuch, born of the same lineage (sagotra),
deprived of sight or hearing, and likewise one defiled by epilepsy.
[33] Indeed, these are remembered as the faults of the groom; they are proclaimed as the faults of the bride.
One should avoid giving [the daughter] in such cases, whether before or after [the marriage].

“Niṣkāntaḥ” means one whose habit is to travel to other regions. “Dāsaḥ” means a servant. “Liṅgasthaś codarī yadi”: if one who bears the insignia of a religious order (*āśrama-liṅga*) does so merely for the sake of filling his belly. “Prāk” means prior to the commencement of marriage. “Paścāt” means after the formal betrothal (*vāgdāna*). Manu says:
“A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father’s house at will until death.”
But one should never, under any circumstances, give her to a man devoid of good qualities.
The intended meaning here is that [the bride] should not be given to one devoid of virtues; however, a menstruating woman must not be worn [as a garment].
Yama says: "One should give a maiden who is still naked according to one's ability to a man of good qualities."
But one must never obstruct a woman in her courses, especially not one who lacks virtuous qualities.
"According to one's ability" means when there is the capacity [to give]. "Only a naked girl" means one who is ten years old; he should give her away.
Manu says:
To an excellent groom who is handsome and of equal status... [34]
One should give that maiden to him according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached [marriageable age].

“Superior” means by virtue of family, character, and so forth. “One who has not reached [the proper age]” means even one who has not yet attained the age specified as being suitable for giving in marriage. Āśvalāyana says:
“One should first examine the family [of those who are] ‘from the mother’s side and from the father’s side’”; as stated previously, one should give the daughter to a wise man.
Śātātapa says:
A bridegroom should be sought who is a suitor, endowed with noble birth and good character,
handsome, learned, wise, young, and free from defects.
Regarding the section on the qualities of a bride, Yājñavalkya states:
"A bridegroom who possesses these very same qualities, who is of the same caste, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*),
carefully tested for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people [is recommended]."
Nārada said:
A man must be examined for his virility by the very characteristics of his own limbs;
if he is a man without deficiency, he is worthy to obtain a maiden.
His knee-bones and shanks are well-knit; his shoulders and neck are firmly set;
his body and skin are thick and firm; and his gait is steady and unhindered.
If his semen floats upon the water and his urine is frothy, he shall be a male by these characteristics;
however, by the opposite signs, he is a eunuch.
In the treatise, sixteen types of eunuchs have been observed by the wise;
the method for their treatment, both curable and incurable, has been explained in due order.
The Nisarga-ṣaṇḍa and likewise the Baddha-pakṣa-ṣaṇḍa [were destroyed] by the curse of Agni,
by the anger of their preceptor, and likewise by the wrath of the gods.
[36] The envious, the impotent, he whose semen is wind, the one whose vulva is in the mouth,
the one whose seed is discharged prematurely, the bashful, and likewise the husband of another woman.
In that regard, one should perform the two [penances] called *pakṣa*, which cannot be remedied otherwise, for one month;
the time for this triad is traditionally held to be one year in sequence.
The other four who have been mentioned—the envious, the impotent, and so forth—must be abandoned like outcasts; and likewise women whose virginity has been violated.
Even when her husband has failed in his duties toward her, a woman whose seed was sown fruitfully may,
according to tradition, wait for another husband for half a year.
Even for a modest man, the penis falls limp through union with a bold woman;
she should then attend to that one whose vigor has failed with caresses.
If a man who belongs to another woman should become unfaithful toward his own wife, she may obtain another husband; this is the decree of Prajāpati.

[37] Women were created for the sake of offspring; women are the field and men are the seed-bearers. The field should be given to one who possesses the seed; one who lacks the seed does not deserve the field.

“Subaddha” means well-knit. “Jatru” is the joint between the neck and the shoulders. “Ghāṭā” is the back part of the neck. A “nisargaṣaṇḍha” is one born entirely devoid of sexual organs and testicles. A “baddha” is one whose testicles have been removed. A “pakṣaṣaṇḍha” is one whose sexual potency is intermittent. One becomes so “from the curse of a guru,” or “from the wrath of a god,” meaning from anger arising out of reviling a deity. An “īrṣyāṣaṇḍha” is one whose semen is paralyzed due to jealousy regarding his own wife. A “sevya” is one who, despite being served by a woman in many ways, has lost desire or never experiences desire. A “vātareto” is one for whom, during intercourse, there is merely the emission of wind through the penis. A “mukhebhaga” is one who performs the function of the vulva only in the mouth of another. An “ākṣiptaretāḥ” is one whose semen flows backward at the time of ejaculation. A “moghabīja” is one whose semen is not capable of causing conception. A “śālīna” is one whose penis falls away upon the presence of a bold woman. An “anyāpati” is one who possesses virility only toward a woman other than his own wife. “He should wait for a month” means he should wait for the duration of a month. A maiden should not be given to these men if they were known to be such beforehand. If she is given out of ignorance, then in the case of those who can be cured, one should wait until the treatment is completed; however, in the case of those who cannot be cured, even if she has already been given, she should be taken back and given to another.
[38] Now follows the alternative regarding wives; on this matter, Manu says:
For the twice-born, women of their own caste are recommended for marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [castes] shall be the preferred wives in successive order.
The wife of a Śūdra is only a Śūdra woman; those two and his own [woman] are prescribed for a Vaiśya;
those two and his own for a Kṣatriya; and those three and his own for a Brāhmaṇa.

The meaning is as follows: when a maiden of the same caste is available, she alone is recommended in the primary option (*praśasta prathamakalpe*). In her absence, for one who has sexual desire, these maidens of the *kṣatriya*, *vaiśya*, and *śūdra* castes are to be married in that order. Even there, in the absence of each preceding one, the succeeding one is to be married. However, one who is free from desire but incapable [of maintaining] the stage of life (*āśrama*) should abide by the vows of a *snātaka* alone.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi: "In the absence of a maiden, he should observe the vows of a *snātaka*; or else, he may procreate a son with a *kṣatriya*, a *vaiśya*, or a *śūdra* woman—so say others."
Yama says:
For all, one’s own wives are the primary dharma. Furthermore, according to the traditional order, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives.
Manu declared that for a Kṣatriya, three wives are to be known in successive order as lawful; and for a Vaiśya, two wives of lower status are likewise lawful.
A Śūdra shall obtain a wife from his own caste; among them, the offspring shall be equal.
This equality is intended with respect to the discharge of the father's debt, which is the motive for the procreation of sons.
Regarding this, Nārada follows immediately after [the discussion on] commonality of caste:
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are three other wives in the direct order [of castes];
likewise, for a Śūdra, there are three other husbands in the inverse order [of castes].
Two wives are prescribed for a Kṣatriya, and one for a Vaiśya. It should be known that a Vaiśya may have two husbands: one of his own class and the other a Kṣatriya.
"Another" means of a different caste; for a Vaiśya, one [wife] is understood as being from his own caste. For a Vaiśya, two husbands are to be known as "others"—this is the remainder [of the sense].

Vasiṣṭha says: "A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives according to the order of the castes, two for a Rājanya, and one each for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. Some allow [marriage] even with a Śūdra woman, excluding the sacred mantras; however, one should not act in that manner, for from it follows a certain degradation of the family and, after death, the loss of heaven."
Yājñavalkya says: As for what is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra wife by the twice-born,
this is not my opinion, because from her one is born oneself.
Viṣṇu: A Śūdra woman can never be the wife of a twice-born man for the sake of dharma;
she is declared to be for his pleasure alone, for him who is blinded by passion.
“Only for the sake of pleasure,” meaning that she does not become a partner in dharma. Manu says:
“For a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, even when they are in distress...”
In no circumstance whatsoever is a Śūdra woman eligible to be a wife.
The phrase "for the sake of religious duties such as *śrāddha*" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry a woman of a low caste..."
Indeed, families quickly sink into the state of Śūdras along with their lineages.
Manu [states]:
"According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls;
according to Gautama, by the birth of a son [to her]; and according to Bhṛgu, by having that as one's offspring."
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
In all instances, the phrase "the opinion of Gautama, the son of Utathya" is to be supplied. Śaṅkha says:
Even in times of distress, a twice-born man must not take a Śūdra woman as his wife.
[42] Because for one who has been born from her, no atonement is prescribed.
One who is an ascetic, devoted to sacrifice, and the best among the upholders of all dharma,
certainly incurs the status of a Śūdra by partaking in a Śūdra’s Śrāddha on the thirteenth day.
But for those among whom a Śūdra born into the family is led into the state of sapinda-relationship,
they all descend to the status of Śūdras, even if they have conquered heaven.
The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite must certainly be performed for one born into the family after twelve Śrāddhas have been completed, when the thirteenth Śrāddha arrives.
One who is unworthy of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, as well as a Śūdra, is likewise excluded;
therefore, one should avoid a Śūdra woman as a wife with every effort.
Yama says: A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Śūdra woman remains in a state of birth-impurity for three days;
moreover, if he conceives a child with her, he is indeed fallen from his status as a Brāhmaṇa.
A killer of a Brahmin is not truly a killer of a Brahmin; rather, the husband of a Vṛṣalī is a killer of a Brahmin.
The fetus that is born there becomes a killer of a Brahmin by virtue of that [act].
[43] Hārīta says: A Brāhmaṇa who has gone to a Śūdra woman shall immediately go to a downward state;
if he then conceives a child in her, he falls instantly—of this there is no doubt.
No other slayer of a Brahmin exists; rather, the husband of a Vṛṣalī is the slayer of a Brahmin, for by him the embryo conceived in her has been killed.
Uśanas says:
There might be atonement for one who drinks liquor or for one who kills a knower of Brahman;
but for one born of a Vṛṣalī woman, no atonement is possible.
Manu, Yama, and Hārīta state:
"For one who has drunk the foam from a Śūdra woman's mouth, for one who has been defiled by her breath,
and for one born of her— no atonement is prescribed."
“Of the yellow-foamed”: of that which has yellow mouth-wine (*mukhāsava*).

Regarding this, they say: "Uśanas falls [from his caste] by marrying a *vṛṣalī*"; others say he does not fall. Vasiṣṭha states that there are four wives prescribed in the *Brāhmaṇakalpa*, to be taken in successive order. There is doubt as to whether he falls or does not fall. Hārīta says he falls by reason of the *vṛṣalī*. Śaunaka says he falls upon the birth of a son. Gautama says he falls by reason of their offspring. Thus says Hārīta.

Regarding one who procreates among women of lower castes, there is a doubt as to whether he falls [from his caste] or does not fall. He does not fall in the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, because of their connection with sacrifice; however, he who procreates with a Śūdra woman falls due to that act of intercourse. Furthermore, by procreating with all [lower castes] when the [higher] caste is lost, he does not incur sin. This is the meaning of the section: for the twice-born, if a maiden of their own caste is not available, even maidens of successively lower castes may be married in order. Likewise, when the cause for taking a second wife exists, or upon the death of the first wife, if a maiden of the same caste is unavailable, successive [lower-caste] wives may be taken.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The daughters of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are not to be married by the twice-born;
however, after [marrying] a Brāhmaṇī, they may in some cases be married."

The phrase "in some cases" (*kvacid eva*) refers to when there is a specific cause for taking another wife, such as the death of the first wife. However, regarding a Śūdra woman, this is the distinction: if among the other [permitted wives] no offspring can be produced, she may also be married solely for the purpose of procreation. Regarding the decline of the lineage (*varṇakṣaye*), the statement of Hārīta says that one does not incur sin by begetting children from all [wives]. Yet, even then, she does not become a *sahadharmacāriṇī* (a partner in religious duties), because of the statement of Viṣṇu: "She shall not be [a partner] for the sake of Dharma. The prohibition against marrying a Śūdra woman applies only when the others are available. As for the deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the marriage to a Śūdra woman and the birth of sons and grandsons from her, that too refers to such a marriage [under normal circumstances]. The hearing of specific censure, however, is intended to demonstrate the greater gravity of the fault.
Thus ends the section on substitutes for a wife;
now follows the determination of the sequence regarding the bride and the groom,
as stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
A man three times as old as his wife should marry her; thus say Manu and Yama.
A thirty-year-old man should wed a charming twelve-year-old girl.
A man of twenty-four years quickly fails in his duty with a woman of eight years.
In the Mahābhārata:
A man of thirty years should take as his wife a maiden of sixteen who is still naked (nagnikā);
or a man of twenty-one years may obtain a girl of seven.

[46] Thus, the meaning of these statements is as follows: A girl up to eight years of age should be married to one who is exactly three times her age. Beyond that, up to twelve years of age, she may be married to one whose age is slightly less than three times hers. Above twelve years of age and up to sixteen years of age, she is most highly commended when married to one whose age is two and a half, three, or slightly less than three times her own. Even if she is married at a very young age, she remains a wife; however, she does not serve the purpose of procreation properly. Furthermore, even if religious duty (*dharma*) suffers, one should perform the marriage out of regard for the fact that she is merely younger, even if it is done with haste.
Now follows the determination of those who may give away a maiden.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"The father, the grandfather, the brother, a *sakulya* (a distant relative), and likewise the mother..."
In the absence of the preceding giver, each subsequent person who is in his natural state is the giver of the maiden.

Viṣṇu states: "The father, grandfather, brother, a kinsman (sakulya), maternal grandfather, and the mother are the givers of a maiden. In the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is the giver, provided he is *prakṛtistha*.
[47] "Prakṛtistha" means free from defects such as loss of caste (*pātitya*), insanity, and so forth.
Kātyāyana says: The father himself should give away his own legitimate daughter; in his absence, her own kinsmen;
then the maternal grandfather [should give] another, or the mother should give her daughter born according to the law.

In this context, "relatives" (bāndhavāḥ) refers to the paternal grandfathers and others who, as stated in other Smṛtis, are authorized to give away a maiden in marriage. "Another" (anyām) means one who is not an aurasa daughter. "Dharmaja" means one produced through the practice of *niyoga*. Likewise:
"When the relatives have gone on a long journey or are minors (*pogaṇḍa*)."
But at the proper time, a mother may give even her own biological daughter.
“Pogaṇḍa” means one incapable of legal transactions. “At the proper time” (samaye) refers to the occasion suitable for the giving away of the girl.
Now, regarding the self-choice marriage of a maiden (kanyā-svayaṃvara), Nārada says:
But when there is no one at all [to choose her], the maiden should approach the king;
with his permission, she should herself choose a husband after examining him.
[48] He should practice dharma together with one who is of the same caste and similar in family, appearance, age, and learning; and from that, he should procreate sons.
"Therefore," that is, because of that boon; Yājñavalkya says:
"In the absence of givers, however, a maiden may choose her husband herself."
"Fit to approach" (*gamya*) means worthy of being approached on account of [the man's] family, character, and so forth.
Manu says:
"A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years."
But after this period of time has passed, she may find a husband of equal status.
If she should approach a husband on her own when not being given away,
she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he whom she approaches.

A woman choosing her own husband (svayaṃvarā) shall not take for herself ornaments given by her father, nor those given by her mother or her brother; if she were to take them, it would constitute theft.
One who takes away a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his authority as master.
[49] “Enas” refers to the cause of becoming a female slave.
Baudhāyana says:
A woman who has reached puberty should wait for her father’s command for three years.
Then, in the fourth year, she shall find a suitable husband.
When a suitable [bridegroom] is not available, one may resort even to one who lacks good qualities. Viṣṇu states: "A maiden, having waited for three menstrual periods, may herself choose a husband."
But when three seasons have passed, she is always capable of conceiving a child from herself.
A maiden who sees her menses in the house of her father before she has been consecrated is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; one who carries her away does not incur sin.

Gautama: Having passed three menstrual periods, a maiden may unite herself with one who is blameless, having set aside her paternal ornaments. If he does not give her away before the period [of menstruation], he is at fault. Some say [the time limit is] until she has put on the [marriage] garment.
Yama: [50]
If a maiden remains in her father's house for twelve years without being given away in marriage, the guilt of foeticide falls upon that father; she shall then choose a husband for herself.
And one should never despise a wife who has come to one of her own accord;
Manu, the son of Svayambhū, declared that such a woman should be known as a harlot.

And this waiting for three years applies when, despite the father and others making efforts for some reason, the giving [of the girl] does not take place; and the waiting for three seasons applies when the father and others remain indifferent even though a bridegroom with the aforementioned qualities has appeared, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "When she is of equal status and desirous, she may be requested by suitors," and so forth.
Likewise:
"A maiden should wait for three seasons and then inform her kinsmen."
If they were all to refuse her, they would all be equal to killers of embryos (bhrūṇahan).
"Bhrūṇa" here means an embryo;
[specifically] one that is most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*).
But if, through the negligence of the father, a girl [is born] here...
It should remain after its proper measure of time has passed;
for if it is not given away and remains beyond the proper time, it destroys the giver, just like a heavy sacrificial fee that is withheld too long.

"Exceeding the time" (*kālātiriktā*) means that the time for giving has passed; the meaning is that it is just as when a teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*), if not given, destroys the giver by becoming a cause for the arising of sin. Likewise:
"A father should give away his daughter while she is still naked (pre-pubertal), out of fear of [her reaching] the time of menstruation."
For while she remains in her season, the fault falls upon the father.
For as many seasons as the menses touch a maiden who, though desiring [a husband] and being asked by suitors of equal status, remains unmarried,
for that many embryos have been slain by her.
"To one's mother and father"—this is the declaration of the Dharma.
“With equals” means in terms of family and so forth. Baudhāyana says:
One should give a daughter who is still a *nagnikā* (pre-pubertal) and a follower of dharma to one possessed of good qualities.
Alternatively, one should not detain a menstruating woman for a man who is devoid of good qualities.
"Even to one devoid of virtues"—that is, even to one lacking such qualities as noble birth, good character, and beauty;
likewise:
"He who does not give away his daughter, though she has reached puberty, for three years..."
He undoubtedly incurs a fault equal to that of killing a Brahmin.
"He incurs" means he attains [sin]. If he does not beg, it would be thus; but if he begs, then for each individual season, Manu has declared that there is a fault, a mortal sin (pātaka).

This is the meaning: if no one at all asks for the maiden, then after three years there is the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). If, however, one does not give her to a suitor of equal status who asks for her, then for every season that passes there is the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). And in this case, the transgression is indeed the fault of killing an embryo; so say Atri and Kaśyapa. "But if a maiden, remaining uninitiated (*asaṃskṛtā*), should see her menses while in her father's house..."
The fetus-killing belongs to her father; that girl is considered a Vṛṣalī.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, should choose such a girl as his wife—
one should know him to be an untrustworthy man, unfit for the company at a meal, and the husband of a Vṛṣalī.

[53] Paiṭhīnasi: As long as her breasts have not emerged, so long should she be given away. If she has reached puberty, both the giver and the receiver fall into hell; the father and the grandfather are born as worms in excrement. Therefore, she should be given away while still a girl (*nagnikā*). Aṅgiras:

A girl who has not yet reached puberty is called *gaurī*; once she has reached puberty, she is *rohiṇī*. A dark-complexioned girl without developed breasts is *śyāmā*, while one who lacks breasts altogether is *nagnikā*.

Regarding the term "avyañjanakucā": she is one for whom the secondary sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) and breasts are non-existent; the meaning is that her hair and breasts have not yet emerged. Likewise:
"When the secondary sexual characteristics have been employed, Soma consumes the maiden."
But when she has breasts, the Gandharva Vahni consumes her while she is menstruating.
Therefore, a father should give away his daughter while she is still devoid of pubic hair, her breasts are free from dust, and she has not yet been enjoyed by the Moon or other [planets].

“Vyañjanāni” refers to the manifested secondary sexual characteristics, namely the body hairs. [54] Regarding the dissolution (*saṃvarta*): when the time for the appearance of hair has arrived, Soma should enjoy the maiden.
But during the period of her menses, the Gandharva Vahni consumes the woman who has her courses.
Therefore, one should marry off a maiden before she reaches puberty;
indeed, the wise recommend that the marriage of a girl take place when she is eight years old.
Kaśyapa says: A girl seven years old is a Gaurī; one ten years old is a Kanyā;
when the twelfth year has arrived, she is designated as a Kumārī.
Soma resides in the condiments when one eats; the Gandharvas in the breasts;
Vāyu in the arrival of the folds of the skin; and Agni is established in the menses.

Therefore, a father should not give his daughter in marriage if she is devoid of secondary sexual characteristics, lacks pubescent breasts, or has not yet been enjoyed by the Moon and other [planets].

Upon reaching puberty, a girl destroys her family through improper conduct, she destroys her ancestors by nursing at the breast, and she destroys both her sacrificial merits and her charitable works once her menses have begun.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: A girl who has not yet reached puberty is called Gaurī; once puberty has arrived, she is Rohiṇī;
one who lacks the marks of sexual development is a Kanyā; and one devoid of breasts is a Nagnikā.
[55] A girl of seven years is Gaurī; one of ten years is Nagnikā;
at twelve she becomes a Kanyā, and beyond that, she is Rajasvalā (menstruating).

The *gaurī* who is seven years old is the primary [type]. The statement, "A *gaurī* is one who has not yet attained her menses," also refers to this same [category]. Furthermore, the statement of Saṃvarta, "Marriage for a girl of eight years is recommended by the wise," also refers specifically to her who is seven, because the eighth year is simply the completion of the seventh. According to the statement of Gautama, "But the *nagnikā* is the primary [type], prior to the assumption of clothing," she is one who is ignorant of wearing a garment. She is defined as a ten-year-old who lacks breasts for the purpose of establishing the absence of fault in marriage; however, the previously mentioned [seven-year-old] alone is truly praised.
Therefore, before menstruation has begun, the father should give his daughter in marriage once;
otherwise, a great sin would touch him—such is the rule for the virtuous.

The rule for the virtuous is that she is to be given away before the onset of passion (*rajas*); otherwise, if passion has arisen, great sin would touch this donor because of the gift—this is the meaning. [56] Manu, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati state:
"Once does a share descend; once is a maiden given."
He says "I give" once; these three [acts] are each performed only once.

Just as a "share" (aṃśa), meaning a portion of inheritance, is made to "fall once," and just as one giving property such as cattle says "I give" only once, so it is also in the giving away of a daughter. Nārada says:
"This rule is recorded for the five forms of marriage, beginning with the Brāhma."
Giving may be performed with regard to the qualities [of the recipient] even toward the three beginning with the asuras.

The meaning is this: among the Brāhma and other [classes], including the Gandharvas, "this" mode consisting of a single gift [of the bride] applies. However, among the Āsuras, Rākṣasas, and Paiśācas, the meaning is that even one who has been wedded may be seized and given to another.
Likewise:
"If a suitor more excellent than the groom should come while the bride's dowry has already been received... [57]
In that case, even speech connected with virtue, wealth, and pleasure may be false.

“*Śulka*” means a price; this refers specifically to the *āsura* form of marriage, though it also serves as an illustration for the other three forms of marriage, since a bride-price is impossible in all of them. A “statement joined with *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*” is one such as: “This girl must be given by me to you. Another reading is *pratiśravaḥ*. It is thus: “In matters of *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*, she must not be transgressed against.
Yājñavalkya says: “A maiden is given only once; he who carries her off shall be subject to the punishment for theft.”
Even if she has been given away, one may take her back if a more excellent suitor arrives first.
Likewise:
"One who seizes a girl already given in marriage shall be fined and shall pay the expenses along with interest.
"Superior" (*śreyān*) means free from the defects of the bridegroom to be described later. "Along with interest" (*sodayam*) means together with the profit.
Manu says: A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her away once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being.
And thus, neither others nor any other virtuous men have ever done this:
that after having granted permission to one person, it is then given to another.
And "falsehood regarding a person" refers to the sin incurred by speaking untruth concerning a person;
as it has been stated: "One kills a hundred [by lying] about horses, and a thousand [by lying] about a person. "Having promised" means having agreed to give.
Kaśyapa said: Listen to the destination reached by that fool who commits a falsehood regarding a maiden— whether it be her father, or her mother, or her brother, or her husband’s younger brother.
Just as a hawk does not turn back and just as the wind moves forward,
so do men who commit falsehood regarding a maiden go to hell.

"Another" here refers to the person entitled to give the gift. "Those who speak falsely regarding a maiden" are those who tell lies concerning the giving away of a daughter. Kātyāyana states: "Even when a girl has been promised to many, if she remains unmarried..."
And she shall obtain that supreme boon from all of them as the very first boon.
Whoever subsequently obtains that which was given by the groom, it shall be his;
however, if she departs before being married, the groom shall take back what was previously given.

Having promised to give [a daughter] after first receiving wealth from many [suitors], if she remains unmarried and many suitors arrive, then among them all, the first suitor—the very first—shall obtain that maiden; the others, however, shall receive the gift of the *malaya* (the bride-price). Thus says Nārada:
"And the man who, having accepted a maiden, departs for another country..."
Having passed over three suitors, she may choose another bridegroom.
"Having accepted" means having taken possession of her who has been verbally betrothed. Kātyāyana states:
"He who, having given the bride-price as well as the woman's property (*strīdhana*) for a maiden, should depart..."
It should be worn for one year, and then it may be given to another according to the prescribed rule.
Now, if a suitor should arrive, she should be accepted for three years;
after that time, the maiden may be given to another as he desires.
But when a maiden who was previously given has been married by another,
she should be given back to the one to whom she was originally promised, even if she has already been consecrated through the rites.
But when a maiden given by another is married by a suitor,
Bhṛgu maintains that he acquires her through time and according to the prescribed rite once she has been consecrated.

“Woman’s property” (*strīdhana*) refers to the signet ring and so forth. “News” (*pravṛtti*) means tidings of her well-being. This [rule] regarding the giving back of the bride to the previous suitor—even after she has been married—should be understood as applying before the period of waiting mentioned immediately above.
Yama states: “If a maiden has been given by word of mouth, but her suitor dies...”
And a maiden who has been obtained through mantras belongs to her father alone.

In this case, the ritual consecration consists of the taking of the hand itself, accompanied by the recitation of mantras. Vasiṣṭha states: "If, after a girl has been given with water and word, the bridegroom should die..."
And she shall not be led away by means of incantations; she belongs to her father alone.
Manu says:
If the giver of the bride-price dies while the bride has already been given away,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the girl herself consents.
Immediately after the rule regarding *niyoga*, Manu states:
"If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this following procedure."
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she being clad in white garments and pure in her vows—
he shall unite with her in private once each season until she gives birth.
“According to rule” means according to the Gṛhya-śāstra. “Purity of vows” refers to the restraint of speech and other faculties. Now, Nārada says:
“But that man who, having accepted an unblemished girl, should abandon her...”
Even if he is unwilling, that person to be converted should nevertheless marry that very same girl.
If there is a defect in the girl, the gift is fruitless and the giver incurs a fine of ninety-six [paṇas];
likewise, there shall be the return of the bride-price and the withdrawal of the girl.
By concealing one's own faults, the transgression becomes twofold in effect;
the gift to the bridegroom is lost, and the woman returns [to her family].
"Expiation" (*atyaya*) means punishment. "Loss of what was given" (*dattanāśa*) means the forfeiture of the dowry that has been paid.
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"That man who takes the bride's hand without having disclosed a defect [in himself]..."
Or if he should make a request, the son would not obtain what was given.
Even in the case of a defect in the girl, this law applies: the giver shall be fined, and the bridegroom likewise;
the giver shall return what was received, but never once when [the couple] has already had sexual intercourse.

“Both the giver and the bridegroom are to be punished”—this means that if the defects of the girl have not been disclosed, the giver is to be punished; if the defects of the bridegroom [have not been disclosed], the bridegroom is to be punished. Regarding the phrase “of those who have already procreated,” this refers to those who have already begun [the marriage]. Sumantu states: Even if she has been married, a girl who is defective—being afflicted by a contemptible caste, occupation, character, or disease—and whose virginity remains intact, may be abandoned; however, one whose virginity has been violated must be maintained. A bridegroom likewise becomes liable to be abandoned if he possesses these very same defects.

"Contemptible" means lacking auspicious marks and other such qualities. "Of another caste" means inferior in comparison to [the groom's] caste. "Marred by action" means corrupted by a mortal sin (*pātaka*). "Marred by character" means immoral. "Marred by disease" means afflicted with leprosy and other such ailments.
Nārada and Kātyāyana state:
"One should not defame an unblemished maiden, nor should one defame an unblemished groom."
If a fault exists, there would be no fault for those two who abandon it to one another.
“Doṣe” refers to leprosy and the like; “doṣaḥ” means sin. Manu says:
“Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon a girl who is blameworthy.”
Whether she is diseased, corrupted, or approached through deception;

"According to rule" means preceded by the offering of water and other such rites. "Despised" means having ill-omened physical marks. "Corrupted" means her affection is directed toward another. "By fraud" means by means of showing one girl while giving another in marriage, and so forth.
Likewise:
"The mantras for taking the hand are established as applying only to virgins."
For men, there is never [a marriage] with women who are not kanyās, for they are indeed those whose mantras and rites have been lost.
A giver who fails to disclose prior defects— such as being insane, afflicted with leprosy, or having already engaged in sexual intercourse— is liable to punishment.
“Established” means those who have been assigned [to duties] by means of purificatory rites and so forth. “Among those who are not virgins” refers to those who possess defects.
Now, regarding the relationship between women and men, Nārada says:
In the case of a man and a woman, the formal choosing (varaṇa) is prescribed first;
after the choosing comes the grasping of the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa), for the relationship is indeed of two kinds.
