“From the connection,” meaning from the characteristic act of taking the hand in marriage. “The choosing”—“He should send suitors who are friends, assembled and accompanied by those who know the mantras,” as stated in the *Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra*. “Of two characteristics” means of two kinds.
Likewise:
"The choosing of those two is said to be indefinite because of the perception of faults;
the taking of the hand accompanied by the mantras is the definitive characteristic of a wife. [65]

"Indeterminate" means that there is no rule establishing their status as wives. "Because of the observation of defects" refers to the fact that the scriptures observe the return of a maiden due to defects such as impotence and so forth. "The marriage mantras" are those forming part of the ritual procedure of marriage, beginning with "I take your hand for the sake of prosperity. Manu says:
"For their auspiciousness, there is the rite of *svastyayana* and the sacrifice to Prajāpati."
In marriages, they are honored because the giving [of the bride] is the cause of ownership.

“*Svastyayanam*” refers to such passages as “May you, sirs, pronounce blessings,” and so forth, as well as “Place ten sons in her; make him the eleventh husband,” and so forth. “The sacrifice of Prajāpati” is a rite having Prajāpati as its deity. “In marriages” means that which is performed during a wedding for the sake of auspiciousness and for the purpose of dispelling the defects of inauspicious marks. “The giving [of the girl] effects ownership”: by the very act of giving, the relationship of master and owned arises between the bridegroom and the maiden, and the father’s ownership ceases. On this point, Manu and Kātyāyana [state]:
The mantras of taking the hand are the definitive characteristic of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise as occurring at the seventh step.

“Completion” (*niṣṭhā*) means finality; and here, completion consists in the fulfillment of the status of being a wife. “At the seventh step” means when the girl has reached the seventh step. On this point, Yama says: “Neither by water, nor even by speech is one called the husband of a maiden.”
Husbandhood arises at the seventh step through the sacrament of taking the hand.
“With water” means by the prior gift of water; “with speech” means by the gift of words. Thus says Hārīta.

For virtuous men, providing seats, salutations, rising to greet them, and the offering of *arghya* and hospitality are the means for accomplishing their religious duty (*dharma*). There is no transgression regarding the giving of these to such men by a maiden, except in accordance with the actual facts of the case. Regarding those who are impotent, outcastes, away on a journey, renunciants, or deceased, Prajāpati says that they are not considered [as husbands] through the water-rite nor by word alone. Some maintain that if one should accept [the bride] after bathing, one should give [the fee] to him; however, this is because the rule there is incomplete and involves a specific number. Others hold that it is accomplished by the mantras of taking the hand. That too is established for the first three lower castes by the taking of the arrow, the goad, and the staff respectively. Even in those cases, wifehood is not established merely by the grasping of the hand; for one should know that the status of husband and wife is complete only at the seventh step.

The meaning of the term "āsana" (the sitting) is as follows: regarding the offering of *arghya* and other honors to those who have come for the purpose of choosing a bride (*kanyāvaraṇa*), "the transgression of the maiden" (*kanyāyā atikramaḥ*) means the cessation of her status as a maiden; it does not mean that she becomes ineligible for being given to another suitor. Regarding the phrase "except in accordance with the truth" (*anyatra yāthātathyāt*): this means except in the case of a truthful statement concerning the giving of the maiden. It has been stated by the words "in the case of a eunuch," etc., that even when a truthful statement is made regarding others such as eunuchs, there is no transgression. And in these cases, the cessation of maidenhood occurs both upon the formal gift preceded by water (*udakapūrvadāna*) and upon the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*). As for the statement, "By water alone [is the gift] for the foremost of the twice-born," and so forth, that is merely the commencement of the gift; such is the opinion of Prajāpati. Others, however, believe that the completion of the gift occurs through acceptance according to the prescribed rule (*vidhipūrvaka*). To this he says, "Having bathed," etc. He refutes that as well with the words, "In that case," etc. "Because the procedure is incomplete" (*akṛtsnavidhānāt*) means because the ritual rule is not fully established. The reason for this is: "Because of the connection with a number" (*saṃkhyāyogāt*). And that has been stated by Nārada [12.2]:
"Taking the hand [in marriage] after the choosing [of the bride]—that is marriage, characterized by two features.
Even so, [the author] says "taking the hand," etc., because it is incomplete:
"The taking of the hand accompanied by the fixed mantras is the defining characteristic of a wife."

Because of the use of the word "niyata" (fixed/established) in this verse of Manu [8.227], others maintain that the completion of the marriage (*vivāhasaṃpatti*) occurs immediately after the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "that too for the first [classes]," etc.: "for the first," meaning for Brāhmaṇas; "in lower castes," meaning among Kṣatriyas and so forth, if there is a goad (*pratoda*). One should not entertain doubt regarding these cases where the taking of the hand is absent. The taking of the hand must indeed be performed, since the taking of arrows and other items is prescribed, the taking of the hand is thereby established. Even so, the status of husband and wife (*jāyāpatitva*) is not complete; he now states how it becomes complete: "For the whole," etc. By this, for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the principal rite of marriage (*pradhāna-vivāhakarma*) consists of leading the bride as far as the seventh step (*saptama-pada*), accompanied by mantras and characterized by the taking of the hand and other acts. And this alone is what brings about the status of being a wife (*jāyatva*). For a Śūdra, this very same rite is performed without mantras.
Manu says: "The sacramental rite of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known regarding the marriage ceremony with women of different castes."
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman during a marriage with a man of higher caste.
Yama:
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste;
as it is observed among women of different castes, I shall describe that sequence.
The Vaiśya woman takes the goad; the Kṣatriya woman takes the arrow;
the Śūdra woman indeed takes the fringe of the garment, while the woman of excellent complexion takes the hand.
[The term “daśā” means the hem of a garment; “for the sake of the hand” means for the purpose of taking the hand.
Circumambulation of the fire is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; for the Rājanya and Vaiśya, it is circumambulation of the teacher. “Parikarma” means performing a circumambulation [Manu].
For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is commended;
but for the other castes, it is by mutual desire.
“By mutual desire” means through the reciprocal affection of the bride and the groom. Paiṭhīnasi states:
“One should take the hand of a Brāhmaṇī woman including the thumb; that of a Kṣatriya woman with the arrow; that of a Vaiśya woman with the goad; and that of a Śūdra woman by the hem of her garment.”
The *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*:
This rule is prescribed for those who seek a maiden in marriage:
they propose while facing west, and they accept while facing east.
In both cases, one should proceed with the father and daughter in succession;
for those who give away a maiden, it is the same for both the father and the daughter.

“Of both sides,” that is, of the mother’s side and the father’s side. “One should recite in succession,” meaning one should proclaim them in order starting from the third generation. Regarding the phrase “those who give the girl”: it is not only he who seeks the girl in marriage who should recite the lineage of fathers and sons on both sides; rather, the meaning is that those who give the girl—the givers of the bride—should likewise recite the lineage of fathers and sons on both sides.
Now, regarding the different types of marriage, Manu says:
"Of all four castes, [these marriages] are beneficial or harmful both after death and in this world."
Learn these eight forms of marriage for women in brief.
The phrase "marriages of women" indicates that the woman is the one to be consecrated by the sacrament. Nārada says:
"Eight types of marriages have been proclaimed for the sake of the sacraments of the social classes."
Of these, the first is the Brāhma marriage, and likewise the Prājāpatya.
The Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura;
the Rākṣasa follows immediately after that, and the Paiśāca is the eighth and lowest.
Of these, however, four beginning with the Brāhma are declared to be lawful;
the Gāndharva may be common [to all], while the other three are likewise lawful.
[71] "Common" means neither superior nor inferior.
According to the sequence of Nārada, Gautama states that after marriage,
the first four are lawful, while some say there are six.

Hārīta says: Now, eight forms of marriage occur: the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, the Āsura, the Rākṣasa, the Paiśāca, the Mānuṣa, and the Kṣātra. Of these, the first seven [are valid] on both sides. Among them, one should accept the Mānuṣa in the absence of [the others]. Regarding the phrase "of these, the first": among those, the first three marriages are the initial ones. "On both sides" means they rescue seven generations each on the maternal and paternal lineages; this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Of these" refers to the three. "In the absence [of the others], the Mānuṣa"—one should obtain that.
Furthermore, Hārīta states:

"They declare that a woman wedded from among any one of these [classes] is a lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). And although all types of marriage are unsuitable for all castes, nevertheless, she becomes the lawful wife of whichever man for whom a specific type has been prescribed."
Vasiṣṭha:

There are six forms of marriage—the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Gāndharva, the Kṣātra, and the Mānuṣa. Having enumerated the Brāhma, Ārṣa, Daiva, Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, and Prājāpatya marriages, Āpastamba says:
[72] Of these, the first three are commended; each preceding one is superior to the next. Manu and Yama state that the first are the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, and likewise the Āsura.
The Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and the lowest.
I shall declare to you all that which belongs to each social class (varṇa), the virtues and faults of each, and the merits and demerits pertaining to their offspring.
One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [forms of marriage] in order; for a Kṣatriya, four; and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, those same [four], excluding the Rākṣasa form, which are lawful.
The wise know that the first four [forms of marriage] are praiseworthy for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone is for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of the five [marriages], three are considered lawful and two unlawful here;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura should never be performed.
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.

[73] Regarding "in procreation" (*prasave*), it means in offspring. "Virtues and defects" (*guṇāguṇān*) refers to merits and faults. "In succession" (*ānupūrvyā*) means according to the order specified. "Commended" (*praśastān*) means those that produce distinguished unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*). "Inferior" (*avarān*) refers to those below, namely the Āsura, Gāndharva, and Paiśāca forms. "Separately" (*pṛthak pṛthak*) means one by one. "Mixed" (*miśrau*) means those in which the characteristics of both are combined. For example, when there is mutual affection between the bride and groom, yet the father does not give the girl away and the marriage proceeds by abduction, the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa forms are combined. — Pārthasthānasi.

The *brāhma*, *prājāpatya*, *ārṣa*, and *daiva* [forms] are for the Brāhmaṇa; the *gāndharva* and *āsura* for the Rājanya; the *rākṣasa* for the Vaiśya; and the *paiśāca* for the Śūdra. Among all these, the *ārṣa* is authoritative. "Ārṣa" refers to the word of Devala.
Following the sequence of Nārada, after the enumeration of the forms of marriage, Devala says:
These four common forms of marriage, involving a dowry, are known [to be prescribed];
and the Rākṣasa form is prescribed exclusively for the Kṣatriya because it is particularly recommended for him.
[74] Baudhāyana is of the same opinion.

Of these, four belong to the Brāhmaṇa; among them, each preceding one is superior to the next. For the others, each succeeding one is more inferior. Even there, the sixth and seventh follow the duties of the Kṣatriya, because the Kṣatriya is preceded by that [Brāhmaṇa] status. The fifth and eighth belong to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra respectively, for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra have wives who are not restrained [by sacred marriage rites], being occupied with agriculture and service. Some praise even the Gāndharva form of marriage for all classes, because it is based on mutual affection. It is known from tradition: "As is the marriage, so is the offspring."

“Four” [are] “praiseworthy”—this is the ellipsis. The meaning is that each preceding one is more praiseworthy than the next. “Of the others,” namely the Gāndharva and so forth, each subsequent one is less praiseworthy. “The sixth and seventh,” the Āsura and Rākṣasa forms, “follow the dharma of the Kṣatra,” that is, they follow the dharma of the Kṣatriya; and that dharma consists of the excellence of bestowing wealth and possessing strength. Since a Kṣatriya possesses the aforementioned chariot (the power of force), there is the possibility of those two types of marriage for him. “The fifth and eighth,” the Gāndharva and Paiśāca forms, belong to the Vaiśya and Śūdra respectively. They are “those whose wives are unrestrained,” meaning their women are not restricted. Here, “wife” (*kalatra*) refers to all women. By this, daughters of those two castes are suitable for the Gāndharva and Paiśāca marriages. Their state of having unrestrained wives is due to their being authorized for agriculture and service, and because they are characterized by affection. For all castes, “as is appropriate” means according to the connection with either a quality or a defect. “Correspondingly endowed” means possessing those respective qualities or defects.

[75] Manu says: Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring becomes blameless; through blameworthy ones, it becomes blameworthy among men. Therefore, one should avoid those that are blameworthy.

In this matter, the following rule is stated by Nārada: the Prājāpatya, Ārṣa, Daiva, and Brāhma forms are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa; the Gāndharva form, however, is permissible for him as it does not contradict the Dharma. Although the Āsura form is also declared by Manu to be lawful for him, it is inferior to the Gāndharva and should only be performed in extreme distress.
Furthermore, the Paiśāca and Āsura forms should never be practiced under any circumstances.

This is because it was stated by Manu himself. However, the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca forms of marriage must never be performed by a Brāhmaṇa, as it is declared: "Six [forms of marriage] are for the Brāhmaṇa in order of precedence. As for the statement by Baudhāyana that the Ārṣa is superior to the Daiva, that refers to the procreation of offspring through the mere practice of common religious duties; in that regard, Manu has declared the superiority of the Daiva form. Furthermore, the superiority of the Gāndharva form mentioned by Hārīta is intended for all [classes] with respect to the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice) Gāndharva, as it is defined as: "When a maiden herself chooses [her husband], that is the Gāndharva. As for what is stated in the works of Paiṭhīnasi, Hārīta, and the Mahābhārata—that a marriage involving the forcible abduction of a maiden under the terms of the Rākṣasa, Āsura, Kṣātra, or Paiśāca is praiseworthy—that applies only to the Kṣatriya. The Brāhma and Daiva forms, however, belong only to the Brāhmaṇa and not to others, following the description of the Brāhma marriage in the Mahābhārata.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this dharma has been declared for virtuous Brāhmaṇas.

Because of this statement, because the *daiva* form involves giving [the bride] to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and because the priesthood is impossible for Kṣatriyas and others; whereas the *paiśāca* form belongs to Vaiśyas and Śūdras. As for the mention of the *rākṣasa* as superior for the Vaiśya, that refers to the *āsura* form, based on the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "The *rākṣasa* occurs when one takes her hand with a white [garland]. However, the *ārṣa*, *prājāpatya*, and *gāndharva* forms are common to all, because they are not censured and are appropriate. But for those born of mixed castes (*saṃkara*), the marriages other than the *brāhma* and *daiva* are according to their respective castes.
Now, regarding the characteristics of a Brahmin, Manu says:
"Having clothed and honored him personally, [one should give] to one who possesses learning and virtuous conduct."
[77] Summoning [the bridegroom] and giving away the daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
"Having clothed her," meaning having caused her to put on a pair of garments. Devala says:
"Then [he should give] a modest, auspicious girl, endowed with noble lineage and youth."
Having adorned [the bride], one should give her to a worthy man; this marriage is called the Brāhma rite.
"A virtuous woman" means one free from the aforementioned defects of a maiden. "To a worthy man" means to one endowed with the aforementioned characteristics of an excellent groom.
Vyāsa says: Having clothed her and adorned her, and having circumambulated the fire three times...
One should give while specifying the name and lineage; this is the Brāhma rite.
Saṃvarta says:
Having adorned her with ornaments and honored her well, one should give the daughter to a suitable bridegroom through the Brāhma form of marriage.
"Supūjitām" means honored with flowers, sandalwood paste, and so forth. Yama says: "They know that maiden who is given away with water as a *brahmadeyā*."

[78] The designation "gift for Brahman" (*brahmadeya*) is used among the faithful; it is for the purpose of establishing the practice of being a "purifier of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*) for one born from that [gift]. Hārīta says:

"Without censuring [the recipient], without deliberating with others, having given a pair of garments according to rule, [one should say]: 'May dharma be practiced together'—this is the manner of a Brahmin."

“Without reproaching,” meaning not uttering words of blame; “without suspecting others,” meaning not harboring doubts regarding faults in others; “according to rule,” meaning preceded by the *madhuparka* offering and other rites.
Āpastamba states:

“In the *brāhma* form of marriage, having ascertained the family, character, learning, and health [of the groom], one should bestow the daughter upon him for joint performance of duties, after having adorned her according to one's ability.”

“*Sahatvakarmabhyaḥ*,” etc. The meaning is that one who is desired as a companion—that is, as one who shares in the performance of rites such as the *dhāna*—is authorized; for that purpose, one should perform the presentation in this manner. Thus says Baudhāyana:
“Having ascertained [the student’s] learning and character, one should give [the Veda] to a seeker who is a religious student (*brahmacārin*); that is the rule regarding the Brahman.”
[79] “To a *brahmacārin*” means to one who has not yet had contact with women. “To one who desires” means to one who wishes for it.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

“In that case, a man of the same caste (*savarṇa*) should give an unveiled girl (*nagnikā*) to a man of the same caste who is known [to be suitable] and who is known [to be desirous]; that is the *brāhma* [form of marriage].”
"Known" means [known] by her family and so forth. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Therefore, one should give away a maiden who is still naked (i.e., unmarried) along with gold; this is the Brāhma marriage."
In the *Śreṣṭhavarānuvṛtti* section of the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"When will you, endowed with faith, give your daughter to a worthy suitor,
having adorned her according to your means and satisfied him with wealth?"

“Having adorned” means having adorned with excellent [ornaments]. “With wealth” means with cattle, gold, and so forth. The phrase “having filled [her] according to one’s ability” is to be applied to both cases. In the continuation of the section on the Brāhma marriage, Saṃvarta says: “By the giving away of a daughter, he attains abundant spiritual merit.”
[80] One who acts thus is called "virtuous" by the good, and he obtains abundant fame.
The particle *iti* should be understood as following the word *sādhu*. Thus: a hundred *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifices multiplied by a hundred [become an *atirātra*].
By giving a woman who has been consecrated with oblation-mantras, one attains the state of a man.

“Puruṣīm” means a maiden. Since the *Gṛhya-sūtras* prescribe the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) immediately after the giving [of the bride], it should be understood by implication that she has been consecrated by the oblation-mantras after being given. Kaśyapa says: “[The merit of one who gives] ten thousand oxen, capable of bearing the yoke...”
Giving according to the rules to a worthy recipient is equal to the giving away of a daughter in marriage.
But he who, according to truth and dharma, gives his daughter in marriage to her son,
attains a station after death such as that of Dakṣa Prajāpati.
"By truth" means by that which is free from deceit and the like. "He causes to touch" means he unites with the supreme. [81] In the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Having heard of the giving away of the daughter, the fathers along with the grandfathers..."
Being truly liberated from all sins, they go to the world of Brahmā.
Devala said:
Having given three daughters according to the prescribed rule, having protected them in accordance with justice, and having offered them [in marriage],...
Neither the father nor the mother who has given birth to a daughter goes to hell.
"Strīprasūtinī" means one who gives birth to daughters. This is from the *Smṛti*:
"That [result] would not come about through the Agnihotra and other rites; rather, it comes from the Brahman or from a Brāhmaṇa."
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving a maiden in marriage according to the prescribed rites.
In the *Brāhmānuvṛtti*, Saṃvarta states:
"Having given that maiden away, the father, honoring her with ornaments, clothing, and seats,
attains heaven during festivals and occasions of prosperity."
Thus ends the definition of the Brāhmaṇa;
now follows the definition of the Daiva.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"When a sacrifice has been properly commenced and the officiating priest is performing his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the Daiva rite."
“Samyak” means correctly, that is to say, without error. [This refers to] the officiating priest performing the ritual.
Devala says: Having brought the girl, adorned with gold, into the interior of the sacrificial altar...
But when he gives her to the officiating priest, this marriage is designated as the Daiva.
Yama:
Having adorned the officiating priest, the marriage is called Daiva. Hārīta: [Thus it is said].

"At the conclusion of the sacrifice" (*vedyante*), a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) is to be given to the bridegroom at a portion of the sacrificial altar (*vedyā*). It is one's own that is to be given to the bridegroom, and not what has been received from the bridegroom, for that would entail the status of being an *ārṣa* marriage.
[83] Baudhāyana.
When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are being led inside the altar (*antarvedi*), that which is given to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is "pertaining to the deity" (*sa daiva*).
This means the gift given to the priest for the purpose of giving when the sacrificial fees are being led [into the hall].
[This is stated] in the *Ādityapurāṇa*.
But he who gives away his daughter by the Daiva marriage rite,
having opened wide the door and provided an excellent staircase for the sun;
He then proceeds to ascend above the world of the sun.
Now, regarding the definition of a Ṛṣi,
Manu says therein:
"Having taken one pair of cattle or two, according to the law..."
The giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule—this is called the Ārṣa dharma.

"According to dharma" means for the sake of kindness, and not with the intention of a bride-price (*śulka*). And the mention of "a pair of cattle" should be understood as referring to a case where the giver of the girl himself is unable to give a further gift, yet desires to provide an additional benefit to the girl. Devala says:
"That which is the giving away of a girl together with a pair of cattle..."
The sages know that [verse] to be the seer's own, belonging to the lineage of the Teacher.

“Together with a pair of cattle (gomithuna)” means accompanied by the pair of cattle received from the bridegroom. “To one who is praiseworthy” means to one endowed with the characteristics as previously described. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “In the Ārṣa marriage, a pair of cattle and a pair of garments [are given]; furthermore, all ornaments and the woman’s property (strīdhana) should be given.”
“Woman’s property” (*strīdhana*) refers to something else as well, such as ornaments and so forth. Baudhāyana says:
Having first offered the oblations of parched grain (*lājāhuti*), [the bridegroom] should perform the *ārṣa* rite with two cows.

Of the four [types] mentioned previously, two are the first: "with two cows. The phrase "together with a pair of cows" is to be supplied as an adjunct. Now, regarding the definition of the *prājāpatya* [penance], Manu says:
Having addressed them with the words, "May you both perform dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite.

The *prājāpatya* [form of marriage] is that in which one gives away the daughter after making an agreement with these words: "May both of you practice dharma together, remaining faithful to one another. Devala says:
"The giving [of the bride] for the sake of performing dharma together, due to the binding of an agreement..."
The marriage of a maiden by adorning her alone is the rite of Prajāpati.
“*Samayabandhanaṃ*” (the binding of the agreement) is the making of a covenant that the two shall move together. Gautama says:
in the *prājāpatya* [form of marriage], it is the mantra of union, namely, “May dharma be practiced together.”
Viṣṇu is [the giver] who bestows what is requested;
"prārthitapradāna" means the giving of that which has been requested.
[86] Now, regarding the characteristics of an asura, Manu says:
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter by one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
“Non-giving” (āpradānam) means taking or seizing. “Out of one’s own will” (svācchandyāt) means by one’s own desire, and not through dependence on the father of the maiden. Devala states:
Having paid the bride-price (śulka) for the maiden, the formal giving away (supradāna) according to the prescribed rule [is required].
This sixth form of marriage, in which wealth is the motive, is called the Āsura.
He for whom wealth is the cause is such [an Āsura marriage]. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"When one gives after bargaining for a bride-price, it is the Āsura [form]."
"Having bartered," that is, having sold;
so says Hārīta.
That which is given or accepted from others when they have suspected one of hypocrisy or deceit is *āsura*.

[87] "By others" means by other people. "Through hypocrisy and deceit" means that when a suitor is known to be hypocritical or deceitful, one personally demonstrates a lack of hypocrisy and a lack of deceit; giving a gift after having thus ascertained him is *āsura*. Furthermore, Hārīta says:
through a bride-price (*śulka*), it is *mānuṣa*.
And this is another name for *āsura*.

Vasiṣṭha says: "Having made a bargain, she is purchased for wealth; that is the human [form]. Therefore, it is known as a purchase that 'one hundred [cows] plus an extra chariot should be given to the father of the daughter.'"

The phrase “dhanakrītī” (bought with wealth) implies that she is one who exists [in such a state]. “Atiratham” means that a hundred cows plus an extra chariot should be given; this is the meaning. By the word “iti ha,” there is a citation from the Śruti regarding the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, intended to show that the primary purpose of the purchase is for her to be bought for another [purpose], such that, having been bought, she moves about with others. Kaśyapa says: “A woman who has been purchased with wealth is not ordained as a *patnī* (wife).”
"She is not for the gods, nor is she for the ancestors," Kaśyapa said to that maidservant.
Āpastamba:
"The giving away and the sale of a child are not permitted. Manu: [same].
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not take a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, one effects a concealed sale of the daughter.
Yama said: We have never heard of such a thing, even in former births—
that evil sale of a daughter for a price designated as a "bride-price."
[89] Regarding the rite of the seers (*ārṣa*), some say that the pair of cattle is the bride-price (*śulka*); that is indeed false.
Even if it is very small, such a thing is likewise nothing other than a sale.
Those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property—
whether it be her vehicles or her clothing— are sinners who go to a downward state.

The acceptance of wealth in the *ārṣa* and *āsura* forms of marriage has been mentioned; in that regard, this prohibition is heard: "And there is no possibility of the *ārṣa* and *āsura* [forms] without the acceptance of wealth. In this matter, the settled rule is as follows: there is fault in accepting wealth for one's own sake; however, in accepting wealth for the sake of the girl, there is the fault of selling her. The mention of "women's property" (*strīdhanāni*) occurs here by way of context. "They subsist upon" (*upajīvanti*) means they enjoy it. By this, even those relatives of the bride who subsist on the wealth given for the purpose of honoring the girl share in the fault; therefore, what has been accepted must not be used by oneself. — Kaśyapa.
Those who, deluded by greed, bestow their own daughter for a bride-price are sellers of themselves; they are sinners who create great defilement.
They fall into a terrible hell and destroy their lineage up to the seventh generation.
Furthermore, for every going and coming, a toll is prescribed;
"going and coming" refers to the father of the girl's going and coming for the purpose of requesting her hand in marriage.
Manu:
"That the kinsmen do not take a fee for them is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure benevolence."
“Kindness” (*ānṛśaṃsya*) means compassion.

Āpastamba states: “In marriage, the giving [of a gift] to one who has a daughter is heard of as being for the sake of desire and for the sake of dharma. Therefore, a hundred [cows] plus a chariot should be given to one who has a daughter; therein he should perform the rite of union. Regarding this, the term “purchase” (*kraya*) is merely a figurative expression, for [the act] is fivefold by virtue of dharma.

The meaning is as follows: it has been stated that neither the giving nor the purchase of offspring is permitted. Anticipating the objection—“How then can there be the acceptance of a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) and so forth in the *ārṣa* marriage?”—the author says “In marriage,” and so on. That which is given to the father of the bride in marriage is for the sake of a specific desire (*kāmya*). It does not have as its object the production of a son equal to a seer (*ṛṣi*), because of the scriptural statement: “As is the marriage, so is the offspring. “He should make that into a pair (*mithunīkuryāt*): this means he should make that given chariot, etc., or the hundred cows, into a pair. The meaning is that he should bring about the state of husband and wife (*jāyāpatitva*). In the word *mithuna*, the substitution of *y* for *m* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage, because the distinct meaning of the two members of the compound is not dissolved. As for the word “purchase” (*kraya*) used in another Smṛti regarding that girl wedded in the *ārṣa* marriage, that is merely a verbal expression; there is no actual purchase there. The reason for this is: “For the connection arises from Dharma. For it is caused by Dharma that there is no bride-price (*śulka*).
Now, regarding the definition of the Gāndharva form, Manu says:
"The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through desire [is the Gāndharva marriage]."
That, however, should be known as the Gāndharva [form of marriage], which arises from desire and involves sexual union.

“Mutual union” (*anyonyasaṃyoga*) refers to the formal agreement between the bride and groom. “Pertaining to sexual intercourse” (*maithunya*) means that which is beneficial for sexual intercourse (*maithunya*), which is the act of a couple (*mithuna*). Devala says:
“The meeting of a woman and a man in private by themselves is [sexual intercourse].”
That Gandharva marriage, which has affection as its cause, is considered the fifth.
Gautama says: The Gāndharva marriage is the union of two who desire each other after having adorned themselves.
[92] The word "having adorned" implies "having adorned oneself."
Viṣṇu [states]: The Gāndharva [form of marriage] occurs between two who have mutual desire and is devoid of the giving by the mother and father;

that is, having adorned oneself independently of the mother and father—this is the implied sense. The phrase "devoid of the giving by the mother and father" refers specifically to the Svayaṃvara (self-choice) Gāndharva.
Hārīta:
When the maiden herself chooses [her husband], that is the Gāndharva [form]. Vasiṣṭha: [So it is].
If one should detain a willing woman of equal status while desiring her, that is the Gāndharva [form of marriage].
Āśvalāyana says: "Having made a mutual agreement, he should marry her; that is the Gāndharva."
Now, regarding the characteristics of a *rākṣasī* marriage, Manu states:
"Having killed, having cut, and having broken [the way], [she takes her] from her home as she cries out and weeps."
[93] For one who carries off a maiden by force, the Rākṣasa form of marriage is prescribed.
"Having killed" means having struck; the word "of the bride's kinsmen" is to be supplied as the object. "Crying out" means calling to her own kin out of fear. Devala says:
"Furthermore, the abduction of a maiden may take place by force, that is, by violence."
A marriage based on valor is considered the seventh, the Rākṣasa form.
"By force" means having overcome.
Āśvalāyana says: "Having killed and split open their heads, one should carry away a weeping woman from those who are weeping; that is the Rākṣasa [form of marriage]."
“From those weeping”—the remainder of the sense is “from the relatives of the girl.
Hārīta states: “The Rākṣasa [form of marriage] occurs because of the specific fear of capital punishment or physical assault resulting from royal patronage.”
The meaning is that when one abducts a maiden by instilling fear of execution, punishment, and so forth, by relying upon a king, that is the *rākṣasa* [form of marriage].
Vasiṣṭha states: "That in which they carry her off by force is the *kṣātra* [form]."

[94] Hārīta says: "The *kṣātra* [form of marriage] consists in winning [the bride] while she is adorned. This means that for one who is victorious in battle with a view toward obtaining a maiden who has been adorned for the purpose of marriage, the acquisition of that maiden constitutes the *kṣātra* form.
Now, regarding the characteristics of the Paiśāca [form of marriage],
Manu states therein: "When he approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged..."
That eighth, known as the Paiśāca, is celebrated as the most wicked among marriages.

“In private” means in a secluded place. “Approaches” means he performs acts such as embracing, but does not actually enjoy her sexually; for if her virginity were destroyed, it would follow that the sacramental rite of taking the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) could not take place.
Devala says: “He who carries off a maiden while she is sleeping or intoxicated, even out of passion...”
The eighth marriage is said to be the Paiśāca, which has negligence as its cause.

[95] "From sleep" means from a dream; "from intoxication" means from being intoxicated by drinking liquor; "from calamity" means from disturbances such as those caused by kings and so forth. [The phrase "of those who possess a maiden" is to be supplied as the remainder; for there is a statement of Āśvalāyana: "The Paiśāca [form occurs] when [the bridegroom approaches] those who are asleep or intoxicated"]. Yājñavalkya says: "The Paiśāca [form occurs] through the deception of a maiden."
“By means of the pretext of a maiden” means by deceiving a girl. Hārīta says:
[The *paiśāca* rite arises] from the union with a woman who is addicted to drinking liquor and sexual indulgence.
Because of the addiction—that is, the attachment—of the girl’s father and others to drinking liquor and to sensual enjoyments such as singing and dancing.
Now, Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana state:
"If a girl has been forcibly carried off, provided she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras..."
She should be given to another according to the prescribed rule, just as a maiden is given away.

And this abduction of the maiden prior to the consecration by mantras is to be understood as occurring when another suitor possessing superior lineage, character, and so forth has been obtained. Yama says:
"If the suitor should in any way lack lineage and character..."
In that matter, mantras are not the cause, nor would there be falsehood regarding the maiden.
"Having forcibly abducted a maiden who has not yet reached puberty, one should give her again to a virtuous man; thus said Śātātapa."

“Knayānṛtam” refers to the sin of acting otherwise than one promised regarding the giving of a daughter in marriage. “Samākṣipya” means having forcibly taken her away. Śātātapa says: “One who takes a girl from a family inferior in lineage and character does not incur guilt.”
Mantras are not the cause of that, nor would there be any falsehood regarding the maiden.
"Having forcibly abducted a maiden whose virginity is intact from a sinful man, one should give her to a man of good family, character, and virtue; thus said Śātātapa."
But a maiden who has been married and has reached her husband yet has not had sexual intercourse returns to him as a bride once more; she is exactly like an unmarried girl.
"From a wicked man" means from one who is devoid of proper form.
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"Whether he be of another caste, an outcaste, or even a eunuch."
[97] One who is engaged in forbidden acts, or a kinsman, or a slave, or even one afflicted by a chronic disease;
Whether the husband is impotent or has been deprived of his virility by medical means,
she may be given to another even if already married, along with her wedding garments and ornaments.
After the four types of marriages beginning with the Gandharva, Devala states:
"Once these marriages have been entered into, the marriage rite as traditionally prescribed is declared to be performed by the three castes according to custom, with fire as witness."
“The nuptial rite” refers to the rites such as the *jāla-homa* (the offering for the net) that constitute an integral part of the marriage ceremony;
this is stated in the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*.
According to the ritualists, [this applies] to marriages of the *brāhma*, *ārṣa*, *daiva*, and *prājāpatya* types.
The ritual for the fire-oblation was declared first; thereafter, the marriage ceremony is prescribed.
Among the Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, and Rākṣasa forms of marriage,
the wedding ceremony is prescribed first, and the fire-oblation follows afterwards.
Now, regarding the merits and defects of the marriages, Manu states:
"Whatever merits have been proclaimed by Manu for each of these marriages..."
Listen all of you, O Brahmins, as I recite it correctly.
The son of a Brāhmaṇī who has performed meritorious deeds liberates ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin.
The son born of a Daiva marriage purifies seven generations before and seven after himself;
the son born of an Ārṣa marriage purifies three before and three after; and the son born of a Kāya marriage purifies six before and six after.

The word *daśa* (ten) is connected with each of the words *pūrva* (former) and *apara* (latter), because of the designation “twenty-onefold. *Brāhmī* refers to one wedded through the *brāhma* form of marriage. *Enasaḥ* means from sin. Regarding the term *pitṝn* (ancestors), sons and others are also included by the word *pitṛ* through the function of *ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (retaining its own primary meaning while indicating another). *Daivoḍhajā-sutaḥ*: one wedded by the *daiva* rite is *daivoḍhā*; one born of her is *daivoḍhajā*, and her son is *daivoḍhajā-sutaḥ*. The shortening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasor bahulam*. In some readings, the text is “the son of a *daivoḍhā* woman” (*daivoḍhāyāḥ sutaḥ*).
Having described the *prājāpatya* marriage, Yājñavalkya says: "That [offspring] is *kāya*; he born from it purifies six ancestors on each side along with himself. Gautama says:
Virtuous sons purify three generations on the father’s side, ten on the divine side, and ten on the side of Prajāpati.

Āśvalāyana says: one purifies twelve descendants and twelve ancestors on both sides; one purifies ten descendants and ten ancestors on both sides; one purifies eight descendants and eight ancestors on both sides; and one purifies seven descendants and seven ancestors on both sides.

"Lower" means those belonging to one's own lineage who are below [oneself]. And these four statements refer, respectively, to the Brāhma, Daiva, Prājāpatya, and Ārṣa forms of marriage, because they are mentioned immediately following them. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the Prājāpatya, one gives oneself along with seven ancestors and descendants; in the Ārṣa, five; in the Daiva, three; and in the subsequent [forms], there is no emphasis on ritual action."
Viṣṇu [states this] following the word "marries" (*pṛṇāti*).
Prajāpati’s son [Manu] says there are four [types of marriage].
Devala speaks immediately after the enumeration of the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma.
Sons born of a woman given in marriage in these four ways purify the lineage of both the giver and the receiver up to the seventh generation.
[100] Manu and Yama state: "In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma rite, in their proper order,
sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born."
Possessed of beauty, endowed with virtues, wealthy, and renowned,
having abundant enjoyments and being most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
When other [types of marriages] are practiced, sons who speak cruelly and falsely,
and who hate the Veda and the Dharma, are born from improper marriages.
Regarding the observances following marriage, Āśvalāyana states:

"From this point forward, the couple shall eat food that is neither pungent nor saline, remain celibate, refrain from personal adornment, and sleep on the ground—either for three nights, twelve nights, or a year.
The *Brahma Purāṇa* [states the same].

Once the marriage has been performed, the groom must live as a celibate student for one year, provided the bride is eight years old; in that case, the man shall remain so for three times that duration.
“Threefold” means fourteen years. Likewise:
“Alternatively, twelve days [are equivalent] to thirty years at all times.”
If a girl should be twelve years old and endowed with beauty and good qualities, [she may be given].
If a sixteen-year-old girl is obtained when he has reached the full thirty-two years of age,
then he must dwell for six nights with self-restraint.
When a maiden is twenty years old, one must certainly stay there for three days;
beyond that age, even those who are self-restrained should stay for only one day and night.
Thus ends the section on the varieties of marriage in the Gṛhasthakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great Sandhivigrahika.
Now, taking an additional wife.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"A wife who drinks liquor, who is untruthful in conduct, who is antagonistic,
who is diseased, who is injurious, or who constantly squanders wealth, may be superseded by taking another wife."

“Drinking liquor”: here, it should be understood that this refers to a woman of the twice-born castes. “Of untruthful conduct” means one who behaves improperly. “Adverse” means one who acts to the detriment of her husband. “Diseased” means afflicted by a disease that renders her incapable of performing household duties. “Violent” means one whose habit is to beat her sons, female slaves, and others. “A squanderer of wealth” means one who causes the loss of property through negligence and the like. The word “always” is to be construed with “of untruthful conduct” and the subsequent terms. Yājñavalkya says: “One who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, a rogue, one who is barren, a squanderer of wealth, and one who speaks unpleasantly.”
A woman who gives birth only to daughters, as well as one who hates her husband, may be superseded by another wife.
"A remarried woman (adhivinnā), however, must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
"A rogue" (dhūrtā) is one whose primary characteristic is deception. "One who gives birth only to daughters" (strīprasūḥ) is one who gives birth to female children alone.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One may marry a woman who is of an unpleasant disposition or one who hates men, or even one who is favorable.
"Of an unpleasant disposition" means she possesses a character that causes displeasure to her husband. "Hates men" means she who hates her husband. (Manu).
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately.
In this context, the word "should take another wife" (adhivettavyā) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Devala says: "A husband should wait for eight years if his wife has given birth excessively."
Ten [days] for Vandyā and Vindhyā, and twelve for Strīprasūtinī.
Then, one desiring a son should, according to the law and in accordance with dharma, obtain a wife through the prescribed ritual;
for there is nothing in this world superior to obtaining a son, as they (women) bring forth many offspring.
[104] She has but one son, and her habit is to speak like a man. Hārīta says: she is childless in the ninth year, but in the tenth year, her children die.
In the eleventh year, she gives birth to a daughter who speaks unpleasantly from the very start.
If a man, having married one woman for the sake of desire, wishes to marry another,
he should marry the second after satisfying the first previously wedded wife with wealth, provided he is capable of doing so.
A Śūdra may have one wife, a Vaiśya two, a Kṣatriya three, and a Brāhmaṇa four; for a king, there may be as many wives as he desires.

"Excessive procreation" (*atiprasavā*) refers to menstruation (*prasavaḥ*), which is the flow of blood (*rajas*); it is so called when it has passed even its proper time. "Vindhya" means one who is defective (having a hole, etc.). "Progeny" (*prasavāḥ*) refers to offspring. "Capable" (*samarthaḥ*) means capable of providing wealth for her satisfaction; this is the implied sense. The alternative regarding the waiting period of eight years and so forth should be understood as being established in consideration of the wife's age and physical capacity. However, regarding those grounds for supersession (*adhivedana*) where no specific time limit is heard in the scriptures, one should wait for as long as it takes to ascertain whether that defect persists—for example, in the case of a chronic illness, one may supersede her and marry another woman after the first marriage. One should perform the marriage with another woman subsequent to the marriage with the first wife.
Manu: A daughter who may be afflicted by disease, yet is endowed with good character,
should be informed and superseded [by another wife], but she must never be treated with contempt.

Yājñavalkya says: One should give an equal amount as a compensation for supersession (*ādhivedanika*) to a wife who has been superseded. If no separate property (*strīdhana*) has been given to her, half of that amount is prescribed.

‘Ādhivedanikam’: the meaning is that whatever—such as ornaments and the like—is given for the purpose of taking a second wife to one wife, that very same amount must also be given to the superseded wife.
Manu says:
"But a woman who has been superseded, if she should depart from the house in anger..."
She must be restrained immediately, or else abandoned in the presence of the family.
Nārada says:
A man who abandons a wife who is compliant, not wicked in speech, virtuous,
and a mother of children, shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.
Thus ends the section on supersession.
Now follows the procedure for the announcement.
In this regard, Manu, Śātātapa, Yama, and Baudhāyana state in the second [chapter]:

"He who enters into marriage and the Agnihotra while his elder brother remains unmarried is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*."
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him, the woman through whom he is married,
as well as the giver and the officiating priest— these five all go to hell.

And here, the officiating priest (*yājaka*) is the *ṛtvij* at the *homa* that forms part of the marriage ceremony and at the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires). Regarding this, Hārīta states: "When the elder brother has not been given his share (*anirviṣṭa*), the younger brother who takes his share becomes a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder), and the elder brother becomes a *parivitta* (one superseded). The girl who is given away in such a case is a *parivedinī*; the one who gives her away is a *paridāyin*; and the officiating priest is a *parikartṛ*. All of these are outcasts (*patita*)."

‘*Anirviṣṭe*’ means one who has not performed marriage. Because of the use of the suffix *niṣṭhā*, even while the elder brother’s marriage remains unaccomplished, the younger brother has no entitlement to marry; therefore, even a simultaneous marriage (*sahavivāha*) should not be performed. By the word ‘brother’ (*bhrātṛ*), only a uterine brother (*sodarya*) is meant. Since the application of the word ‘brother’ is possible even for a half-brother (*sāpatnya*) and others due to their connection with the quality of having a common cause, there is no need to assume a primary denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*) for it. And the *Śātātapa-smṛti*, stating “the sons of a paternal uncle,” etc., speaks in favor of this principle. Kātyāyana says in the *Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa*:

He who performs the marriage or the establishment of the sacred fires while his elder brother remains unmarried or without having established his fires is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.
The one who causes a younger brother to marry before the elder and the younger brother who so marries both certainly go to hell;
even if they have performed the prescribed penance, they partake of only three-quarters of the merit [of their offspring].
The meaning is that they are partakers of three-quarters of the fruit of the sin, which is hell.
Likewise: "A moneylender, a royal servant, and a farmer likewise..."
And one should examine a person who has been away from home, even if he returns in haste after three years.
If [the husband] has gone abroad, one should observe [the vow] for a year;
but when he has returned from there, she should perform a quarter-penance (pāda) for purification.

[108] Regarding the phrase “even though hurrying”: it should be construed as “even though he is hurrying. If he hears that the suitor is residing in another country, such as with a moneylender or similar person, then even while “hurrying”—that is, acting with haste—he should wait for three years for the marriage. However, if he performs the marriage after waiting for one year while the suitor is away and remains unseen, then upon the suitor’s arrival, he should perform the quarter-penance (*pāda-prāyaścitta*) for superseding a younger brother in marriage. Thus says Gautama.

If the elder brother has disappeared, there is a penance of six years; if he is heard from, one must go to him; but if he has entered the religious order (pravrajita), there is no obligation. By extension, for a Brāhmaṇa, this applies for twelve years regarding a brother connected through learning; likewise for an elder brother, some say that for a younger brother there is a period of six years regarding the marriage of a daughter or the kindling of the sacred fires.

If an elder brother has not married and has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), and he remains away from home, the younger brother shall wait for twelve years, or eight years, or six years, while the elder brother is unheard from; this waiting is for the purpose of having the elder brother perform his marriage and the establishment of the fires. If the elder brother has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), there is no further obligation to go to him. For a Brāhmaṇa who has gone abroad for the sake of acquiring knowledge, the waiting period is twelve years, or according to the opinion of some, six years. Regarding the total number of years to be waited, there is an option based on the age and capacity of the younger brother. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.
If one does not wait for an elder brother who has not yet returned from his journey for eight, ten, or twelve years, he becomes liable to penance.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"But for twelve years indeed [one should wait] for an elder, on account of the connection with dharma and artha."
It is right to wait for a brother who is heard of again and again.
One who is insane, sinful, afflicted with leprosy, fallen from his caste,
impotent, or suffering from consumption should not be waited for [to receive the funeral cake].

“Āmayāvī” means one who suffers from a severe illness; the long vowel [in *āmayāvī*] is according to the rule “the term *āmaya* is to be added everywhere,” as stated in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* regarding one who is not excessively ill. Furthermore, the suffix *matup* (expressing possession) is remembered to be used even in the sense of intensity (*atiśāyana*). Śātātapa says:
“In the case of one who is impotent, one who has gone to another country, one who has fallen from his caste, or even a mendicant...”
And there is no fault for one who marries a younger sister when he is devoted to the study of the Yoga scriptures.
[110] There is no fault in lamenting for those who are lame, dwarfish, humpbacked, stammering, or dull-witted, nor for those who are blind from birth, deaf, or mute.

There is no fault in superseding the sons of a paternal uncle, the sons of a co-wife, or the sons of another man's wife, when it comes to the union with a wife and the maintenance of the sacred fires.

“Gadgada” means one whose speech is indistinct. A “jaḍa,” on the other hand, is one incapable of grasping [the teaching] even when taught repeatedly. Regarding women of others, those such as Dattaka and Kṛttimā are brothers. One is observed to be detached through application to the Yoga-śāstra.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
“Those residing in another country, eunuchs, those with only one testicle, and those who are not uterine brothers...”
A Vaiśya, one accused of a crime, an outcast, one equal to a Śūdra, and those who are excessively diseased;

Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, hunchbacked, dwarfish, or crippled; those who are very old, those with weak constitutions, those dependent on agriculture, and those belonging to the king.
One does not incur sin by marrying a younger brother who has married before his elder, provided that the elder is desirous of wealth, or is acting out of lust, or is a womanizer, insane, or a thief.
"Ekavṛṣaṇaḥ" refers to a specific type of eunuch who has only one testicle. "Equal to Śūdras" means those devoted to occupations such as cattle-herding. As it is said:
"Cattle-herders, traders, as well as artisans, actors, servants, and usurers—one should treat these Brāhmaṇas like Śūdras. [111]
Thus, according to the statement of Manu: "Kuṇṭhaka" means one who is handless. Regarding the phrase "of the teacher and of the king," the meaning is "those who are to be practiced by the king."

In this matter, the following is the settled rule: the injunction regarding a twelve-year wait applies as a duty to the younger brother when the elder has gone abroad for the sake of wealth or learning and is heard of again and again. However, the waiting for ten or eight years, as prescribed by Ātreya, depends on the age and capacity [of the younger brother], or on hearing news of the elder residing in another country, or on such circumstances. The six-year wait according to Gautama applies when the elder has gone abroad for the sake of dharma, wealth, or learning and is not heard of at all. As for the three-year wait, since it has already been mentioned in the context of dharma and wealth, it applies by process of elimination to the younger brother who is in great haste when the elder has gone abroad being addicted to pleasure, serving the king, or engaged in agriculture.

In this regard, just as with the establishment of the *agnihotra* fire, even when the *āvasathya* (domestic) fire is established by a younger brother while the elder has not yet done so, the status of a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) certainly arises; for Kātyāyana uses the term "establishment" (*ādhāna*) to refer to the act of establishing the fire in general, and Gautama uses the phrase "in the taking of another's fires" (*kānyāgnyupayameṣu*) to refer to the mere appropriation of the fire, as well as because of established custom. Hārīta says:
"How can one among all uterine brothers become a *parivettṛ*?"
But wives are abandoned neither by the Agnihotra nor by sacrifice.

This passage is intended to demonstrate the greater gravity of the fault in taking a wife when one's elder brother is still unmarried; it does not mean that there is no fault in performing the *paryādhāna* (the kindling of the sacred fires).

"He who enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti* (one superseded). [112]

For Manu has established the fault even in that case, and a separate penance has been prescribed for *paryādhāna* (the act of kindling the sacred fires after a brother has already done so). By this very reasoning, the statement "seven brothers who kindle the fires [in succession]" is also explained.
And likewise, Āpastamba states:

"Among those who have kindled the fires while the elder brother is still living (*abhinirmukta*), those who have kindled them after the elder has died (*abhyudita*), those with deformed nails (*kunakhī*), those with black teeth (*śyāvadanta*), those who have not performed the *agrāvidhi*, those who have married before their elder sister (*didhiṣūpati*), those whose younger brother has kindled the fires first (*paryāhita*), those who have sought a bride for themselves while the elder was available (*parīṣṭa*), and those who have married before the younger brother (*parivitti*)—among these, in each successive case, the impurity and the resulting loss of caste are more severe."

By saying this, it is stated that the abandonment of one's wife is a greater fault than the failure to maintain the sacred fires (*paryādhāna*). The same applies to the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathya-ādhāna*), since Gautama, in the rule "the younger [brother] in the acceptance of brides," prescribes the taking up of the fire alone without distinction. Śātātapa states:
"Neither the sacred fires, nor the Vedas, nor ascetic penances abandon [a man for such a transgression]."
Nor is there a funeral offering for a youngest son, nor for a daughter whose marriage has been fruitlessly delayed.
Thus ends the section on the *Pravēda* festival in the *Gṛhakalpakaṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Hṛdayadhara.
[113] 5 Now follows the establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya).
In this regard, Katyayana states in the Chandogaparisista:
"If a girl has been given by someone through word alone, he who is about to place the final fuel-stick on the fire must not place it at all; otherwise, he commits a fault."

“At once” (*sapadi*) means at that very time. “The final fuel-stick” (*antyāṃ samidham*) refers to that which pertains to the time of the *samāvartana* (the student’s return home). This is what is meant: he for whose sake the girl’s father has already promised to give her away while [the boy] is still in the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*), he, having established the sacred fires at that very time, should perform in those fires the subsequent rites accomplished by fire, such as the *samāvartana*. The sentence should be construed without interruption as follows: “Having established the fires, he should indeed place the final fuel-stick into them. And so it is stated in the *Gobhila-gṛhya-sūtra*.
Whenever he places another kindling stick on the fire, desiring to take his wife's hand, he should offer that very oblation; that indeed becomes his domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*).
Likewise:
"If that maiden, while still unmarried, passes away..."
There is no such violation of the tantra for him; therefore, he may marry another woman by that very same [rite].

By the word "tantra" here, according to the context, the performance of the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathyādhāna*) is intended. "By that very [fire]" means, by implication, by the fire that has been established. Likewise:
"And if he should not obtain another girl, even though he is requesting one..."
Having internalized that fire within himself, he shall quickly become one who has entered the higher stage of life.
“Having made it one’s own” means having made it identical with oneself, that is to say, having superposed it upon oneself by means of a mantra. According to Pāraskara:
the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathya*) takes place at the time of marriage; according to some, at the time of [the father's] death and so forth.
"At the time of inheritance" means at the time of receiving a share of the estate. Paiṭhīnasi says:

"One should kindle the nuptial fire and, according to the proper time, place fuel-sticks into it every evening. [The mantras are] 'To Agni, to Prajāpati, to Anumati' in the evening; 'To Sūrya, to Prajāpati, to Anumati' at the morning time."

[115] Hārīta says: One is a householder because of the taking of a wife and because of the performance of domestic rites; therefore, he is called "one who dwells in a house. From the sacrifice performed as a master of the house, the duties of the householder stage proceed.

Having stated, "having taken a wife and established the sacred fires," the five sacrifices and other duties were prescribed as to be performed subsequent to the establishment of the Śrauta fires. By this [verse], it is stated that those [sacrifices] also take place prior to the Śrauta establishment. Therefore, they are to be performed by the householder (*gṛhastha*). And he is a householder "because of the taking of a wife for marriage and because of the Gṛhya injunctions. The "marriage fire" (*audvāhika*) is the fire used for wedding rites. The "Gṛhya injunctions" refer to the injunction regarding the performance of rituals prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras; therefore, due to those two aforementioned reasons, being a "house-dweller" (*gṛhoṣita*), i.e., a householder, he performs the *pākayajñas* from that point onward. Starting precisely from then, the duties of the householder come into effect.
Manu and Viśvāmitra state:
"A householder should perform the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*) according to the rules in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five sacrifices and the daily cooking."

"In the nuptial" means taken at the time of marriage. "Domestic rites" refers to the *pākayajña* and other such rituals. "Cooking" means the act of preparing food. "Daily" means that which is performed every day. Baudhāyana states:
"The fire [obtained] from the marriage of a wife and so forth—performing rites in that fire prior to the formal establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*)."

According to Āpastamba and others, in the case of the *sarvādhāna* (the rite of laying all the fires at once), this is for the purpose of ensuring that domestic (*gṛhya*) rites are performed in the ordinary fire (*laukika*).
Yājñavalkya states: "A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the marriage fire (*vivāhāgni*)."
And even when brought by the giver, the Smārta fire is [to be used] for the Vaitānika fires.
A *vaitānika* is one for whom the *vitāna*— that is, the sacrifice— is the purpose.
Now, regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and other rites, Vasiṣṭha states:

"A Brāhmaṇa must necessarily establish the sacred fires and perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the animal sacrifice, and the Sautrāmaṇī. For this is a mandatory duty and is likewise described as a debt."

“Naiyamikam” means that which pertains to a fixed rule (*niyama*), that is, what is constant. “Ṛṇasaṃstutam” means that which is proclaimed as being for the purpose of discharging a debt, by such passages as, “A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born... and so forth. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

“Having taken a wife, one should sacrifice with the seven *haviryajñas* ending with the *agnyādheya*, *punarādheya*, *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *dākṣāyaṇa*, *cāturmāsya*, *paśu*, and *sautrāmaṇī*.”

“Punarādheya” is a specific mode of re-establishing the sacred fires. “Dākṣāyaṇa” is a specific mode well-known among ritualists, consisting of the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) with repetition at every lunar phase according to a fifteen-year rule. Paiṭhīnasi says: “Agni is indeed the deity of human beings; therefore, one should establish the fire, for the deities have Agni as their mouth. He carries the oblation (havya) to the gods and the ancestral offering (kavya) to the ancestors. The evening and morning bali-offerings, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Naveṣṭi, the Aṣṭakā, the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), and the Pitṛyajña—these are the Pākayajñas.”
In the phrase "he carries the *havya* to the gods," the word "Agni" is the ellipsis. In the phrase "the *kavya*," the verb "carries" is the ellipsis. Hārīta says:
"One should constantly perform the *pākayajñas*, and one should constantly perform the *haviryajñas*."
And he who desires imperishable dharma should [employ] gentle means according to the prescribed rule.

The gentle one should perform the rites on the eighth day; the commencement of the fortnight; the *śrāddha* at the new moon and other times; the *śravaṇa-karman*; the *āgrayaṇī* rite; the *āśvayujī-karman*; the procedure for the *caitrī*; the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*); the *agnihotra*; the *darśapūrṇamāsa*; the *cāturmāsya* rites; the *paśubandha*; the performance of the *sautrāmaṇī*; and the Soma sacrifices—the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*. [119] By the word "new moon and others" (*amāvāsyādi*), the *śrāddhas* of the *aṣṭakā* and so forth are included.
Devala said:

The seven forms of the *pākayajña* (cooked-sacrifice) are: the *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *ahuta*, the *śūlagava*, the *baliharaṇa*, the *pratyavarohaṇa*, and the *aṣṭakā-homa*. The seven forms of the *haviryajña* (oblation-sacrifice) are: the *agnihotra*, the *agnyādheya*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the *ayanayajña*, the *cāturmāsya*, and the *sautrāmaṇī*. The seven forms of the *somayajña* (Soma-sacrifice) are: the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*. Thus, the sacrifice described in the *Adhvara-veda* consists of twenty-one types. The great sacrifices (*mahāyajñas*), such as the *vājapeya*, *aśvamedha*, *rājasūya*, *pauṇḍarīka*, and *gosava*, are the seasonal sacrificial rites (*kratavas*).

"Etāvat" refers to the duration of time; this sacrifice (*yajña*)—the performance of vows, gifts, and so forth—is a sacrificial session (*sattra*). As for the commencement of the five-fold sacrifices (*pañcapadā-yajña*), the sacrifice is "performed" (*kṛta*); the oblation (*homa*) offered with reference to the gods is "offered" (*prahuta*); the giving of cooked food and fire to a Brāhmaṇa is "unoffered" (*ahuta*); the offering of bali-oblations to the guardians of the site and the elemental spirits is the "ox on a spit" (*śūlagava*), a sacrifice of a bull dedicated to Rudra which has the *sthālīpāka* as its constituent part; the "offering of bali" (*baliharaṇa*) is [the sacrifice] to the serpents; the "descent" (*pratyavarohaṇa*) is the descent performed on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, as stated in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*: "When the sun has set, they should offer the *sthālīpāka*," and so forth; the "solstice sacrifice" (*ayanayajña*) is the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśuyāga*). Regarding the phrase "etāvat... kālam uddiśya": the meaning is that one should observe the duration of time consisting of the sacrificial sessions (*sattra-aṅga*) from twelve nights up to a thousand days. "Five-fold" (*pañcapadā*) means that one performs the five types of *sthālīpāka* sacrifices, the *havis* sacrifices, the *soma* sacrifices, and the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) in the form of a sacrificial session (*sattra*).

Baudhāyana says: From the *agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires) onwards, these [rites] become perpetual (*ajasra*). Namely: the *agnyādheya*, the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the animal sacrifice during the northern and southern solstices, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* offering at the beginning of each season, and the *jyotiṣṭoma* in the spring—thus [constitutes] the attainment of security (*kṣemaprāpaṇa*). "Perpetual" means they must be performed at their own prescribed times. The "*ṣaḍḍhotṛ*" is the oblation offered at the beginnings of the six seasons with the mantra beginning "Speech is the hotṛ. "Attainment of security" means the avoidance of the transgression caused by non-performance.
Manu says: One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night;
and indeed, one should perform the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice at the end of the full moon month.
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the seasonal sacrifices;
at the end of the sun’s course, he should perform the animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and desires to live a long life should not eat new grain for a month without having first performed the sacrifice of the new harvest and the animal sacrifice.
[121] Without having offered to the fires with fresh food and with animal oblations, those fires— despised by the consumption of fresh food and meat— desire to devour one's very life-breaths.

"At the beginning and end of day and night" means at the morning and evening twilights (*saṃdhyā*). "At the end of the season" means at the conclusion of the menstrual period. "With four-month sacrifices" refers to the *Cāturmāsya* offerings. "With an animal oblation" means with the sacrificial offering of an animal. Hārīta says:

"In the Agnihotra, one should eat what has been won by sacrifice, not what has been won by other means. By kindling with wood, one conquers the vegetable realm; by water, one conquers the waters; by milk and the like, [one conquers] milk, clarified butter, and so forth; by rice and barley, one conquers the plants; and by animals, one conquers animals."

"Conquered by sacrifice" (*yajñābhijitam*) means conquered by a person through the performance of sacrifice; it is obtained from the *Abhijit* [sacrifice], or perhaps from that very source. Now, one might object: "In that case, how can there be no fault in eating the fruits of trees and the like, the milk of buffaloes and other animals along with its derivatives, or even wild animals, since these are not fit for sacrifice? To this he replies: "By means of wood," and so forth. "Produced from a tree" (*vānaspatyam*) refers to fruits and such things originating from a forest tree (*vanaspati*). "By means of water" refers to the water used for sprinkling at the time of cooking and so on, as well as the products of the cow (*gavya*) employed in the sacrifice. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), curd and other such items are included. "By means of an animal" refers to a goat or similar creature employed in the sacrifice. The connection is: "He does not conquer domestic or wild [animals]."
Yājñavalkya says: Every year the Soma sacrifice is to be performed, as well as the animal sacrifice at each solstice;
likewise, the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed.
In the absence of these, a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a deficient rite with available materials, for it yields no fruit.

The *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice is an alternative (*anukalpa*). Regarding the phrase "when wealth exists": when the primary means for performing the rite is available, the reason why one "should not perform a deficient rite" is that [such a rite] "yields no fruit"—this is the implied sense. Viṣṇu states that one should sacrifice when there is a continuation [of the rule];
and one should perform the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice in the autumn and summer, as well as upon the ripening of rice and barley.
[123] Jābāla says: A twice-born man should always perform the Vaitāna oblations in the evening and in the morning;
indeed, he should also perform them with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and with the Pūrṇamāsa sacrifice likewise.
One should perform the *naveṣṭi* at the ripening of the grain, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices at the beginning of each season,
the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* at the start of the solstice, or even once a year.
At the end of the year, having sacrificed with the Soma sacrifice, he is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Yama said: Even a householder should sacrifice with the Agnihotra day and night.
One should worship the ancestral deities with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Hārīta says: There is no duty higher than the Agnihotra; there is no austerity higher than the Agnihotra;
there is no gift higher than the Agnihotra; there is no self-restraint higher than the Agnihotra.
There is no higher good than the Agnihotra; there is no greater glory than the Agnihotra.
There is no higher perfection than the Agnihotra; there is no higher goal than the Agnihotra.
There is no station higher than the Agnihotra; there is no vow higher than the Agnihotra—[that] which the wise worship, free from dualities and devoid of desire for fame.
Thus, this [truth] is subtle, like fire hidden within wood in the Agnihotra rites,
and [concealed] in the Śukriyas, the secret texts, the Niṣads, and the Upaniṣads.
The great-souled ones study it; it shines forth in the Agnihotra sacrifice.

"In the *śukriyas*," that is, in the sections concerning the *pravargya* rite; "in the secret texts," that is, in the hymns such as the *aghamarṣaṇa*. [The connection is: they recite the subtle Supreme Self in the *śukriya* and other texts; He shines forth in the *agnihotra* sacrifice. Likewise:
"Purified by the *agnihotra* and other rites, self-restrained, and having conquered his senses..."
One attains what is subtler than the subtle, just as there is a void in the sky.
Well-performed Agnihotra sacrifices lead to the supreme goal;
herein lie both heaven and liberation for whosoever desires to go there.
“The Supreme Brahman is subtler than the subtle. “Just as there is a cavity in the sky”: the meaning is that it is brought forth from the cavity within the great space. [Jābāla]:
Having tasted the nectar of contentment, the man who knows the Dharma, with his mind fixed on That—
And by means of desire, the Hotṛ priest of the Agnihotra shall attain his own light.

Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states: "One should worship Agni alone and no other deity; it is known [from scripture] that one should think, 'May I become Agni. One should not go on a journey. If he should go on a journey, the prescribed ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for one who has gone abroad applies; he should offer the *prāśita* portion at the re-establishment of the fire (*agnyādheya*). In the case of the *navaiṣṭi*, the same applies to the domestic fire (*aupāsana*); the ritual attendance mentioned in the *Kalpasūtra* is to be performed—this is the remainder [of the sense]. 'The *prāśita*' is the portion to be consumed by the sacrificer. Thus, in the *navaiṣṭi* connected with the domestic fire, the sacrificer's portion belonging to one who is away on a journey should be cast into the fire."
Aṅgiras:
Whatever one offers according to the rules, whether it be worldly or Vedic,
through the Vedic rite one attains heaven, while the worldly rite is a means to heaven.
"Laukika" refers to that which is based on tradition (smārta); "vaidika" refers to that which is based on revelation (śrauta). He attains heaven—or liberation. Devala says:
