Having established the *agnihotra* fire, one should not abandon it even for the sake of saving one's life.
For all the Vedas have that as their purpose, as do the birth of a Brahmin in this world.
Manu says: Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning,
nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*.
For these fall into hell, as does the one for whom they sacrifice;
therefore, the officiating priest (hotṛ) should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and a master of the Vedas.

“Alpavidyaḥ” (one of little learning) is one who is ignorant of the substitutes for expiation and so forth. “Bāliśaḥ” (an infant) is one under sixteen years of age. “Ārttaḥ” (one who is afflicted) is one tormented by disease and the like. “Asaṃskṛtaḥ” (one who is uninitiated) is one devoid of the sacramental rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception). “Yasya” refers to the *agnihotrī* (the maintainer of the sacred fire); the word “his *agnihotra*” is to be supplied as the ellipsis. “Vaitānakuśalaḥ” is one skilled in performing rituals accomplished by means of the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*). This is a prohibition against girls and others who might otherwise have been obtained here as substitutes for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in the *agnihotra*.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: “The offering must not be made by a priest or anyone else in the absence of the husband and wife.”
For if it occurs when neither of the two parties is present, the ordeal would indeed be useless.
If one who has maintained the sacred fire departs with his wife, having crossed the boundary,
it is prescribed that he must perform the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) once the time for the fire-oblation has passed.
When the forest has been consumed by the fire of a traveling fire, one who is composed should protect the sacred fire; once it has been extinguished, the re-establishment of the fire is prescribed.

“Boundary” (*sīmā*) refers to the boundary established by the formal installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) and so forth; the meaning is that if the wife and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) remain within each other’s respective boundaries and the time for the *homa* offering passes, there must be a re-installation of the fires. “Destruction” (*nāśa*) means non-appearance [of the fire]. “Concentrated” (*samāhita*) means one who exerts proper effort in guarding the fire.
On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
“Having obtained his livelihood in accordance with dharma, bathing daily and hospitable to guests...”
A householder who is devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice does not suffer, provided he performs it correctly.

[Hārīta]: One who performs the *pākayajña* sacrifices without spilling becomes purified from all sins committed through slaughter. The Śruti states: "As food is for living beings, so is the *agnihotra* for Agni. Just as living beings who do not eat fall into a state of wretchedness or die, even so those whose *agnihotra* fire has been interrupted fall into a state of inferiority or die, even if they possess other sacrificial rites (*kratu*). Therefore, the Śruti says: "For the sake of maintenance (*bhṛtyai*) or for the sake of support (*dhṛtyai*), those without offspring fall into wretchedness and cause their own destruction; such is the *agnihotra*."

The sacrificer is the creator of life; indeed, life itself is the *prāṇāgnihotra*. Just as [the fires] become satisfied and capable, so too, through the uninterrupted *agnihotra*, the fires, being satisfied and pleased, manifest in the sacrifices. He who, having been initiated for the lifelong sacrificial session (*sattrāya*) until old age or death, performs the introductory rite of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), becomes a Soma-sacrificer by means of the Full Moon oblation—since he manifests in the vegetable offerings, the milk-offerings (*sānnāyya*), and the animal sacrifice—and nourishes the Soma with the New Moon offering. Therefore, those who understand the New and Full Moon sacrifices as the completion of the *darśa* are purified from the very beginning and attain immortality, surpassing others by their excellence. That [sacrifice] is of two kinds: worship with material substances (*dravyejyā*) and worship of the Self (*ātmejyā*). When one worships with a motive, either intending the fruit "let there be this very material substance" or with some underlying desire (*sopadha*), that is worship with material substances.

Now, he who possesses knowledge of the Śruti, Smṛti, and the Self, and who worships Vaiśvānara—who is the oblation that is like nectar, consisting of the deities and the self—as the Self, that is the sacrifice to the Self. This has also been stated in a Ṛk verse: “Recognizing the Self within the Self in the inner ordinance, in the highest heaven, as Vaiśvānara, the guest who bestows [blessings]; the wise man goes forth every evening with delight. They honor this heroic guest; may we, as immortals, traverse these worlds.”

“*Askannapākayajñaḥ*” means one whose *pākayajña* (cooked-sacrifice) is not spilled. The phrase “*askannapākayajñaḥ*” is a restatement of what was previously mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating the result. With the passage beginning “*yathā prajānām aśanam*” and ending with “*śrutiḥ*,” he states the necessity of performing the *agnihotra* by means of the worldly example of eating. “*Anaśnantyaḥ*” means not eating; “*pāpīyastvam*” means emaciation. “*Kratunopapannena*” refers to well-known sacrifices such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. “*Avasīyastvam*” means inferiority. “*Dhṛtyai*” means for the sake of maintaining one’s own state; “*guptyai*” means for protection. With the passage beginning “*āyuṣkṛd yajamānaḥ*” and ending with “*saṃbhavanti*,” the capacity for subsequent sacrifices is demonstrated through the example of the *prāṇāgnihotra* (the fire-sacrifice of the vital breaths) for those satisfied by the *agnihotra*. “*Āyuṣkṛt*” means one who performs the *prāṇāgnihotra*; by the word “*āyuḥ*,” the *agnihotra* dedicated to the deities of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc. is indicated, because it is the cause of increasing life. “*Tṛptāḥ*” means capable. “*Jarāmaryāya*” means having old age and death as its limit. With the passage beginning “*jarāmaryāyaivam*” and ending with “*atrekād anyair*,” it is stated that by undertaking the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices right from the start—beginning with the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite—one becomes purified. But by other performances extending until old age and death, due to the abundance of practice (*atirekāt*), one attains immortality (*amṛtatvam*). Because *soma* can be produced from herbs and so forth, one causes the *soma* to swell through the *somayāga*. With the passage beginning “*sa dvividhaḥ*” and ending with “*sañcarema*,” specific results are stated according to the specific qualification of the sacrificer. “*Sopadham*” means accompanied by conditions such as occasional rites (*naimittika*). Here, in the phrase “*śrutyādīty*,” the word “*jñāna*” (knowledge) is connected individually with each of “*śruti*” and the others. “*Amṛtam*” is Brahman. “*Havirbhūtam*” means having the nature of an oblation; it has the nature of the deities (*adhidaivata*). “*Adhyātmabhūtam*” means having the nature of the sacrificer. “*Vaiśvānaram*” means the cause of the heating of Vaiśvānara. Thus, the sacrifice performed when one has attained such a state is “*sātmejyā*” (sacrifice with the self). “*Vaiśvānaram atithim*” and so forth refers to Vaiśvānara in the form of a guest. “*Ādadānam*” means serving with respect. “*Antarvidhau*” means in the internal sacrifice. “*Ātmani*” means in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). “*Ātmānam*” means the individual soul (*jīvātman*). “*Abhisaṃvidānaḥ*” means perceiving them as one through the practice of meditation. “*Aratiḥ*” means one whose attachment to external objects has departed. “*Parame vyomani*” means in the supreme ether, in the ultimate reality, that is, in the Supreme Self. The meaning is that he attains oneness with That and experiences the state of becoming Brahman (*brahmībhāva*). “*Pratisāyam*” means every evening, at the time of the *homa*. This is for the purpose of indicating the time and equipment for the obligatory (*nitya*) ritual.

Furthermore, Hārīta says: From the syllable (akṣara) Brahman comes into being; from that, ritual action (karman); from that, the season (ṛtu); from that, Parjanya; from that, food (anna); from that, the beings (bhūtāni) were born.
From sacrifice (yajña), offspring (prajā) arise on all sides; sacrifice sustains offspring.
From sacrifice all this being has arisen; sacrifice is the essence, these bodies are its forms.
Those ignorant people who utter censure against the sacrificer—
those senseless ones do not incur the sin that is repelled by the sacrifice.
Indeed, there is no world for one who does not perform sacrifice; one who does not sacrifice finds no happiness.
Having failed to offer sacrifice, his soul unpurified, he falls like a withered leaf.
By sacrifice the worlds shine stainless;
by sacrifice the gods attained immortality;
by sacrifice they were liberated from many sins.
He attains the worlds of the supreme Viṣṇu.

"From the Imperishable," that is, from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It is first perceived by the knowers of Brahman, as seen in such scriptural passages as, "This Rigveda is His very breath. "From that," meaning from the Veda. "Action" (*karman*) refers to ritual performance. "Sacrifice" (*kratu*) refers to the *yāga*. "On all sides" (*viśvataḥ*) means everywhere. "Bodies" (*tanūḥ*) refers to physical forms. "Borne by sacrifice" (*yajñāpoḍham*) means carried away by sacrifice. As stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Those twice-born who perform the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices..."
[132] There is never again a return for them from the world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, Hārīta says:
one attains a divine state;
likewise.

Day by day, through the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, Āgrayaṇa, Cāturmāsya, Iṣṭi, Paśubandha, and other rites performed according to rule, there arises "pravṛtti" from the surplus of one's livelihood; "pravṛtti" means performance. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.

One who is faithful by nature but lacks the desire [to perform rites], yet is lazy regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), should not fail to establish the fires. And one who is capable [of performing them] should not fail to offer the Soma sacrifice; that is, one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice [despite being capable] is at fault.
"Lacking desire" means not being covetous of the wealth of others. "Capable" means competent; and competence consists in the possession of wealth, learning, and so forth. — Manu.
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, if a twice-born man drinks Soma when the substance is very small, even though he has previously drunk Soma, he does not obtain its fruit.

“Sufficient for three years” (traivārṣika) means that by which one’s subsistence will be maintained for three years. “Dependents” (bhṛtyāḥ) refers to those who must necessarily be supported. Yājñavalkya says:
“That twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may drink the Soma juice.”
One whose food supply lasts for a year should perform the rites pertaining to the Soma sacrifice first.

“Prāksaumikīḥ” refers to the rites such as the Cāturmāsya and others that occur prior to the Soma sacrifice. This applies even to the obligatory (nitya) context, because the expression “he drinks the Soma” is used without qualification. It has been stated that one who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain should perform the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice every year; since this is so, Yājñavalkya has also prescribed the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice for those who lack those [other sacrifices]. Manu says:
“One should regularly perform the Vaiśvānarī iṣṭi at the completion of each year.”
[134] When the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices cannot be performed for the sake of expiation, [the following applies].

"Kḷptānām" means those prescribed as necessary. "Niṣkṛtiḥ" means the removal of the transgression incurred by not performing them. "Asaṃbhave" means when the previously mentioned wealth, cattle, and so forth are unavailable.
Likewise: "A person of faith who has conquered his senses should perform other meritorious acts."
But one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with small sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, does not give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the Prājāpatya rite at the establishment of the sacred fires,
he remains one who has not established the fires.

“Other meritorious acts,” such as giving and so forth, which are accomplished through great wealth, [are not possible] for one who has little wealth; here, “little wealth” is relative to the prescribed number of one hundred and twelve [cows] and so on. “The horse belongs to Prajāpati” because, by its very nature, the horse has Prajāpati as its deity. “He is one who has not established the sacred fires” means that he does not obtain the fruit of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) rite.
[135] Regarding the duties of kings, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One who does not possess sufficient resources should not perform a sacrifice; for it is said that one who lacks the means for a year's subsistence should not sacrifice, as misfortune falls upon the kingdom and misfortune covers the sacrificer at the performance of the sacrifice.

"Misfortune" (*aniṣṭam*) refers to the non-performance of what is beneficial. "The performance of the sacrifice" (*yajñasavanam*) refers to the sacrifice itself, for it "covers" him—that is, it binds him with sin.
Again, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
The officiating priest, endowed with the power of mantras and possessed of the qualities of medicinal herbs,
attains the gods through sacrifice, yet he does not attain them as long as he has not received his sacrificial fee.
The social classes are established in each stage of life and become manifest through their respective duties;
therein, the Brāhmaṇa is the instructor of the rules, conduct, and dharma.
That teacher who performs the purificatory rites is to be fully honored and worshipped;
all sacrificial fires have him as their mouth, and it is traditionally taught that all the gods have Agni as their mouth.

The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and the Atharva-Aṅgirasa hymns—these have been studied by the Brahmins; they are the sacrifices accompanied by the distribution of sacrificial fees.

Those by whom sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been properly obtained from wealth and so forth are called "those who have received the fees" (*āptadakṣiṇā*). By this means, the giving of complete sacrificial fees is established through the medium of the Brahmins.
[136] Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"A twice-born man must not perform the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) even with a single wife."
One should know that as unperformed—that which all [the rites] follow after.
The churning for the fire must be performed separately by these virtuous wives of equal caste, who are senior in age, with great effort and using many sticks.
But he should not appoint a Śūdra woman, nor one who acts out of malice or hatred,
nor one who stands under a curse, nor one who has had sexual intercourse with another man.
Then, whichever one among these is most capable,
or whichever one has arrived, should churn the fire as desired.

The purposes are accomplished when they undertake [the rite] together with their authority. By this it is stated: for one who has many wives, the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) must not be performed even in the absence of a single wife. Among many wives of various castes, only the eldest of all should perform the churning of the fire. Even among those of the same caste, if they are all virtuous (*sādhvī*), each should perform the churning separately. "Until the emergence of the fire" means until the fire issues forth from the two kindling woods (*araṇī*). "One who does not abide by the instruction" refers to one who transgresses her husband's command. "Then," meaning after the churning; "among these" wives, "she who is more capable" should perform the service of the fire. "More capable" means competent to perform the attendance upon the fire and so forth. Among those who have approached—that is, standing nearby—any one of them may attend to the fire according to her own will.
[137] Yājñavalkya says: Having cremated a virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire,
the husband shall take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule, without transgressing the law.

“Vṛttavatīm” means one who possesses the practice of her own dharma as previously described; “vidhivat” means according to the manner of marriage as previously described. Following the duties of women, Manu says:
“A twice-born man [should marry] a woman of the same class who possesses such conduct and who dies before him.”
One who knows the Dharma should cause [the body] to be cremated with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial vessels.
Having given the sacred fires to his wife who has died first during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the formal re-acceptance of the fires.
"In the final rites" refers to the rite of cremation.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"If the eldest wife of a man with many wives goes astray through illicit conduct..."
Regarding this, some authorities desire a re-establishment of the sacred fires, but Gautama does not.
[138] Having cremated his wife— who was a suitable match and previously established as such—
with fires, he who has taken a wife should, without delay, establish the sacred fire with the ritual vessels.

“*Abhicāraḥ*” means transgression. “*Pūrvasaṃsthitām*” means one who has previously died. And this mention of the *agnihotra* is intended as an illustration for the *smārta* (domestic) fire as well. This practice pertains specifically to the death of the senior wife of the same caste (*savarṇa*), because the word *bhāryā* and others are used without distinction to denote any wife in general. Nor is it the case that these [fires] are attended to when the wife has died; rather, since it is established in the context of the fire-sacrifices (*agnikratu*) without distinction that the fires must be abandoned upon the death of the senior wife alone, by virtue of her being the primary wife. As for those [verses], however:
Even when his wife has died, he must not abandon the Vedic fire;
for that ritual act, performed under a specific condition, he should complete throughout his entire life.
If one should ever burn his own wife with the Agnihotra fire,
she does not become a woman, nor does the burner become a man.
If he should cremate a second wife with the sacrificial fires while the first wife is still living,
that act is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor.
But when the second wife has died, he who abandons the *agnihotra* sacrifice should be known as a renouncer of the Veda (*brahmojjha*), as should he who abandons his desires.

Regarding the scriptural statements such as "with the mantra for spreading the sacrificial grass (barhis-taraṇa), behind the fire, for many [wives]," since these concern the spreading of the sacrificial grass and are distinct from other matters, their basis is at least doubtful; they apply solely to the case of the death of a wife of a different caste who is the second [wife].
Now, regarding the performance and non-performance of sacrifices, Baudhāyana says:

At the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra, "O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, whatever debt I incurred while not playing the dice—bestowing life upon you from every side," one who is about to begin the *agnihotra* should employ the *daśahotṛ* formula; one about to begin the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *caturhotṛ*; one about to begin the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *pañcahotṛ*; at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*; and at the *soma* sacrifice, the *saptahotṛ*. Thus it is known. For the Brāhmaṇa states: "At the beginnings of rites, one should offer with these; thus purified, he attains the world of the gods."

The *daśahotṛ* and other such specific mantras, beginning with "The altar is the offering-spoon" (*citiḥ sruc*), have been mentioned for the commencement of rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).
On this point, Āpastamba says:

From the time of the taking of the hand (marriage) onwards, the conduct for the two householders is as follows: eating at two times of the day and not being satiated with food; on the *parvan* days, there is fasting for both, which means eating only at other times and being satiated with food; and whatever may be dear to them, that they should eat on this [first] day, and they should sleep on the ground, avoiding sexual intercourse. On the following day, there is the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking); its procedure is explained by the *pārvaṇa* rite. The world constantly teaches: wherever one intends to establish the fire, there one should draw three lines facing east and three facing north, sprinkle them with water, and kindle the fire; having poured out water to the north or the east, one should place another vessel there so that the vessels are not empty of water.

“From the taking of the hand” means after the marriage ceremony. “Of the two householders” refers to the husband and wife. “At the two times” means in the evening and in the morning. “Non-satiety” means the cessation of overeating. “Of food” (*annasya*) is a genitive used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe ṣaṣṭhī*) in connection with a word meaning satisfaction (*su-hita*). “On the *parvan* days” means on the full moon and new moon days. “Of both” refers to the wife and husband. Here, fasting (*upavāsa*) must indeed be observed by not eating. Regarding the domestic fire, they maintain that one should eat the cultivated and wild forest produce after having anointed the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, and the dwelling; and that very same meal [is prescribed] at another time. However, the meal occurs immediately after the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), or at the two times of evening and morning. But because of the statement of Kātyāyana, “In the afternoon, he should eat the food for undertaking the vow,” and because of the rule of the Āpastamba school, “And there is satiety of food,” this refers specifically to the new moon day. For the full moon day, the *Kalpasūtra* states: “Those intending to fast on the full moon day should not eat to complete satiety.”

[142] And whatever may be pleasing to these two—any one of the prescribed items such as clarified butter, curd, and so forth—on this very day, but not on the previous day. "Below" means not on a bed or similar furniture. "On the following day" means on the first lunar day (*pratipad*). "Service" refers to the husking of grain and other such rites. "With the *pārvaṇa*," that is, with the *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) performed on a festival day (*parvan*). "He should kindle" means he should set it ablaze. "Having poured out water" in whichever direction; "another" refers to a different supply of water. "Cushions" and so forth, beginning with the *samā*. "Constantly" means for as long as the performance lasts. —Hārīta.
On the day following [the preparation], even for the sake of rites for the gods and ancestors, one should not exceed the fast (*aupavasta*).

Regarding the phrase "on the day following" (*śvo bhūte*), this refers to when a rite for the gods or ancestors is to take place on the next day, even if it is other than the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. "Fast" (*aupavasta*) refers to specific dietary restrictions; it is that which is prescribed by the statement: "He observes the vow (*vrata*) consisting of food without beans, without meat, and with abundant clarified butter. — Paiṭhīnasi.

It has been stated that on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*) the food is sacrificial; one must not speak in anger nor utter falsehoods. One should not engage in idle conversation with people. Pure, self-controlled, vigilant, skillful, and having conquered the senses, one should sacrifice. After midday, having eaten sacrificial food, having bound the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and fuel (*idhma*), and having performed the encircling of the fires, one should not go abroad and should sleep on the ground—or, if he so desires, he may sacrifice. On the full moon day, having shaved his beard, adorned himself, and anointed himself, he should enjoy perfumes, flowers, and the like. For the ancestors indeed desire purity; the gratification of Brahmins according to the ritual for the ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) has already been explained.

"On the *aupavasathya* day" means on the day preceding the day of the sacrifice. "Food" (*bhakta*) refers to that which is to be eaten. "The consecration of the fire" (*agniparigraha*) here refers to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that the deities, beginning with Agni, are to be worshipped. "Anointed" (*abhyakta*) means with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth. "Satisfying the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*) pertains to the full moon and new moon days. The meaning is that one should feed many [Brāhmaṇas] "according to the ritual of the *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhakalpena*), that is, in the manner of a *śrāddha*. — Baudhāyana.

"One who wears unwashed garments is pure. Therefore, whatever may be connected with sacrifice and the like, all that one should perform wearing unwashed clothes. The wife, the sacrificer, and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should put on clothes that have been washed, aired, and are not soiled. This applies from the commencement onwards in long Soma sacrifices. In every case, the officiating priests should act according to what has been traditionally handed down. For example, in the Abhicaraṇīya sacrifices, the animal sacrifices, and the Medha offerings, the officiating priests should proceed wearing red turbans and red clothes; and in the Vṛṣākapi rite, they should wear variegated clothes and variegated numbers [of garments]. Thus it is.
Their garments should be made of linen; in the absence of those, they may be made of cotton or wool.

Among garments, a new (unwashed) garment is the best; a sacrifice performed by one wearing such a garment is pure. "Upavātāni" means dried [in the wind]; "akliṣṭāni" means without holes. "In long Soma sacrifices" refers to those Soma rites that extend over a long period of time. As for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), however, they perform all the rites exactly as prescribed—wearing whatever kind of garment has been prescribed for them. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning with "tathaitad" ("so indeed this..."). "Abhicaraṇīyam" refers to the means for performing sorcery, such as the Śyena sacrifice and others. "Citravāsasaḥ" means those wearing variegated garments. Regarding the phrase "when the Vṛṣākapi [hymn] is being commenced," since the context concerns only the wife and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) through the passage beginning with "linen garments" (*kṣaumāṇi*), this is a rule prescribing different garments for the *Ādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires).
[145] Yama says: A black antelope skin is for a Brāhmaṇa, a tiger skin for a Kṣatriya, and a goat skin for a Vaiśya;
however, a garment of hemp or linen may be used by anyone.

Baudhāyana says: The sacrificial ground (vihāra) is to be approached from the north; likewise its completion. In rites for the ancestors (pitrya), it is the reverse. One should wash what has been struck by the foot. Having touched a limb, one should touch water or a wet cloth. Thus it is known: in cases of cutting, splitting, digging, burning, casting away, and in rites for the ancestors, the Rākṣasas, the Nairṛtas, the Rudras, and in malevolent (abhicārika) rites, one should touch water.

One should not protect oneself by means of a sacrificial accessory that possesses a mantra. The internal parts are the sacrificial accessories; the external ones are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The wife and the sacrificer are more internal than the officiating priests. Clarified butter (*ājya*) is more internal than the sacrificial accessories; the oblations (*havis*) are more internal than the clarified butter; the animal victim (*paśu*) is more internal than the oblations; Soma is more internal than the animal victim; and the fires are more internal than Soma.

Just as the officiating priests do not turn away from the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), [the sacrificer] turns toward his right shoulder while facing east; facing west, he turns toward his left. The space between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap is the entrance (*tīrtha*) of the sacrifice. Where there is no *cātvāla*, the *āhavanīya* fire serves as the *utkara*. From there, the performers—the sacrificer and his wife—should enter. This applies whether the rite is unfinished or completed; the path of movement is from the region of the *utkara*. One should not place into the fire a piece of wood or a fuel-stick (*samidh*) that has not been sprinkled with water, has not been brought forward, or is damp. The Brahman and the sacrificer proceed in front of the *āhavanīya*; according to some, behind the *āhavanīya*. To the south of the *āhavanīya* is the seat of the Brahman, and to the west is that of the sacrificer. To the north of the northern hip (*uttarā śroṇi*) is the seat of the Hotṛ; the *utkara* is the seat of the Āgnīdhra. To the rear of the *gārhapatya* is the seat of the wife. At each respective time, the spreading of *darbha* grass should be performed upon these seats. A water-pot should be kept for each person for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*). Once initiated, the sacrificer must observe the vow: he shall not speak ill of others, nor become angry, nor weep; he shall not look at urine or excrement. Upon seeing something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the sun is the best of lights. O Initiation, do not forsake me!"

*Vihāra* means that which is moved about; *vihṛta* refers to the fire that has been carried forth. It is said to have its "access" (*upacāra*) on the northern side, meaning that its commencement of entry is on the northern part. "Exit" (*apavarga*) is the departure at the conclusion of the ritual; that too is likewise on the north. Regarding "rites for the ancestors" (*pitryeṣu*), such as the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and others, both of these [entry and exit] are "reversed," meaning they are performed on the southern side of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). "Touched by a foot" (*padopahatam*) means touched by a foot. Regarding the sacrificial implement, the *sruva* ladle, and so forth: one should touch oneself [only] above the navel. For the *Taittirīya Śruti* states: "The part of a person above the navel is pure (*medhya*), while that below is impure (*amedhya*). "Hem" (*sik*) refers to the edge of a garment. One should perform the touching of water (*udakasparśana*). With "that which possesses a mantra": whatever rite is performed in the sacrifice with a mantra, one should circumambulate oneself with that implement, such as the *sruva* ladle. At that time, one should not hold it anywhere other than upon one's own body.

The reason for this is as follows: "The internal members of the sacrifice" refers to those that are not external; "from the members of the sacrifice" means from the *sruva* ladle and other such implements. "Clarified butter and oblations" refers to those in the form of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Regarding the phrase "according to the ritual": in whichever ritual action a priest is engaged, he should not, at the time of completing that action, go elsewhere from the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) of his own accord except for necessary business—this is the meaning. When he turns around while facing east, he should turn his right side toward the center (i.e., clockwise). When the sacrificer, facing west, turns around, he should likewise turn his left side toward the center (i.e., clockwise).

“Between” (*antareṇa*) means in the middle of the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*. They call the “sacrificial passage” (*yajñatīrtha*) the entrance for the officiating priests and others for the sake of the sacrifice. “In the absence of a *cātvāla*” (*acātvāle*) refers to sacrifices such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) which lack a *cātvāla*. The phrase “between the *āhavanīya* fire and the *utkara*” is to be supplied as a continuation [of the previous rule].

“Thence” means by that path. “The performers” refers to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). “They should proceed” means they should enter. “When completed” means when the sacrifice has concluded. “Movement” means wandering; the ellipsis is that this is not outside the *utkara* area. “Unattained” means obtained without effort. “Behind” means to the rear. “To the west of that” means to the west of that *brahman*’s station; the ellipsis is that this refers to the northern hip of the altar (*vedi*). “The *utkara*” is the location of the *āgnīdhra*; this is to be supplied as the context. “Behind the *gārhapatya* for the wife” means in the region behind the *gārhapatya* fire; here too, the word “location” is to be supplied. “In those” locations and at those times, “the initiated one,” being possessed of the vow (*vrata*), should remain. He states these very things: “Slander of others” means he should not speak anything contrary regarding another. “Impure” refers to urine and feces. “The unbound,” etc., is the mantra ending with “May she not abandon me.”
Hārīta says:

For the sake of elevating him to the state of the gods, he is consecrated by this rite; through that consecration, he attains equality with the gods, co-residence with them, and union with them. Therefore, they say that one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is indeed equal to the gods. He becomes established in the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* verses, in the worlds, in the lights, among the gods, or in Brahman. For he gratifies these [fires] every day, morning and evening; and they purify him every day, morning and evening. Day after day, with Agni as their mouth, they stand ready for his oblation, morning and evening. Therefore, even among those who know the sacrificial offerings (*havirvid*), one who has not maintained the sacred fires is more meritorious than those who have, provided he does not neglect his own duties. Consequently, one should never be a person who fails to perform the *agnihotra*.

Just as one would not eat the food of a person after having invited and appointed Brāhmaṇas for him, so too [one should not eat] what one eats before the oblation has been offered; therefore, one should eat only after the *abhijit* [moment]. One should not speak untruth, nor vulgar speech; one should not be unrestrained, nor impure; one should not go to the wives of others, nor stand with them; one should not drink water while naked, nor kindle the fire with wood that is wet or rotten while impure; one should not travel during the two times of the fire’s vigil (at dawn and dusk). On the *parvan* days and in times of distress, one who is away from home should remain silent at those times. Every day, having mentally meditated upon the *agnihotra*, and having remained standing, one should know it to have been offered by means of the mantra. Regarding the vow, one should address the couple who are present; or, when the sun has set, one should restrain speech until sunrise, or until both [the morning and evening] offerings have been made. One should offer the *agnihotra* oneself, or attend to it elsewhere. Having approached in the evening, having circumambulated and paid homage, one should depart in the same manner. In the morning, one should not blow on the fire with the breath, nor offer oblations with things unfit for sacrifice; one should give the remains of the offering to a Brāhmaṇa.

One who is grown-up, a youth, or even one who is not a child, should not offer the fire-oblation at nightfall. "Equal to the gods" means comparable to the deities. "The Agnihotra-sacrificer is seated" refers to one whose Agnihotra is performed while seated, being free from the interruption of the oblation. "Having summoned" means having appointed him; having sat down for the purpose of eating the *śrāddha* meal, one should eat that which belongs to him by oneself. In this very way, he who eats what has been offered [is said to eat the sacrifice]. "Conquered" (*abhijitam*) means preceded by an offering; "indecent" (*aślīlam*) means vulgar—one should not speak such things, this is the connection. "Unrestrained" (*aniyataḥ*) means one whose senses are not controlled. "Not entered" (*nāviṣṭaḥ*) means not having a single support. "Fire-time" (*agnivelā*) is the time for the oblation and giving. And one should not enter during the festival days (*parvan*), this is the connection. If one must travel, one may do so in times of distress according to the degree of necessity, provided one has not performed the formal rite. Then, having meditated upon the fires mentally every day, having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), and knowing the oblation has been made through the mantra, one should "vow" (*vratayet*), i.e., eat. "Having come" means having returned from the journey; having performed the attendance, one should speak. The meaning is that one should not say anything without first performing the attendance to the fires. "When set" (*nimrukte*) means when the sun has gone down. "Until sunrise" (*ā udayāt*) means until the rising of the sun. "Until the oblation" (*ā homāt*) means until the completion of the evening oblation. This restraint of speech until sunrise should be understood as applying to one who desires specific results, since it is not a general rule. "On both sides" means both in the evening and in the morning. "By himself" means by his own self. "Elsewhere" means when there is another person performing the Agnihotra oblation. "He should attend the fire himself" means he should stand nearby while meditating. He states the sequence of duties that must be performed daily: having removed [the ashes], and without performing the circumambulation, one should perform the three rites beginning with the attendance even in the morning. "Without *darbha*" means without the connection of *darbha* grass to the right hand. "With non-sacrificial items" refers to beans and the like.

Furthermore, Hārīta says: On the day of the vow (*vrata*), one should avoid black gram (*māṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), honey, meat, food belonging to others, and sexual intercourse. One should not release speech at an improper time while under the vow. During a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasatra*), one may eat new grain; during the ritual season (*ṛtu*), one may approach one's wife. One who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should not eat honey, nor milk, nor the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*). Or, one should observe the rules for the consecrated, the rules for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or the rules for the *iṣṭi* sacrifice after having performed it.

The initiated one (dīkṣita), wearing linen garments, with matted hair, a girdle, a sacred thread, and a turban, shall sit upon a black antelope skin. The initiated one must avoid releasing speech, shedding tears, rubbing [the eyes], bathing, urinating, lying down uncovered, looking [at things], being startled, brushing the teeth, and going out. When yawning or laughing, he should cover his mouth with his hand. He should not void urine, excrement, or spittle in the sun. These are the rules for the initiated.

The sacrificer should avoid anger, egoism, fear, despondency, meanness, and greed; he should worship the gods with oblations and the Brahmins with food and sacrificial fees—these are the rules for the sacrificer. He should avoid attachment to various wombs and dwellings; he should not attend to impure objects belonging to water, fire, wind, the moon, or the sun—these are the rules for the sacrifice.

One should not look at an animal being slaughtered, nor touch the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or the stakes. Thus it is fixed: a sacrifice performed by those of mixed character is corrupted; the sacrificer leaks away, encounters misfortunes, enters all wombs, or is cut off from his life-span. Therefore, one should choose officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are endowed with noble lineage, learning, good conduct, and virtuous behavior. With sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), they make his sacrifice one that milks all desires. Following the sacrifice, the sacrificer, following the sacrificer, should bestow offspring and cattle. When a sacrifice is offered with plants, animals, and *soma*, they complete it with sacrificial fees. A sacrifice struck down by fees is truly struck down. "With sacrificial fees they complete his sacrifice that milks all desires"—thus he gives the fee. By it, he sacrifices for the world of the Moon. What he gives to the *hotṛ* priest, by that he sacrifices for the world of Agni; what to the *udgātṛ*, by that for the world of Parjanya; what to the *hotrāsaṃsin* priests, by that for the quarters; what to those who perform favors, by that for this world; what to the obedient one who has studied the Vedas (*anūcāna*), by that for the heavenly world. As much land as he gives, for that many misfortunes he sacrifices away. When he gives to one who is worse, he thinks: "By this fee I redeem myself."

"The Moon is indeed Brahman; as long as the moon does not perish, so long does what is sacrificed and given by him become inexhaustible. 'O Hotṛ, I give you speech; I redeem it with this sacrificial fee'—Agni is the Hotṛ; as long as Agni does not perish, so long does what is sacrificed and given by him become inexhaustible. 'O Udgātṛ, I give you hearing; I redeem it with this sacrificial fee'—Parjanya is indeed hearing, and Parjanya is the Udgātṛ; as long as Parjanya does not perish, so long does what is sacrificed and given by him become inexhaustible. 'O Adhvaryu, I give you the eye; I redeem it with this sacrificial fee'—that fire over there is the sun, and the sun is the eye; that sun over there is the Adhvaryu; as long as that sun does not perish, so long does what is sacrificed and given by him become inexhaustible. 'O Hotrāśaṃsin priests, I give you my limbs; I redeem them with this sacrificial fee'—the quarters are indeed the Hotrāśaṃsin priests, and the quarters are the limbs; as long as the quarters do not perish, so long does what is sacrificed and given by him become inexhaustible. Now they also cite this here:
The Brahmayajña remained among the Brāhmaṇas;
therefore, the Brāhmaṇas are its purifiers.
Therefore, they are entitled to a share of the sacrifice.
In a sacrifice, a sacrificial fee should be properly given to the Brahmins.
There are three sacrifices; the third of these is the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Through the vital breaths, the sacrifice proceeds by means of the application of ritual action (*karmayoga*).
Therefore, one should indeed give a more abundant sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
A wise person, desiring the abundance of sacrifice, should give.
The Yajus indeed divided the sacrifice into its respective portions; yet they did not [attain it] through the application of ritual action alone.
Having recognized this majesty within the Yajus-texts, [they attained it]. [154]
And the wealth of the performer should be given to those who know the Yajurveda.
By means of phonemes, morae, syllables, vowels, feet, half-verses, and pauses; by means of invocations, hymns, and the application of rituals at their proper times.
But for those who are the bearers, there is indeed the gift of fortune.
Dharma is sacrifice; by those who know dharma, dharma is performed as an action for the sake of karma according to dharma.
O Brahmins, dharma protects the worlds therein.
Therefore, the wealth of dharma should be bestowed upon those who know it.
When Sūrya was destroyed by the darkness of Svarbhānu, then the worlds were not manifest, nor was there sacrifice, nor was there the sacrificial session for the sake of peace;
[to him] be homage!
Therefore, they declare that sacrifice is the wealth of the three [classes].
Friends, allies, kinsmen,
and performers bring about the sacrifice through various means; therefore, the sacrifice cannot be accomplished without assistance.
Therefore, the wise person should worship [it] in this way and not otherwise.
Through logic, through wealth, by means of pure officiating priests, and by the renunciation of jewels and sacrificial fees,
the sacrifice leads to desired worlds endowed with all objects of desire.
One should lead [the soul] to Virāj, the foundation of the world of Brahman.
Those who know the truth declare Viṣṇu to be the sacrifice here; they also say that he is the fire and the guest of the sacrifice.
Therefore, in the sacrifice, by means of various applications of substances—
Having become threefold, one should indeed satisfy the sacrificial fire.
They call him Agni, Rudra, and Time,
for these creatures are indeed his delusive manifestations;
by satisfying him alone, they become immortal.
Those who do not know him are fashioned for him like food.
For Agni is both father and mother here; Agni is brother, protector, and guardian from evil deeds.
Indeed, Agni is the giver of sons, wife, and prosperity.
And they say that fire is the deliverer from all misfortune.
By means of fire alone, the gods attained godhood; likewise, by means of fire alone, they attained all the worlds and immortality.
Having performed austerity, they attained the worlds of Agni by means of fire alone.
Having conquered [the senses], the seers proceed toward becoming Brahman.
Therefore, a hero who has heard the scriptures, who acts according to the law, who maintains the sacred fires by following the prescribed rule with devotion—
being patient, self-controlled, stainless, and free from sorrow— [attains the goal].
May he go to the worlds frequented by sages and gods.
Healthy, prosperous, glorious, fragrant, and composed of clarified butter, he may travel at all times through pleasant and gentle regions, praised by the sky-dwellers.

"Released from death, he goes to the world of Brahman. Thus [it is said]. "On the day of the vow" (*vratye*) means on the full moon day and so forth. "One who has undertaken the vow" (*vratopetaḥ*) means one who has observed the rules of speech and conduct. "At the improper time" (*akāle*) means before the time for preparing the oblation (*havir-kṛta*). "Having approached the fire" (*agnim upetya*) means having gone near the fire. "He should not turn back" (*na paryāvarteta*); turning back means turning one's back toward the fire.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bearing [the fire] with the two [verses] containing the words *vrata* and *kāma*": when he would wear a garment, then, having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with these two verses joined with the words *vrata* and *kāma*—namely, "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (*tvam agne vratapā asi*) and "To you, O best of the Aṅgirasas" (*tubhyantā aṅgirastama*)—he may dwell elsewhere.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "again" (*punar*) is as follows: one should dwell elsewhere out of fear. Having performed the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) before sunset and at the first sunrise with the two mantras, "May the mind-light rejoice" (*mano jyotir juṣatām*) and "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (*tvam agne vratapā asi*), one should perform the *darśa* and other sacrifices. Having sacrificed, one should eat only of the new grain; that is to say, one should eat the new harvest. Regarding the phrase "in long sacrificial sessions" (*dīrghasatreṣu*), this refers to sessions lasting a hundred nights and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or the remainder of the oblation consisting of milk and so forth," the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) is to be supplied as: "one should eat the remainder of the sacrifice consisting of milk, curds, and the like."

The sacrificer is both initiated and uninitiated. The release of speech occurs after the response to the question, "Release the speech of the initiated. "When the stars have risen" means when the stars have appeared. "Open sleeping" refers to sleeping outside the wife's hall (*patnīśālā*). "Amazed" means astonishment. "He should cover with his hand"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "his mouth. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Having entrusted the fire to his own wives and likewise having appointed a priest..."
A Brahmin who has business while traveling abroad should not remain away for long, even if it is for a false reason.
Even while traveling, one should perform the daily rites with the mind, remaining untiring;
being pure, one should sit down and perform everything at the proper time.

"Having entrusted" (*nikṣipya*) means having handed over for the sake of service. "[Having settled]" (*vikalayya*) means having established. "Having appointed a priest" (*parikalpyartvijam*) means for the purpose of performing the *agnihotra* and other rites, for the purpose of the milk-oblation and other duties, for the sake of wealth sufficient for the maintenance of those who must necessarily be supported, and for the sake of security. "In vain" (*mṛṣā*) means without a necessary purpose. Even for the sake of a necessary purpose, "not for long" means not exceeding the period of absence prescribed by the various *kalpa-sūtras*.

Vasiṣṭha says: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should not approach a dark-complexioned woman for pleasure. A "dark-complexioned woman" is one who exists solely for sexual enjoyment and not for dharma.

"Having piled the fire" means having performed the sacrifice involving the construction of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*). "A dark-complexioned woman" means one of the Śūdra caste; the meaning is that he should not approach even his own married wife [if she is of such a caste]. Hārīta says:
"But with material of a *tāmasa* nature, and likewise with *ṛtvij* priests who are *tāmasa*..."
Resorting to a state of darkness, it is called a sacrifice characterized by darkness.
But through sacrifice, giving, and austerity performed with a tamasic disposition, one will surely take birth in hell; thus one should recognize tamasic prosperity.
When performed with materials of a passionate nature, by priests of a passionate nature,
and by one who has adopted a passionate disposition, such a sacrifice is called *rājasa*.
Through the Rājasūya sacrifice, as well as through charity and austerity,
one obtains birth in hell or heaven, and a kingdom that is both cruel and endowed with prosperity.
But when a sacrifice is performed with pure materials, by pure officiating priests,
and while one maintains a pure disposition, it is called a sāttvika sacrifice.
But through sattvic giving, sacrifice, and likewise austerity,
there is certain residence in the world of the gods, as well as union with the gods themselves.
"Tāmasa" means black. That which is acquired through fraudulent gambling, theft, and similar acts of violence, or by means of deception, is declared to be "black."

Thus it was spoken by Nārada. Furthermore, because the officiating priests proceed with the sacrifice while affected by the defect of a *tāmasa* disposition, the *tāmasa* nature of both their gifts and austerities should be understood in the very manner just described. “*Tāmasī* prosperity” consists of such forms as sovereignty over barbarians (*mleccha*) and the like. “*Rājasa* wealth” is variegated (*śabala*). And that is declared to be *rājasa*:
“[Wealth] acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, tolls, the practice of crafts, and what is obtained from one who has received a favor is designated as *rājasa*.”

[160] Thus spoke Nārada. The cruelty of kingship consists in the harming of those who should not be harmed and so forth. "Sāttvika substance" means pure. And that is as follows: wealth acquired through learning, valor, austerity, a daughter, a disciple, or a patron—this sevenfold wealth is to be known as pure; such is the sāttvika type.
Thus it was spoken by Nārada. Manu says:
A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should not beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice.
For a Cāṇḍāla who begs for the sake of performing a sacrifice is born again after death [in that same state].
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all, goes to the state of a crane or may even attain the state of a crow.

The meaning is that one should not perform a sacrifice after having accepted wealth from a Śūdra for the purpose of performing a sacrifice. Wealth acquired even from Brāhmaṇas and others for the sake of a sacrifice must be given away entirely; if it is not given, however, one shall become a Bhāsa or a crow. A "Bhāsa" is a domestic cock. "Samāḥ" means years. [161] Hārīta:

A sacrifice performed with improper materials fails; one performed by those who are not officiating priests falters; one performed by the ignorant is fruitless. One performed with mixed elements does not achieve its purpose; one that is incomplete lacks luster; and one devoid of ritual rules is exhausted. That which is deceptive, unstable, fraudulent, and yields little fruit, or which prescribes no sacrificial fee and is untrue—these are the defects of sacrifice, by which a sacrifice, when afflicted, becomes fruitless.

“*Asaddravyam*”: acquired through improper means. “*Sravati*”: it goes to fruitlessness. “*Anṛtvijaḥ*”: those lacking the characteristics of a learned priest (*anūcāna*) and so forth. “*Avidvān*”: even the sacrificer who is ignorant of the ritual acts. “*Abhāvukaḥ*”: one who provides no protection. “*Saṃkīrṇaḥ*”: a perpetrator of the sin known as *saṃkara*. “*Asiddhārthaḥ*”: one whose purpose remains unaccomplished. “*Akṛtsnaḥ*”: incomplete, lacking the constituent parts of the sacrifice. “*Ajyotiḥ*”: devoid of splendor; that is to say, lacking power. “*Vidhihīnaḥ*”: devoid of the prescribed procedure regarding the primary and subordinate rites. “*Chadma*”: hypocrisy. “*Adhruvaḥ*”: yielding fruit for only a short time. “*Sopadhaḥ*”: performed for the sake of desired fame and the like. “*Upadiśati*”: it becomes exhausted. “*Upasṛṣṭaḥ*”: afflicted by the defects known as *upasargas*.
[162] Manu says:
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—
they too are the officiating priests of Śūdras, and are censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who perform constant sacrifices while serving the fire of a *vṛṣala*, the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
“Proponents of Brahman” means proponents of the Vedas. “Vṛṣala” means a Śūdra.
On this point, Chāgaleya says:
“He who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, should maintain the Agnihotra fire.”
The donor does not obtain the fruit, and the doer shall go to hell.
Manu says:
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the lack of even one component—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa— while a righteous king is in power;
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but lacks the means for sacrifice and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from him— whose family is in distress— for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice.
He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for a Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices.
If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—
one may take [wealth] from the households of these two without hesitation.
One may take from a non-giver who is constantly taking [from others],
provided that his sacrifice is thus extended and his merit increases.

“Pratiruddhaḥ” means undertaken, not delayed. “Ekāṅgena” means by one limb, such as the right hand or another. “Āharet” means he should take from him that substance which constitutes a part of [the gift] while it is being offered; this is the meaning. However, in the absence of a Vaiśya, two or three limbs may be taken even from a Śūdra, because of the statement: “The Vaiśvadeva [offering] belongs to the Śūdra. It should be seized by force from the house of a Śūdra; by the phrase “for there is nothing belonging to a Śūdra,” he indicates that the wealth of a Śūdra is unfit for use in sacrifice. “Ayajvā” means one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice. “Ādānanityaḥ” means one who is intent on acquiring wealth by both censurable and non-censurable means. “Adātā” means one whose habit is not to give. Since both terms—“of a non-giver” and “not giving”—are employed, a member of the three higher castes (traivarṇika) should first be requested. If, when requested, he does not give, then one should take it from him without hesitation.

Gautama says: The acceptance of property from a Śūdra is permitted for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage or in connection with religious duties (*dharma-tantra*). Furthermore, one may accept it from a Śūdra who possesses many cattle and whose ritual duties are not neglected—specifically, from one who owns a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, or from one who owns a thousand cows but does not offer the Soma sacrifice. If he has not enjoyed the seventh [generation of] wealth and his accumulation is still insufficient, he may declare this when questioned by the king; he must then be supported by him. However, if he is endowed with learning and good character, there is no fault in failing to support him during a time of distress regarding religious duties.

The appropriation of another's property that has not been given, even without permission, refers to as much wealth as is necessary so that the marriage may be accomplished; and this applies when there is a risk of the marriage being delayed, on the part of the giver of the girl. "Interruption" (*prasaṅga*) refers to the cessation of an already commenced religious duty (*dharma-tantra*), such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to draw forward the phrase "for the sake of accomplishment" (*siddhy-artham*). Here too, one should take and appropriate only that amount of wealth by which that [marriage] is accomplished, because taking more would result in the offense of theft.

From where is this to be accepted? To this he says: "from a Śūdra. If one cannot obtain it from a Śūdra, one may take it from another person of the three higher castes who will be described later. "One whose actions are not deficient" means one who is devoid of actions for invisible (transcendental) purposes that require wealth as a means. The mention of "cows" is intended to include their value as well. He states another cause for taking the property of another: "and without having eaten on the seventh day. This refers to the sequence of meals at morning and evening; it means eating only as much as necessary for sustenance until the time of the seventh meal, and not for the purpose of accumulation. Furthermore, regarding the occasion of theft, if he is seized by the king, then he "should declare" it—he should speak of it—and must not remain silent out of fear. Regarding "in the case of an affliction to his religious duties," this refers to one who suffers such an affliction to his religious duties. For one possessing these three aforementioned occasions, this applies to the primary cause.
Aṅgiras: Grain found in a threshing floor or a field, water found in a pond or a well,
and milk found in a cow-pen— these may be taken even from one whose food is otherwise unfit to be eaten.

But when the sacrificial portions have been cut off and the offerings have been cooked, one should perform the *iṣṭi* sacrifice without modification; one must not cause that which has been well-performed to be lost.

“From one whose food is not to be eaten” means from a Śūdra or similar person. And this grain and so forth should be accepted only for the purpose of completing the required quantity when there is a fear of the interruption of a sacrifice. “Unmodified” means free from modifications such as having too much food. On this point, Baudhāyana says: “If fire is placed upon impure matter or the like, one should re-establish it by churning and perform the Pavamāneṣṭi. In cases of differences regarding purification, place, mantra, substance, preparation, or time, priority belongs to the former among fires.”

The meaning is that when impure substances have been cast into that fire, one should consign it into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), perform churning, and then carry out the *Pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifice.
Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states:

"One should provide a substitute based on similarity in respect of stalks, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, shoots, juices, scents, and so forth; in the absence of all these, barley becomes the substitute."
Āpastamba:
One does not choose as a priest (*ṛtvij*) one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor one who haggles over the fee. One who is unlearned is ineligible to officiate.

He who haggles, saying, "I will cause you to sacrifice only according to this specific arrangement of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā-kalpa*)," is a haggler. An "unlearned" person is so even if he is wealthy compared to those who know the sacrifice.
On this point, Śaṅkha says:
"A wise man should not abandon a previously acquired livelihood that is pure by virtue of his occupation, birth, sacrifice, study, and [righteous conduct]."
When a Brahmin, endowed with these very same qualities, performs a sacrifice for one whose wealth has been acquired through righteous means, then a gift may be accepted from him.

The meaning is that one should not, at the very time of the initial consecration (*ādhāna*), abandon a priest who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities and so forth, and then appoint another priest for subsequent sacrifices such as the *darśa* and others belonging to the northern tradition (*udīcya*).
Thus ends [the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great domestic chaplain (*mahāsandhivigrahika*).
In the section on the householder, this is the sprout of the chapter on domestic life.
Now, the duties and occupations of the brahmins.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"This entire ordinance concerning the five sacrifices has been prescribed for you;
now hear here the ordinance concerning the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born."

Hārīta says: He should teach and study, he should officiate at sacrifices and perform sacrifices for himself; he should accept gifts and give them. A Brāhmaṇa is traditionally said to have these six duties.
Through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the like, as well as through giving and receiving gifts,
the twice-born attain the Virāj heaven, accompanied by celestial chariots.

“Virājaḥ” means shining. In the phrase “from sacrificing, studying, and so forth,” the ablative case is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*). Here, by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), both sacrificing (*yajana*) and studying (*adhyayana*) are included.
As Manu says: “Teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, sacrificing for others, likewise...”
Giving gifts and receiving them are indeed the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
[168] Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts.
“Pure” means that for accepting gifts from such a person, no specific expiation is traditionally prescribed.
Regarding the rules for livelihood, Āpastamba states:
"Inheritance, gleaning ears of grain, picking up single grains, and other things not previously claimed [are permissible]."

“Dāyādya” refers to the taking of inheritance; a “dāyāda” is one who takes (ādatte) the inheritance (dāyam), such as a son or other heir, and the act of that person’s receiving wealth is what is meant. “Aparigṛhīta” means ownerless, such as wild rice (nīvāra) and the like. Hārīta says:
They declare the householder to be of two kinds—the settled (śālīna) and the wandering (yāyāvara). The wandering householder is more meritorious and superior to the settled one.

In all undertakings, he possesses many *śālās* (halls/abodes); thus he is *śālīna*. Alternatively, he is *śālīna* because he is established (*līna*) in his own modes of livelihood (*ātma-vṛtti*) within a *śālā*. He is of two kinds: the *gṛhya-śālīna* and the *tretā-śālīna*. The *gṛhya-śālīna* is one who, having fathered a son, performs the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) after a year, or one who is devoted to service; he too is of two kinds: one whose livelihood is well-established and one whose livelihood is not well-established. Of these two, the one whose livelihood is not well-established is superior; he has been explained. A well-established livelihood consists of officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and agriculture (*kṛṣi*).

*Śālā* means houses. *Śālāvān* means possessing a bed and a comfortable seat. "One who possesses a domestic hall" (*gṛhyaśālīnaḥ*) means one who possesses a domestic hall. "One who possesses the three halls" (*tretāśālīnaḥ*) means one who possesses the hall for the three sacred fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*. "When a son has been born, they should perform the *ādhāna*"—this is the ellipsis. In the phrase "the *ādhāna* when a son is born" (*jātaputrāyādhānam*), the word *jātaputra* ends in the nominative plural; the reading with the vowel *yā* is based on the opinion of Śākalya. Or, after a year, he who is intent on service. He who is intent on service, that is, one who performs the attendance upon the domestic fire—after a year has passed, he should perform the *ādhāna*; this is the meaning. "One who has performed the *ādhāna* once and is not yet prosperous, subsisting by gleaning ears of corn and the like. "He is explained"—he too is described as one who has a prosperous livelihood, having taken a wife and performed the *ādhāna*, and so forth. "Prosperous" (*saṃpannaḥ*) means one whose livelihood is prosperous.
Furthermore, Hārīta states:
"From teaching, there arise livelihoods supported by truth (*ṛta*), livelihoods supported by nectar (*amṛta*), livelihoods in times of distress, and livelihoods in times of calamity.

'Truth' refers to gathering ears of grain (*uñcha*) or living by gleaning; 'nectar' refers to what is obtained from virtuous people without being asked for. From teaching arises the livelihood supported by pupils. Livelihood through wealth and livelihood in times of distress [are also mentioned]. Among these, the preceding ones are superior. And the phrase 'from teaching' is an illustration for livelihoods as prescribed."
Manu says:
A Brahmin should live in times of non-distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no harm at all toward living beings, or at least very little harm.
For the sake of accomplishing the mere necessities of life,
one should accumulate wealth through one's own irreproachable occupations, without causing affliction to the body.

One may live by means of the Ṛta and the Amṛta, or by the Mṛta and the Pramṛta, or even by the Satya and the Anṛta; but one must never, under any circumstances, live by the Śvavṛtti (the dog's mode of life).
Gleaning ears of grain (uñcha) and picking up single grains (śila) should be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Alms obtained by begging are *mṛta*, while agriculture is traditionally remembered as *pramṛta*.
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed subsist by it;
service is explained as the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.

“Droha” means causing pain to others, not killing, because the latter is excessively forbidden. “Yātrā” means the maintenance of life. By the word “mātra,” the taking of wealth for the sake of enjoyment is excluded. Following the recurrence of the word “from truth” (ṛtāt), Yama says: “The first four are the most excellent modes of livelihood for Brāhmaṇas.”

Gautama states, following the word "of a Brāhmaṇa": "Agriculture and trade, provided they are performed by himself, as well as usury. "Usury" refers to the lending of money for the sake of interest. Its separate mention here is intended to authorize it even when performed by oneself, because it is stated in another passage that "the profession of usury is lawful."

Hārīta says: Having established the sacred fires, one should provide for one's livelihood by means of gleaning ears of corn or picking up single grains, or by receiving what is offered unasked from virtuous people, or by officiating at sacrifices for the righteous, or by begging from the good for the sake of the gods, ancestors, and men. Paiṭhīnasi says:
Now, one who intends to practice the duties of a householder should maintain his livelihood without violating the law. Manu says:
"He may be one who possesses a granary of grain, or he may be one who possesses a jar of grain."
Or he may subsist for three days at a time, or even be one who does not store anything for the morrow.
And among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior to the preceding in terms of dharma, O best knower of the world.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the Brahmasattra.

“*Kusūladhānyakaḥ*” means one who possesses grain measured by a *koṣṭhikā* (granary). “*Kumbhī*” is a particular type of earthenware vessel. “*Tryahaihikaḥ*” means one for whom there is grain sufficient for three days’ livelihood; *aihika* refers to that which pertains to effort (*īhā*) in this world, and he is so called because his *aihika* [provision] lasts for three days. Grain that exists for tomorrow is “*svastana*” [literally, "belonging to tomorrow"]; according to the rule “*śvasastuṭ ca*,” the suffix *tuṭ* is added, and thus one who possesses such is a “*śvastanikaḥ*” (one who provides for tomorrow). One who is not a *śvastanika* is an “*aśvastanikaḥ*,” meaning one who washes [his bowl] immediately after eating.

Regarding the measure of the *kusūla* (granary) and *kumbhī* (jar): for one who takes only as much grain as is necessary to sustain his own family for one day, there is a threefold increase in the days of sustenance compared to the next day’s requirement; this is understood accordingly. It should be understood that for both the *kusūladhānyaka* and the *kumbhīdhānyaka*, there is likewise a threefold increase in the number of days for each subsequent stage. Furthermore, this adoption of specific modes of livelihood is intended for the sake of spiritual excellence (*dharmātiśaya*) and pertains only to householders in general, not specifically to the *yāyāvara*. This is because, immediately after describing the progressive superiority of these four types, the text states, "Among these, one performs six duties," which implies that the six modes of livelihood here include trade (*vāṇijya*), since there is no reason to exclude the previously mentioned modes of livelihood such as *uñcha* (gleaning).

Trade is not prescribed for a *yāyāvara* (one who wanders from place to place), whose six duties consist of gleaning (*uñcha*), living by grains (*śila*), begging (*ayācita*), and agriculture (*kṛṣi*) along with trade (*vāṇijya*). "By three" means by gleaning, living by grains, and begging; "by two" means by gleaning and living by grains; "by the *brahmasattra*" means by gleaning. The term *brahmasattra* refers to gleaning, because it constantly protects (*trāyamāṇa*) the Brahmins.
[173] Yājñavalkya and Viśvāmitra state:
"One may possess a granary (*kusūla*), a jar of grain (*kumbhīdhānya*), enough for three days, or even enough for a single day."
Or one may live by gleaning ears of grain; among these, each subsequent mode is superior.
[Hārīta]:
A *yāyāvara* is so called because he sustains his own livelihood through his virtuous conduct (*śīla*).

He is a *yāyāvara* because he travels while staying for ten nights at a time; or, he is a *yāyāvara* because he sustains himself by means of various choices (*vara*) within his own kingdom and his own means of livelihood. He is of two kinds: one who has set out (*kṛtaprasthāna*) and one who has not yet set out (*akṛtaprasthāna*).

He for whom, after having caused the shaving to be performed according to rule, they establish the directions, the ritual materials, and so forth, by means of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice with its mantras at sunrise on the eastern side, is one who has performed the departure (*kṛtaprasthāna*). Now, he for whom, after having performed the shaving according to rule, they set forth the directions, the ritual materials, and so forth, by means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice with its mantras at sunrise, is one who has not performed the departure (*akṛtaprasthāna*).

His status as a seer becomes equal to that of Brahmā; by the first [verse], he is released from sin. By the second, he attains illumination among the gods and a world equal to theirs. By the third, he achieves the state of a Brahmarṣi and comes to abide in the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, abiding in Brahman, one should not—without being invited—engage in lying down, sitting, eating, walking about, rising, giving, or bestowing gifts.

On the festival days (parvan), he should perform the piling of the fire-altar, the attendance upon the fire, and the oblation himself; or, having brought the offerings to their respective places, he should present them to the Gārhapatya fire. He should perform the bali-offerings and homas as prescribed, avoid proclaiming his own specific merits, and renounce those pursuits that obstruct dharma.

Now there are eight modes of subsistence (*vṛtti*): *uñcha*, *śila*, *ayācita*, *upapanna*, *sandarśana*, *babhru*, *skanna*, *kuddālakāpotī*. By whichever one of these modes—whether the best or the next best—he may perform the sacrifice according to his livelihood. There are five places for *uñcha*: a threshing floor, a place where grain has been pounded, a cow-pen, a granary, and salt. They say that what is reaped, what is fallen, and what is permitted is *śila*. From Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas he obtains what is not asked for; some say even from Śūdras. In times of distress, showing himself, he may take for his own sake; they cite this rule: "One who shows himself should beg."

One should plow five furrows with a leafy branch until the shoulder of the ox becomes tawny. A spade-bearer shall pay the king’s share; otherwise, there is a specific purpose for this when the means of subsistence arise. Having performed the Soma sacrifice, piled the fire-altar, and given away all one's possessions, one should join the thumb and ring finger, attach them to the neck, and take [the grain] one by one like a pigeon; some say that from what is broken, one follows a broken way of life. Having gathered [the grain] by these means of subsistence, one should act as previously described.

Having withdrawn his self through the *kṛcchra* penance for six months, he observes the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*); thus he is a "Yāyāvara. He attains the supreme Brahman, the nectar of immortality, having gone to which one is not born again here. [The word] "yāpanāt" means from contraction. "Eight" refers to the modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*) to be described, beginning with *uñcha*. On the previous day, the shaving and the *Āgneyī* sacrifice should be performed. But in the morning, when the sun has risen, by means of the *Vaiśvānarī* sacrifice, one should set out in this direction, bringing the materials—rice, barley, and so forth.
He for whom the officiating priests establish and arrange the directions, materials, and so on, is one who has completed the departure (*kṛta-prasthāna*).

But for one who has not yet set out, having had the shaving of the hair and other rites performed as before, when the sun has risen in the morning, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) direct the materials for the directions and so forth, saying: "In this direction, you must bring this substance of rice and the like. [The meaning is: he becomes radiant, shining toward the gods;
that is, the first [direction] belongs to Agni, the second to Vaiśvānara, and the third to the Viśvedevas. Thus, he becomes manifest to the gods.

The suffix *tasi* in the word *amantrataḥ* is used in the sense of the instrumental case (*amantraiḥ*). One should not perform acts such as lying down without a mantra. "Acceptance" (*upādāna*) means receiving a gift. Regarding the phrase "on the festival days" (*parvasu*), the repetition of acts such as shaving—which would otherwise be required by virtue of being an *āhitāgni*—is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

The offering at the *gārhapatya* fire is prescribed for him as soon as it becomes available. Now, regarding the specific stages of life (*āśrama*), such as that of the wandering mendicant (*yāyāvara*) and others: the statement “now there are eight modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*)” and “by one or another” is intended to prohibit the mixing of these modes. The word “*yāpayet*” means “he should pass”; the word “time” (*kālan*) is to be supplied as the object. A “cow-pen” (*go-sthāna*) is where barley and other fodder are given to the cows. A “granary” (*dhānya-karaṇa*) is a threshing floor; a “reaping-field” (*lavana*) is a field because of the etymology “that in which reaping occurs. Here, “permitted” means neglected by the owner. Regarding the phrase “showing,” when the owner is present, he should take even the neglected grain and so forth only after showing it. Regarding “for his own sake”: showing himself before the owner of the goods, he should beg for the purpose of enjoyment sufficient for his mere livelihood, and so forth; the meaning is that he does not beg by verbal request. He should have a brownish-brown shoulder-yoke carried. Regarding “with a leaf-branch” and so forth: a “leaf” (*parṇa*) is a *palāśa* tree; with its branch, he should have a shoulder-yoke of the brownish-brown color of a bull carried as far as it can be turned. He should have it carried for a measure of five finger-breadths. This refers to the ground obtained by right. Some, however, read “twenty-four furrows” (*sītā*). And this “carrying” lasts until the time of sowing seeds. Elsewhere than with a spade, or elsewhere than in the case of giving a share to the brownish-brown shoulder-yoke, there is an option. He describes the “dove-like” (*kāpotī*) mode: “from specific kinds of food” and so forth. When, through obtaining what is unasked for and so on, there is an abundance of specific foods, he should perform the *Soma* sacrifice and other rites, and then practice the aforementioned *kāpotī* mode. Having hung it around his neck, the word “vessel” (*pātra*) is to be supplied, referring to the *praveśikā* and other types.

“Some say that ‘from the distinct [there is] a distinct practice.
