When [the term] *sati* occurs, this very *kāpotī*—the taking of individual seeds from a *goṇī* (a large measure) or similar source that has been split or torn apart—is what they consider to be the “distinct-and-non-distinct practice. Therefore, here too, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), such as the taking of all one's property and so forth, is exactly the same. And because this is a specific type of *kāpotī*, its mention follows immediately after that. As before, the sequence beginning with the offering to the *gārhapatya* fire and so on applies; the phrase “one should perform *kṛcchra* penances for six months” is to be supplied. Since no specific [type of] *kṛcchra* is mentioned, they are *prājāpatya* penances. “Having withdrawn the self” refers to the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*). The verb “should perform” is to be supplied here as well. One by whom the self (*ātman*) has been withdrawn—that is, turned back—from sense objects is “one who has withdrawn the self.”
Baudhāyana says:

Now, for those who follow the dharma of householders, those who move about in chariots, and those who descend [from higher stages], who subsist by nine modes of livelihood—because they subsist by these, it is called "livelihood" (vṛtti).

Because they depend on a hall (*śālā*), they are called *śālīna*. Because they move in a circular sequence, they are called *cakracara*. Because they go by means of an excellent livelihood (*vṛtti*), they are called *yāyāvara*. We shall explain these in detail. There are nine [types of livelihood]: the six-turner (*ṣaṇṇivartanī*), the spade-method (*kauddālī*), the fixed (*dhruvā*), the washing-method (*saṃprakṣālinī*), the root-gatherer (*samūlā*), the protector (*pālinī*), the gleaner (*śiloñchā*), the pigeon-method (*kāpotī*), and the seeker of what is already prepared (*siddhecchā*). There is yet another tenth livelihood for these, which exists alongside the ninefold livelihood. And there is yet another tenth livelihood for these, which exists alongside the ninefold livelihood.

Having shaved his hair, beard, body hair, and nails, he should prepare: a black antelope skin, a water-pot, a staff, a climbing plant, and a *kutha* mat. Having performed the *traidhātavīya* sacrifice, or the *vaiśvānarī*, he shall set out. At dawn, when the sun has risen, he kindles the fire according to the Sūtra; having melted clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons and taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati in the *āhavanīya* fire, reciting: "O Lord of the Dwelling, recognize us," and following this with the verse, "O Lord of the Dwelling, with your auspicious assembly... He offers the oblation. According to some, everyone who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should do so. Then, having again heated the *sruk* and *sruva* and prepared the butter in the *sruk*, he stands at the edge of the village or at the boundary of the village. There he builds a hut or a cell, or enters one already built. Regarding the items prepared—the black antelope skin and the rest—he should employ each for the purpose for which it was intended.

The attendance upon the sacred fires is well known; the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is well known; the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice is well known; and the practice of offering oblations of harvested herbs as part of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) is observed. [He offers them] either silently or with the formula: "I offer what is pleasing to all the gods. Then he sprinkles them with water, either with the formula: "I sprinkle what is pleasing to all the gods," or silently. Having prepared them, they cook them. For him, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts cease, as do other sacrificial rites. And his food for the vow consists of sacrificial substances: namely, mixed with ghee, mixed with curd, meatless, without pungent salt, and not stale. He observes celibacy, or he may approach his wife during her season. At every change of the moon, he has his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, and follows the rules of purification.

Regarding the phrase “of those desiring the Dharma”: here, the one who wanders with a wheel (*cakracara*) is intended by the term “one desiring the Dharma,” because he desires a superior degree of Dharma even more than a *yāyāvara* (one who moves from place to place), owing to his sequential adoption of the various modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*). “He prepares” (*upakalpayate*) means he produces. A “load-bearing pole” (*vīvadha*) is a carrying-pole for burdens. A “bundle of *kuśa* grass” (*kuśahāra*) consists of an axe, a digging-stick, and so forth. Regarding the phrase “he shall set out”: when he is about to set out, he should perform the rite dedicated to Vāstoṣpati according to the prescribed procedure. “Having recited” (*anudrutya*) means having repeated [the mantra]. “It becomes as seen” (*dṛṣṭaṃ bhavati*) means it becomes just as it is seen in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). “The offering for undertaking the vow” (*vratopāyanīyam*) is that which is to be brought forward for the sake of the observance; the word “he brings” (*bahvati*) is to be supplied. “Without meat” (*apiśitam*) means excluding meat. The rule of purification is external, by means of earth, water, and so forth; the internal [purification] is by means of truth, self-restraint, and so forth.
[180] Again, Baudhāyana says:

Regarding this "six-fold plowing" (*ṣaṇnivartanī*), he performs exactly six turns of the plow without interruption. He either leaves a portion for the owner of the land or takes it with permission. Before breakfast, he should be a plowman, using two oxen whose noses are not pierced and whose testicles are intact, driving them with a goad without striking them, repeatedly encouraging them. Because one performs six turns according to this rule, it is called "six-fold plowing."

*Kauddālī* refers to one who, near a body of water, digs with a spade, a ploughshare, or a sharp piece of wood, sows seeds, and produces bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs. Because she works with a spade (*kuddāla*), she is called *kauddālī*.

Standing on the *dhruvā* brick, he wraps his head with a white cloth, saying: "For prosperity, I wrap your head. He takes up a black antelope skin, saying: "You are Brahman-splendor; for Brahman-splendor, you. He purifies [himself] with the *pavitra* blades using formulas that do not contain the word "water. He takes up a water-pot, saying: "You are strength; for strength, you. He takes up a carrying-pole, saying: "You are grain; for nourishment, you. He takes up a staff, saying: "O friend, protect me.
Then, having gone outside and muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, he mutters the consecration of the quarters.
"May Earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, and the quarters;
may Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—the deities who protect the husband—protect me.
Having recited the *mānastokīya* verse and entered the village, he shows himself at every door of the house along with his load; this is called "being seen" (*sandarśanī*).
In the absence of movement after movement, and likewise in the absence of non-movement,
that which remains constant therein is proclaimed as "the Constant" (dhruvā).

"Samprakṣālanī" means that there is no throwing away or discarding of herbs once they have grown, nor is there any hoarding; rather, having washed the vessels, one turns them upside down—thus it is "samprakṣālanī.

"Samūhā" means that in places where there is no prohibition, whether on paths, in fields, or in open spaces, wherever herbs are found, she gathers them together by means of a broom and subsists upon them—thus it is "samūhā.

"Pālanī" means "not causing harm"—this is what is expressed by this term. She desires rice grains from which the husks have been removed, or she protects seeds for virtuous people—thus it is "pālanī."

*Śiloñcha*: This refers to subsisting by means of *śila* (gleaning) at various times. It means gathering a single ear of grain (*kaṇiśa*) here and there—whether in uncultivated places, on paths, in fields, or in any unobstructed space where herbs are found—and sustaining oneself with these gleanings from time to time; thus it is called *śiloñcha*. *Kāpotī*: This refers to subsisting like a pigeon (*kapota*). It means gathering a single herb here and there with one's fingers—whether in uncultivated places, on paths, in fields, or in any unobstructed space where herbs are found—and doing so from sight alone, like a pigeon; thus it is called *kāpotī*.

"Siddhecchā" (one who desires cooked food): one who, exhausted by his modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*), due to old age or the depletion of bodily constituents (*dhātu*), desires cooked food from virtuous people is called *siddhecchā*. For him, there exists the imposition of the status of a self-realized one (*ātmasamāropaṇa*); he has the same outward appearance as a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), with the exception of the sacred grass ring (*pavitraka*) and the ochre robe (*kāṣāyavāsa*). Alternatively, "Vānyā" (one who subsists on wild grains): one who subsists by means of other things—namely trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and medicinal herbs; or by wild grains such as *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, *jartila*, and so forth—is called *vānyā*. If there is an adherence to these modes of livelihood, he "sinks down" because of them. Furthermore, they cite this example: [The verse follows...]

"Having relied upon the higher mode of life, and later having relied upon the even higher, that fool who stands in the state of a wandering mendicant would desire the status of a householder. Thus it is said.

A *nivartana* is a plot of land measuring thirty *daṇḍas* by means of a staff (*daṇḍa*) ten *hastas* long. That [land] has been thrice ploughed by one's own hand. "To the owner of the land": the suffix *ini* is used here because he possesses land, according to the rule for words such as *vrīhi*. "Before the morning meal": this is an *avyayībhāva* compound; the meaning is that one should plough before eating during the day. "Masti" (is it "mastināma"?). "With testicles" (*samuṣkaḥ*): meaning with the scrotum. "Causing to rise" (*abhyucchandayan*): meaning causing to rest. "He does" (*karoti*): he prepares or cultivates. "When it has passed" (*vṛtte*): when the time has elapsed. "In each turn" (*avārtāyām avārāyam*): this repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended to show continuity. "Storing" (*prakṣepaṇam*): the depositing of grain and so forth in a granary or similar place. The meaning is that holding [the produce] in the hands of another may also be done in another manner. "In places where there is unobstructed access" (*apratihatāvakāśeṣu*): because they are taken simply by sight, as their movement is unrestricted. "The depositing of that" (*tasya samāropaṇam*): for one who subsists on gleaned grain once the crop is harvested, it becomes the internal depositing (*samāropaṇa*) of the sacred fires within oneself.
Manu says:
"Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭis prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices."
One should never follow worldly ways for the sake of a livelihood;
rather, one should live the pure, straightforward, and honest life of a Brahmin.
One who seeks happiness should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering.

“*Pārvāyanāntīyāḥ*”: the state of being both a *parvan* and the end of an *ayana*; having formed [the compound] as *stārkikarmaṇaṃ*, the suffix *cha* (or *añ*) should be applied according to the rule for words ending in a long vowel (*vṛddha*). “*Lokavṛttaṃ*” refers to the praise of wealthy patrons and the like. “*Ajihmām*” means free from crookedness. “*Aśaṭhām*” means devoid of pride and similar vices. “*Śuddhāṃ vṛttim*” means a livelihood free from impurity or confusion. “*Jīvet*” means he should maintain the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa. [184] 9
Now, regarding conduct in times of distress,
Manu says:
A Brahmin seeking a livelihood may gather grains by gleaning or picking them from anywhere at all.
Accepting gifts is inferior to gleaning ears of grain; even more than that, gleaning is praised.

In the absence of his primary means of livelihood, he may gather grains by gleaning and picking even from a person of lower status, but he should not accept gifts; for gleaning and picking are more commendable than accepting gifts. In the absence of those two, he may take even from a gift. Manu says:
"One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the well-performed duty of another."
For one who lives by the dharma of another falls immediately from his caste.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: For him, his own duty alone is better, even if performed in small measure, than that which is practiced out of inferiority. A Brāhmaṇa who serves the base would be reborn among the base. Therefore, one whose conduct follows the praised tradition may accept gifts from anyone; yet he should not seek personal satisfaction from them. He may perform the priestly office for the three other castes at will. Having obtained his livelihood from them in accordance with dharma, he should apply it toward religious duties.

“Of him” means of that Brāhmaṇa. “His own duty” (*svadharma*) refers to the means of his own livelihood. “Even if it be small” means even if performed in any manner whatsoever. “An inferior person” (*avara*) refers to a Kṣatriya or others. One who practices the convention (*samaya*), that is, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), of those who are praiseworthy and disciplined is called “one who follows the practice of praiseworthy conventions. “From all” means he may accept [gifts] even from a Śūdra or others. “Thereby,” that is, by accepting gifts from a Śūdra and so forth. “Satisfaction” (*tṛpti*) refers to a lower form of enjoyment. “In accordance with dharma” means according to the scriptures. Regarding this alternative course (*apatkalpa*), Gautama states, with the phrase “of a Brāhmaṇa” being understood as a carry-over.

Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are permitted for all [classes]. Each preceding one is more weighty than the following. In the absence of that, one may follow the occupation of a Kṣatriya; in its absence, the occupation of a Vaiśya.

[186] "For all" means even for those who are not recommended. "Weightier" means more prone to fault. As for the statement of Manu, "Receiving gifts is the lowest," which is a censure of receiving gifts, that is with reference to the highly recommended practice of sacrificing for others.
— Vasiṣṭha.

Or rather, they may themselves cultivate sesame seeds and sell them; for it is well known that officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice is permissible once one is free from debt. Furthermore, they cite this:
"The best of the twice-born blaze like fires through their recitations and burnt offerings, but they are extinguished by the acceptance of gifts, just as fires are quenched by water."
“By acceptance”—the remainder [of the sentence] being “by that which is forbidden. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
“In times of distress, for a Brāhmaṇa who has parents and many dependents, subsistence from those living in the immediate neighborhood is an alternative means of livelihood.”

[187] Where, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa whose parents are endowed with good conduct and virtues, there is a weakness in his means of livelihood, he should report it. Whatever they may say, that shall be his duty (*dharma*). In the case of a Kṣatriya, there is an "exclusive adherence" (*abhiniveśa*) to the three occupations of a Brāhmaṇa—namely, officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts—provided he turns away from them. Even if he cannot subsist in this way, he should live by the occupation of a Vaiśya.
"Alternative" (*vikalpa*) means deliberation. "Exclusive adherence to the Kṣatriya [duty]" means being fixed in the occupation of a Kṣatriya.

Immediately after [practicing] *śiloñcha* and so forth, the wise man [should subsist]; in the absence of that, by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or the occupation of a Vaiśya. In a time of distress (*āpad-kalpa*), he may accept gifts from those who are not virtuous (*asādhu*). He should not perform actions that cause a confusion of livelihoods (*vṛtti-saṃkara*), but rather [perform those that cause] a confusion of castes (*varṇa-saṃkara*) for the sake of purifying his lineage. "In a time of distress" means when the occupation of a Vaiśya is impossible. Here, "not virtuous" refers to one whose acceptance of gifts is inferior compared to agriculture and other such means. The statement that "one's own duty, even if defective, is better" (*śreyān svadharmaḥ*)—which asserts the superiority of accepting gifts and so forth—refers specifically to the acceptance of gifts from Śūdras and others.
Regarding the continuation of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, Baudhāyana says:

"In the event of inability to do so, he may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because that is the next closest [duty]. Gautama says: "No; even for the sake of laughter, a Brāhmaṇa should not take up arms. For the duty of a Kṣatriya is exceedingly fierce for a Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
For the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or to prevent the intermixture of castes,
a Brahmin and a Vaiśya may take up arms out of regard for dharma.

The livelihood of a Vaiśya should be followed; however, it should be understood that this is apart from the wielding of weapons according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because for a Brāhmaṇa, the wielding of weapons is prescribed solely for the sake of dharma. Yājñavalkya states:
"In times of distress, a twice-born man may subsist by the dharma of a Kṣatriya or even by that of a Vaiśya."
Having crossed over the goal and renounced it, one should purify oneself on the path.
“Having overcome the calamity”—this is the connection with the consequence of transformation.
Nārada says:
"In times of distress, the next [lower] mode of livelihood is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa."
Therefore, the livelihood of a Vaiśya has been declared; it is never inferior.
A Brāhmaṇa should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brāhmaṇa; for those two acts lead to their downfall.
[189] For those two, there exists neither superior nor inferior karma;
for, having abandoned middling karma, they are indeed common to all.
Having crossed over his distress, a Brāhmaṇa, when wealth has been acquired through the occupation of a Kṣatriya,
should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation after performing a purificatory rite for himself.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, out of passion, delights in that very mode of life— he is fallen from the path, a mere bowman (kāṇḍapṛṣṭha), and is proclaimed unfit to sit in the row for a meal.
Baudhāyana says that a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*— the lowest of Brahmins—
should personally engage in usury, agriculture, and trade.
In times of distress, a twice-born man who acts otherwise incurs sin.
Having attained his desire, he should also honor the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins;
when they are satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify that fault for him.
A merchant or a moneylender should give clothing, cattle, gold, and so forth;
a farmer should give food, drink, vehicles, beds, and seats.
Having given a twentieth part to merchants for a hundredfold [return] on cattle, gold, and so forth,
a merchant shall be free from the fault of usury when feeding Brāhmaṇas.
In the Mahābhārata: "From coarse food and pungent seasoning, from soft and unctuous meals,
and from not being a servant to others— he who desires more than this goes downward."
In all these statements, it should be understood that the Brāhmaṇa may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya in times of distress.
Now, regarding agriculture,
Manu says:
"A Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya, though living by the occupation of a Vaiśya..."
One should diligently avoid agriculture, which is dependent on others and consists primarily of violence.
People consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.
And this agriculture is to be regarded as censurable only when other occupations for a Vaiśya are impossible. Baudhāyana says:
"Agriculture leads to the destruction of the Veda; the Veda is the destroyer of agriculture."
One who has the capacity should perform both; however, one who lacks the capacity should abandon agriculture.

Hārīta says: A plough with its yoke-pole is not found among Brahmins. If, in times of distress, one should act according to established custom, one should do so according to the purpose. "According to the purpose" means without exceeding that amount by which the distress is overcome.

Baudhāyana says that one should be a plowman before the morning meal, with his nostrils unsewn and his testicles intact, not piercing [the ground] with a wooden pin, but repeatedly encouraging himself. Pārthasārathi says:

"One should plow a field with two bulls that have their testicles intact during the summer heat; and one who gives [land], he should sow sesame seeds"—thus is the *lāṅgala* known as the "enemy-creeper. *Parīraḥ* means its end. *Suśevam* means having a beautiful nose; Soma obtains the outer part, thus it is called *somapitsaru*. He plows that up, or he obtains a cow (or a goat). Therefore, "he plows" and "he should sow sesame seeds" is a statement for the sake of food. "The enemy-creeper is the plow," and so forth, is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Plowing is indeed that [means of livelihood] which arises from agriculture, [as opposed to] sacrificing for those for whom it is forbidden or accepting gifts from such persons.
Vasiṣṭha:

Therefore, one should plow before breakfast with two oxen that have testicles, are not gelded, and are not worn out. In the summer, he should offer water. He should employ the plow, which is sharp-edged (*pavīravat*), very pleasant (*suśeva*), and has a handle for Soma-gathering (*somapitsaru*). It digs up cattle, sheep, goats, horses, mules, donkeys, and camels, as well as the fat, beautiful, and excellent young woman. "The plow, the chariot-bearer, with its pole. The plow is sharp-edged (*pavīra*); it is possessed of heroes (*vīravat*), possessed of good men, and possessed of oxen. It is very pleasant (*suśeva*) because its nose is auspicious; indeed, its nose is auspicious, for by means of its nose it digs up and casts away [the earth] from afar. Its handle is for Soma-gathering (*somapitsaru*), for Soma reaches its handle. It digs up cattle, sheep, goats, horses, mules, donkeys, and camels, as well as the fat, beautiful, and excellent young woman—lovely to behold and the first among the young.

*Parīraṃ* is *phālaḥ* (the plowshare); likewise, the plow (*lāṅgala*) is *pariḥ* (the surrounding part), for the author of the *Nirukta* says: "That which purifies the earth is thus *parīrava*. To illustrate the meaning of *parīravat*, Vasiṣṭha says: "like a man, like an ox. *Suśevam* means "having a beautiful face. *Nāsikā* is the tip of the plow. *Apavidhyati* means "he casts away pride" or "he eradicates it. *Somapī* means "one who attains *soma*"; this is formed with the suffix *ṇini*. The elision of the vowel *ā* of the root is a Vedic anomaly. *Soma* refers to barley and the like, according to the *Śatapatha-śruti*: "Food, indeed, is *soma*. *Tsaruḥ* is the place where the animal is harnessed. *Tad udvapati* means "he produces that [growth]. *Prapharvyām* means "possessing excellent joints"; the change of letters here is a Vedic anomaly.
Hārīta says:

In times of distress, they say that agriculture is the means of subsistence. One who practices agriculture should do so as if for a long-term investment; having yoked the oxen, he should avoid using children, the elderly, the emaciated, the afflicted, and others. He should drive them slowly with a short goad. He must not strike them with sticks, fists, clods of earth, elbows, knees, or halters, nor should he harass them by running alongside or shouting at them. He should not drive them on festival days (*parvan*) or during the periods of twilight. If they have been yoked for two ploughs, they should be released after being unyoked and groomed. Like gentle beings, one should provide them with drink, food, and other necessities in the shade. One should protect them from worms, insects, *kilītaka* beetles, gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, and predatory animals; and from cold winds, heat, and rain by providing shelter, removing them from danger, scratching their ears, using smoke and fire, and keeping them in windless, well-covered, and well-strewn enclosures. For those that are exhausted, injured, stuck, or afflicted, one should provide medicine, fodder, salt, oil, and other such things as required. One should perform the rites of offering oblations (*bali*), fire-sacrifices (*homa*), and so forth, during the fanning, cutting, threshing, winnowing, and excessive winnowing of the grain.

Devala says: "Having bathed and having adorned a bull, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, thinking, 'This is the merit of the descendants of Surabhi. Having given a sixth part to the king and a fifth part to the Brāhmaṇas, one should satisfy them.
Furthermore, they cite this here:
This sacrificial post has been set up here in the midst of the fields by the ploughing farmers;
therefore, one should unweariedly give gifts of food, grain, wealth, and dakṣiṇā.
Having broken the earth, cut down plants, and killed insects and ants, farmers purify themselves by means of the *khalayajña*; of this there is no doubt.

[195] “*Āyojya-vat*” means like that which is prescribed for the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) and in the domestic rites (*gṛhya*). “*Aratni*” is a cubit, a hand with the fingers extended. “*Drāvaṇam*” means driving away. “*Dvihala-kṛte*” means for the purpose of plowing again. “*Pariyoga*” is the yoking of the plow; the meaning is that one should also do so at the beginning of the furrows. “*Avamṛjya*” means having removed dust, mud, and the like with the hands or other means. “*Mṛduvat*” means without being angry. “*Kilītaka*” refers to a specific kind of blood-sucking insect found on the udders and other parts of cows and other animals. “*Nivṛttayaḥ*” are *camara* flies. “*Sṛmarāḥ*” are small flies that move in swarms. In the event of such afflictions from worms, insects, and the like, one should protect them by removing them as appropriate. “*Sannaḥ*” means exhausted or dejected. “*Vilagnaḥ*” means stuck or submerged in mud and the like. “*Yathārtham*” means one should feed these distressed animals with medicinal herbs, fodder, and so forth. “*Pavanam*” means the removal of fatigue. “*Atihāraḥ*” means bringing [the cattle] from the threshing floor to the house. “*Saurabheyāṇāṃ puṇyam*” means one should feed the Brahmins with the thought, “May there be prosperity for the descendants of Surabhi.”
Bṛhaspati says: Having given a sixth part to the king, a twentieth to the deities,
and a thirtieth to the Brahmins, one incurs no fault by practicing agriculture.
Hārīta says: A plough for dharma shall have eight oxen; for those seeking a livelihood, six oxen;
for the cruel, four oxen; and for those who have slain a Brahmin, two oxen.
Likewise,
the training and riding of young horses is not recommended,
nor that of those who are old or weak; such is the word of Prajāpati.
Devala says:
One should not cause emasculation to be inflicted upon a man, nor upon draft animals.
One should not yoke an old animal, nor one that is exhausted, nor one that is diseased, even if it be a pair.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Kaśyapa, and likewise Surabhī;
Indra, Pracetas, Parjanya, Śeṣa, Candra, Arka, and Vahni.
Baladeva is the plow, the earth is the two bulls—Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
Jānakī Sītā is the two oxen, and their movement is the journey itself.
These twenty-two auspicious lords of creatures have been proclaimed;
cows should be worshipped during auspicious rites, at the commencement of agriculture, and on great festivals.
[197] With water for honor, flowers, incense, garlands, and various jewels,
according to the prescribed ritual, accompanied by ritual fees, fire offerings, and the gratification of Brahmins.
Then, accompanied by the abundant sound of musical instruments played by birds,
he himself, having bathed and being well-adorned, should plough the ground with a plough.
One should proceed toward the auspicious northeastern direction, the quarter of Indra, moving by degrees;
then, having performed a circumambulation to the right, one faces the north.
Having released the two bulls and the seed, the man— endowed with auspicious marks,
joyful, well-clothed, and wearing a garland— should sprinkle it with water from a golden vessel.
Facing the east, one should place [the vessel] upon the ground together with a golden bowl;
having sown the seed right there, it should be eaten together with one's kinsmen.
And a festival should indeed be celebrated, filled with the sounds of singing and instrumental music.
Likewise: One should not drive a barren cow, nor should one oppress a milch-cow with a heavy load;
bulls should never be put to work anywhere during the cold season.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "He who, having looked well at the back and the shoulder region of a bull, makes it carry a heavy load, shall indeed carry a hundred loads."
In the Rāmāyaṇa: "He who, fearless of sin, drives a weak, exhausted,
and foolish ox, shall become a killer of cows and incur evil."
He who shall drive a hundred-strong, powerful bull,
provided with fodder and offerings, shall incur no sin.
In this regard, it should be understood that in all statements concerning the occupations of Vaiśyas during times of distress, the authority belongs to the Brāhmaṇas.
Alternatively, regarding trade in that regard, Manu says:
"But this [trade] results in a deficiency of dharma for one who abandons skill in dharma."
The merchandise of a commoner, from which the set-aside portion has been removed, may be sold to increase one's livelihood.
One should exclude all liquids, cooked food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, livestock, and human beings.
And all woven cloth, whether dyed or not dyed— such as that made of hemp,
linen, or wool— as well as fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs [are pure].
Water, weapons, poison, meat, soma, and all types of perfumes; all wild animals, fanged creatures, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals—[200].
Tin, lead, iron, and all other metallic substances;
as well as hair, skin, bones, fat, sinews, and gallstone.

“Viṭpaṇyaṃ” means the merchandise of the Vaiśyas. “Uddhṛtoddhāraṃ”: that which is extracted is the *uddhāra* (extract); this refers to meat and the like, which have been removed. “Rasāḥ” here refers to substances primarily consisting of the six tastes, such as sweetness and so forth. “Apoheta” means one should abandon. “Kṛtānnaṃ” means cooked food. “Aśmānaḥ” means stones, such as rubies (*padmarāga*) and others. Since the prohibition of salt and other substances is already established by their being [included under] “tastes,” their repeated prohibition is for the purpose of making known the gravity of the fault. “Snāvāni” means tendons. Yājñavalkya says: “Fruits, stones, linen, *soma*, humans, cakes, and climbing plants...”
Sesame-water, rice-gruel, juice, alkali, curd, milk, ghee, and water.
Weapons, fermented liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, stone, and sacrificial grass;
earth, leather, flowers, blankets made of goat hair, hair, buttermilk, poison, and land.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals,
lead, vegetables, medicinal herbs, oil-cakes, livestock, and likewise perfumes;
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, he must never sell "creepers," such as *guḍūcī* and others; "alkalines," such as *yavakṣāra* and others;
nor safflower, coconut, eggplant, or *pūtika*.
Soma, the Śleṣmātaka tree, sacrifice, water, and righteousness are all [efficacious] in every respect.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Even so, if he cannot subsist [by the prescribed means], he may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya; therein, having set aside the materials for the Saṃvatsara-sattras, he should acquire wealth with the remainder. This is excepting flowers, juices, perfumes, wine, meat, boiled rice, sesame, vegetables, curd, milk, soma, water, honey, indigo, silk, vessels, foodstuffs, raw jute, iron, stone, blankets, weapons, poison, humans, linen, black antelope skins, single-hoofed animals, and the like.

Regarding the phrase "of the year-long sacrificial sessions" (*saṃvatsarasatrāṇām*), having set aside wealth for the purpose of performing the duties that must necessarily be fulfilled throughout the course of a year, one should engage in trade with the "remainder. [202] This is stated by Gautama in his discourse following the section on Brāhmaṇas.

His forbidden merchandise consists of perfumes, liquids, prepared foods, sesame, meat, linen, skins, dyed garments, washed clothes, milk and its derivatives, roots, fruits, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and unwholesome items; as well as animals when associated with slaughter, and always bulls, heifers, young cows, barren cows, and milch-cows or oxen—so say some. Regarding "unwholesome," this refers to poison and the like. A "vaśā" is a barren cow. A "kumārī" is a cow of very young age. A "vehat" is a cow that destroys her own offspring.
This follows from the recurring term "forbidden merchandise"; thus says Vasiṣṭha.
Among domestic animals, those with solid single hooves are forbidden; likewise all wild animals, those with manes, and fanged creatures.

[203] Āpastamba says: Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. If he should engage in commerce, he must exclude articles that are unfit for sale: human beings, liquids, elephants, perfumes, food, skins, a cow that has recently calved, phlegm, water, young sprouts, fermenting grain, long pepper and black pepper, grain, meat, weapons, and the hope of merit. He should especially not sell sesame and rice among grains.

"Excluding those things among commodities that are not for sale": this means excluding from commodities such as rice and the like those items which are not fit for sale. "Śeṣma" is the resin of a tree used as a means for joining leather and other materials. "Tokma" is a seed that has slightly sprouted. "Kiṇva" is the substance used as the cause for the production of liquor. "Sukṛtā" means well-prepared; the meaning is that sesame seeds and rice grains [are forbidden] in the midst of grain. Paiṭhīnasi states: "Learning, charitable works, sacrifices, cows, conch shells, and wool—these are not to be sold."
Having begun with the statement that "these things are not to be sold by a Brāhmaṇa," Uśanas lists:
"silk, poison, husks, *kutapa*, water, soma, perfumes, linen, dyed cloth, silk (*kauśeya*), skins, woolen blankets (*kambala*), and so forth.
[204] Here, "*kutapa*" refers to a Nepalese woolen blanket.

Baudhāyana says: "He who sells sesame seeds sells the ancestors; he who sells rice grains sells his vital breaths; and he who, while bargaining, gives away his daughter sells his shares of merit. Regarding the prohibition of sale, Vasiṣṭha, Manu, Paiṭhīnasi, and Baudhāyana state in their verses that among grains, sesame seeds [are not to be sold].
They say:
"Moreover, they cite this:
'Whatever else one does with sesame seeds other than eating, anointing, or giving them away...'"
Having become a worm in excrement, he sinks down along with his ancestors.
Yama says: [Theft] of juices, perfumes, sesame seeds, lac, salt, clarified butter,
land, fire, milk, goats, sheep, oil, horses, water, and clothing;
One who sells meat, black antelope skins, or all kinds of merchandise; and one who sells oily substances, liquids, and even living beings.
The wise declare that one who speaks of the merit of giving is a killer of an embryo;
even he who speaks of the merit of giving under oath is a seller thereof.
And of all the elements of tin, lead, and iron; as well as of diamond, mother-of-pearl, coral, gems, and gold.
And the maker of a counterfeit is also called a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*).

"Oily substance" refers to sesame seeds and the like. "Of beings" means of living creatures. "In an oath" means in the making of a vow. The syntactical connection is that he is one who speaks of the merits of giving. [This is stated] in the *Mahābhārata*.
For in this world, the wise censure the sale of Soma;
O dear one, they condemn both those people who purchase it and those who sell it.
Having reached the realm of Vaivasvata, they go entirely to the Raurava hell.
Chāgaleya said:
One should not sell the Vedas, nor indeed should one sell the sacred fires.
For those men who sell the Dharma, that very hell arises for them.
Therefore, there is no sale of the Veda, nor likewise of the Agnihotra;
rather, there is its proclamation, its study, and its acceptance preceded by inquiry.
[206] Conducting sacrifices for others, teaching, and debate constitute the sixfold sale of the Veda.
Regarding this, Vyāsa also states in the following verse:

"The term *agnihotra* here refers to the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*). Furthermore, "conducting sacrifices" and "teaching" here refer to those performed for a fee, and "debate" here refers to that conducted for a wager.

In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*: "O Lord of Birds, wealth produced from the sale of the Vedas, that which is earned by a woman, and that which is obtained from a drunkard, should not be given to the ancestors or the gods."
He who, through persistent entreaty, gives a gift to a Brahmin goes first to hell, and the Brahmin follows immediately after.
As many syllables as are employed for the sake of [extracting] meaning from the Veda,
so many instances of killing an embryo does the seller of the Veda incur.
Yama says:
"But one who sells cows shall become a worm in a cow-pen for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on those cows."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should not sell items that must not be sold—namely, sesame, curd, honey, salt, lac, liquor, meat, cooked food, women, men, elephants, horses, cows, bulls, perfumes, liquids, linen, black antelope skins, soma, water, and indigo. By selling these, a Brāhmaṇa falls from his status immediately.
[207] "Nīla" refers to a garment of blue color.
Hārīta as well, and Manu, Vasiṣṭha, and Śātātapa in their verses, state:
"One must never be a seller of what is not to be sold.
Thus he says.
One falls immediately from one's caste by selling meat, lac, or salt.
Manu says:
"By intentionally selling other goods that are forbidden for sale in this world..."
A Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
"Of others" means other than lac, salt, meat, and milk. "He incurs" means he attains [the sin]. Hārīta says:
"But he who, having gathered his provisions, awaits a famine..."
One who gives inferior value and honor is indeed declared to be a thorn of famine.
But he who, through pride in his low and mixed lineage, takes away the impurity [of others],
is called by the wise "the remover of the impurity of living beings," for he himself is that very impurity.

“*Hīnārghamānadāthā*” means taking a high price with a low measure; that is, selling after having taken [the goods] at a low value. “*Durbhikṣakaṇṭakaḥ*” means a thorn or enemy to people during a famine. “*Hīnasaṅkaramānaiḥ*” means by a low or small [measure], by “*saṅkara*” (mixing) with inferior substances, and by “*māna*” (measure), which is a qualification based on the smallness of the substance to be measured. He who steals through these means—[stealing] what is impure or dirty because it is a cause of sin—is [described as such].
Now, Vasiṣṭha, having stated the mantra that establishes the plow as the cause for [obtaining] cattle and so forth:
For how indeed could one turn up the plowshare except for the sale of grain?
"Turn up" means he would produce [cattle and so forth]; this is the implied meaning. — Manu.
Having personally undertaken agriculture and produced [the crop],
the farmer may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long.
"Recently stored" means not kept for a long time, so as not to exceed the proper value. "For the sake of dharma" means for the accomplishment of necessary rites that must be performed with wealth;

likewise, when one is unable [to afford it], for the sake of medicine, and similarly for the purpose of sacrifice—if sesame seeds must necessarily be sold, they may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
Thus, from the words of Nārada:
"Likewise, flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors."
Cooked food may be exchanged for uncooked food, and sesame seeds are equal in value to grain.

“Prepared food” (*kṛtānna*) refers to cooked rice, barley meal, and so forth; “unprepared food” (*akṛtānna*) refers to raw rice and the like. “They are to be bartered” (*nimātavyāḥ*) means they are to be exchanged. Gautama states:

“The exchange of flavors for flavors, and of animals, as well as of salt, prepared food, and sesame seeds, is permitted; however, for the purpose of immediate need, cooked food may be exchanged for uncooked food of equal value.”

"And of animals" means by means of animals. "In the sense of immediate time" refers to the use of raw grain at that very moment; for a counter-exception is made specifically against one for whom the sale of cooked food is forbidden.
Sesame seeds do not turn into oil, nor do cows turn into milk. Their juice is not for sale; as are cows, so are sesame seeds.
[210] Hārīta says: However, the sale of liquids and the like is not at all blameworthy, nor is that of sacrificial fees for the sake of a sacrifice; such is the word of Prajāpati.
There is no fault in the exchange of liquids and other such items. The meaning is that even the sale of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of a sacrifice is not blameworthy.

Vasiṣṭha states: "Liquids may be bartered for liquids, whether they are equal or inferior in value, but salt must never be exchanged for liquids. Sesame, rice, cooked food, knowledge, and human beings are also permitted to be exchanged."

The suffix *tasi* is used here after the third-case ending of the words *samataḥ* (from equality) or *hīnataḥ* (from inferiority). Thus, the meaning is that flavors may be exchanged for those that are equal or inferior, but one must not take more than what is given. Regarding the exchange of sesame for rice, Āpastamba states: "A mutual restriction has been prescribed among these: food for food, humans for humans, flavors for flavors, fragrances for fragrances, and knowledge for knowledge. One should conduct transactions with goods that are not purchased for sale. One should not rely excessively on unprocessed grasses and wood such as *muñja* and *balvaja*; having obtained a livelihood there, one should desist."

“With goods not purchased for sale” means those obtained by means other than buying. Although *muñja* and *balvaja* are already included under the term “grass,” they are mentioned specifically here to permit their sale. “He may apply himself” means he may become attached [to that livelihood]. “Livelihood” refers to the primary one—this is the ellipsis.
Baudhāyana says: “Unprocessed grass and wood may be sold. Furthermore, they cite this:

"One-tusked animals, stone other than salt, and yarn that has not been dyed—these are items that a Brāhmaṇa may not sell. Here, "stone" refers to rocks; "other than salt" means anything besides salt. This sale of stone should be understood as permissible only in extreme distress, because other Smṛti texts prohibit such sales altogether. "Not dyed" means not colored with safflower or similar dyes.
Nārada says: However, for a Brāhmaṇa, the following may be sold: fine wood, grasses, perfumes, and *erakā* grass, with the exception of heavy wood, cotton, and *kuśa* grass. [212]
A split bamboo stalk that has naturally withered, fruits of the jujube or the *iṅguda* tree,
and a rope made of cotton thread, provided that it remains unaltered.

“Erakā” is a specific kind of grass; “tūla” is [the fiber] of the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*) and so forth; “vidala” is bark. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One should collect materials from pure wood, jujube (*badara*), *iṅguda*, *bilva*, cotton, and unprocessed threads.”
Hārīta:
If one cannot subsist on the aforementioned occupations, one may sell dry wood and grass, or one may tend cattle.
Śaṅkha and Likhita: [same as above].

A Brahmin who has fallen into distress and desires to live may, by resorting to a livelihood that is one step removed [from his own], say "This is for sale, this is for sale. He should desire the price only once.
Now, regarding the tending of cattle:

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should guard the cows. While they are drinking, one should not drink; while they are standing, one should not sit down. One should not drive them up by oneself, but should gently strike them on the back with a moist branch. One should not lead them down to a watering place that is difficult of access, uneven, or has little water. One should attend to those that are young, old, diseased, or afflicted, remaining calm. And one should provide medical treatment according to one's ability. This is the specific duty (*dharma*) regarding cows; otherwise, there is ruin. "One should attend" means one should care for them. This duty applies specifically to cows, not to goats and other animals.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, having treated the earth with contempt out of delusion, a man is cast into the Avīci hell;
pierced by the breaths of the cows, he is consumed by the fire of hell."
Therefore, one should quickly lead the way with the bark of milk-exuding trees, speaking these words: "O illustrious Mother, please come; the calf calls for you."
Even any ordinary man who is slain in battle for the sake of cows and Brahmins goes to the state of Śaṅkara; how much more so, then, those such as Brahmins themselves?
Now, regarding indolence:

In these statements, it should be understood that the authority refers to a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress. Regarding this, Nārada says: "A Vaiśya may indeed overcome his distress through the practice of usury at will;
however, even in the most dire calamities, there is no usury for Brāhmaṇas."
Vasiṣṭha and Paiṭhīnasi state in a verse:
"A Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya shall not pay usury. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who, having taken goods at a low price, gives them back at a high price..."
He is indeed called a usurer, and is censured among those who discourse on Brahman.
Having extracted a loan by means of another portion and having taken it;
and likewise Baudhāyana says:
"He who, having extracted wealth at a low price, gives it back at a high price."
He who bestows that which is of excellent color and great value.
Yama says:
He who takes goods at a low price and gives them back at a high price is indeed called a usurer,
as are those who lend on interest.

“Fair price” (*samargham*) here refers to the price that is permitted for ordinary trade; “high price” (*mahārgham*) refers to a price exceeding that which is permitted by the scriptures. This is because trade is permitted for a Brāhmaṇa only in times of distress. The phrase “they lend food at interest” is the ellipsis to be supplied. Bṛhaspati says:
“When enjoyment [of the debt] exceeds double [the principal], and when compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) is accepted...”
Afterwards, the interest on the principal is also to be paid; that usury is censured.

“Bhoga” (usufruct) is the taking of interest exceeding the doubled principal. “Cakravṛddhi” (compound interest) is interest upon interest itself. “Sodayam” (with interest) means more than the amount fixed as the value to be received. Nārada says:
“The interest that is declared for grains is called usury.”
Paiṭhīnasi says: One should avoid usury. Moreover, they cite this:
A usurer and a killer of an embryo, when placed upon a scale, [the former outweighs the latter].
"The killer of an embryo stood upon the tip [of the scale], while the usurer balanced with it.
Thus [it is said]. The usurer has been mentioned previously;
after the discussion on great interest (*bṛhadvṛddhi*), Hārīta says:
He placed the killer of a Brahmin and the usurer upon a scale;
the killer of a Brahmin ascended onto the ten-million-fold weight, while the usurer remained unweighed.
Chāgaleya said:
A Brahmin should not practice usury; it is worse than the killing of an embryo.
For he once weighed the killing of an embryo and usury together upon a scale, and they were found to be equal.
There is no sin for those who kill a fetus, no sin for the husband of a low-caste woman,
no sin for those who set fire [to the forest], and no sin for one who harms his teacher.
Manu weighed the growth of all sins against the killing of a fetus [and found them equal].
A Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should never employ interest.
However, for the sake of pleasure, virtue, or wealth, one may give even a small amount to a wicked person.

“Vṛddhim” means censurable interest. “Dharmārtham” means for the sake of a necessary obligation. “Pāpīyase” means to one of low birth. “Alpakam” means as much of the increase of wealth as is required to accomplish the necessary task. Regarding the application to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, Vasiṣṭha states: “Or they may, at their will, give [interest] to one of low birth who has failed in his duties.”
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Some say one may give ten [paṇas] at will to a debtor who is worse off; however, one should not take interest that is higher, nor indeed that which is lower.

The meaning is that one should give ten paṇas for each person who is worse off. One should understand that 'lower' or 'higher' refers to the interest in comparison to the rate prescribed by the scriptures."
Vasiṣṭha says:
Listen to the rate of interest proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha for a moneylender:
five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; thus the law is not violated.

A five-māṣa interest is to be taken on twenty kārṣāpaṇas; for it is stated in the words of Nārada: "One should know that a māṣa is indeed the twentieth part of a kārṣāpaṇa. Thus, "five māṣas" are equivalent to an eightieth part. And this interest is to be taken month by month.
"A moneylender may take an eightieth part from every hundred per month," according to the statement of Manu.
Bṛhaspati says:
The interest shall increase by one-eightieth part until the principal has doubled;
lent for seven years less one-third, there is no doubt of this.
Vyāsa says:
When there is a pledge, the monthly interest is declared to be one-eighth; when there is a mortgage, it is one-sixteenth;
and for a loan without collateral, the monthly profit is two percent.

“Eighty” means the eightieth [part]. And this very [fraction], when combined with its own eighth part, is “with an eighth part” (*sāṣṭabhāga*). “Without pledge” (*nirādhāne*) means free from a security.
Manu says: “He may take two percent per hundred, remembering the duty of the virtuous.”
For one who takes two per cent does not become a sinner for the sake of wealth.

Just as one who takes an eightieth part does not become a sinner regarding wealth, so too one who takes two percent per hundred incurs no fault; and in this matter, the rule is established as referring specifically to secured loans (*sabandhaka*), following the statement of Vyāsa: "In a secured loan, the share is eighty," and so forth. Hārīta states:

On twenty-five *purāṇas*, the interest for one month is eight *paṇas*; thus, over six months or four years, it amounts to two-fold. This interest is called righteous interest (*dharmavṛddhi*); by means of this, one does not fall away from righteousness.

“*Purāṇa*” means sixteen *paṇas*. A *paṇa* consists of four *kākiṇīs*, according to common usage. “*Dviparyāgatam*” means doubled. “*Saṃtiṣṭhate*” means it remains fixed; that is to say, it does not increase further. Manu says: “Two, three, four, and five per hundred [per month] are equal.”
One may take interest for a month, according to the successive order of the social classes.
[220] “Dvika” refers to that principal sum upon which a two-fold increase is granted; likewise for three-fold and so on. “Equal” means not exceeding the proper measure. Yājñavalkya states:
“The interest shall be one-eightieth part every month when there is a pledge.”
According to the sequence of the castes, there are one hundred [years], or otherwise two, three, four, or five [hundred].
"Otherwise" means in the absence of a pledge.
Now Vasiṣṭha:

"Furthermore, the creditor shall receive from the debtor the principal as it was given, along with interest at the rate of two, three, four, or five percent per month, according to the order of the castes."
Gautama says: "Some say it should not exceed one year. Manu says:
One should not take back interest exceeding one year's duration, nor that which is not sanctioned;
likewise, compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and bodily interest [are forbidden].

From a month up to a year, the interest must be determined even by its total amount. One should apply the practice such that what increases in a month is the same as that which [increases] in a year, and not more than that. "Unseen" means not sanctioned by the scriptures; the meaning is that one should not take interest exceeding five percent. Interest such as *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) and others should also not be accepted.
Its nature, however, is stated by Yājñavalkya: "Compound interest is interest upon interest; monthly interest is that which is paid every month."
Bodily action performed through desire would be that which is caused by the body, consisting of bodily karma.
Bṛhaspati says: Many means of livelihood have been proclaimed by the seers;
yet among all of these, they know usury to be the most excellent.
Due to drought, fear of kings, or calamities such as rats, there may be loss in agriculture and similar pursuits; however, such [loss] is not found in usury.
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, by night or even by day,
in heat or in rain, or at midnight, the increase does not cease.
Whatever profit accrues to those who travel in various directions and subsist on diverse merchandise,
that same profit arises for him when he properly engages in lending at interest.
[222] 13 Other modes of livelihood in times of distress.

Now, there are other modes of livelihood in times of distress. Regarding this, Manu says: "Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of subsistence."

“Vidyā” refers to sciences other than the knowledge of the Vedas, such as the science of Garuḍa (gāruḍa) and others. “Śilpa” is the work of painting and so forth. “Bhṛti” is wages. “Vipaṇi” is trade. “Dhṛti” is contentment. Yājñavalkya says:
Agriculture, craftsmanship, contentment, learning, usury, a cart, and a mountain [are means of subsistence].
Service, the vicinity of water, alms, and [other means] are the modes of livelihood in times of distress for a king.
[223] Bṛhaspati says: In the case of misfortune, the means of livelihood are trade, agriculture, commerce, and farming; as well as marshy lands, mountains, and service to a king.
“Vaṇik” means trade;
“chāgaleyaḥ”; “śakaṭaṃ,” “śākinī,” “gāvaḥ,” “jālam,” and “aspandanaṃ vanam.”
A marshy region, a mountain, a king, and nine means of livelihood during a famine.

A "cart" (*śakaṭa*) is that which provides a livelihood through the hiring out of vehicles for transporting grain and other goods. A "garden" (*śākinī*) is a vegetable plot. A "net" (*jāla*) refers to catching fish. "Stationary living" (*aspandana*) is remaining in one place; this is because it is free from excessive expenditure and involves the acquisition of grass and other such resources. A "forest" (*vana*) is [a livelihood] through the gathering of fruits, roots, and so forth. A "marshy region" (*anūpa*) is a land with abundant water, [providing a livelihood] through the gathering of lotus stalks, tubers, and the like. A "mountain" (*parvata*) is [a livelihood] through the extraction of red chalk and other minerals. Thus says Hārīta.

They consider a cart with five oxen to be one that is yoked but lacks security, one with ten oxen to be a slaughterhouse, and one with a hundred oxen to be a slaughterhouse during the rainy season; therefore, one should not travel by cart at night nor during the rains. Those who know the Dharma say that if one subsists on a cart for a month, one falls [from dharma], for they say that by means of it, Agni, the gods, guests, the household, and the sacrificial implements are provided.

One should prepare a hundred-rooted bundle of sugarcane leaves for the purpose of sacrifice. Here, "burden" (*bhara*) refers to a heap of rice and other grains being placed upon it. "Lack of security" (*ayogakṣema*) is due to its being accompanied by the yoke and the cart-driver. "Cart" (*anaḥ*) means a wagon. Even with security (*sayogakṣema*), there is a ten-rooted bundle at night; likewise, a hundred-rooted bundle during the rainy season. By bringing fire-utensils, sacrificial fuel, flowers, fodder, rice, and so forth, one becomes free from sin through this act performed for the sake of sacrifice, and not for the sake of livelihood or similar purposes. Thus says Gautama.

In every way, one may subsist by means other than Śūdra labor when unable to do otherwise; some say this even when there is danger to life. However, the rules regarding the mixing of castes and forbidden foods remain. Yet, when there is danger to life, even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms.

"In every way" means by means of prohibited trade, mixing of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), and so forth. "In case of inability" means when there is a failure to perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. "By non-Śūdra work" means by work other than that of a Śūdra, such as eating the remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭabhakṣaṇa*), crafts, and so on. "Even that" refers even to the work of a Śūdra. "In a life-threatening crisis" implies for oneself and those who must necessarily be supported. "Likewise, mixing of castes" refers to sitting together with them, and so forth. "Unfit food" refers to garlic and the like. "Restraint" means cessation [from it]. "One may take up a weapon" implies for the purpose of preserving one's life. — Aṅgiras.
For one who is diseased, for one who is impoverished, for one who has fallen from his family,
or for one who has set out upon a journey, the practice of begging is prescribed.
This [mention of] being afflicted by disease and so forth is intended as an illustration for the impossibility of alms-food being prepared in any way whatsoever. Hārīta says:
"Alms-food may be collected from members of all four castes, or it may consist of food from a single source among the twice-born and others."
Among the twice-born, they praise only alms-food and not food from a single source.
Sages who are experts in dharma praise alms obtained by one's own labor, acquired according to the rules and without malice, as being equal to the wind.

“By one’s own duty” means by the purpose of study and so forth as previously described. “According to the rule” means in the manner established by such [injunctions] as “as much as required for one’s needs” and “without deceit. “Equal to the wind” means by virtue of its purity.
Manu says:
“Likewise, by one who has not eaten for six meals, at the time of the seventh meal...”
One who has fallen away from his duties must perform them according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found,
it must be told to him who asks, provided he does indeed ask.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he may take the property of a bandit or one who neglects his religious duties if he has no other means of livelihood.

“By the method of not providing for the morrow” means by using [only] what is sufficient for one day. A “dasyu” is a thief. “One devoid of rites” is one who is lacking in obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rituals. The meaning is that [food] may be taken even from those two types of Brāhmaṇas.
Yājñavalkya says: “Having remained hungry for three days, one may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa.”
Having accepted it, the accused must explain it in accordance with the law.
"Having accepted" means having taken.
Following the phrase "of substances and so forth," Gautama states:
"When questioned by the king, he should report to those who have not neglected their duties regarding the seventh [day], those who have not eaten, and even those who have not accumulated [wealth]."
“The seventh mealtime”—the word “mealtime” is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Hārīta says:

The practice of medicine, subsistence through a paramour, and living off a bull or a Vaiśya; the livelihood of a merchant, a trader, a moneylender, a liar, or a gambler; the practice of litigation, servitude, sophistry, or breeding horses; serving as a royal agent, living by deceit, or the practice of fraud; the theft of another's property—these constitute sinful modes of livelihood. Those who live by such sinful means are ordained for hell and are reborn in evil wombs; therefore, one should not adopt an improper mode of livelihood.

“Living by procreation” (*upapatyupajīvanam*) means living off one’s wife or another man’s wife. The release of bulls among the women of others for the price of a bull from cattle, horses, and so forth—this is its name, “the practice of the bull” (*vṛṣavṛtti*). A “merchant” (*vaṇik*) is one who sells merchandise. A “peddler” (*kirāṭī*) is one who sells items not fit for sale, such as ghee, oil, rice, and the like. Living by the profession of usury is “the practice of a moneylender” (*vārdhuṣikavṛtti*). This is a livelihood based on falsehood. “The practice of a gambler” (*kitavavṛttitā*) is the profession of gambling. “The practice of litigation” (*vivādavṛtti*) is living by being addicted to quarreling. “The practice of a servant” (*praiṣyavṛtti*) is being a servant. A “logician” (*tārkika*) is one who lives by the science of argumentation, skilled in quibbles and the like, who lives by the suppression of true knowledge. This is the fourfold “practice of the horse” (*aśvavṛtti*). “Royal service” (*rājapauruṣyam*) is the taking of bribes by pointing out the fear of the king. Theft (*steyavṛtti*) is the seizing of another’s property through deceit, manifesting a lack of integrity. “Those instructed in hell” (*nirayānuśiṣṭāḥ*) means those who have been made to undergo the torments of hell.
[228] Devala says: One should not live by practicing medicine, astrology, fortune-telling, cart-making, oil-pressing, liquor, weighing, or even by being a teacher to one's own son.
Lac, madder, meat, honey, iron, and poison—even a low-born man who does not live by these is noble; he is excluded from such activity.
“Appearance” refers to a means of livelihood such as that of a prostitute and the like. “Being a teacher to one’s son” means receiving wealth from a son by virtue of being his teacher.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should not seek a livelihood that is interrupted, nor one that is undistinguished, nor one that is excessive, nor one that is equal, nor one that is deficient, nor one that is contemptible, nor one that is ruinous.

“*Antaritā*” means interrupted, such as a Kṣatriya adopting the livelihood of a Śūdra. “*Avaśiṣṭā*” refers to that which takes the form of accepting impure gifts and the like, when pure gifts are available. “*Adhikā*” is that which pertains to a caste higher than one’s own. “*Samā*” is that which is incapable even of performing necessary duties or supporting dependents. “*Hīnā*” is that which pertains to a lower caste. “*Kutsitā*” is that acquired through censurable acts. “*Anarthakarī*” is that which is harmful. Manu says: “One should not seek wealth through addiction [to vice], nor by forbidden action.”
[229] Because it does not exist in objects being conceptualized, nor even in suffering, from whichever source that might arise.

“By addiction” means through attachment to singing, instrumental music, and so forth. “While [means of subsistence] are being provided” means while there exist wealth sufficient for livelihood that has come down from ancestors and others. “From here and there” means from those such as the accused or the outcaste. Yājñavalkya says:
“One should not strive for wealth that obstructs Vedic study, nor from here and there.”
And one should always remain content, without falling into the error of contradiction.
Laghuhārīta states:
"He who is entitled to perform a particular rite is declared to be its servant;
therefore, a most excellent twice-born man should never perform such work himself."
But as for the one who was previously authorized, if he causes the ritual to be performed, he shall go to a terrible hell; for that result belongs to him for whose sake it was done.

“Whose wealth it is, his is the fruit thereof. This means that one should perform religious duty (*dharma*) with the master’s wealth, distinct from the wealth given for the sake of subsistence (*vṛtti*). Bṛhaspati and Vyāsa state:
“An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son...”
"Even after committing a hundred wrongs, she must be maintained," so Manu has declared.
“Hundred improper acts” here refers to censurable modes of livelihood.
Dakṣa [states]:
“The means for accomplishing the welfare of those to be supported should be pursued only during the third parts of the day.”
Mother, father, teacher, wife, offspring, the destitute, and those who have sought refuge.
The guest who has arrived, the fire, kinsmen, one’s own people, the destitute, and likewise the helpless person who has sought refuge— this group is declared to be the Pauṣya class.
Furthermore, the group of dependents for one endowed with wealth has been described;
one must give to those who possess knowledge, otherwise one shall go to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always support those who are dependent;
the maintenance of those who are to be supported is praiseworthy and a means to attain heaven.
Hell awaits him who oppresses his dependents; therefore, one should support them with diligence. That man alone truly lives who is supported by many.
Yet other men, though living, are as if dead, being merely preoccupied with filling their own bellies; some live for the sake of great wealth, while others live for the sake of their families.

One who is distressed even by his own belly is unable to provide for others for his own sake. "Accomplishing wealth" means the acquisition of *dharma*. "A dependent in distress" means one who has taken refuge while being in a state of misery, but not everyone. "A guest" (*abhyāgata*) is one who is unrelated and has come from another village. "A kinsman" (*jñāti*) is a paternal relative. "A relative" (*bandhu*) is a maternal relative. "One without a protector" (*anātha*) is one who is deprived of a supporter such as a father. "A knower of knowledge" (*jñānavit*) is one who knows the Vedas and the Śāstras. Now follows the procedure for receiving gifts (*pratigraha*).
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"O best of the twice-born, one should seek wealth from praiseworthy members of the twice-born,
or even from any twice-born person whatsoever, but never from a Śūdra."
A Snātaka who is perishing from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; but not from anyone else—this is the settled rule.
Yājñavalkya:
One who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, a pupil, or one for whom he performs sacrifices;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who rely on fallacious reasoning, heretics, and those who act like herons.
"Haitukas" are those devoted to the doctrine of logic, who stand outside the Vedic tradition (*trayī*).
Nārada says: "Because of the manifold nature of objects and because of the divinity of the Great-Souled Ones..."
The acceptance of gifts from kings is more meritorious than from others, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
Both the Brahmin and the king are indeed observers of firm vows;
there is no difference between them whatsoever, because both are devoted to the protection of the subjects and the dharma.
They say that even for a sharp-witted king who knows the Dharma, who is grateful, and who rules over the impure for the sake of protection, his wealth is indeed pure.
Just as the confluence of pure and impure waters attains equality in the ocean, even so does the influx of wealth to a king.
Just as gold situated in a blazing fire attains purity,
so do all acquisitions of wealth attain purity when entrusted to a king.
A Brāhmaṇa, remaining steadfast in his own duty, may seek his livelihood from the king;
however, when he has the means, he should not accept gifts from the wicked.
How is it that the king is not a deity— he by whose word an impure man becomes pure, and who instantly makes the pure impure?
Those who know this divine nature of the king of immeasurable splendor accept his gifts and are not tainted in any way.

“*Aśucīn*” means those who have committed offenses. “*Devatvam*” (the state of being a deity) is so called because they have been consecrated by Manu and others as having the nature of the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Following the practice of gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*), Manu says:
“By those who are suffering and desiring base metals or wealth, the lord of the earth [should provide them].”
He should be entreated by Snātaka Brahmins; if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.
[233] Unplowed land is better than plowed land; likewise, cattle, goats, and sheep;
gold, grain, and food—each preceding one is less culpable than the following.

“Base metal” (*kupya*) refers to wealth such as bronze and the like, other than gold and silver. “By those who have taken the bath” (*snātakaiḥ*) means by Brahmins. “Other” refers to bronze and so forth. “Wealth” (*dhana*) refers to gold and the like, other than base metal. “Unwilling to give” (*aditsan*) means devoid of the desire to give. “He deserves abandonment” (*tyāgam arhati*) means he should not dwell in that kingdom; thus says Medhātithi. “Uncultivated” (*akṛta*) means unplowed. “Food” (*anna*) means cooked food. Baudhāyana states:
His livelihood shall be sought from Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and chariot-makers; he should beg while standing and remaining silent.

A *rathakāra* is one born from a *māhiṣya* father and a *karaṇī* mother. "He should desire to obtain" means he should seek what is unasked for; this is the implied sense. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: When begging, he should state his specific purpose. He should not perform a public display on a stage, nor should he beg food without specifying it from a woman, from one who has not attained legal majority, or from one who does not have sufficient provisions nearby. Whatever purpose he begs for, he must accomplish that very purpose. He should announce the remainder to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or give it to someone else who is most virtuous.

“*Nimitta*” refers to occasions that prompt begging, such as weddings and the like. “*Raṅga*” is a place for dancing and so forth; “*avatāra*” therein means going to that location for the purpose of begging. “*Aprāptavyavahāra*” is one who is less than sixteen years of age. “*Aparyāptasaṃnidhāna*” means situated in a place or time unsuitable for giving. “*Anuddiśya*” means without specifying. “*Anyam*” means something other than what has already been done. The verb “*bhikṣeta*” (he should beg) is not connected with [the phrase] “not a woman,” and so forth.
Manu: “One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the *rājanya* lineage.”
For those who live by the very guise of butchers, oil-pressers, and tavern-keepers;
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a courtesan is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten courtesans.
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, the acceptance of gifts from him is terrible.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in due course, go to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃghāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pūtimṛttika.
The Iron Spike, the Razor-edged Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-leaves, and the Pit of Burning Iron Coals.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king.
A *sūnī* is a meat-seller; a *cakrī* is an oil-presser; a *dhvajvān* is a vintner; a *veśyā* is a courtesan.
[This applies] to a king who is not born of the *rājanya* caste and who acts according to his own will.
The acceptance of gifts from such a person is terrible; though it tastes like honey, it is like poison.
For Brahmins who have been consumed by royal offenses and whose selves are unrefined,
there is no rebirth, just as for seeds that have been scorched.
Therefore, the wise avoid accepting gifts from a king;
instead, they replenish themselves with the food of the gods and the food of the twice-born.
In the same way, the queen, the royal ministers, and the family priests—
all those who follow the duties of kings— are joined with half of that sin.

“Those of unrefined soul” refers to those who engage in the acceptance of gifts from censurable kings. “They nourish themselves again with the food of deities and the food of the twice-born” means that they nourish themselves even with the property of the gods and the property of Brahmins—which is preferable—rather than accepting gifts from a king; this is the intended meaning. Hārīta says:
“A king indeed commits ten thousand slaughter-house sins every day.”
He performs those very same [actions] at night; such is his terrible acceptance [of gifts].
Half of that [share] belongs to the ministers, and half of that to the commander-in-chief and the chief justice;
then half of that, and again half of that, accrues to those who have taken refuge [with the king].
Aṅgiras:
That twice-born man who for six months eats the food of a Śūdra, which is censured,
shall live as a Śūdra and, upon death, is reborn as a dog.
These faults arise here from accepting gifts from a Śūdra alone,
even for the sake of one's teacher, guests, and especially dependents.
One may accept the food of a Śūdra but not eat it oneself;
according to the opinion of Aṅgiras, there is no fault in this for one who acts out of a desire to show favor.
"Of one engaged in showing favor" means of one engaged in showing favor toward the teacher and others, as will be described hereafter.
Regarding Yama: "Those twice-born who accept [gifts] from a deceased person within ten days..."
For a hundred thousand years, they shall dwell in hell.

“Within ten days of a deceased person” means during the period of impurity caused by death. Aṅgiras states: “For unhusked grain is purified by [purificatory] rites; therefore, it is traditionally held to be pure.”
Therefore, the raw [mercury] should be taken even amidst dead metals and fluxes.
A Brahmin should avoid cooked food; likewise, a Kṣatriya should avoid cow-grain;
from Vaiśyas all grains may be accepted, and from a Śūdra coins may be taken.

"By means of *saṃskāras*" refers to such acts as breaking and crushing. A "*paṇa*" is a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika*. All of this should be understood as applicable to one who has fallen into distress (*āpadgata*), because for a *śūdra* whose wealth is otherwise entirely unacceptable as a gift, the acceptance of a *paṇa* is permitted for the sake of purification.
[238] In the section concerning those excluded from the *pāṅktya* (those unworthy to sit in a row for a meal), Manu, immediately after mentioning those who officiate for *śūdras*, states:
"Even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, having accepted a gift from him out of greed..."
It quickly goes to destruction, like an unbaked clay vessel in water.

Hārīta: What is accepted from those who have fallen [from their caste] or who have committed evil deeds leads away from heaven and is unfit for sacrifice; one does not thereby attain meritorious goals. One who, having overcome a Brahmin seeking wealth for the sake of the gods or ancestors, prohibits that gift from being given to another and accepts it himself, incurs the evil deed of that person. Having accepted it for the sake of a debt, he sinks into the state of a thief if he fails to apply it to those purposes; if he accepts it for his own sake, he binds himself. By accepting gifts through these improper means, one prepares for hell. Bṛhaspati:
Even though it does not belong to him, he takes from the virtuous and bestows it upon them;
thus, making himself the master of the wealth, he delivers himself across the difficult-to-cross [ocean of existence].
Yama said:
"But he who, having received [a gift] from here or there, gives it back again—
when he asks the king, 'To whom does the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) belong?'"
Whatever misdeed may have been committed, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
a righteous person overcomes it all by accepting [the gift] and then giving it away again.
But for those who are attached to receiving gifts and never to giving them,
Vaivasvata has declared that there is no upward journey for them anywhere.
“Attached” means clinging.
Yājñavalkya says:
[One may take what is necessary] for the sake of honoring gods and guests, and for the maintenance of teachers, dependents, and so forth.
One may accept gifts from anyone for the sake of one's own livelihood alone.
“Livelihood for oneself” means that which consists of the sustenance of one’s own life.
Manu says:
“Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests...”
One may accept from all sources, but one should not satisfy oneself with that.
[240] But when the gurus have passed away, or when living at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always receive it from a virtuous person.
Even when capable of receiving gifts for these purposes,
one should not accept them from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy.

“Gurus” refers to parents and others. “Desiring to rescue” means wishing to uplift those who have fallen into distress due to hunger and so forth. “Wishing to honor” refers to deities and guests; the meaning is that this is for the sake of fulfilling obligatory duties. “From all [sources]” means from both the virtuous and the non-virtuous. “But he should not satisfy himself with that” means that he should not use it for enjoyments and the like beyond what is necessary for the mere maintenance of life. “Or he may live at home without them” means that even while his gurus and others are alive and capable of providing a livelihood through other means, he should receive alms only from the virtuous and righteous for the sake of his own subsistence.
Gautama says:
