Fuel, water, roots, fruits, honey, protection from fear, a bed, a seat, a dwelling, a vehicle, milk, curds, grain-porridge, mustard seeds, *priyaṅgu* seeds, and leaf-vegetables are not to be refused from anyone; provided, however, that one has no other means of subsistence except for a Śūdra, and that these items are used for the maintenance of ancestors, gods, teachers, and dependents.

“*Abhyudyatam*”: brought forward for the purpose of giving, such as firewood and other items; however, milk, curds, and vessels, even if not specifically brought forward for giving, are present in the giver’s house and so forth. These, being given unasked, must not be refused. “*Āvasatham*”: a dwelling or house. “*Mārgam*”: venison. Regarding the phrase “and other things for the maintenance of ancestors, gods, teachers, and dependents,” the meaning is that other items given for the sake of *śrāddha* ceremonies and the like must also not be refused. Sumantu says:

Even for those whose food is forbidden, there is no fault in taking flowers, fruits, roots, vegetables, grass, wood, and grain that are situated in a field, as well as water from a pond, and milk situated in a cow-pen.
Here, "field" refers to the place of production. Thus says Āpastamba.

Honey, uncooked food, a path, meat, land, roots and fruits, protection, a pasture, a dwelling, a draft animal, and clothing are things that may be accepted from one who is fierce (*ugra*). These too must have been brought forth by a resident pupil (*antevāsī*).

"Protection" means defense. "Pasture" (*gavyūti*) means a cow-path. "Fierce" (*ugra*) refers to one who acts contrary to the scriptures. "Brought forth by a resident pupil" means carried by a disciple (*antevāsī*). Thus says Hārīta.

They might take raw grain or tasteless cooked food, and there would not be sufficient abundance. Even if one cannot provide for oneself, one may consume gold or livestock after giving them away; one should not remain in such a state indefinitely, but should desist once a livelihood is obtained.

“Āma” refers to raw rice grains and the like. Because of the use of the genitive case in the phrase “of prepared food” (*kṛtānnasya*), one may accept even from a low-caste person (*ugra*) a small amount—just enough to maintain one’s dependents—of either prepared food or unfermented liquor (*virama*) that is devoid of flavors such as salt. “They would not be in times of plenty” means that if people were not easily found to be givers of requested food, then it would be a famine. As stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
“Even from kings who are evildoers, virtuous men accept gifts.”
They desire nothing other than the earth, for this is indeed the supreme purifier.
Manu says:
One may accept from anyone fuel-wood, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered spontaneously, honey, and the gift of safety.
One should not reject a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables.
[243] Since it is impossible for Abhaya to give the primary gift, this is cited for the sake of illustration. "Maṇayaḥ" means jewels.
Aṅgiras and Baudhāyana are mentioned first:
"The grain situated in the threshing floor and field, and the water situated in the pond and well."
Even from one whose food is not to be eaten, that milk which has entered into a cow-pen may be accepted.
When the sacrificial portions have been interrupted, as well as the *āgrayaṇa* offerings, one should perform the unmodified *iṣṭi*; one must not let the merit of what has been well-performed perish.
One may accept cooked food from Brahmins, *godhūma* grain even from Kṣatriyas,
all kinds of grain from Vaiśyas, but nothing at all should be accepted from Śūdras.
However, grain that has been brought into the field or onto the threshing floor, even if it is outside the dwelling house, may be taken at all times even from Śūdras; this is the opinion of Aṅgiras.
It is observed that each of these items may be accepted by the best of the twice-born according to their respective castes;
nevertheless, even from among the twice-born, milk is to be drunk, as is the opinion of Aṅgiras.

"And when interrupted" means at times such as when the wings [of the ritual] are being performed. Likewise, regarding "in the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifices," the meaning is that for the sake of achieving the full completion of the sacrifice, one may accept grains and so forth as described—even from one whose food is unfit to be eaten—until that completion is attained. Here, "milk" refers to water.
Furthermore: "Whatever grain may be heaped together, whether in a threshing floor or in a field..."
It should be accepted at all times, even from Śūdras; this is the opinion of Aṅgiras.
Milk that has been placed in a worthy vessel is always pure;
however, milk from a Śūdra who has come to one's own house may be accepted only when it has been transferred into another vessel.
If a Brahmin, having turned away from a Śūdra's house, should consume milk or even curd,
that too is recorded in the Smṛti as Śūdra-food (śūdrānna).
Raw meat, honey, ghee, parched grain, milk, as well as medicinal herbs,
molasses, buttermilk, and juices may be accepted even from a Śūdra who has desisted [from offering them].
Vegetables, fish, lotus stalks, bamboo shoots, roasted flour, sesame seeds,
sugarcane, fruits, and oil-cake may be accepted from anyone.

"At all times" means even during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth, and for all social classes (*varṇa*). "Flavors" (*rasāḥ*) refers to salt and the like. "Husks" (*kambūkāḥ*) refers to the broken grains of rice. Yājñavalkya says:
"Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, milk, fish, fragrances, flowers, curd, and earth..."
Meat, bedding, seats, and roasted grains should be refused, but water should not be.
One may accept even from a person of evil deeds what is offered unasked,
except in the case of an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy.
Jābāla says:

One should personally accept food offered at one's own home from anyone; having received it for one's own auspicious welfare, one may employ it oneself, but one should give it to a servant only as a last resort.

“Śubhāyātam”: one should make for oneself that which has come in an irreproachable manner; however, that which has come in a reproachable manner should be made useful for those who must necessarily be supported—this is the meaning. Manu says:
"Alms that have been brought, offered, and not previously solicited..."
Prajāpati considered that [the sin] should be seized even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblation, who treats her with contempt.
One should avoid even food offered by a physician who has killed a patient, a blood-letter,
a usurer, a eunuch, and an unchaste woman.
A "śalyahartā" is a surgeon.
[The verse continues: Yama says: [One should not eat the food] of a physician, a hunter, a Vaiśya woman, or a gambler.
One should avoid even food offered by a eunuch or one who has recently given birth.
Prajāpati has declared that alms which are offered spontaneously, brought forward unasked, and presented before one, may be eaten even from a person of evil deeds.
One may eat the food of even a thief, provided he is full of faith,
but never that of one who performs sacrifices for many, nor of one who initiates many pupils.
Likewise:
"The water of one who practices medicine, a hunter, a surgeon,
a fisherman, a eunuch, or a woman of the Kulata caste, is not accepted even if it has been drawn up."
Vasiṣṭha:
Weapons, poison, and liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa. Śaṅkha and Likhita: [The same].
One should neither give nor accept liquor. In the *Ādityapurāṇa* it is said:
"What will that brahmin accomplish by accepting a 'two-faced' [cow]?"
There are a thousand nooses of Varuṇa, resembling the flames of a cruel torrent of fire.
One fetter is released after a full thousand years;
he who accepts a cow with two faces reaches this very state.
Yājñavalkya says: A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
for by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward.
[248] Manu says: Having authorized the rule for the righteous acceptance of gifts, one should not perform the acceptance of a gift in the morning, even if one is perishing from hunger.
One who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds,
or clarified butter without knowledge is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold and food increase life; land and a cow nourish the body;
a horse [increases] the eye, clothing the skin, ghee luster, and sesame seeds progeny.
But a twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study, and who delights in accepting gifts,
sinks down along with that very recipient, just like one in water using a boat made of stone.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear from whomsoever he receives a gift;
for by accepting it even from an outcaste, he sinks like a cow in the mud.
Even if he is capable of accepting gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, his spiritual luster (brahmatejas) is quickly extinguished.

“The rule regarding acceptance is lawful”: this refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for accepting gifts. Regarding gold and food, the meaning is that they "consume" and "burn," respectively, [the lifespan]. "From whatever": from anything whatsoever, even if impure. "Attachment" (*prasaṅga*) means excessive attachment. Yājñavalkya says:
"Even though capable of accepting gifts, he who does not accept them..."
Whatever worlds belong to those who are generous and virtuous, he attains those abundant realms.
Yama said:
"Better than visiting all the gods, better than performing all sacrifices,
and better than the gift of ten million cows, is the non-acceptance of gifts by that [person]."
Vyāsa says: He who is constantly a beggar is not a fit recipient for heaven;
he causes distress to living beings just like a thief.
In the Mahābhārata:
For one whose desire for wealth is for the sake of dharma, the absence of such desire is superior;
for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
The phrase "for the sake of dharma" refers to religious acts other than those that are obligatory (*āvaśyaka*).
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, after stating that accepting gifts at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) yields no merit, it says:
"Therefore, one should not accept gifts at a sacred ford or at holy shrines."
And the twice-born man should remain vigilant regarding all signs.
Thus concludes the procedure for receiving gifts.
[251] 14 Now, the occupations and livelihoods of the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Three duties cease for a Brāhmaṇa with respect to a Kṣatriya:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts."
It is the established rule that these [prohibitions] should likewise cease with respect to a Vaiśya;
for Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them.

The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya. However, the true duty consists of giving gifts, study, and sacrifice.
The study of the Vedas is the distinguished duty of the Brahmin; that of the Kshatriya is protection;
and that of the Vaishya is the work of trade—these are the specific duties within their respective spheres.
"These are the Brāhmaṇas" refers to the Brāhmaṇa caste. "Vārtā" consists of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. "Viśiṣṭāni" means excellent. Parāśara [1.67.70] states:
"The subjects must be protected by the Kṣatriya, who carries a weapon in his hand and is fierce."
Having conquered the enemy armies, he should protect the earth through righteousness (*dharma*).
The smithing of iron, as well as the protection of gems and livestock,
trade, and agricultural labor— these are declared to be the occupations of the Vaiśya.
"Pracaṇḍavān" means endowed with heroic men.
In the context of the recurring themes of giving, study, and sacrifice, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"The Kṣatriya follows the very same dharma as the former [the Brāhmaṇa]. His livelihoods consist of acquiring enemies, protecting from wounds, judicial proceedings, inflicting punishment, and providing instruction."
The *vaiśya* follows the same duties as the former [the *kṣatriya*]. His livelihood (*vṛtti*) consists of agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, breeding livestock, and lending at interest.

"The duties of the former" refers to study, sacrifice, and giving. "Acquisition by means of weapons" (*śastrārjana*) is the earning of wealth through arms. "Protection from injury" (*kṣatatrāṇa*) is the safeguarding [of others] from harm. "Legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) is the removal of doubt between plaintiff and defendant. "Instruction" (*anuśāsana*) is the establishment of the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*) in their respective duties. "Breeding livestock" (*yonipoṣaṇa*) is the maintenance of cattle and other animals for the sake of profit. "Cattle-rearing" (*paśupālya*) is the protection of animals for wages. — Hārīta.

The Kṣatriya, who has completed his vows and bathed [upon graduation], has as his duty the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), study, sacrifice, and giving; he maintains his livelihood by taking a sixth part [of the produce] through the subduing of the unruly. He is a partial observer of Vedic vows. The Vaiśya has as his duty study, sacrifice, and giving; he maintains his livelihood through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. “*Dhanurvedaḥ*” refers to one who has acquired knowledge of weapons through ritual bathing. The same applies to the *veda* and the *vrata*. “*Abhijitānām*” means the taking of a sixth part of the enemy’s land and other possessions. “*Vedavratāvekadeśī*” means one who has achieved his purpose even through a single portion of the *veda* and the *vrata*.
Regarding the phrase “*brahmādadhāt*,” Baudhāyana states that this continues [in the following context]:

for the prosperity of the *kṣatriya*, there is the power of the *kṣatra* joined with study, sacrifice, giving, and the protection of weapons, treasuries, and territory; for the prosperity of action among the *vaiśyas*, there is work joined with study, sacrifice, giving, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
Paiṭhīnasi states:

"Study, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, vigor, not fleeing from battle, and sovereignty are the duty (*dharma*) of a Kṣatriya. "Vigor" means majesty; "sovereignty" means independence from the control of others.
Āpastamba:

The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, inheritance, gleaning ears of grain, and other things not previously claimed.
These same duties apply to a Kṣatriya, with the exception of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts, and with the addition of wielding the rod of punishment and warfare.

[254] The duties of a Vaiśya are like those of a Kṣatriya, with the exception of fighting with weapons; they additionally include agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. Following the recurring rule that for the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are primary, Gautama begins by stating, "For a king, the additional duty is the protection of all beings," and so forth, and then adds: "If another [member of the twice-born] should live by that [kingly] occupation, he should do so according to that mode of livelihood."
"Another" refers to one connected by mere birth. "Him," the king. "By that occupation," namely, by the wielding of weapons. Devala says:

The duty of the Kṣatriya consists of: the study of the Vedas, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, worshiping the gods and ancestors, serving Brāhmaṇas, protecting Vaiśyas and Śūdras, collecting taxes, tolls, and the one-sixth share [of produce], maintaining the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), suppressing the wicked, supporting the virtuous, avoiding litigation, upholding righteous conduct, training in and practicing the use of elephants, horses, chariots, and weapons, relying on the methods of the treatises, overseeing the treasury and the army, and possessing the self-reliance, heroism, power, and fortitude gained through the suppression of enemy forces, forest tribes, thieves, traitors, the proud, the trusted, and high-born officials; as well as energy, valor, capability, and not begging. The duty of the Vaiśya consists of: the performance of dharma through study, sacrificing, and giving; service to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas; avoidance of evil; supporting one’s wife; agriculture; cattle-rearing; carrying loads; trade in merchandise; and livelihood through dancing, singing, playing musical instruments, and performing on stage.

“*Bali*” is a tribute. “*Kara*” is the fixed payment of wealth collected from artisans, farmers, and laborers. “*Śulka*” is the toll on goods at ferries and such. “*Living on a sixth share*” refers to grains and other produce; this is the implied meaning. “*Saṃsthā*” means established order or boundary. “*Śikṣā*” means instruction or the science of training. “*Upāyas*” are the means, such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest. “*Gāyanam*” here refers to singing. “*Tālāvataraṇam*” here refers to instrumental performance. “*Raṅga*” is the arena for wrestling; however, in this context, it indicates the art of wrestling itself. Baudhāyana says: A Vaiśya may live by usury, provided it be at the rate of five *māṣas* per twenty-five [units].
"Twenty-five" [kārṣāpaṇas].
Manu: But a Vaiśya who has performed the sacramental rites and taken a wife...
He should be constantly devoted to his livelihood and to the protection of the cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya should not entertain the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
One should understand the relative value of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven textiles,
perfumes, and liquids by means of their *argha* (monetary worth).
One should know the sowing of seeds, as well as the qualities of the field and the seed; one should understand all the methods of measurement and all the applications of the balance.
He should know the essential and non-essential nature of merchandise, the merits and defects of regions,
the profit and loss of commodities, and the methods for increasing the number of livestock.
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing and using goods, as well as buying and selling.
One should exert the utmost effort to increase one's wealth through righteous means,
and one should diligently provide food for all living beings.

“Metals” refers to copper and so forth. “Strength and weakness” means deficiency or excess. Regarding “the sowing of seeds,” he should be a knower of the proper method of sowing seeds—whether densely or sparsely—in a manner conducive to the full growth of the crop; the ellipsis implies that he should be a knower of the qualities of his own fields and seeds. “Methods of measurement” refers to the various types of measures. “Methods of weighing” refers to the ways of holding the scales. “Of goods” means of commodities for sale. “Quality” here refers specifically to its enduring nature even over a long period of time. “Servants” are laborers. “Wages” is the remuneration corresponding to the work performed. “From the application of placement” means by means of the specific way they are stationed.
Immediately after prescribing the Vaiśya’s mode of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa, Manu states:
"A Kṣatriya who has reached a state of distress may live by all these means;
however, he must never at any time consider his own superior mode of livelihood as inferior."
“Having gone to a [difficult] way” means having fallen into calamity. “He might think” means he would accept it. Likewise:
A Vaiśya, unable to subsist by his own duty, may even live by the occupation of a Śūdra.
One should not engage in improper acts, and one who is capable should turn away from them.
“Improper acts” (*akāryāṇi*) refer to such things as clearing away food-leavings and so forth. Likewise:
“He who, being base by birth, should live through superior occupations out of greed.”
The king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately.
In this context, the "superior" one is the Brāhmaṇa. In the Kālikā Purāṇa it is said:
"Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are indeed prescribed for the Vaiśya."
Nevertheless, one should never engage in agriculture with two oxen.
From two bulls and two enemies, for a duration of half a watch (prahara),
the twice-born man should join them two by two in pairs and cause each one to be performed according to the Dharma.
One should diligently provide them with oil-cake, grass, and water;
having thus prepared the smoke and the coloring, one should then cause [the ritual] to be performed.
O great sage, even by cultivating land as thin as a bamboo leaf, a Vaiśya who exerts himself in agriculture shall never come to grief.
Having set aside one-sixth for the king and one-fifth for the cultivator, and having satisfied the artisans, the subjects, and their heirs there, [he should proceed].
A prosperous man should invest his surplus in his own fields and threshing floors;
he should practice the rearing of cattle and establish his dwelling in a sheltered location.
It was secluded, level, and bright, provided with pillars that were not harsh to the touch,
and contained a collection of goats, sheep, cows, and female buffalo.
One should perform [the ritual] in such a way that it never becomes contradictory to others—
such as dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, cats, mongooses, and so forth.
A Vaiśya practicing his own duty should never accept as a gift salt,
honey, liquor, sesame seeds, curd, ghee, or milk.
Beeswax, lac, leather, indigo, poison,
weapons, meat, asafoetida, and likewise three kinds of pigments;
Food prepared with molasses and oil-cake, fruits such as eggplant,
weapons and missiles, water, the gods, and various kinds of fermented liquids.
A Vaiśya shall not sell śaileya, kutapa, or other such items.
In the Mahābhārata: "A Vaiśya, adhering to the path of the righteous, should never sell sesame seeds, grains, or liquids for the sake of trade."
[259] 15 Now, the properties of substances are possession, non-possession, and ownership.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, the performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous."

“Acquisitions of wealth” (*vittāgamāḥ*) are the means of obtaining riches. “Inheritance” (*dāyaḥ*) is wealth acquired through lineage. “Gain” (*lābhaḥ*) refers to [the discovery of] buried treasure and the like. “Conquest” (*jayaḥ*) here means the overcoming of an enemy in battle. “Lending” (*prayogaḥ*) is usury. “Application of labor” (*karmayogaḥ*) includes agriculture, trade, and so forth. Gautama states: “The owner [is established] in respect of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding. What is obtained is the additional [means of livelihood] for a Brāhmaṇa; what is conquered is for a Kṣatriya; and what is earned by labor (*nirviṣṭam*) is for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra.”

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be understood as the ellipsis for each term. "Purchase" (*kraya*) refers to wealth acquired by buying. "Partition" (*saṃvibhāga*) refers to a gift from a friend; this is the view of Bhartṛyajña. "Acquisition through possession" (*parigraha*) refers to wild buffalo and the like that have not previously belonged to another. "Discovery" (*adhigama*) refers to what is obtained from mines and so forth; these are lawful sources of property common to all social classes (*varṇa*). "That which is additional for a Brāhmaṇa" refers to what is acquired through gifts and the like, which is his unique source. "Conquered" (*vijita*) refers to what is gained in battle, which is the additional source for a Kṣatriya. "Earnings" (*nirviṣṭa*) refers to what is acquired through labor. Nārada [4.43–55]:
All activities have wealth as their root; effort is prescribed for its acquisition.
Its preservation, increase, and enjoyment constitute its threefold method in due order.
Furthermore, that [practice] should be known as threefold: pure, variegated, and black; its division, moreover, is to be understood as sevenfold.
Wealth acquired through learning, valor, austerity, daughters, disciples, sacrificial clients, or inheritance—
these seven kinds of wealth are pure, as is the prosperity from which such wealth arises.
That which is obtained through idleness, agriculture, trade, tolls, crafts, or following one's occupation,
as well as what is received from a benefactor, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling with dice, theft, distress, forgery, violence,
or by means of fraud is declared to be *kṛṣṇa* (black wealth).
By means of that, buying and selling, giving and receiving,
as well as various activities and even the enjoyment of wealth, proceed.
Whatever a person performs with whatever kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both in this world and after death.
Furthermore, that is traditionally held to be twelvefold according to the respective castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama):
three types are common to all, while the wise know the remaining nine types to be specific.
Inherited property, a gift of affection, and what is acquired together with one's wife— these three kinds of wealth belong in every way to all social classes without distinction.
One should know that the specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa has three characteristics:
that which is obtained through gifts, from a patron for whom one sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil.
They say that there are also three kinds of specific wealth for a Kṣatriya:
that acquired through battle, from imprisonment, and from fines in legal proceedings.
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics:
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; while that of a Śūdra consists of service through favor.
This is the lawful acquisition of wealth for all social classes;
by the opposite means it would be unlawful, unless there is a grave emergency.

“Obtained through learning” means acquired by means of study and so forth. “Through valor” means by victory and the like. “Through austerity” means by means of recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), propitiation of deities, and so on. “Obtained from a daughter” means received from the father-in-law or others together with the daughter. “Obtained from a pupil” means received as a gift. “Rise” means the fruit. “Of that kind” means pure. “Attendance” means service. “Side-gain” means obtained through bribes and the like. “Distress” means suffering. “Counterfeit” means things that are mere semblances of wealth. “Daring act” refers to risky expeditions and the like; here, “fraud” means the mixing of other substances. “By that” means by the threefold [means]. “The remainder” means that which is not common. “Tax” means *kara*. “Legal proceeding” means judicial process. “From favor” means resulting from the bond of service.

[262] Viṣṇu [58.1–10]: Now, for one in the householder stage of life (gṛhāśramin), wealth is of three kinds—white, variegated, and black. Whatever funeral rite (aurdhvadehika) he performs with white wealth, having attained the state of a deity, he enjoys that. Whatever he performs with variegated wealth, he enjoys that in the human state. Whatever he performs with black wealth, he enjoys that in the animal state. All that is acquired through one’s own occupation (vṛtti) is white; what is acquired through the occupation of an immediate predecessor is variegated; and what is acquired through the occupation of a remote predecessor or an inferior occupation is black. That which is inherited, a gift of affection, and what is obtained together with a wife are also white.
The wealth of all [these] is declared to be "white" without distinction.
That which is obtained through bribery or taxes, or acquired from the sale of what ought not to be sold,
or received as a reward for a service rendered, is declared to be "stained" (śabala).
That which is obtained through gambling or theft, by means of counterfeits or violence,
and that which is acquired through fraud, is declared to be "black" wealth.

Buddha: One should perform ritual acts with wealth acquired through righteous means; [the sources of such wealth are] study, officiating at sacrifices, receiving gifts, inheritance, purchase, partition, and finding.
Bṛhaspati [Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.24.1].
Whatever is obtained by means of a livelihood, one should use it for protection and increase,
as well as for enjoyment together with one's kinsmen, the poor, the helpless, and those who seek assistance.

In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "Since the sacrifices consisting of cooked offerings (*pākasaṃsthā*), the sacrifices consisting of oblations (*havissaṃsthā*), and the sacrifices consisting of Soma (*somasaṃsthā*) are all established upon wealth for human beings, one should therefore strive for the acquisition of wealth."
In the Mahābhārata: "For all the activities of a man of small intelligence who is deprived of wealth perish, like small streams in the heat of summer."
From famine to famine, from affliction to affliction, from fear to fear,
those who are poor and do evil pass on even further into death after death.
Those who possess faith, are well-self-controlled, wealthy, and perform auspicious deeds go from festival to festival, from heaven to heaven, and from happiness to happiness.
A house devoid of gold, lacking servants, with little food and no milk products—such is the home of those who live like wretches; it is but another form of hell.
Wealth should be acquired through righteous means; wealth obtained through righteousness is of three kinds. A man should strive diligently to make righteousness his supreme goal.
One who desires prosperity should perform his duty with one part,
pursue pleasure with another part, and increase his wealth with the remaining part.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (34.11–12): A self-possessed person should set aside one quarter of his wealth for the sake of the next world, and with the other half, he should provide for his own maintenance, including the fulfillment of daily and occasional obligatory rites.
One should increase by one-quarter, then by one-eighth, and so on, the portion that constitutes the root of wealth;
in this manner, my son, through right conduct, wealth attains fulfillment.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"If a wealthy twice-born man does not perform dharma that can be accomplished through wealth,
his mind being overcome by greed, he does not obtain the fruit thereof."
Therefore, one should set aside one-third of one's wealth for the purpose of livelihood,
and two parts for the sake of dharma, because life is transient.

Having acquired wealth through irreproachable means— whether by means of excellence in Vedic study, by association with Brahman-sages, or indeed through the practice of offerings, restraints, and austerities in mountains, oceans, and forests— the householder should maintain the life of a householder. [265] 16

Now, regarding the duties, laws, and occupations of Śūdras: in those cases where the word "service" (śuśrūṣā) is not explicitly mentioned in the scriptural statements, it should be understood that the entitlement belongs to the twice-born (dvijāti), as they are required [to serve]. The word "dharma" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Regarding this, Manu says:
For a Śūdra, the highest dharma leading to ultimate liberation is indeed the service of illustrious householders who are Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
Pure among those of the highest castes, gentle in speech, and free from egoism,
one who constantly takes refuge in Brahmins attains superiority by birth.

In this context, the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are superior. "Dependent on Brāhmaṇas" means one who, even while intent on serving Kṣatriyas and others for the sake of livelihood, has dedicated himself to the Brāhmaṇas. "Superiority by birth" refers to excellence of caste. Bṛhaspati [Saṃhitā 529] states:
"Purity, service to Brāhmaṇas, and constant freedom from anger."
Likewise, for a Śūdra, the ritual action is understood here to be the mantra of salutation.
Āpastamba: Service is the duty of the Śūdra toward the other castes; the highest good is greater toward the preceding caste. Parāśara [1.71]: [The same].
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is the primary characteristic of his dharma;
whatever else he may do shall be fruitless for him.
Hārīta says: "They do not declare that a Śūdra has a means of livelihood; his livelihood is solely the service of the three higher castes. Some say his duty is giving gifts.
But if a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, should wish to serve the Kṣatriya,
or if he desires to live, he should do so by serving a wealthy Vaiśya.
For the sake of heaven and for the sake of both worlds, he should support only Brāhmaṇas;
for once the title of "Brāhmaṇa" has been attained, that indeed constitutes his fulfillment of duty.
Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him.
[267] He should provide for his livelihood from his own household as is appropriate,
having considered their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they support.
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments,
the chaff of grains, and old household utensils.

“Should propitiate” means he should maintain [the service]. “One who has acquired the title of Brāhmaṇa” refers to one by whom the designation “this is a servant of a Brāhmaṇa” has been obtained. “Other than that” means other than serving the Brāhmaṇas, such as vows, fasting, and so forth. “By them” means by those twice-born ones. “From his own family” means from the wealth intended for his own family. “According to ability” means according to one’s capacity. “Dexterity” means skill in performing tasks. “The maintenance of dependents” refers to sons, wife, and so forth. “Remnants” (ucchiṣṭa) refers to what remains after guests and others have eaten. And this eating of remnants applies to one who has not yet taken a wife; for another [who has], there is the entitlement to perform domestic sacrifices (pākayajña). “Pulakas” are inferior grains. “Appurtenances” (paricchada) include things such as umbrellas and sandals.
Gautama.

The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he is of a single birth. For him as well, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required], as is rinsing the mouth and the washing of hands and feet—some say this alone suffices. His duties are the performance of *śrāddha* rites, the maintenance of dependents, devotion to his own wife, and service to those higher than himself. He should seek his livelihood from them. He may consume worn-out shoes, umbrellas, clothing, mats, and the like, as well as food-remnants. He may also subsist by manual crafts (*śilpa*). Even if impoverished, he should support whoever provides him with wealth. Furthermore, he may accumulate wealth for the sake of those [higher castes] with their permission. The ritual formula for him is the salutation (*namaskāra*). Some say that he should perform sacrifices himself using *pākayajña* offerings.

[268] “Of one birth” (*ekajātiḥ*) means having a single birth, because he lacks the birth consisting of the *upanayana* (initiation). “Of the higher ones” (*uttareṣām*) refers to the superior classes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. “A *kūrca*” is a seat made of grass. “For that purpose” (*tenārthena*). “Deprived” (*kṣīṇaḥ*) means lacking a livelihood. “By him” (*tena*) refers to the Śūdra. “The higher one” (*uttaraḥ*) refers to the Ārya; the word “deprived” (*kṣīṇa*) is understood to carry over here. “For his sake” (*tadarthaḥ*) means for the sake of the Ārya. “His” (*asya*) refers to the Śūdra. “Accumulation” (*nicayaḥ*) means a collection of wealth. “Himself” (*svayam*) means he should do it himself; the meaning is that he should not have it done by his wife, son, or others. “With *pākayajña* sacrifices”—thus says Vasiṣṭha.

Service to these [twice-born] is the Śūdra’s means of livelihood; his hair and dress are unrestricted. Or, for all [castes], except for the loosened topknot (*muktaśikhā*). “To these” refers to those of the three higher castes. “Unrestricted” means free from the rule that “this much must be given. “Unrestricted hair and dress”: the construction is that all are unrestricted regarding both hair and dress for the Śūdra. “For all,” meaning for the Brāhmaṇas and the others. “Except for the loosened topknot” means that the state of having a loosened topknot must not be performed by anyone. —Baudhāyana.

For Śūdras who are under the authority of Āryas, there is shaving every half-month or month. Their procedure for sipping water (ācamana) is like that of the Āryas. [269] “The procedure for sipping water” refers to the manner of performing the sipping of water. “The sacred thread (upavīta)” refers to the arrangement of the garment and so forth. “Those dependent on Āryas” means those who are not independent, such as those living by crafts and the like. Manu says:
Śūdras who live according to the law must have their hair shaved every month;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and their food consists of the remnants of the twice-born.

"Of those who abide by the law" means those devoted to the service of the twice-born. "The ritual of purity" refers to the manner of removing birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), performing ritual sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth.
Yājñavalkya and Viśvāmitra state in the first [chapter]:
"The Śūdra’s duty is the service of the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant."
Or he may live by various crafts, while practicing what is beneficial for the twice-born.
Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites,
he should not neglect the five great sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.

“Delight in his wife” means that his supreme delight is in his wife alone, and not in common women or the wives of others. Regarding the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), it is done “with the *namaskāra* mantra,” that is, with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*, accompanied by the deity in the dative case.
Manu says: “But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born... [270]
Having fallen into distress regarding his children and wife, he may live by the labor of an artisan.
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the works of artisans.
“*Atyayaḥ*” means a hardship.
Parāśara [1.72]:
Salt, honey, liquor, or buttermilk, curd, ghee, or milk.
One should not find fault with those of the Śūdra caste; one may sell [goods] to all of them.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: A Śūdra who engages in the sale of all commodities incurs no fault,
with the exception of honey, leather, liquor, lac, and meat as the fifth.
Furthermore, this prohibition against the sale of honey and other such items should be understood as not applying to a Śūdra except in times of extreme distress. Vyāsa states:
"It is certain that a Śūdra does not fall [from his caste] in this case."
Nor indeed does he deserve ritual refinement here;
nor does he enjoy the dharma enjoined by the Veda,
nor is there even a prohibition against dharma in the Veda for him.

“And here a Śūdra does not fall,” even by selling meat and so forth. “Sacrament” (*saṃskāra*) here refers to initiation (*upanayana*). “Enjoined by the Veda” (*śrutiprayukta*) means that which is based on the Śruti, such as the Agnihotra and other rites. “From dharma” means from that which is declared in the Śruti. Manu says:
“There is no sin for a Śūdra, nor is he entitled to sacraments.”
He has no authority over the Dharma, nor is there any prohibition against the Dharma.
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who practice the dharma of the virtuous, do not incur blame when acting except through the use of mantras; rather, they receive praise.
For in whatever measure one who is free from envy abides in virtuous conduct,
in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the next.
For even a capable Śūdra should not accumulate wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
“Excluding mantras” means excluding Vedic mantras.

Āpastamba says: “Veneration must be shown to those of superior caste, and to those who are older; for one who is elated becomes arrogant. The arrogant transgresses his own duty. Indeed, upon the transgression of duty, there is hell.”
“Worship” (*pūjā*) refers to acts such as salutation and the like. “Of those who are older” means even among those of the same caste; this is the sense. Gautama states:
“All should serve each other in ascending order of seniority; when there is a conflict between an Ārya and a non-Ārya, there is equality of action regarding the task.”

“Of the noble and the ignoble”—that is, between those of superior and inferior birth—there is equality when they transgress their own duties; the meaning is that there is no mutual relationship of worshiper and worshipped. Manu says:
“An ignoble person performing the duties of the noble, and a noble person performing the duties of the ignoble...”
Having reflected, the Creator said: "They are neither equal nor unequal."

“They are not equal” because one [of them] is superior by birth. “Nor are they unequal” because even those of superior birth, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, may perform lowly work. Therefore, the intended meaning is that service and so forth should not be performed for him by the other. As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: “Consequently, there is indeed dependence upon all their duties.”
Those twice-born ones conquer their own worlds through great hardship.
By the mere service of the twice-born, this Śūdra becomes entitled to perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
he conquers his own worlds and is therefore more blessed than that [other Śūdra].
O tiger among sages, he has no restriction regarding what may or may not be eaten, nor indeed regarding what may or may not be drunk; for that reason, he is called "the virtuous one."
In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*, in the section concerning the *śūdra*:
"He should be a giver of what is unasked; he may resort to agriculture for his livelihood;
he should listen to the Purāṇas daily, and perform the worship of Narasiṃha."
In the Mahābhārata:
A Brāhmaṇa, blazing like fire, is to be served from a distance by a Śūdra;
however, he may be touched and attended upon by a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
The station of a Brāhmaṇa is that of Brahmā and Prajāpati; that of a Rājanya is that of Indra; that of a Vaiśya is that of the Maruts; and that of a Śūdra is that of Gandharva.
Devoted to their respective duties, they go to their respective stations.

Thus ends the section on Livelihood (*vṛttiparvan*) in the *Gṛhasthakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great Sandhivigrahika (Minister of Peace and War).
[274] 17 Now, the observances of one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka).
Regarding this, Manu says:
"A twice-born Snātaka living by any one of these modes of livelihood should observe these vows,
which lead to heaven, long life, and fame."
One should perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas constantly and without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.

Regarding the phrase “by any one mode of livelihood,” because it is a restatement (*anuvādaka*), the singular number is not intended to be restrictive; thus, there is no contradiction even if one subsists by multiple modes of livelihood. “Vow” (*vrata*) is a specific resolve prescribed by the scriptures, such as: “This must be done by me; this must not be done. “Revealed in the Veda” (*vedodita*) means that which is made known by the Veda through direct perception or inference. “One’s own” (*svakam*) means that which is prescribed for one’s own stage of life (*āśrama*). “Constantly” (*nityam*) means throughout one’s entire life. “Unwearied” (*atandritaḥ*) means free from laziness. “According to one’s capacity” (*yathāśakti*) means that if it is impossible [to perform everything], one may proceed even with the omission of some minor auxiliary parts. Vyāsa says: “The duty (*dharma*) pertaining to the castes and stages of life is considered to be based on the actions prescribed in the Veda.”
For the learned man, performing Vedic rites, attains his desired goal.
Vedic ritual action is primary, while other [actions] are subordinate;
one who is intent on the subordinate, thereby subverting the supreme authority, goes to a downward state.

“Dependent on the Vedic actions” means dependent on the essential points of the Vedas. “Established in the qualities” means established in the traditional codes of conduct (*smṛti*). “The supreme authority” is the Veda; [as stated by] Manu and Vasiṣṭha:
“The daily study of the Veda according to one’s ability, the performance of the great sacrifices, and forbearance...”
They swiftly destroy all evils, even the most heinous crimes.
“Study of the Vedas” here refers to the *brahmayajña* and other such rites.
Āpastamba says:

“He who is a performer of duties regarding the acquisition of wealth, a provider at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), a driver who avoids what is not a sacred site so that there may be no danger, a gatherer of men, and an enjoyer of pleasures not forbidden by dharma—he thus conquers both worlds.”

“Yoktā” means industrious. “In matters joined with dharma” refers to prescribed duties, not to those that are unrighteous or purposeless. “Tīrthe” means in a worthy recipient. “Yantā” is one who has desisted from giving to unworthy recipients. Regarding the word “yataḥ,” the meaning is that even to an unworthy person, such as a thief or one driven by fear, [gifts] should be given. “Manuṣyān” refers to laborers and the like. “Bhogān” refers to saffron and other such luxuries. Saṃvarta says:
One should perform domestic rites, but the primary duty is the nourishment of one’s own wife.
He should approach his wife during her fertile period; thus he attains the supreme goal.
"The supreme dharma," is the ellipsis. Sumantu says:
"Eating the remnants of others' food, approaching one's wife during her season, and performing the rites for the five sacrifices."
And for a householder, association with equals is prescribed.
“And association with equals” is to be understood [as the rule] when no superior [alternative] exists. Manu says:
“One should always practice associations together with the most excellent.”
They lead the family to excellence; one should abandon those who are base.
By associating with the most excellent and avoiding the base, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; but through the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra.
"In *pratyavāye*," that is, in the case of contrary conduct;
Bṛhaspati says: "One should practice truth even more extensively, and one should always approach the Lord."
One should not engage in groundless hostility or dispute with anyone.
A friend is considered superior to kinsmen, relatives, and those with whom one is related by marriage; therefore, one should not treat a friend as equal or inferior through any effort.
For in this world, that [friend] who is a vessel for protection from grief, hostility, and fear, and for joy and confidence,
as well as a friend in times of calamity, is indeed superior to one's own kin.
Excessive intimacy with one who is not an equal is censurable.
Vasiṣṭha said: "The practices of eating, excreting, and recreation..."
But those who know the Dharma should act with great self-restraint;
speech, intellect, and vigor, as well as austerity, wealth, and life itself, must be kept most closely guarded.

“Exertion” (*nirhāra*) is the elimination of urine and feces. “Dwelling” (*vihāra*) is the pursuit of women. “Yoga” is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). “Guarding of speech” (*vāggupti*) is by means of avoiding false speech and the like. “Guarding of the intellect” (*buddhigupti*) is by means of avoiding impure intentions and the like. “Vigor” (*vīrya*) is capability; its protection is the absence of employing it in an improper place. “Austerity” (*tapas*) is celibacy and so forth; its protection is the avoidance of causing wonder. “Most guarded” (*guptatame*) means most unrevealed. Skillful [one]: life-span, wealth, domestic secrets, mantras, sexual intercourse, and medicine.
Austerity, dharma, and humility—these nine are always to be guarded in secret.
That which is appropriate, the clearing of debt, giving, mortgaging, and selling; the giving away of a daughter, the ritual release of a bull, and secret, contemptible sin.

“Household flaw” refers to envy and other such vices that are causes of misfortune. “Lending” is the investment of wealth for interest. “Debt” is the taking on of a loan; it is the purification of debt itself. “Giving” is the gift of immovable property, such as land. “Mortgage” is a pledge. Manu [says]:
Of age, occupation, wealth, sacred learning, and lineage...
One should move about here in this world, practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect.

“Appropriateness” (*sārūpya*) means suitability. By this, it is meant that dress and other such matters should be made suitable to one’s age and so forth. Viṣṇu [71.5–7]: One should adopt a dress corresponding to one’s age, learning, lineage, wealth, and country; nor should one be arrogant.
Manu and Vasiṣṭha [MDh 4.145–46]:
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should daily recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.

"For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, who are always self-restrained, and who recite prayers and offer oblations, no misfortune exists. "Auspicious conduct" refers to practices such as applying yellow pigment (gorocana) to the forehead at dawn and so forth. "Misfortune" refers to the loss of what is desired and the like.
Cows are purifying and auspicious; upon cows the worlds are established.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all evil.
Cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and yellow pigment—
these six limbs of the cow are always supremely auspicious.
The water from the horns of cows is meritorious and destroys all sins.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: Now, the following are the destroyers of Rākṣasas: the meat of a goat, gold, silver, copper, sandalwood, and gems; clarified butter, mustard seeds, linen, a black antelope skin, an elephant, barley, *lāja* grains, a mirror, *priyaṅgu*, yellow orpiment, and realgar; a cow, a full water-jar, an elephant, the *śamī* tree, *palāśa* flowers, and *darbha* grass. Furthermore, the study of one’s own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is always auspicious, as is keeping vigil during the first watch of the night for the three social classes (*varṇas*).
"Elephant" (*nāga*) means a tusker; "darbha" means *kuśa* grass; "flowers" refers to blue lotuses and the like.
Regarding the Earth, Viṣṇu spoke these words to Lakṣmī:
"I dwell in the sun, in the moon, in the cloudless sky rich with hosts of stars, and likewise in the earth."
Likewise, [he beheld] her swaying, pendulous breasts,
which shone like Indra’s bow accompanied by lightning.
Likewise, upon pure gold and silver,
on jewels and stainless garments,
and upon the ground and rows of white palaces.
In temples adorned with banners.
Or likewise upon fresh cow dung, or when a lordly elephant is in rut, or a horse is in its prime,
or a bull is likewise filled with pride.
Likewise, toward a Brahmin who is likewise endowed with Vedic study.
Upon a lion-throne, an *āmalaka* fruit, a *bilva* fruit, an umbrella, a conch, and always upon a lotus;
in a blazing fire and a stainless sword.
And I am always present within the mirror-image.
Upon full water-jars accompanied by fly-whisks and palm-leaf fans, and upon ornaments and charming vessels for pouring water.
And I abide in the soft, as well as in the newly arisen and arrogant.
Likewise in milk, in clarified butter, in grassy meadows, in honey, and in curd;
likewise in the body of a woman, in the body of a maiden, and in the bodies of the gods.
In the bodies of ascetics and performers of sacrifice.
I stood here when my hero had emerged from battle, whether he was dead or had departed from this world to heaven; I stood here at the sound of the Vedas and the blast of conch shells.
And amidst the sound of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and the resonance of musical instruments and other noises.
Likewise, during a royal consecration, a wedding, or a sacrifice; when a man has bathed his head and it is not yet dry;
among white flowers; and on mountains.
amidst delightful fruits and the best of rivers.
In lakes filled with white lotuses, upon the earth covered with young grass, amidst clusters of lotuses,
and among calves and young animals full of joy.
In a virtuous man who is devoted to righteousness.
One who is devoted to proper conduct, learned in the scriptures, modest in dress as well as elegantly attired,
with perfectly clean teeth yet appearing as if covered in impurity—
And toward one who is excessively devoted to eating sweet foods.
Content with his own wife, devoted to dharma, preeminent among beings, free from overeating,
always virtuous, and with fragrant limbs—
And among those who are constantly anointed and adorned.
To one who stands firm in truth, is devoted to the welfare of beings,
endowed with patience, or free from anger;
who is well-restrained in purpose and skilled in the affairs of others.
Always well-conducted toward those with virtuous minds.
“O you with hanging breasts,” meaning one who bears pendulous breasts. “In the refined” means in the Sanskrit language. “Among the Arjunīs” means among cows.
In the *Mahābhārata*, I dwell in truth, O fortunate and well-restrained one.
When a man is engaged in his duties—
free from anger, devoted to the divine, grateful, self-controlled, and always elevated by truth—
I do not dwell in a man who is habitually inactive,
nor in one who is an atheist, a hypocrite, or ungrateful;
nor in one whose nature is divided, nor in one who behaves with cruelty toward men.
Nor indeed among thieves, nor among the naked, nor among fools.
And where those who possess little splendor, strength, or essence of being neither rejoice nor become angry,
O Queen, I do not dwell in such places.
Among men whose desires have not yet been fulfilled.
He who desires nothing for himself,
whose inner self is offered up by its very nature—
to him [it belongs], and not to those others who are always intent on meager contentment.
O Goddess, I do not dwell among men.

[282] I dwell among those who are virtuous in character, who know the Dharma, who have disciplined themselves, who serve their elders, who are self-controlled, who understand the Dharma, and who are great-souled.
I dwell in women who are skillful, self-controlled, devoted to the gods and the twice-born,
truthful in their conduct, and naturally humble.
One who leaves her household goods scattered about, acts without consideration, always speaks in opposition to her husband,
delights in the house of another, and is shameless— [such a woman is to be abandoned].
I avoid such a woman as this.
Fickle, unchaste, and promiscuous, she is devoid of virtuous conduct, fond of quarreling,
and constantly addicted to sleep and reclining.
I avoid such a woman.
Among truthful women who are always pleasant to behold, endowed with good fortune, and possessed of virtues;
among maidens, vehicles, and ornaments—
In sacrifices and in oblations accompanied by rain.
I dwell among the blossoming lotus ponds and beneath the starry canopies of autumnal nights.
Upon the mountains, in cow-pens, as well as on battlefields and in lakes filled with blooming blue and white lotuses,
and by rivers resounding with the sweet cries of swans—
In those [forests] beautified by the sounds of the *krauñca* birds as they were being crushed.
I dwell eternally in these rivers, which are adorned with trees on their broad banks, frequented by ascetics, perfected beings, and brahmins, and abound with abundant water.
In rivers whose waters are agitated by sunas, crocodiles, and makaras.

In that house where [the fire] is constantly offered oblations and sacrificed— whether it be upon a rutting lordly elephant, a bull, a king, a lion-throne, or a virtuous man— [there dwells prosperity].
And one honors cows, Brahmins, and the deities.
And at the proper times, offerings of flowers are made; I always take up residence in that house among the twice-born who are constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas.
I dwell always in the Kṣatriya who is ever devoted to dharma, in the Vaiśya devoted to agriculture,
and in the Śūdra constantly engaged in service.
I dwell with single-minded devotion in Nārāyaṇa, having become his very body through my entire being;
for in this Viṣṇu resides the most exalted Dharma.
And here, there is likewise Brahminical conduct and amiability.
O Lord, I do not dwell within the body;
it is not possible for me to say here [where I am],
other than that I dwell by my very nature within that person.
He increases in virtue, fame, wealth, and desire.
Likewise, Śrī said to Indra:
"Formerly, I dwelt among the Asuras, bound by their virtuous conduct;
but perceiving their sons to be perverse, I chose to dwell with you."
But while the elder members of the assembly were telling truthful stories,
those inferior in virtue laughed and showed malice toward all the elders.
At night they spoke aloud, and there they kindled the fire low;
sons addressed their fathers, and women addressed their husbands.
Those foolish people did not observe impurity for them;
in thought, deed, and word, their devotion remained unrestrained.
Grains were scattered about as food for mice;
milk remained uncovered; and he touched clarified butter while still impure from eating remnants.
The hoe, the grain-basket, the scattered vessels of bell-metal,
and all the household implements— the housewife must not look after them.
Those dwelling in hermitages who have destroyed their own dwellings do not reflect upon that; established in improper conduct, they harbor mutual hatred.
Those Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and those who are clearly untruthful—
there is no difference between them whatsoever regarding honor and contempt.
In the Mahābhārata:
"They indeed resort to necklaces, ornaments, dress, gait, posture, and immobility—
following the conduct of the wicked, like those who are dependent."
Women in male attire and men wearing female dress attained supreme joy in their sports, amusements, and diversions.

The gifts brought from various cities and bestowed upon those worthy of them did not fail to reach their recipients, even when such opportunities were rare, due to his lack of atheism and his devotion to truth.
In the presence of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, the young bride gave instructions to the female servants; and she spoke to her husband as she went along facing him in conversation.
Even with great effort, a father should indeed protect his son's wealth;
yet, dwelling in such a state of misery, he divided it out of agitation.
"Since my conduct has been corrupted by them and they have not remained within the bounds of proper behavior,
O Lord of the Gods, it is my resolve that I shall no longer dwell among the Dānavas."
Likewise: "Doves in the house are auspicious, as are parrots and mynas;
these are praised in the home, as indeed are oil-drinking insects."
Hārīta says: He in whose house these—
the first three *vyāhṛtis*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *namaḥ*, and *vaṣaṭ*—
are always present, dwells indeed in the world of Brahman.
Likewise: He whose eye consists of the Veda, whose speech consists of the sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis),
and whose body consists of splendor— how could he ever despair?
Paiṭhīnasi: For one who has offered the Agnihotra, performed his daily rites, completed his silent prayers, and is standing on the road.
Those divine worlds above which the Brahmins aspire, and all those who are indeed the seers (ṛṣis);
Viṣṇu [81.90]: One who desires dharma and has conquered his senses should practice that conduct which is properly declared in the Śruti and Smṛti and is followed by the virtuous.
Manu [4.178]: By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that, he does not come to harm.
By means of that mode of performance, one "does not perish," meaning one is not harmed. And this refers to an optional matter. Hārīta says:
"Through action one attains the worlds; through action one is released from the inauspicious."
Through action one obtains everything whatsoever that one desires in the mind.
Through auspicious action characterized by non-violence, the wise man attains liberation;
O brahmins, I tell you this: nothing whatsoever can be attained without action.
“Non-violent” means free from prescribed injury. “The wise man” here refers to one who knows the Supreme Self. “Without action” means devoid of the duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama).
Vṛddha Śātātapa says:
“One should do tomorrow’s work today, and the afternoon’s work in the forenoon.”
For death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished.
And this [rule] is intended to show extreme respect and applies to matters where no specific time is fixed.
"Whatever action depends on another, that one should avoid with effort."
Whatever may be under one's own control, that indeed one should cultivate with effort.
All that is under the control of another is suffering; all that is under one's own control is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.
Whatever action brings satisfaction to one's inner self while performing it, that one should perform with diligence; but one should avoid the opposite.

That which is under one's own control is dependent upon the request of another; and this is stated in whatever way possible for the purpose of demonstrating a commitment to contentment whenever wealth arises. By the words "the action while performing," and so forth, [it refers to] self-satisfaction. The repetition is for the purpose of making known that this is a vow (*vrata*) of the *snātaka*. Laghu-Hārīta says:
"Even in the forest, faults arise for those who possess passion."
The restraint of the five senses within one's home is austerity;
for him who engages in blameless action and whose passion has ceased, his very home is a grove of penance.
He is skillful in the sequence for the performance of the six duties:
twilight prayers, bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, study of the scriptures, worship of the deity,
the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and hospitality toward guests— even if these are performed only partially due to lack of capacity.

“Looking” means looking toward the guest. “Or even a small portion, due to inability” means that if one lacks the capacity to feed the guest, one should set aside even a small amount of food. Yama says:
What is the use of celibacy if one indulges in a wife?
And what is the use of fasts if one eats the leftovers?
What would silence avail if one speaks the truth?
And what would truth avail if one is cruel?

Hārīta says: A householder is one who speaks the truth, is always contented, approaches his wife only during her fertile period, is constantly habituated to bathing, is ever free from anger, does not cause distress to others, is not deceitful, is constantly devoted to water-rites, constantly wears the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), is constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), seeks righteousness, avoids the food of outcasts, is free from passion, greed, and delusion, is devoid of stinginess regarding wealth, and is not envious.
"Not deceitful" means free from guile. "Crooked" means dishonest. "Constantly devoted to water-rites" means one who carries a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) filled with water.

Kāśyapa said: One who has established the sacred fires, who is devoted to his own wife, who bathes and approaches her only during her season, who performs the sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, spirits, men, and Brahman; who provides hospitality to one, two, three, or four Brahmins; who is intent on vows, observances, silent recitation, burnt offerings, and mantras; who is devoted to his mother and father; who eats only the remnants of food after his dependents and children have been fed; who is not envious; who eats whatever is available; and who avoids those who weigh, measure, pierce, or inform against others—such a person is united with prosperity.

In this context, "vows" (*vrata*) refers to the restraints (*yama*). "Mantras to be recited" (*japyamantra*) refers to the *Sāvitrī* and others. "One who desires anything" (*yatkiṃcāśī*) means one who is not greedy for flavors. A "divider" (*bhedaka*) is one who causes dissension regarding the rules of conduct (*samaya*) and so forth. An "injurer" (*vedhaka*) is one who pierces the vital secrets of others. A "slanderer" (*sūcaka*) is a backbiter. [Vasiṣṭha, Hārīta, and Baudhāyana state:
"One who is constantly engaged in ritual bathing (*nityodakī*), one who constantly wears the sacred thread (*nityayajñopavītī*)."

A Brāhmaṇa who constantly recites his own Veda, avoids the food of outcasts, approaches his wife according to the rules during her season, and offers oblations in the prescribed manner, does not fall from the world of Brahman.

Uśanas: Therein, one who has completed the vow of Vedic study (vedavidyāvratasnātaka), being pure, constantly performing ablutions, and always wearing the sacred thread, should perform the daily twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at both times and be habituated to bathing.
Gautama [1.9.68].

He should be devoted to truth and righteousness, noble in conduct, a teacher of the disciplined, purified by cleanliness, and intent upon sacred learning; he should always be non-violent, gentle, firm in action, and characterized by self-restraint and generosity. A *snātaka* who conducts himself in this manner, seeking to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from misfortunes, never falls from the world of Brahman.

“Possessing the true dharma” means being true to one’s word. “Noble in conduct” means one whose behavior is pleasing to the noble. “Teacher of the disciplined” means an instructor of the virtuous. “Refined by purity” means one who exerts effort in purification. “Gentle” means free from harshness. “Firm in action” means one who completes what has been begun. “Intending to liberate” means for the sake of liberation. This is to be connected with the phrase “of such conduct. [Thus says] Viṣṇu:
[One should practice] constant service to the three aims of life, the giving of food, the worship of the gods, and the gratification of Brahmins.
Having performed the study of sacred texts and the libations to the ancestors, the householder goes to the abode of Śakra.

Manu [4.175]: One should always exert oneself in truthfulness, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity; and one should instruct disciples in accordance with the Dharma, restraining speech, arms, and belly.

“Disciples” (śiṣyāḥ) are those to be instructed, such as sons and others. “Restraint of the arms” (bāhusaṃyamaḥ) is not causing harm to another by means of the upper arm. Parāśara says: “As long as one offers oblations, studies, gives gifts, and even teaches.”
As long as he mutters prayers and worships the gods, he is called a twice-born.
[291] Yama said: The sages asked,
"What are the characteristics of Dharma, and upon what is Dharma established?"
What is the dharma agreed upon by all, and what is the ultimate goal of dharma?
Yama said:
Austerity is the supreme dharma; giving and sacrifice are characterized by the absence of greed.
Dharma stands upon the boundary of moral order and proceeds through established convention.
Truth is the ever-arisen Dharma; truth is that which is devoted to Dharma.

"Supreme austerity" means having austerity as its primary element. "Establishment" refers to the boundary of conduct. "Truth" is the speaking of things as they truly are. By the second occurrence of the word "truth," Brahman is meant here.
[He is] Dakṣa.
He who possesses a disposition for renunciation, who is endowed with patience and is compassionate, is declared a true householder; one does not become a householder merely by means of a house.
Compassion, modesty, fortitude, faith, wisdom, renunciation, and gratitude—
he who possesses these qualities is called a liberated householder.
[292] Yama said: Purity, study, and constant charity—these are designated as the objects of focus.
Having attained this Brahminhood which is difficult to find, one should cultivate these with diligent effort.
In this regard, the meaning is that one who is diligent must apply effort toward purification and other such duties. Śātātapa says:
"One should always be intent on purity, as well as having conquered the senses regarding the body."
Free from anger toward all beings, acting virtuously, and speaking kindly.
Bṛhaspati said:
Truth, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—this is the characteristic of dharma.
From dharma come happiness and knowledge; from knowledge, liberation is distinguished as supreme.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is the duty; in the Tretā age, sacrifice is prescribed;
in the Dvāpara age, ritual worship is proclaimed; and in the Tiṣya age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are the duties].

"Tiṣya" refers to the Kali age. That merit which is obtained in the Kṛta age in one year, is obtained in the Tretā age in three seasons, in the Dvāpara age in three fortnights, and in the Kali age in a single day.
Through compassion, righteousness, generosity, austerity, and celibacy,
having subdued the collection of the senses, one may attain the world of Brahmā.
Manu [4.246]: Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
one attains heaven through non-violence, self-restraint, charity, recitation, and likewise through vows.
Harita says: self-restraint, compassion, generosity, and firmness in one's vows.
They declare that for a Brahmin, abiding in noble birth, sacred learning, good conduct, and virtuous behavior constitutes self-restraint.
Compassion toward all beings is mercy; sharing [one's wealth] is charity;

and the unwavering performance of the rules for deity-worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and meditation at the three junctions of the day constitutes firmness in one’s vows. For those who observe these rules, the evil of the three junctions perishes; their austerity increases, and they attain the radiance of Brahman. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should be observant of the rules at the three junctions of the day.

The mention of the word "of the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇasya*) is for the purpose of emphasizing his particular diligence regarding these [duties]. "Conduct" (*śīla*) refers to Brāhmaṇical behavior and so forth. "Non-transgression" (*askandana*) means being endowed with all its constituent parts or being unerring. "Observances" (*niyamāḥ*) consist precisely of the worship of deities, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and study (*adhyayana*). "The performance of them" (or "the performance of observances") means at the three junctions (*trisaṃdhya*), that is, at the time of the three daily junctures. The meaning is that their performance should be carried out according to what is appropriate. Again, Hārīta says:

Stability, being known through the uninterrupted Veda, not being born of improper union, and having an unbroken lineage of seers—these are the qualities of a family. The sixfold sacred learning (*śruta*) consists of the Vedāṅgas, Dharma, knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātma*), and stability.

Patience, self-restraint, compassion, charity, non-violence, reverence for the guru, purity, bathing, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), austerity, study of one’s own Veda, truthful speech, contentment, and firmness in vows—these are the virtues.
Gautama: One should protect oneself from all [harm]. Yama: [The same].
One should indeed protect the body, the field of Dharma, with great effort;
for from the body flows Dharma, just as water flows from a mountain.
Vyāsa says: One should not become attached to sense objects; one should practice restraint of the mind. By adhering to restraint of the mind, one shall attain the world of Brahman.
Viṣṇu says:
"One should abide by means of self-restraint (dama); restraint is proclaimed to be the control of the senses. For one who is self-restrained, there is this world and the next.
Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.12.2–3.
A self-restrained man should wear garments that are always unwashed, auspicious forest herbs,
and gems belonging to Garuda.
A man should always wear hair that is perfectly clean and free of dirt, be fragrant, and dress in beautiful garments; he should also carry white flowers and remain joyful.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [34.54]:
"Nor should one wear red garments, nor those that are variegated or black;
nor should one exchange one's clothes or ornaments."
"One should avoid cloth that has been bitten by rats and that which is excessively defiled.
In the *Mahābhārata*, "excessively defiled" refers to that which is smeared with liquor and the like.
One's clothing should always be quite different when on one's bed;
indeed, it should be different on the streets, and yet quite different during the worship of the gods.
“In the streets,” meaning in places where one may act as one pleases.
[296] The wise man:
he should not wear gold uncovered by fire.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Whatever evil deed a man performs with gold that remains on his person,
that [deed] of his shall become like a thunderbolt."
One should wear [the gold] on the ring finger of the right hand.

The phrase "by that which resides on the body" refers to the ring finger of the right hand. One should not perform despicable acts with gold placed on any other limb; the intended meaning is that by acting in such a manner, an excess of sin occurs. Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
He who performs all his actions with water filtered through a cloth is a sage, he is a great saint; he goes to the supreme goal.
Likewise:
"That man who enters a temple while wearing sandals goes to the terrible hell known by the name Tāmisra."
In the Mahābhārata: One who has bathed his head with oil should not touch any part of his body;
he should also not eat sesame paste, for thus he attains a long life.
[297] O Lord of the People, one who is wise should offer pleasing unguents to one who has bathed; these should be applied separately with priyaṅgu buds, bilva, tagara,
and kesara.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, among the oaths of the Seven Sages:
"May he who steals the lotus stalks engage in sexual intercourse outside the proper season, indulge in sleeping during the day, and practice mutual hospitality with his wife."
Likewise: By bowing with a devoted heart to cows, Brahmins, sacred fords, mountains, rivers, and deities, a man is not reborn as a preta.
Yājñavalkya [2.255]:
One who is impure from eating should not touch cows, Brahmins, fire, or food with his feet.
From the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
He who indeed voids phlegm, urine,
or excrement in the temple of the Sun, the Lord, shall go to the hells in succession.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [34.30]:
"One who is impure from eating should not speak anything, and he should avoid Vedic recitation.
Likewise [34.44]:
A wise man should never stand with his feet and calves raised.
A man should not enter a burning house, nor should he climb to the summit.
One should not grind one's teeth, nor should one pinch the nose.
A wise person should not yawn with the mouth uncovered, nor should they emit breath or cough; they should not laugh loudly or make noise, nor should they release wind with sound.
One should not utter the sound "huṃ" after smelling a corpse, for a multitude of corpses is indeed auspicious;
one should not approach a wild beast, nor should one stand for long once one has risen.
O Lord of Men, a wise man should likewise avoid excessive wakefulness and sleep, as well as standing and sitting;
he should similarly avoid lying down and physical exercise.
A wise man should avoid from afar those with fangs and those with horns,
as well as frost, O Indra among kings, and likewise the morning mist and the heat of the sun.
One should not sip water for purification with one's lower garment tucked up, nor should one omit the worship of the gods and other deities;
the discharge of phlegm or sneezing is not recommended during a meal.

“In offerings, auspicious rites, recitations, and the like—not in the fire-oblation (homa), nor in the presence of a great multitude. The phrase “with one’s lower garment untucked” is to be supplied [to each]. “In the presence of a great multitude” means in the midst of a great multitude. [This is stated] in the Devīpurāṇa.
A wise person should not consume poison, nor should they play with venomous snakes;
one should employ eye-salve after first cleaning the teeth.

In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.12.6–7]: "Together with those who have married a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, the insane, those with many enemies, those afflicted by insects, prostitutes, the husbands of prostitutes, the base, liars, and dancers..."
A wise person should not form friendship with those who are excessively wasteful, fond of slander, and deceitful; nor should one travel alone on a road.
"atikīṭakaḥ" means extremely miserly; "bandhakī" means an unchaste woman.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [34.89], following the recurring injunction "one should not form friendship," it says:
"Not by those who are constantly suspicious of everything, nor by men devoted solely to the gods."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
Since space is known to be fearsome,
one should never void urine or excrement in an uncovered place, nor should one eat or drink there.
One should not engage in sexual intercourse, and one should avoid "remnants" (*ucchiṣṭa*).
"Remnants" refers to what remains after being consumed.
[As stated] in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [34.7]:
Neither sacrifices nor austerities lead to the prosperity of a man who acts by transgressing the rules of right conduct.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "He who, for the sake of one person— whether for himself or for another— should kill even a single living being, or many, incurs sin at his will."
But when one who is not auspicious is slain, and many prosper happily,
there is no sin nor secondary offense in slaying that inauspicious person.

In the Mahābhārata: "He who, out of delusion, hates the revealed scripture (śruti), the traditional law (pravṛtti), and the treatises spoken by the sages, without understanding them— one should know him to be a slayer of Brahman."
In the Mahābhārata, the words of Śrī to Bali:
"When one is joined by one's retinue in serving the elders..."
And out of delusion, a son will send his father to perform labors.
Śūdras will cause Brāhmaṇas to perform the washing of their feet,
and a Śūdra will fearlessly take a Brāhmaṇa woman as his wife.
Men will always sow seeds in improper wombs;
