there will be confusion regarding ritual vessels of white copper, and even offerings will be made with inferior bowls.
When the entire fourfold order of society becomes devoid of restraint,
then each one of your bonds shall be released in succession.

In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "One should not cause a mixture [of impurity] with one's house, seats, or household utensils with that body or its dwelling which has been struck by the breath of a god or others."
“Struck by the exhalations of gods and others” means due to the absence of appropriate worship.
[Thus end the vows of the *snātaka* in the *Śrīgṛhasthakāṇḍa*.
Now, regarding the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), Manu says [4.204]:

A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas) and not the observances (niyamas) exclusively; for one who fails to practice the restraints while devoting oneself solely to the observances falls.

And this should be understood as applying when *yama* and *niyama* occur simultaneously; since there is no distinction in their being prescribed, the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) arises. Vyāsa says: "Always—even in times of distress: non-violence, truthful speech, celibacy, and freedom from guile."
Non-stealing—these five are both the restraints (yamas) and the observances (vratas).
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and vigilance— these are the five observances (niyamas) and the minor vows (upavratas).
In this context, *brahmacarya* (celibacy) means the avoidance of prohibited sexual intercourse. "Freedom from guile" (*akalkatā*) means being devoid of deceit. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Absence of anger, straightforwardness, purity, proper conduct, and service to the teacher—these are the five observances (*niyamas*)."

"Vyavahāra" (legal procedure) is the practice of the meaning of the scriptures. Although non-anger and other virtues are already included herein, they are mentioned again for the sake of emphasis. Yājñavalkya [3.312–13]:
Celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity, truthfulness, and sincerity.
Non-violence, truthfulness, purity, gentleness, and self-restraint are recorded as the restraints (yamas).
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ,
service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas).

“Meditation” (*dhyāna*) is reflection upon the Supreme Self. “Sweetness” (*mādhurya*) consists of speaking kindly and so forth. “Heedfulness” (*apramādatā*) is attentiveness toward one’s own duties. Hārīta states:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and celibacy are the observances (*niyamas*). [304]

Having withdrawn the limbs from activities like a tortoise, the sight from forms, and speech from things to be spoken—as if one were mute—and having restrained the organs of action, the organs of perception, and the mind, one becomes non-violent (ahiṃsā).
For thus it is said: "By action, by the eye, by speech, and likewise by the mind..."
"Indeed, that which one does not commit as evil—that is non-violence (ahiṃsā), and it is fourfold. Thus says Devala.

In this regard, violence is tenfold: causing agitation, causing distress, inflicting pain, drawing blood, practicing calumny, depriving of happiness, transgression, confinement, obstructing what is beneficial, and killing.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"In brief, that which increases bodily affliction, mental suffering, or even the killing of living beings through hatred is violence."

“Agitation” (*udvega*) is mental unease. “Torment” (*santāpa*) is that suffering which, once arisen, makes one feel as though one’s very self is distraught. “Pain” (*rujā*) is physical suffering. “Transgression” (*atikrama*) is being treated with contempt. “Confinement” (*saṃrodha*) is the prohibition of acting according to one’s own will. “Prohibition of what is beneficial” (*hitapratiṣedha*) is the denial of medicine that would remove suffering.
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: “When lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and the like devour the body of oneself...”
Those men who protect [them] like their own sons go to heaven.
Hārīta says:
This speech is existent for one who is existent; by means of that which is existent, he speaks of what is existent.
That which the existent speaks is this very existent; they call it "truth" (satya).

Just as fire blazes when offered oblations of clarified butter, even so does truthful speech illuminate the self, which is Brahman, by speaking in accordance with what has been received through the food given. Now, just as one who extinguishes fire with water encounters darkness, even so does one who speaks untruth with certainty encounter darkness; therefore, one should not speak untruth. However, one is not defiled by speaking falsely in the following cases: at the purchase of Soma, during the marriage of a daughter, in times of fear, during sexual intercourse, when calming a child, and for the sake of the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas. For thus it is said: "Where there is no killing of living beings, and that which is eternally blameless..."

And that which is true by its very nature is known as truthful speech. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "that which the self speaks through speech. That thing which she speaks as being real and beneficial to herself is truth. "Causing the child to understand" means pleasing the child. "Blameless" means free from vulgarity and the like. "By its very nature" means free from deception. [Manu 4.138].
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak an untruth that is pleasant—this is the eternal law (dharma).
By this, it is stated that one should speak a combination of both the pleasant and the true.
Yama says: "Thousands of well-spoken words and hundreds of well-spoken words..."
All these together are not worth even a sixteenth part of one who has brought [the truth] here.
For compassion toward all beings is extinguished by falsehood;
even by truth it may perish where violence prevails.

By this censure of truth and falsehood, the excellence of silence (*mauna*) has been stated. Hārīta says: "Truth (*ṛta*) is the expression of what is as it actually exists. That which is not true here is falsehood (*anṛta*). That is of four kinds: falsehood regarding transactions (*paṇitānṛta*), falsehood regarding trust (*pratyayānṛta*), falsehood regarding good deeds (*sukṛtānṛta*), and common falsehood (*sādhāraṇānṛta*). Falsehood regarding transactions consists in the practice of buying, selling, and gambling. Therefore, one should not buy or sell out of addiction and the like, nor should one adopt the livelihood of a gambler. For thus he says:"
"The seller praises the merchandise, while the buyer censures its excellent qualities;
and because of their deceptive practices, the Creator has declared the gambler to be untrustworthy.
Thus, there are three types of falsehood regarding conviction: falsehood in matters of trust, falsehood as a witness, and falsehood in legal transactions.
That which one utters or causes to be uttered from a mouth of confidence is called "falsehood of confidence.
That which one determines to be false while standing as a witness—wherein one conceals what is known and assumes the role of a perjured witness—is called "falsehood of testimony.

When, between two disputing parties, one takes the side of another out of friendship, hatred, greed, fear, or negligence; and when one sets aside what has occurred and establishes what has not occurred—that is called "falsehood of worldly transaction. For thus it is said:
Through lack of trust, one destroys three; through a false conclusion, five;
but through lying in legal proceedings, one instantly destroys seven generations.

“Calamity” (vyasana) means deception; “false conclusion” (mithyāvasāya) means speaking untruth; “denial of knowledge” (jñānāpalāpa) means giving false testimony; “pair” (yuga) means birth and death. [308] Yama.
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men.
One who speaks falsely for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsely regarding land. Therefore, one should never speak falsely regarding land.
Regarding women, they say that in sexual enjoyment one is like [drinking] water; in the act of intercourse, one is like [eating] earth.
As with cattle, so it is with honey and clarified butter, as well as whatever else is produced from cattle.
As with cows, so it is with all garments, beds, and seats;
as with horses, so it is with all vehicles, including donkeys, camels, horses, and mules.
The sun and the moon, fire and wind,
heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama constantly observe the conduct of a person.
Therefore, you must never speak an untruth.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always properly restrained— his austerity, his knowledge of the Vedas, his traditional law, and his renunciation— enjoys all the fruits of these.

“By lying regarding five animals, one kills,” means that by speaking a falsehood concerning animals and the like, one “kills” five or more relatives—that is, causes them to fall into hell. The observation of increasingly severe censure is for the purpose of making known the greater gravity of the offense. “In enjoyment and sexual intercourse” means enjoyment produced by a couple. “And everything derived from cattle” refers to milk, curds, and so forth. “In all” refers to sheep and other such animals. [309] Devala says:

Untruth (*anṛta*) is of two kinds: falsehood (*asatya*) and contradiction (*visaṃvāda*). Among these, speaking otherwise than what has been seen, heard, or done is falsehood; the failure to mention things previously promised is contradiction. Untruth arises in a person from disease, hatred, fear, greed, courtesy, apprehension, hypocrisy, or even negligence.
Falsehood is especially [sinful] when intended for the purpose of harming another's life or for the theft of another's property; it is not so [sinful] in cases such as idle chatter.
Therefore, one should never produce those causes of falsehood within oneself;
or, if they have arisen, one should pacify them by means of causes that counteract them.

Hārīta says: Falsehood regarding gifts, falsehood regarding sacrifices, and falsehood regarding austerity—these are the three kinds of falsehood concerning meritorious deeds. When one has given any one of the following—a gift of food, grain, wealth, clothing, jewels, gold, cattle, horses, a maiden, land, or the granting of fearlessness—and subsequently does not give it or does not acknowledge, saying, "It was given by me," that is called falsehood regarding gifts.
For thus it is said: [310] Thus he speaks:
Falsehood regarding food destroys one's birth; likewise, two things are destroyed by falsehood regarding clothing.
Three jewels are destroyed by falsehood regarding gems, and four things are destroyed by falsehood regarding gold.
One kills five by lying regarding cattle, ten by lying regarding cows;
one kills a hundred by lying regarding horses, and a thousand by lying regarding men.
But by telling a lie regarding land, a man incurs double that sin;
and he who, having granted freedom from fear, subsequently harms it, incurs twice as much again.

If one who has declared, "I shall sacrifice," does not perform the sacrifice; or if, having envisioned a great ritual, he performs only a small one; or if he does not bestow his entire property [as a gift], in those cases the *traidhātavī* is the expiation.

But if one, having undertaken asceticism (*tapas*), does not practice it according to the rule, or practices it otherwise, or desists before completion, in those cases the rite dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*) is prescribed, or the common *cāndrāyaṇa* known as the "general" (*sādhāraṇa*). Just as there is a rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*) intended for the welfare of cows and Brahmins which is designated by its own specific name, so too it is said:
"A word joined with a vital point (*marman*) does not cause harm."
Neither in jestful speech nor for the sake of sexual intercourse,
nor when life is at stake, nor when all one's wealth is being seized—
these five falsehoods, they say, do not constitute a sin.

In this context, "wealth" (*artha*) refers to something other than the wealth already promised. "Having given" means having promised. "Commonality" (*sādhāraṇatvam*) arises from the connection with both merits and faults. Just as a lie told for the benefit of cows and Brahmins is permitted, yet a lie told for the sake of a teacher is faulty while in other cases it is faultless; so too it is with lies spoken in times of distress, or those spoken regarding thieves or insults.
Yama says: "A word joined with jest does not cause harm."

"O King, they say that there are five untruths that do not constitute a sin: [speaking falsely] regarding women, at the time of marriage, when life is at stake, and when all one's wealth is being seized."

Devala said: For the sake of performing a marriage, for the purpose of releasing a Brahmin from a curse, for the preservation of living beings, or for the sake of one's own life, one should not falter by speaking a falsehood.

Regarding marriage (*vivāre* [or *vivāhe*? and sexual intercourse: "For the sake of a Brahmin" means for the sake of a Brahmin and for the sake of laughter. Gautama [3.5.29]: "Some say there is no fault in untruth spoken during marriage, sexual dalliance, or jesting; however, one must not speak untruth for the sake of one's teacher. Indeed, by speaking an untruth to his teacher even regarding minor matters, he destroys seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants, both before and after him, through his mind."
Yājñavalkya [1.132]:
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
neither harmful nor false words; one should not be a thief, nor a usurer.
[312] Now Devala says:
Theft (*steya*) is the taking away—whether by force, silently, or secretly—of three kinds of objects: large, medium, and small.

Large objects include guards, fields, houses, gold, silver, ornaments, and the like; medium objects include quadrupeds, bipeds, food, grain, iron, clothing, coins (*kārṣāpaṇa*), tools, and so forth; small objects include ivory, horn, wood, leather, stone, earthenware, and the like.

"By force" (*prasahya*) means by compulsion. "Stealing in silence" (*tūṣṇīṃ haraṇam*) is the taking of property while the owner is not looking, without the use of force. Hārīta says: "They declare that property is of two kinds: sentient (*sacetana*) and insentient (*niścetana*). [The sentient is] animate (*saṅgama*) and inanimate (*sthāvara*). Insentient [property] also consists of non-luminous things, gems, stones, medicinal herbs, trees, earthenware, and liquids; from the theft of such tenfold [property], theft occurs."

Taking what is not given occurs through grasping excessively, through using [property] without authorization, through giving wages to servants [from the master’s share], through returning borrowed items, through denying a deposit, through seizing [property] by means of fraud or calamity, and through employing improper methods; furthermore, it becomes tenfold by including failing to give after promising and misappropriating what has been offered to the deities. Thus it is said: "By failing to give after promising, and by misappropriating what has been given, one goes to various hells and is born among the animal species."
Whatever action has been promised by word but not fulfilled through deed,
that constitutes a debt bound by dharma, both in this world and in the next.

Taking what has not been given by the owner is "taking the unstolen" (*adattādāna*). Taking more than the allotted measure is "taking what was not authorized" (*anatisṛṣṭagrahaṇa*). Using for oneself what was solicited for the sake of gods, ancestors, or humans is "using what was not assigned" (*anirdeśopayoga*). Failing to give wages after making servants perform work is "withholding wages" (*bhṛter adāna*).

Having borrowed something and saying "I do not wish [to repay it]," thus failing to return it, is "refusal to return what was requested. Denying the existence of a deposit because of reliance on a learned friend or family is "denial of a deposit. Fraudulent measures and weights constitute "deceit. "From calamity" refers to the acceptance of gold and other goods for one's own sake from those who do not practice celibacy, as well as the improper acquisition of wealth by ascetics. For thieves, when they have died, are born to benefit their former owners. Therefore, one should neither commit theft, nor cause it to be committed, nor approve of it.

“Endowed with consciousness and presided over by a living soul (jīva). That is of two kinds: immobile and mobile. That which possesses motion, such as humans, cows, and so forth, is mobile; it takes the form of the womb-born, egg-born, and sweat-born. Trees and the like are the sprout-born (udbhijja), which are immobile and “devoid of consciousness,” being unpresided over by a living soul. “Aqueous” refers to conch shells and the like. “Luminous” refers to gold and the like. “Medicinal herbs” refers to rice, barley, and so forth. “Forest products” refers to grass, wood, and the like. “Earthenware” refers to pots and the like. “Juicy” refers to milk, sugar-cane, and so forth. The tenfold nature [of these acts] will be explained according to the modes of giving and taking, and so on. “Failing to give after promising” means not giving after having promised, saying, “This shall be given by me to you. “Non-connection with a deity” means that after designating a substance for sacrifice, saying, “This is the material for the sacrifice,” there is no connection with a deity because the sacrifice is not performed. “Connected with dharma” is to be construed with “that which was promised. “Having caused [the work] to be done”—the word “action” (karman) is to be supplied. “Failure to repay” means non-returning. “They arise for the sake of assistance” means they arise in the form of cattle, heirs, and so forth—this is the ellipsis.
Yama says: By stealing a single piece of gold, a single cow, or even a single inch of land,
one goes to hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
He who takes away gold, gifts of cattle, women, or garments,
goes by turns to these twenty-one hells.
"And regarding the hells," we shall explain them in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*).
Āpastamba [2.2.6] states:

"A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who is a thief or one accused of a heinous crime is born in the next world in an immeasurable hell; [if they escape], the Brāhmaṇa is born as a Caṇḍāla, the Rājanya as a Paulkasa, and the Vaiśya as a Vaiṇa."

Regarding Gautama [2.4.14–22], who is well-known in the world as a thief: "In cases of false testimony concerning small livestock, a witness destroys ten [generations]. For cattle, horses, humans, and land, the penalty increases tenfold; for land, it is the destruction of everything. In the case of stealing [land], there is hell. As with land, so it is with water. And likewise in the case of sexual intercourse. As with livestock, so it is with honey and clarified butter. As with cattle, so it is with clothing, gold, grain, and sacred knowledge (brahman). In the case of vehicles, the penalty is the same as for horses when they are stolen."
[315] Viṣṇu [52.15–17]: Whatever a man who is unrestrained might take from others, by that very thing he shall be deprived, in whatever state he is reborn.
Since both life and the desire for the Dharma are dependent upon wealth,
one should therefore avoid harming living beings for the sake of wealth with every effort.
He who is intent on harming living beings and he who is intent on harming wealth both obtain great suffering; however, between the two, he who is intent on harming wealth suffers more.
Yama said: Hell receives that man of evil deeds who steals the property of the gods, who delights in seizing the property of Brahmins, and whose actions are sinful.
But he who returns to its rightful place divine property that he has obtained from anywhere—
whether it be the property of his guru or the property of a twice-born— he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
That which people call "wealth" is indeed these vital breaths moving outside the body; he who steals another's wealth takes away that person's very life-breaths.
But he who, having stolen the wealth of another, bestows it as a gift, that donor goes to hell; the fruit belongs to the one whose wealth it was.
But those who live contented with the wealth of others and whose lives are like hells—
for them, wherever dust might fall, that place would become more impure than anything else.
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years,
one who steals the property of a Brahmin wanders through hell.
Likewise: "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa shall fall into hell for sixty thousand years;
so too shall he who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa, and the officiating priest who is unworthy."
Bṛhaspati:
One who is subject to purification is cleansed by water and earth, and a sin is removed by expiatory rites;
however, those two—the stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s property and the misappropriator of a deposit—are not purified until that [property] has been restored.
The slayer of a Brahmin and the stealer of wealth—both may be equal, or they may not be equal;
at the end of a kalpa the slayer of a Brahmin is purified, but the stealer of wealth is never purified.
Knowing this, one should not even mentally covet the property of others;
this is especially true regarding the wives of others—this is remembered as the very essence of Dharma.
One who is blind from birth, deaf, mute, or has contracted fingers [is the result] of slandering the wives of others and seeking out the faults of others.
One who conducts himself in this manner protects his parents from great danger;
having spread his radiant fame here on earth, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

[317] Yama said: Having stolen the property of the gods, the property of the guru, or whatever property belongs to the assembly, a man who lives out of greed shall live in the next world on the leftovers of vultures.
The Caṇḍāla recited this verse: "In ancient times, Svāyambhuva Manu declared that he who eats alone, thinking 'I am the master,' partakes of much sin."
The vomit of dogs and of menstruating women, as well as that which is defiled by impurities—
this is ordained as the mode of subsistence for him as he wanders through the world.
The grammatical connection is: "having become an outcaste (caṇḍāla), he lives.
[He is] a Bṛhaspati in giving. One of dull intellect, enveloped in darkness, seizes or causes land to be seized.
Bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, he is born among the animal wombs.
He who seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another,
is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
The giver of land goes to heaven for sixty thousand years;
however, both the one who resumes it and the one who consents to such resumption shall dwell in hell for that same duration.
One who seizes land is not purified even by a thousand tanks, a hundred horse-sacrifices, or the gift of ten million cows.
Land seized by unjust means and land lost through unjust means—
the one who seizes it and the one who causes it to be seized shall destroy the family for three generations.
Brahmanical property, if consumed out of affection, destroys the family unto the seventh generation;
if consumed by force, it destroys ten ancestors and ten descendants.
One should not set one's mind upon the property of a Brahmin, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
things burnt by fire grow back, but that which is burnt by a Brahmin does not grow.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons.
A man may digest iron filings, horse dung, and even poison;
but what man in the three worlds can ever digest the property of a Brahmin?
Those who steal the inheritance of a Brahmin are born as black snakes dwelling in dry hollows within the waterless forests of the Vindhya mountains.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having received a common sacrificial fee, one who, being deluded,
takes it alone and is devoted to a state of atheism, is born as a *preta*."
Hārīta says: Those who know the Dharma understand that non-stealing is the supreme duty;
for those who seize the property of others, no auspicious destiny exists.
Now follows the refutation of the charge of theft.

Regarding this, Āpastamba [1.28.1–5] states: "Kautsa and Hārīta say that whoever regards the property of another as his own becomes a thief; so too does Kāṇva and Pauṣkarasādi. Vārṣyāyaṇi says that there are exceptions regarding the property of others: 'The fodder for camels, the food for draft animals, and the fodder for horses do not prohibit one from taking them from their owners; such usage is not forbidden. Regarding the fodder for camels, the food for draft animals, and the fodder for horses, there is no prohibition by the owner. Hārīta says that in all cases, prior consent is required."

The term *yathākathā* is a Vedic usage meaning "in whatever way. Thus, when such a thing—already taken possession of by another—is being taken away without being given, one "considers it" (*abhimanyate*) as one's own; that is, one appropriates it. *Śamyoṣā* refers to the seed-pods of mung beans, chickpeas, and so forth. *Uṣā* refers to the awns of barley and other grains. *Yugyānām* means of draft animals. *Ghāsaḥ* means fodder. However, those who "prohibit" (*pratiṣedhayanti*) or stop such a thing while it is being taken away from its owner after having been already possessed by another, [are acting rightly]. *Ativyavahāraḥ* means excessive taking. *Viruddhaḥ* means forbidden.
Yama said: There is no theft in taking wood for the sake of fire, nor is there theft in taking grass for the sake of a cow;
there is no theft in the abduction of a maiden who has not been adorned with ornaments, he who takes her away in this manner commits no theft.
Regarding flowers, vegetables, water, wood, as well as roots, fruits, and grass—
the non-taking of these is what the Restrainer (Yama) declared to be non-stealing.
A twice-born man who takes grass, wood, fruit, flowers,
or even light for the sake of cows or Brahmins is indeed not tainted by sin.
Manu [8.339] says: "Roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows— Manu has declared these to be non-theft."
“Vānaspatyam” means that which originates from a tree, such as leaves and so forth. “Agnyarthaṃ” means for the purpose of kindling the consecrated fire. Devala says:
“Wood for the fire is not theft; grass for an animal is not theft.”
Non-stealing is the fruit of the forest; non-stealing is the water of the earth.
Gautama says:
For the sake of cows and fire, one may take grass, fuel, and the flowers of herbs, shrubs, and trees by oneself; or fruits from those that are "unenclosed" (*aparivṛtta*), meaning unguarded.
Yājñavalkya says: A twice-born man may gather grass, fuel, and flowers from everywhere;
"from everywhere" means even from protected places.
Hārīta says:

There is no theft in taking two stalks of sugarcane from the first two stages of life (student and householder). Likewise, there is no theft in taking urine, feces, and so forth, or vegetables in the quantity of a handful from both hands; or from one hand alone. Similarly, some say there is no theft in taking many *śamī* leaves. Nor is there theft in cutting branches of trees that are to be protected, or in taking small amounts [of fruit], or in gathering flowers (*sumanas*) for other purposes, or in taking grass and wood for the sake of the sacred fire, or fodder and water for cows.

[323] Regarding the phrase “*pāṇyoḥ śākaparimāṇe*” (in the case of vegetables measured by two hands): this refers to vegetables measured by the space of two hands. The word “*pāṇiḥ*” (hand) is to be understood as the measure for *śamī* plants; thus, the meaning is “of *śamī* plants measured by one hand. “*Rakṣyaḥ*” means that which is to be protected. “*Arcāpinahanam*” means the covering of an image. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “There is no fault in taking a handful of grain consisting of sesame, mung beans, black gram, barley, wheat, and so forth, even for travelers; likewise for unwholesome leaves, sugarcane, radishes, and in the gathering of vegetables, flowers, and fruits. There is no fault in taking what is known [to belong to another] openly.”

“Śasyam” means fruit. “Of those with unsuitable leaves” means of those lacking nourishment. “Of that which is known” means of that which has been declared as being wholesome; this is the ellipsis. [Thus say] Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana:
“Two [fruits] of trapuṇi and vāruka, five mangoes, and five pomegranates.”
One who takes a handful of dates, jujubes, and the like incurs no fault.
“Urvāruka” means cucumber. Nārada says: A handful of rice, wheat, and other grains is prescribed to be taken.
Or even in the case of barley and wheat, or perhaps of mung beans and black gram.
Those standing on the road may take a single handful of what is not forbidden;
taking vegetables in the quantity of a vegetable is not blameworthy.
Flowers may be taken for the purpose of worshipping the deities;
however, one should know that he who desires more than this is a thief of what is not given.
“Śākapramāṇa” (the measure of a vegetable) refers to two handfuls as stated by Hārīta. Vṛddha-Manu says:
[This applies to] chickpeas, rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and black gram.
Standing on the road, those who are not bound together should grasp a single handful.
"By those who are unbound," meaning unattached and without an owner— thus says Yama:
"A traveler whose livelihood is exhausted [may take] two sugarcane stalks and two radishes."
A Brahmin who takes [grain] from another's field does not incur blame.
[325] 20 Now, regarding purity.
Regarding this, Hārīta says:

Purity (*śauca*) is the path to dharma and other virtues, the abode of Brahman, the residence of prosperity, the clarification of the mind, that which is dear to the gods, the perception of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) within the body, and the awakening of the intellect. We shall explain that two-fold purity further below. For thus it is said:
"The gods protect the pure; the ancestors follow the pure."
The Rākṣasas and others who are of evil conduct are afraid of one who is pure.

“*Dharmādipathaḥ*” means the primary path of *dharma*, that is to say, the means (*upāya*), because only one who is pure (*śuci*) is qualified for ritual action (*karman*). “*Brahmāyatanam*” means the refuge of the Vedas. It is called “*Kṣetrajñadarśanam*” because it reveals the self (*ātman*) as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). “*Dvividham*” (twofold) refers to the external and internal [purification] which will be described by Hārīta himself. Among these, the external consists of purity of lineage (*kula-śauca*), purity of wealth (*artha-śauca*), and physical purity (*śārīra-śauca*). Therein, purity of lineage is freedom from impurity such as that arising from birth or death (*sūtaka*). Purity of wealth is the cleansing of substances used for food and so forth. Physical purity is the washing away of stains from impure matter and the like.
[326] Internal purity is fivefold. Namely: mental, visual, olfactory, verbal, and alimentary. Among these, the mental consists in the absence of the fault of designating what is non-meritorious.
One who is thus skilled [is pure].
Effort toward purity must always be made; the twice-born is said to have purity as his root.
For one devoid of purity and right conduct, all ritual actions are fruitless.
Hārīta says: Seeing a man who has fallen away from purity, the Rākṣasas,
Yakṣas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and others of this kind strike him here in this world.
Knowledge, charity, austerity, renunciation, the performance of rites according to mantra-injunctions,
auspicious customs, and religious observances— all these are fruitless for one who has fallen away from purity.
Yama says:
Whatever has been sacrificed, offered, given, eaten, muttered in prayer, performed as austerity, or studied—
these are plundered by the Yātudhānas from a twice-born man who has fallen away from purity.
Śātātapa says:
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity by those Brahmins who are devoid of purity and do not wear the sacred thread, shall perish; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the holy life (brahmacarya).
Regarding this, Hārīta says:

"Brahmacarya (celibacy) consists of not desiring, not remembering, not forming intentions toward, not looking at, not praising, not speaking to, not approaching, not seeing, and not associating with divine women, human women, as well as those depicted in paintings, on wooden or earthen vessels, and so forth."

And that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is of four kinds. Among these, the constant avoidance of another’s wife is the black; approaching one’s own wife is the dark-red; approaching her except on the prescribed festival days is the red; approaching her during the fertile period is the white; and the state of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) is the stainless. Thus it is said: "By the black one may conquer this world; by the middle [red] one may indeed conquer the intermediate realm; by the white one may conquer heaven, and through the stainless, one attains liberation."

“Divine” refers to Urvaśī and others known from the scriptures. “Situated in a boat” means situated in a boat—that is, fashioned from silver or other materials used for making images. “Absence of prayer” is the lack of the aspiration, “May she be mine. “Absence of resolve” is the absence of the declaration, “I shall do this. “Absence of looking forward” is not gazing directly at her face. “Absence of beholding” is not looking at all her limbs. “Absence of union” is non-proximity. [Excluding] the observances on festival days; “on festival days” means on the new moon and so forth, and “observances” means vows and the like—these are the *yamas*. [328] 22
Now, regarding the observances (*niyamas*):

Hārīta and Yama state in their final verses that the observances consist of the restraint of anger, straightforwardness, lack of deceit, contentment, and service to the teacher. Following these are the observances of speech and the observances of action. As for the restraint of anger: from the mental affliction of anger, there arise diseases such as emaciation, discoloration, and deformity for one who is tormented by it.

Egotism, envy, malice, hatred, and the intent to harm others are forms of anger. Its verbal characteristics include speaking unpleasantly and harshly, as well as various kinds of verbal abuse. Its physical characteristics include seizing by the hair, striking with blows, and so forth, as well as causing the employment of other bodies. When one is afflicted by these, even a wise person falls into despondency; therefore, one should avoid them.
Thus it is said:
"He who, when reviled, struck, or insulted, remains patient and does not become angry,
gives over his own misdeeds to that person and receives all of that person's merit.
Here, "his" refers to the one who reviles and so forth.
Yama said: "Whatever one who is prone to anger sacrifices, offers oblations, or performs ascetic penance—all that is seized by Vairocana; his labor becomes entirely fruitless.
"Of him" refers to the angry person. "Vairocani" is Bali.

Hārīta says: Expiation (*niṣkṛti*) is restraint (*niyama*); restraint is straightforwardness (*ārjava*). Deceit (*chadma*), illusion (*māyā*), and employment of trickery (*vyāja*) constitute overbearing authority (*adhikṛti*). Harshness, guile (*śāṭhya*), partiality, and wickedness—when these are restrained along with any crookedness (*jaihmya*) joined with insincerity—that becomes straightforwardness. For thus it is said: "They call crookedness the station of death; expiation is the station of darkness."
Because he has become the self of all beings, straightforwardness is the state of Brahman.

Smayaniyama (restraint of smiling), sūnāniyama (restraint regarding slaughterhouses), sevāniyama (restraint regarding service), and adaṃbhaniyama (restraint against hypocrisy) constitute *akalkatā* (freedom from guile).

[330] One should avoid pride through the excellence of knowledge, generosity, austerity, sovereignty, and enjoyments. Those possessed by pride become bereft of spiritual luster (*tejas*). It is said that [pride] consists of the sin produced by the five slaughter-houses (*pañcasūnā*). For those who seek wealth are born like seeds as if they were already departed spirits (*preta*). Therefore, one should not establish slaughter-houses for one's own sake. Nor should one serve others for the sake of food through the practice of the three types of crafts or specific forms of service. An ignorant man proclaims his learning; a non-giver, his generosity; a non-sacrificer, his sacrifice; and one who has not practiced austerity, his austerity—desiring the status of an *āśrama* while not being a true *āśramin*. By that very act, the evil karma of those whose livelihood is such is incurred. Thus it is said:
What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self—
he who represents himself as one thing when he is actually another?

“*Chadma*” is deceit; “*māyā*” is crookedness; “*vyāja*” is the presentation of a different matter as a pretext; “*kāṭhinyam*” is mercilessness; “*śāṭhyam*” is the display of passion and so forth in the heart for no purpose; “*vaiṣamyam*” is the secret plotting of injury against others; “*dauṣṭyam*” is the inability to endure the happiness of others. These are the [vices]. “*Niṣkṛtiḥ*” is crookedness, pride, and arrogance. “*Avapannāḥ*” means fallen or degraded. “They are born like seeds”: just as from a seed a corresponding effect is produced, so too from those who are in debt (or of low character) only those of a similar nature are born. There is no fault in taking wealth for the sake of learning and such. Thus, for those of such conduct who are learned and so forth, [the term] “*pratipadyate*” implies the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).
Manu says: Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
for by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras.
After death and in this world, such a Brahmin is censured by those who discourse on the Veda;
for that vow, practiced through deceit, goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, being without the marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks,
takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born into the womb of an animal.
Yama said: Deceit exists everywhere; deceit does not exist in righteousness. For those whose righteousness is corrupted by deceit, there is no dwelling in heaven.
Austerity is not a stain; study is not a stain; the Vedic injunctions that are natural to one's station are not a stain;
the forcible seizure of wealth is not a stain.
Those very same [substances], when spoiled by fermentation, are called *kalka*.

“Kalka” means sin. “Inherent” (svābhāvika) means not adventitious (naupādhika). “Seizing wealth by force” here refers to taking possession of an object without the owner’s consent, whether through error or by action; it does not refer to mere acceptance. On this point, Hārīta says: One who observes the rules regarding slaughterhouses, one who observes the rules regarding service, one who steals or sells what should not be sold, one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, one who accepts gifts from the wicked, one who teaches the Śūdras, one who teaches for a fee, and one who is addicted to receiving gifts—by abstaining from these, one becomes free from greed and contented. For thus he said:
Contentment is the supreme duty; contentment is the supreme happiness;
contentment is the highest good; contentment is the highest fame.

"Contentment is the supreme accomplishment; contentment is the supreme happiness. Thus it is said. "Recitation before a Śūdra" refers to the recitation of the Vedas and other texts in the presence of a Śūdra for the purpose of demonstrating one's own worthiness as a recipient. "Receiving through interrogation" means receiving preceded by a formal recitation. Since contentment is the root of dharma and the other goals of life, the term "contentment" is used figuratively as non-different from them, in the sense that "contentment with receiving is the supreme dharma. Service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) is performed for the sake of the dharma of instruction. In that regard, one should perform service to the teacher for the purpose of attaining knowledge free from worldly action. The specific nature of such service has been explained in the section on the student (*brahmacārikāṇḍa*).
Furthermore, Hārīta says:
One who remains steadfast and serene in the restraints (yamas) or the observances (niyamas) goes to the most excellent worlds.
Falling away from those [states], one enters various wombs;
born therein, one sinks into agonies.
Therefore, a hero who has heard the scriptures and acts according to the law is one in whom neither fame nor virtue suffers;
for Dharma alone is the excellent companion of men.
"He who protects these from the terrible, difficult path of death.
Thus ends the section on restraints and observances (*yamaniyama*) in the *Gṛhasthakāṇḍa* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara.
23. Now, regarding those things that cause the destruction of a family, Yama, Śātātapa, Dānava, and Vyāsa state:
Through the destruction of the property of the gods, through the seizure of a Brahmin’s own property,
and through the transgression against Brahmins, entire families fall from their noble status.
“Devadravya” refers to an object that has been relinquished for the sake of a deity. Yama says: [One is purified] by means of cows, cattle, horses, agriculture, and abundance of wealth.
Families fall into a state of ruin by showing disrespect toward Brahmins.
[Manu]:
By means of crafts, trade, and having only Śūdra offspring;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king.
By officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and by acts of atheism,
families that are deficient in sacred mantras fall from their noble status to that of being base.
But families that are enriched by mantras, even if they possess little wealth,
attain the status of noble lineages and acquire great renown.

“Craft” refers to work such as painting and the like. “Trade” refers to lending money at interest and so forth. “Vehicles” refers to carts and the like. “Service” is the propitiation of others with a subservient attitude. “Atheistic action” is the conviction that there is no fruit such as heaven resulting from this action. [The following are also prohibited: being clever, falsehood, adultery, and likewise the eating of forbidden food.
Likewise, approaching those who should not be approached, as well as violence and theft;
One should avoid these nine acts: practicing non-Vedic dharma, and those excluded from the dharma of friendliness; for they are both sinful deeds and transgressions.
“Excluded from the dharma of loving-kindness” (maitradharmabahiṣkṛtam) means the exclusion of, or abandonment of, both loving-kindness and the dharma; this is the meaning.
Now, as for residence:
Bṛhaspati is the foremost among those who dwell there; the conduct of the Brahmins has been thus proclaimed.
In this world, the arising of virtues and faults is known to be born of association.
One should dwell in a place that is free from thorns, righteous, and healthy, where the ground, garlands, kusha grass, grain, young shoots, water, birds, and people abound.

“Śaṣpa” here means grass. “Naigama” means a merchant. “Kaṇṭaka” here refers to thieves and the like. “Dhārmike” means in a place abounding in righteous people. “Nirāmaye” means in a region naturally free from disease.
Āpastamba [1.15.22]:
“In a village with abundant fuel and water, or where the means of purification are under one’s own control, residence is lawful for a Brāhmaṇa.”
[337] “*Prayamaṇa*” means purification with water, cow dung, *kuśa* grass, and so forth. Baudhāyana [2.6.31–33]:

A righteous person should strive to settle in a village that has abundant fodder, fuel, water, sacrificial wood, *kuśa* grass, and garlands; one from which people exit [for their needs], which is crowded with wealthy folk, well-provided with firewood, inhabited by noble persons, and where the neighbors are not outcasts.
A Brahmin who lives for twelve years in a village whose water supply is a single well, while being the husband of a Śūdra woman, incurs the status of a Śūdra.

"His body covered with the dust of the city, his eyes and face filled with it, dwelling in the city with a self-restrained mind, he will attain perfection"—that is not so. The dust of chariots, horses, elephants, vehicles, and cows is auspicious;
however, the dust of a common crowd, of dogs, goats, sheep, and those without clothing is inauspicious.

“*Upaniṣkramaṇam*” means the path for exiting. “*Analasaḥ*” means industrious. “*Adasyuprativeśam*” means a neighborhood where no thieves are present. “*Udapānodake*” means a place where there is water only from a well; this is the meaning. “*Nagare*” means in a city. “*Puraḥ*” [338] refers to what is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [49.43]: “A city should have high ramparts with elevated walls, surrounded on all sides by a moat, measuring half of a half-yojana in width and eight times as long.”
This is the intended meaning. Yama says:
"In a village where there is water from a single well, a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman [is defiled]."
By [further] rain, one becomes a Śūdra, having resorted to a dark complexion.
“The black-colored one” refers to the Śūdra.
Āpastamba [1.32.18–21]:

One should not frequent low places or regions inhabited by those of low conduct, nor the assemblies of the wicked. If one must enter an assembly, one should approach it after circumambulating it to the right. One should avoid entering cities.

“*Kṣudrān*” refers to places where movement is restricted by water and the like. “*Kṣudrācaritān*” refers to those inhabited by *niṣādas* and other such people. “*Nagarapraveśanāni*” refers to those areas by which one enters a city. The meaning is that one should not resort to them for the sake of dwelling.
Manu [4.60–61, 79]: One should not live in an unrighteous village, nor in one excessively plagued by disease and the like.
One should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one dwell for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people;
nor in one overrun by heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not live together with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with those of the lowest castes, nor with Antyāvasāyins.
“In villages surrounded by unrighteous people”: in those villages which are encompassed by unrighteous persons.
“One should not dwell in the kingdom of a Śūdra, nor in a place crowded with unrighteous people.”
One should not dwell with one who is devoid of physicians, nor for long on a mountain that has been touched by [the dead].
Uśanas says: One should not dwell together with those who are ruined, outcasts, accused, or whose conduct is censured by the world.
Vyāsa says: One should not dwell in a place where these four are not found:
a lender of money, a physician, a learned Vedic scholar, and a river with water.
In that regard, one should certainly not dwell where these three are always present:
a person seeking victory, an old enemy, and people who are constantly celebrating.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [34.113–116]:
"A wise man should always dwell where there is a king who has conquered his enemies, who is powerful, and devoted to dharma; for how could there be happiness under a bad king?"
Where the citizens are well-united and always abide by justice,
and where the people are free from envy, there dwelling brings about happiness.
In that kingdom where the farmers generally do not live in excessive luxury,
and where all medicinal herbs are found, there a wise man should dwell.
Likewise: A wise person should always dwell among those of virtuous character who live together with him,
where the king is invincible and where the earth yields abundant crops.
In the Mahābhārata: "A self-possessed man should abandon that country where a Brahmin, when asked by those seeking [instruction], might proclaim the Dharma with disrespect."
“Of those who are waiting,” meaning those who are threatening.
Who would abandon that place where the conduct of disciples and preceptors is perfectly composed and properly endowed with the scriptures?
Where wise men, established as if in space, would surely speak of faults while being desirous of self-adulation— who, being truly learned, would dwell there?
“Those who abide in space are beyond praise;
likewise,
those places where the bridges of Dharma have mostly been scorched by the greedy.”
Who would not abandon that place, which is like the hem of one's garment set ablaze?

“Bridges of Dharma” (dharmasetavaḥ) are those who establish the boundaries of Dharma. “Cailam” means clothing. One should practice and dwell among virtuous and holy men where one may act according to Dharma without hesitation and free from envy.
One should never dwell in a place where men practice dharma for the sake of material gain, for such people are evildoers.
One should flee quickly from that place where those who desire life engage in sinful deeds, as if from a bed with its coverlet.
One should flee with speed from that kingdom where the king is not present,
nor are the king’s immediate officials, and where the householders eat before [the king]; a self-possessed man should abandon such a realm.
One should dwell in that kingdom where the śrotriyas— those who eat first, who are constant in dharma, and eternal— are those who subsist on officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
Where the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* are properly performed and proceed incessantly,
there one should dwell without hesitation.
Where one might see Brahmins who are impure because they have been driven by the lack of a livelihood,
one should abandon that kingdom as soon as one has approached it, like meat touched by a dog.
Where people, being pleased, might ask [for help] even unasked,
there a self-possessed man, having accomplished his purpose, may dwell with a tranquil mind.
Where there is punishment for the undisciplined and honor for those who have cultivated themselves— [342] Devala says:
Forests, abodes of deities, sacred fords, and shrines;
Therefore, those who die among them in this world go to the worlds of the celestial dwellers.

“A forest” (araṇya) refers to Naimiṣa and the like; “a sacred ford” (tīrtha) refers to the Gaṅgā and the like; “a sanctuary” (āyatana) refers to Avimukta and the like. These are the abodes of the gods. Therefore, the syntactical connection is that they reside in those places.
Thus ends the section on residence. [343]
Now, regarding what should and should not be spoken,
Manu [4.139] states:
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being) or simply say "bhadram" (well-being);
one should not engage in dry enmity or dispute with anyone.

“*Bhadram bhadram*”: the first word *bhadra* refers to things that are auspicious (*bhadretara-vastu*), while the second word *bhadra* refers to its synonyms. This is according to the view of Āpastamba [1.31.13–14]: “One should not say ‘*bhadram bhadram*’; one should rather say ‘meritorious and praiseworthy. [The text continues: “*Bhadram ity eva*”: in that context, only the word *bhadra* should be employed for that purpose. “*Śuṣkam*” means useless. In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.12.22–23]:
“A wise person should never enter into conflict with those who are superior, nor with those who are inferior.”
Marriage and dispute are both desired with those who are equal in status.
A wise man should not initiate strife; he should avoid dry enmity. Even a slight loss should be endured, for one must abandon the pursuit of wealth through hostility.

[344] Viṣṇu [72.72–75]: One should not utter anything vulgar, nor untruth, nor what is unpleasant, nor should one touch anyone on their vital spot (*marman*). Here, "vital spot" refers to a secret defect.

Āpastamba [1.31.8–11]: One should avoid speaking ill of cows, sacrificial fees, and maidens. One should not point out a cow that is longing for [her calf]. Nor should one point out a cow touched by her calf except on a specific occasion. One should not say of a non-milch cow, "She is a non-milch cow"; rather, one should say, "She is capable of becoming a milch cow."

“Even of a cow for which no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed,” that is, even among those cows designated as sacrificial fees such as garments, gold, and so forth; “longing,” meaning she has begun to eat grain and the like; “touched,” the ellipsis being that she has been touched by a calf in order to be suckled; “on an improper occasion,” meaning in the absence of a cause such as a deficiency in the ritual season (*ṛtu*); there is no fault when there is a statement regarding the milking of a cow for the sake of a virtuous purpose. The word *bhavyā* refers to a cow that will become a milch-cow (*dhenu*); the augment *num* is applied according to the rule: “The augment *num* should be stated after *dhenus* when followed by *bhavyā*. Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:

One should not speak of a rainbow, a halo around the moon or sun, or a meteor to another person. One should not do what is disagreeable to oneself, nor should one engage in opposition with the great multitude (*mahājana*). One should not associate with social circles (*goṣṭhī*). [345] “Opposition with the great multitude” means being contrary to the great multitude. Greatness consists in the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas and so forth. “Social circles” refers to idle conversations. Āpastamba [1.31.17]:

One should not say, "May there be no rival for me. If one were to say, "May there be no rival for me," he would produce a hateful enemy. Paiṭhīnasi says: One should not engage in conversation with those who are intoxicated, careless, or insane; nor should one converse with another's wife in private.
“*Apramattaḥ*” means not negligent.
*Sāṅkhyāyana-Gṛhya-Sūtra* [4.11.6]:
One should not converse with a woman who has recently given birth or one who is menstruating.

Gautama [1.9.17–25]: One should not converse with barbarians (mleccha), the impure, or those who are unrighteous. Having conversed with them, one should meditate in one's mind upon those who perform meritorious deeds. One should converse with a Brāhmaṇa. [One should say: "not a milch-cow" regarding a cow that is about to become a milch-cow; "not auspicious" regarding what is auspicious; "a skull" regarding a potsherd; "Indra’s bow" regarding a rainbow. One should not point out to another a cow suckling her calf, nor should one restrain her from doing so. Pāraskara [2.7.10–11]: [The same rules apply.]
One should refer to a pregnant woman as "one who has given birth" (*vijanī*); one should refer to a mongoose (*nakula*) as "with its family" (*sakula*). Regarding Yama:

one should not mention the lunar day (*tithi*) or the fortnight (*pakṣa*), nor should one point out the constellations (*nakṣatra*). One should not, without a specific reason, say, "Today is the second [lunar day]" or "This is the constellation."
Devala says: One should say "Live! to one who sneezes; when addressed with "Live!", he should reply "So be it" (*saha*).
By using the singular form "so be it" (*saha*), there is a prohibition against the arising of anger.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should not inform another that a cow is grazing or moving about in someone else’s field or house. One should not eat when it causes obstruction to cows or Brahmins. Nor should one say, “Let it be driven,” while it is being driven.
The term “obstruction” (uparodha) refers to [the act of] tending to them.
Baudhāyana [2.6.20]:
One should not utter unyoked, harsh, or rough words. Hārīta:
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf that has entered another's favorite field. Paiṭhīnasi says:
One should not point out a cow grazing in another's field, nor a calf drinking from it.
Āpastamba [1.36.10]:
One should avoid praising one's teacher excessively, such as saying, "He has bathed well.
The term "sussnātṛ" (one who has bathed well) is a praise of the bath.
Furthermore, Āpastamba [2.5.11–13]:

One should avoid contradicting the words of a teacher and those who are superior by means of one's own words; likewise, one should avoid censuring or reviling any living being, and one should avoid contradicting other branches of knowledge by means of one's own knowledge.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "the most excellent among the praiseworthy, and the obstruction of knowledge by means of knowledge.
*Sāṅkhyāyanagṛhya* [4.12.9–10]:

"One should not go to a crowd of people, nor should one sit down among them. Having approached them, even if one does not revile them, one should not be a slanderer; for it is said that a slanderer leads a family to ruin."

One who is devoted to his family and its interests, yet habitually visits the houses of others; one who is intent on proclaiming "this happened here" and "that occurred there"; as it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Among commodities, he has excellent merchandise; among cultivations, his cultivation succeeds."
It is highly beneficial for crops, and likewise for cattle, whether they are fit to be ridden or not.
One should say "it is well-prepared" regarding food; likewise, "refreshment" regarding water;
one should say "nectar" regarding milk-rice, as well as regarding barley-gruel and rice-and-pulse porridge.
When shaving has been performed, after sneezing, bathing, or eating,
and for all those who are ill, one should offer words of greeting to others.
The secrets of great-souled ones must never be disclosed; one should avoid addressing elders by their personal names or using the term "thou."
There is no fault in speaking thus regarding both inferior and equal things:

"This is a beautiful commodity among commodities"—one should say this of a commodity for the sake of commodities. "Of many kinds" means "may there be much grain," and so forth. "Among cattle, that which is for carrying"—among cattle, one should call that which is trained and fit for pulling a load "vāhya. "Long-lived" means one should call it "delightful" (*nandana*); this is the sense. "Inferior" refers to those who are younger. Viṣṇu.
One should not engage in contentious speech.
"Contentious" means having reproached [the opponent].
— Yama and Paiṭhīnasi.
Brahmins, cows, gold, water, women, and the earth—these six are beyond reproach; he who censures them is himself censured.
Hārīta says: One should not engage in slander against the gods, teachers, or Brahmins, nor should one obstruct anything being given to them.
Regarding oaths involving Cāṇḍālas, it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
May he who reviles a woman whom he previously enjoyed and who was beautiful in all her limbs be tainted by that sin, as if he were reviling one whose youth has faded.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin of the merciless man who, having eaten another’s food, speaks ill of him.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that very sin which arises from the disclosure of secrets upon hearing the words of another.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"That evil-minded person who says, 'Do not give this to him,' shall not be freed from his sin even after passing through a hundred births."
Viṣṇu [71.83]: One should avoid censuring gods, Brahmins, the scriptures, and great-souled beings.
"Scripture" (śāstra) refers to the source of injunctions.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [34.83–85]:
O God of gods, [this applies] to the twice-born who are virtuous, truthful, and high-souled;
likewise to teachers, those devoted to their vows, as well as to sacrificers and ascetics.
O son, one should not engage in slander even in jest;
one must never listen to those who speak thus when they are ill-mannered.
In the Mahābhārata: "A man who, while being reviled, does not always [call upon] the auspicious Lord Nārāyaṇa, the remover of all sins, quickly falls into the hells."
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
"To say that Viṣṇu is within Rudra, or that Śrī is within Gaurī—
that is the poetry of atheistic mortals, condemned by the scriptures."
“Antaram” means a breach or division. “Kāvyam” means a contemptible authority; this is the meaning. Yama says:
“But he who, while living, censures another and praises his own virtues,” [is a fool].
He is indeed called a usurer, and is censured among those who expound the Vedas.
Devala said: A wise man should never listen to the secrets of others in their home,
nor should he publicly disclose the private affairs of others in an assembly of people.
Yama said:
One should avoid backbiting about others behind their backs;
one should never speak nor listen to wicked speech under any circumstances.
One should never, under any circumstances, speak harsh words to Brahmins; indeed, one must never address such speech to Brahmins at any time by anyone.
One should remain silent during censure and should not offer any reply;
one should neither engage in slander against Brahmins nor cause it to be done.
Whatever is wholesome among the brahmins, practicing that very same auspiciousness,
one should cover one's ears or depart elsewhere from where the censuring and reviling of brahmins takes place.
Through slander one may become a donkey, a dog, or even a pig; by treating others with contempt one becomes a worm, and if one is envious, one becomes an insect.
“*Parokṣāṇi*” means [speech] that is behind one's back; the word *duṣṭavākyāni* (corrupt words) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Hārīta says:
“A Brahmin should abandon slander and the hinting out [of faults] among those of different castes.”
Miserliness regarding the enjoyment of things as prescribed, and [miserliness] toward one's son and disciple.

"Sūcana" means backbiting. "Paribhoga" means the enjoyment of wealth and other possessions after having treated someone with contempt. Regarding the phrase "in those mentioned," this refers to Brāhmaṇas and all the social classes (varṇas).
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*, following the word "water" (*apaḥ*), it is said:
"One should not point out these [waters] as they flow or as they stand still."
“Paricakṣīta” means he should carry it away.
Therefore, one should not speak ill of this Vāyu, that Vāyu who is the Lord;
for he indeed takes away the merit of those who speak ill of him.
Likewise:
"For that duration, the god is remembered as Ugra; however, the god is consecrated [as Rudra]. Therefore, one should not speak of him thus, nor should one utter anything vulgar regarding him."
“For that duration” means for as long as the time of initiation lasts. “Ugra” refers to Rudra. Likewise:
“But he who speaks ill of a yogin who is meditative and desirous of liberation,” [is a sinner].
He shall go to a terrible hell, and so too the listeners; of this there is no doubt.
Manu says: [One should give] to officiating priests, family priests, teachers, maternal uncles, guests, dependents, the elderly,
children, the sick, Brahmins, kinsmen, relatives, and blood relations.
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants.
By avoiding disputes through these means, one is liberated from all sins;
indeed, the householder who conquers by these means triumphs over all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the sovereign in the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.

Sisters-in-law belong to the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice belong to the world of the Viśvedevas; maternal relatives belong to the worlds of the waters; and one's mother and maternal uncle belong to the earth.
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the afflicted should be known as lords of space.
An elder brother is equal to a father; a wife and a son are one's own body.
One's shadow is one's own, but the group of servants and the daughter are most miserable;
therefore, one should always endure being insulted by them without any feverish distress.
“Kṛpaṇam” means an object of compassion. In the Devīpurāṇa:
One should not engage in idle talk with people, nor with Brahmins, nor with those who are affectionate.
There shall be no dispute with the principal person, nor any insult toward the king, at any time.
From conflict with kings, kinsmen, teachers, ministers, physicians, astrologers, and priests, one incurs very great suffering; through their affection, however, one attains happiness.
And likewise:
one should not utter wicked speech, nor harsh speech regarding rivers;
"relatives" and so forth refer to those connected to the king; "astrology" here refers to an astrologer.
In the *Viṣṭhupurāṇa* [3.12.37]:
"He who brings to peace those who are angry, who is a kinsman to all and free from envy,
and who provides consolation to the frightened— that virtuous man has heaven as a fruit that is but a minor result."
They attain tranquility.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* [41.50–52]:
"There was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms."
Whatever man, having risen at dawn, should proclaim his name;
There shall be no loss of wealth for him, and he shall recover even what has been lost.
Thus spoke Maheśvara to Nandin in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Whether one is healthy or conscious, or even one who merely recites the Name..."
He obtains the very fruit of the horse sacrifice; there is no doubt in this matter.
Devala states, continuing from the discussion on the faults of sin:

"Harsh speech, slander, calumny, falsehood, idle chatter, and cruelty—these are the six [faults] consisting of speech. Harsh speech is the direct verbal expression of a fault regarding others' country, caste, family, learning, craft, appearance, conduct, behavior, possessions, body, actions, or livelihood;
as well as any other speech that generates anger, distress, or fear."
And that should be understood as harsh, as well as anything else of that same kind.

[355] To call one who has lost his sight "one with eyes," a *caṇḍāla* a "brāhmaṇa," a *vṛṣala* a "*vṛṣala*," or one who has fallen from grace a "fallen one"— even if done with good intent, it is a fault; by speaking falsely, one becomes a partaker of double the sin.

The indirect utterance of those very same harsh words is slander (*apavāda*). Backbiting (*paiśunya*) is the recounting of faults in the presence of teachers, kings, relatives, or servants for the purpose of harming their interests. Falsehood (*anṛta*) is of two kinds: that which is untrue and that which is contradictory.
Likewise:
"In a region, [falsehood arises] from royal rumors and from the fabrication of reports."
And frivolous speech should be understood as that which arises from the context of joking and excessive laughter.
They know harsh speech regarding the private parts, the excrement, or the urine of others to be *niṣṭhuravāda*; likewise, any other base speech concerning the union of men and women is so classified.
Thus, by speaking such faulty speech characterized by these six types of conceptualization,
one encounters cruel misfortune both in this world and the next.
The welfare and harm of human beings reside solely in speech;
therefore, one should employ speech with vigilance and after careful examination.
Afterwards, a harshly spoken word becomes most difficult to remedy;
moreover, speech joined with fault will swiftly lead to downfall.
“Vṛtta” means moral conduct (*śīla*). “Ācāra” means the performance of daily and occasional rites. “Ājīva” means one’s livelihood.
O twice-born one, having called a non-thief a thief, or a thief a thief, [one incurs sin]. [356]
From such a statement, there would be an equal fault; falsely, it would lead to a twofold defect.
Whether it falls before one's eyes or out of sight, if one sees it fallen, one must not reject it; one should protect oneself by means of oneself.
The tears that fall from the weeping of those who bring false accusations—those strike their children and livestock; therefore, [this is the fate] of those who falsely accuse.
Yājñavalkya [3.263]:
The guilt of one who makes a false accusation is twice that of one who speaks the truth;
furthermore, by speaking falsely, he takes upon himself the guilt of the person falsely accused.
Āpastamba [1.21.20]:
"Having recognized the fault, one should not first proclaim it to others regarding an outcast; rather, one should avoid him in religious duties.
Śātātapa: [357]

Varuṇa may take away the luster of one who has bathed; Agni may take away the fortune of one who offers oblations; and Yama may take away the life-span of one who eats. Therefore, one should not speak during these three occasions.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.18.104]:
"These are sinful heretics; a wise man should not even touch them. Merit perishes from conversing with them, as does that which arises from an elephant."
Thus end the topics concerning what may and may not be spoken.
Now follows the procedure for departing and entering [a village]. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should not travel with untrained draft animals, nor with those whose tails have been mutilated."
Not with those having broken horns, eyes, or hooves, nor with those afflicted by diseases of the eye.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without striking them excessively with the goad.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an ignorant person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.

“By those who are undisciplined” means by the wicked. “By those disfigured by their tails” means by those whose tails have been cut off. “By draft animals” refers to horses and the like. “[When the sun] has not yet stood too high in the sky”—the word “sun” (savitṛ) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Likewise:
“And riding on the backs of oxen is in every way censured.”

Viṣṇu [63.2–17]: One should not set out on a journey alone, nor with unrighteous persons, nor with Śūdras, nor with enemies; neither too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor during the two twilights; nor at midday; nor where water is not available; nor too hurriedly; nor at night; nor continuously [with vehicles that are] afflicted by disease, nor with those lacking limbs, nor with the wretched; nor with cows, nor with those that are untamed. The term "asaṃnihitapānīyam" (where water is not available) functions as an adverbial modifier. "Adāntaiḥ" means "untrained. "Santatam" means "without rest. "Vyālaḥ" means "wicked."
Hārīta says:

"When the previous means of subsistence exist, one should not travel on a path in the dark, nor at the time of the daily observances (*niyamavelā*), nor without water, nor without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), nor alone, nor with *vṛṣalas*.

The phrase 'when the previous means of subsistence exist' implies that they are currently available. 'In the dark' means at night. 'The time of observances' refers to the time for the obligatory rites."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should not set out on a journey alone, nor when fire has fallen out [of the hearth], nor without the sacred thread, nor with a Śūdra or similar person as a companion.
Baudhāyana [1.7.7–8] states:

Therefore, one should not travel on a road without a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), nor from boundary to boundary, nor from house to house; one should not even take a single step, or at most a distance of one arrow-length—so says one [tradition]. The phrase "without a water-pot" is to be applied in every case. The mention of the *kamaṇḍalu* is intended as an illustration for any vessel for water. "A distance of one arrow-length" means a step greater than the distance covered by the flight of an arrow.
One who desires protection for the body should always go with an umbrella in rain or sun, with a staff at night or in forests, and with footwear.
A wise person should wander about without looking upward, downward, or into the distance;
a man walking while keeping his gaze fixed on a space the length of a yoke upon the surface of the earth incurs no fault.
One should not mount a faulty vehicle, nor should one rely on the shadow of a tree belonging to a noble family.
One should not go alone into a deserted forest, nor should one dwell in an empty house.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should not travel at night without a companion, nor on a wrong path or at a crossroads.
In the Skandapurāṇa:
O tiger among the twice-born, for one who enters the forest after uttering "Saunandinī," violent creatures shall never cause him fear anywhere.
[361] Jābāla says: One should not set out on a journey alone, nor at night, nor with a woman;
one should not climb a large tree, nor cross a river by means of one's arms.
Baudhāyana [2.6.21–23]:
One should not set out on a journey alone; nor with those who are outcastes, nor with those who are accused of crimes, nor with a woman, nor with a Śūdra. One should not travel toward evening;
the verb "should separate" (vyapeyāt) is to be supplied [to each clause].
Paiṭhīnasi:
One should not pass between a cow and a Brāhmaṇa. Yama: [The same].
That twice-born man who, being a sinner, interrupts another who is studying nearby,
goes to the womb of a dog, a jackal, or a donkey.
“Nearby” means within the same assembly hall; this is the intended meaning.
Baudhāyana [2.6.13–15]:
One should not pass between the gate-post and the bolt of a city gate. One should not go between two commands, nor should one walk over a rope of calves.
“Indrakīla” means a flagpole; “parigha” means a bolt; “preṣā” means swings. Āpastamba [1.32.25–27]:

One should avoid mounting a donkey vehicle, and one should avoid ascending or descending uneven places by means of one's arms. One should also avoid crossing a river by swimming with one's arms or boarding a doubtful boat.
The remainder of the sense is that one should not climb [upon it]. "Tara" means crossing.

One should not run while it is raining; one should not cross a river in vain; nor should one cross with arms [alone], by a leaky boat, or without having offered water to the deities and the ancestors.
The phrase "he should not cross" is to be applied to each [subsequent item].
Manu says: "He should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of his vision."
“A difficult place beyond the range of sight” refers to forests and the like, which are unknown because they lack a reality that is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Yājñavalkya says: “‘This is my thunderbolt’—thus one should recite the entire mantra.”
One should not go out unsheltered when it rains, nor should one sleep with the head toward the west.

Reciting the entire mantra, “This *vajra* of mine drives away all evil,” one should walk in the rain without a covering until the completion of the mantra. Viśvarūpa maintains that there is no restriction thereafter, because evil has already been destroyed by that much alone. Āpastamba [2.12.11] states:
One should approach [the fire] after circumambulating it clockwise on the ground, while it is being prepared for Agni face-to-face, [ensuring it is] not unestablished.
The meaning is that one should proceed only after circumambulating [the object] on the ground. Manu says:
"Earth, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, and a crossroads..."
One should perform circumambulations around trees that have borne fruit.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (34.42):
"One should perform a circumambulation of a teacher who is superior in learning, as well as a twice-born man.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should circumambulate cows, Brahmins, Indra’s pillar, crossroads, and well-known trees.
Regarding the injunction "one should circumambulate," Viṣṇu states [63.29–32]:

Having seen fire, a Brahmin, a courtesan, a full water-jar, a mirror, an umbrella, a banner, a flag, a *śrīvṛkṣa*, a *vardhamāna*, and a *nandyāvarta*; as well as palm-leaf fans and chowries; an elephant, a goat, a cow, milk, curd, ghee, honey, and white mustard seeds; a lute, *bakula* flowers, fresh cow dung, fruits, flowers, fresh vegetables, yellow pigment (*gorocana*), *dūrvā* grass, and a *prahorā* (a type of bird); as well as turbans, ornaments, gems, gold, silver, garments, seats, vehicles, and meat; and having seen a golden pitcher, a woman bound with seeds, a virgin girl, and fish—one should set forth.

The "Nandyāvarta configurations" are structures made of gold, wood, and so forth, resembling the growth of a *śrīvṛkṣa* tree, well-known from the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and other sciences. The "ornament of the turban" (*uṣṇīṣālaṃkāra*) refers to a crown.
As stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* [243.14–28]:
"Now, O sinless one, I shall describe the auspicious rites such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice."
White flowers are most excellent, and likewise a full water-pot.
O King, aquatic flowers, meat, and wine [are permitted];
cows, horses, and elephants are bound [as sacrificial animals], while the goat is the single animal that is not bound.
The thirty-three gods, wise friends, and the blazing fire;
O fortunate one, a courtesan, durvā grass, and fresh cow dung.
Gold, silver, as well as clothing, and all kinds of gems;
likewise medicinal herbs, O knower of dharma, barley, and white mustard seeds.
A vehicle borne by men, as well as a palanquin,
a sword, a discus, and likewise weapons made of gold or clay.
Ghee, curd, milk, and various kinds of fruits;
the svastika, the vardhamāna, the nandyāvarta, and the kaustubha.
Other auspicious items arranged in various patterns have been set aside,
as well as unbroken grains, white flowers, and a mirror.
Collyrium, yellow pigment, a water-pot, and likewise honey;
the sound of musical instruments, resonant and captivating.
The Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, and Ṛṣabha notes are auspicious, as are the Asura clouds; likewise, dense and glossy clouds with a sound like the trumpeting of elephants are auspicious.
Thunderbolts and rainbows are auspicious when occurring in the favorable direction; likewise, houses facing the favorable direction are praised, especially those facing the lords of the directions.
O knower of dharma, these are praised: faith, devotion, and likewise the honoring of those worthy of honor; and whatever else may be dear to the mind.
In this matter, the satisfaction of the mind alone is the supreme cause of victory;
on one side are all the ritual emblems, and on the other is that which brings satisfaction to the mind.
O King, where there is eagerness of mind, great joy, the attainment of auspiciousness, discourse on victory, the acquisition of blessings, and hearing [the teachings].
These should always be known as bringing victory.

“Nṛpavardhamāna” is a vehicle (yāna) provided with men; it is a throne (bhadrapīṭha).
