The svastikas and kaustubhas are specific arrangements fashioned from gold and other materials. “Anulomas” are those situated at the back. The “lords of the directions” (dikpatayaḥ) are the Sun, Venus, Mars, and so forth.

Now, one should turn back upon seeing those who are intoxicated, insane, or deformed; those who have vomited or purged; those with shaven heads, matted hair, or who are dwarfs; those wearing saffron robes, those who have renounced the world, or those who are filthy; those carrying oil, molasses, dried cow dung, sugarcane, grass, leaves, ashes, charcoal, or hair; and those carrying salt, eunuchs, liquor (*āsava*), hermaphrodites, cotton, ropes, or who have disheveled hair.

[367] “*Kacāḥ*” means hair; “*klībaḥ*” means one without semen; “*āsavaḥ*” means fermented liquor; “*napuṃsakaḥ*” means one lacking the female sexual characteristics. [From the *Matsyapurāṇa*, 243.2–12, 22–25].
Medicines that are effective, black grain,
cotton, dry grass, and fuel consisting of cow dung.
Likewise, firewood, charcoal, and inauspicious clubs;
an anointed person, one who is filthy, one with a shaven head, and likewise a naked man.
One with disheveled hair, one afflicted by old age, one wearing saffron robes,
as well as a madman, a eunuch, a wretched person, or a neuter;
Iron, a cripple, as well as leather and hair-ties,
and likewise oil-cakes and other such things from which the essence has been extracted.
Empty vessels, a dead body, a corpse wrapped in cloth,
and other such things as these are recommended for sight.
A wind that is unwholesome, harsh, broken, and terrifying, and a sound saying "Come! from the front is auspicious, but not one from behind.
"Go!"—this is said later; but to say "Go! first is censured.
"Where are you going? Stay! Do not go! What is the use of your going there? [368]
Furthermore, other sounds that are inauspicious portend misfortune on the road;
likewise, the presence of carnivorous beasts near banners and such is to be censured.
The shaking of vehicles, the clinging of garments, and likewise the striking of the head upon the doorframe or similar obstacles for one who has gone outside;
The wind, harsh and carrying grit, has arisen from all directions, blowing upon the umbrellas, banners, weapons, and likewise the inauspicious flags.
Likewise, a twice-born man who acts in a contrary manner is to be known as base and a bringer of fear;
whereas one who is favorable, gentle, affectionate, pleasant to the touch, and brings happiness is auspicious.
Those who are coarse, have harsh voices, are fierce, carnivorous, and contemptible—
such persons should be known as inauspicious when serving food or when rain falls during the festival.

“Medicines combined” refers to those such as the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) taken together. “Black grain” refers to sesame, mung beans (*māṣa*), and so forth. “Bondage” refers to shackles and the like. “Carnivorous animals” refers to vultures and the like.
Likewise:
“When a sign is seen, first there is destruction by means of the signless.”
A wise man should worship Śaṅkara and likewise Madhusūdana;
when the second [shadow] is thus seen, he should enter his house with a lamp.
Vasiṣṭha [12.42]: One should not go to a sacrifice uninvited; if one should go, one should return by walking around it clockwise.
"Uninvited" means not having been summoned.
Vṛddha-Manu says: One may go at will to pay homage or out of a desire to see the performance of a sacrifice;
one may even wander from house to house in secret, but not without a purpose.
“From house to house” means from one dwelling to another. “Secretly” means in a hidden manner. “Without cause” means without a specific purpose.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should not go to a place where execution or imprisonment is occurring, nor to a forest fire, nor to the private quarters of a husband and wife, nor to the source of the sages. Nor [should one go] to the source of the sages, nor to a place where execution or imprisonment is occurring.

“Not a crowd of people gathered for the purpose of execution or imprisonment. “A forest fire (*dāva*)” means a wildfire; one should not go near it. “The birthplace of the sages (*ṛṣi*)” means their place of origin; Mādhavasvāmin says this refers to Kapālagrāma and similar locations. Manu [4.73]:
“And one should not enter a village or a house by a way other than the gate, nor if it is devoid of ritual observance (*avrata*).”
And at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
"One should not wander about at night. Āpastamba [1.31.23]: [One should not wander about at night.]
One should enter a village by a path. If one enters, one should mutter this ṛc, "Obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the dwelling (vāstoṣpati)," or another verse addressed to Rudra.
"By a path" means by way of the road.
Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.
One should not drink with outsiders, those who are unrighteous, or those who have not drunk water. One should not eat without first giving a morsel [to others].
As stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (14.56):
"Those who travel in the same company with a man who is destitute and seeking food..."
Having set aside their own food, they eat this; these are the consumers of phlegm.
Regarding the failure to return of the sons of Dakṣa who had gone out to search for their brother, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa [1.15.100] states:
"From that time forth, O twice-born one, a brother who sets out to search for his brother perishes; therefore, a wise man should not do so."
Thus concludes the procedure for departing and entering.
Now, regarding those who are not to be transgressed against and not to be disregarded,
Manu says:
A wise man [should not show disrespect] toward deities, a guru, a *snātaka*, a teacher, or a minister.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of a tawny cow.
One should never step on one's own shadow when it belongs to a eunuch,
an outcast, a Caṇḍāla, enemies, or someone afflicted with disease.
"Prājñaḥ" means one of excellent intellect;
[this refers to] Yājñavalkya. [The verse continues:
"The shadow of a deity, an officiating priest, a *snātaka*, a teacher, a king, or another's wife..."
One should not step upon blood, feces, urine, phlegm, or the remnants of one's own body-unguents.
[373] Manu says: Having eaten at a śrāddha, or having eaten meat, one should not frequent a crossroads during midday, at midnight, or at either of the two twilights.
One should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy,
nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
“Udvartana” refers to substances such as saffron used for removing dirt. “Apasnāna” is water used for bathing. “Niṣṭhyūta” is that which has been spat out, such as betel-leaf and the like.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should not stand together with those who are arrogant or deceitful.
“Arrogant” means undisciplined. “Deceitful” means one intent on the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and so forth.
Viṣṇu [63.19–23]: One should not stand at a crossroads; nor at the foot of a tree at night, nor in an empty dwelling; nor [on] grass, nor in a pen for tethering cattle.
Hārīta states:
One should not stand upon a threshing floor, refuse, water used for ritual bathing, husks, ashes, bones, skulls, hair, or a vehicle.
[374] "Threshing floor" refers to a container such as a bullock-cart or similar vessel. "Refuse" refers to *kuśa* grass and other materials used for sweeping. "Skull" refers to the elbow.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should not step upon the footprint of a snake. Nor should one stand upon a heap of husks, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, grass, or refuse;
"saṅkara" here means refuse.
"One should not stand upon hair, nor upon ashes, bones, or skull fragments.
Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [34.25].
A wise person should not step upon husks, charcoal, bones, fragments, ropes, garments, and the like, nor upon leaves on a path or on the ground.
Āpastamba [2.12.5]:
A Brāhmaṇa should not step upon anything that has not been sprinkled with water after it has been swept by hand; nor should he sit on the ground without a covering.
Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.12.13–15, 28]:
A crossroads, a sacred tree, cemeteries, groves,
and the proximity of wicked women should always be avoided at night.
A wise person should not step over the shadow of one worthy of worship, a deity, a flagstaff, or clarified butter;
nor likewise over hair, bones, thorns, impure substances, sacrificial offerings, ashes, or chaff.
One should avoid from afar a woman who is wet from bathing or one who is menstruating;
one should never step over phlegm, feces, urine, or blood.
In the *Devīpurāṇa*: "One should not stay in an empty house, nor on a mountain peak,
nor in a cremation ground, nor ever in the temples of the gods."
One should not trust a cow that has recently calved, nor among women;
as stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (34.85):
"One should not sleep on a bed higher than [one's teacher], nor occupy a seat superior to his."
Likewise [35.30]: A wise person should never stay in gardens or similar places at improper times;
nor should he converse with wicked people, nor with women who lack heroic virtue.
Thus, these are not to be assailed and not to be presided over.

Now, regarding those things not to be looked upon, Viṣṇu [71.17–21] states: One should not look at the rising sun; nor at the setting sun, nor at the eclipsed sun; nor at it when obscured by a cloth; nor at it when reflected in a mirror; nor at it at midday.
“Eclipsed” means seized by Rāhu. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should not look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun, nor at it when it is full. They perform [the rites] for him according to the rule.
“Āpyāyanam” means worship with the *arghya* offering and other rites. “To him” refers to the Sun. Hārīta says:
One should not look at a naked woman or man, nor at the moon or sun at their rising or setting.
Yājñavalkya: One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one who has recently engaged in sexual intercourse;
nor should one look at urine or feces, nor at the stars while impure.
Devala says:
Men who are impure should never gaze upon both the sun and the moon, nor upon the stars in their entirety, nor upon other planets.

The best of men should not look upon those who have fallen from their caste, those with missing limbs, Cāṇḍālas, or those defiled by leavings of food; nor should he converse with such people, even if they possess wealth.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.12.11]:
"O Lord, one should not look at celestial luminaries when they are obscured by impurities.
Likewise:
If a man suffers a loss of income for a year,
virtuous people should always look upon the sun after first looking at him.

In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [35.33, 35]: "Having touched or conversed with those who revile the deities, the ancestors, the true scriptures, sacrifice, or the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), one becomes pure by beholding the sun."
Having observed likewise a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a fallen corpse,
a group of unrighteous women who have recently given birth, and naked men of the lowest castes;
Those who carry out the dead and those who take pleasure in the wives of others—
this indeed is the means for the wise to purify themselves.
[378] In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having seen an ungrateful man, who is despised even in the hells,
O Goddess, the Moon, Fire, and Sun should be beheld for the sake of purification.
There is an option regarding the use of *soma* and other substances according to what is possible. Hārīta says:
One who is veiled, one who is impure from eating, or one who has something unclean between his teeth should not speak. He should not look upward at the celestial lights, nor at gods or trees.
"Avaguṇṭhita" here means one whose head is covered.
Gautama says: "One should not look at another man's wife when she is naked."
*Sāṅkhyāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* [4.11.1]:
One should not look at a naked woman except during sexual intercourse; likewise, one should not look at an untrustworthy person or one who performs improper acts.
"Untrustworthy" means an enemy; "one who performs improper acts" means a sinner. The word "should not look" is to be supplied [to both].
Regarding the continuation of the injunction "one should look," Viṣṇu states (71.22–31):

One should not look at the face of an angry teacher; nor one's own reflection in oil or water; nor in a mirror that is soiled; nor at one's wife while she is eating; nor a naked woman; nor anyone urinating; nor a tethering post; nor a fallen elephant; nor a bull or similar animal engaged in combat while situated on uneven ground; nor a madman; nor an intoxicated person. Manu also says:
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease.

An excellent twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one giving birth;
so say Śaṅkha and Likhita.
One should not stand near wells or pits; one should not look down into a well; one should not leap over it.
Manu says: One should not gaze at feces or urine.
Thus are they to be contemplated.
Now, regarding things not to be given to a Śūdra,
Manu and Yama-Vasiṣṭha state first [Manu 4.80–81]:
"One should not give advice to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for a sacrificial oblation."
One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe any other vow for him.
For he who teaches him the Dharma and he who likewise instructs him in the vow— both go together with that very person into the darkness called "unrestrained."

“*Matiḥ*” refers to the understanding regarding what ought and ought not to be done. “*Ucchiṣṭam*” is the remnant of food remaining in the eating vessel. “*Haviṣkṛtam*” refers to items such as the *puroḍāśa* cake prepared for the purpose of an oblation (*havis*). “*Dharma*” refers to the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and so forth. Furthermore, this prohibition against giving the leavings of food applies to unattached *śūdras*; however, with respect to those who are dependent, it is said: “Food that is leavings and worn-out garments should be given. [10.115]

This is because it was stated by Manu himself. However, the other prohibitions pertain to all Śūdras. Since the violation of the duties of a caste (varṇadharma) through greed and so forth is already accounted for by the general prohibition, there is no need for a specific injunction regarding that. Yama says:
"He who teaches a Śūdra, and he who is taught by a Śūdra..."
Both of them shall remain submerged in hell for a hundred autumns.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra; nor the remains of food or sacrificial offerings [nor sesame seeds]; nor should one teach him the Dharma or his duty. Śaṅkha and Likhita:

One should not give to Śūdras rice-and-pulse porridge, milk-rice, cakes, meat, curd, honey, clarified butter, or a black antelope skin; nor should one give them leavings, sacrificial offerings, or anything that has been prepared for another purpose.
The subject at hand is the festival.
Āpastamba [1.31.25–26]:
One should not give the remains of food to a non-Brāhmaṇa; if one should give it, one should remove the teeth, place [the food] upon them, and then give it.
In this context, the non-Brāhmaṇa is the Śūdra. Having scraped [the teeth], he should place—that is, deposit—the dental impurities into that remnant; this is the sense.
Now, regarding the avoidance of anger and other such faults, Āpastamba states [1.31.28]:
"One should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings."
"Bhūtadāhīyān" means those things which cause the burning of the body.
Furthermore, Āpastamba [1.23.4–5] says:

"Now we shall set forth the faults that cause the burning of the elements (bhūtadāhīya): anger, joy, greed, delusion, deceit, malice, falsehood, excessive eating, calumny, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of yoga. Their eradication is rooted in yoga."

“Excessive eating” (*atyāśa*) is consuming too much food. “Wrath” (*manyu*) is the persistence of resentment arising from the desire to overcome others. “Lack of self-mastery” (*anātmya*) is a lack of self-control. “Inactivity” (*ayoga*) is idleness. Hārīta says:
One should properly restrain the impulses born of the stomach, the genitals, desire, anger, and joy.

[383] Gross defects arise in all the organs of action through which, when afflicted, one encounters various calamities; therefore, one should be pure and moderate in diet. The teachers state that "when food is pure, the inner being (*sattva*) becomes pure. Among these [defects], fire is the most intense because it causes suffering in both worlds. Hārīta, moreover, says that one should restrain—that is, pacify—them.

Nourishment is the seed of passion; its emission outside the fertile period (*ṛtu*) would constitute a fault, whereas its emission during the fertile period is explained by the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Because the world proceeded from the gods and others, the first [period] is for the sake of sacrificial observance; the second is for the sake of the perfection of austerity (*tapas*); the third is for the sake of the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*); and the fourth proceeds from intention (*saṃkalpa*), arising from the desire of the heart, and binds one through affection. That desire, characterized by longing, is of many kinds; overcome by it, even though already satisfied, one sinks into the whirlpool of desires within the cycle of birth and transmigration (*saṃsāra*) across various worlds. That very thing is fire. For the Śruti says, "Desire is indeed the Lord Vaiśvānara. Its restraint is intention (*saṃkalpa*), which has been explained.
And on this point, there are two verses in the Kāmagīti meter:
"In both engagement and withdrawal, I am the guarantor in every respect.
In all matters, I am according to reality; apart from me, nothing exists."
"He who perceives me as I truly am in all things and in all beings—he goes to the end of the path, and not others who speak of desires. Thus it is said.

Overcome by the fire of anger, one is held in low esteem even by one's own kin; one does not overcome others and becomes untrustworthy. One fails to discern what ought or ought not to be done, or what should or should not be said. Obsessed with the thought that "I shall follow the sequence," one regards teachers who speak for one's welfare [and yet leads oneself to the world of hungry ghosts]. Having experienced terrible torments there, resembling those of hell, one is born among cruel, predatory animals. There, one falls under the power of all living beings. Gradually attaining human status, one comes to be hated by all people. For anger is of the nature of *tamas*; its restraint is forbearance (*kṣamā*), which has been explained. Overcome by the fire of greed, one considers even that which is being used for meritorious purposes to be excessive. One becomes a source of ruin for sons, wives, and kinsmen, and even for friends, relatives, and dependents. One desires the acquisition of things even from those of wicked conduct. Because of the pursuit of wealth therein, one is born among animals. For greed is of the nature of *tamas*; its restraint is contentment (*saṃtoṣa*), which has also been explained. Thus it is said:
The one born of the stomach, that of the seed, that born of desire, that born of anger, and that born of the limbs—
he by whom these are indeed conquered is remembered as a practitioner of the five-fold heat (pañcatapas).
[385] The impulse of speech, the impulse of the mind, and the impulse of anger...

"One who restrains these impulses— the impulse of the tongue, as well as the impulses of the stomach and the genitals— that Brahmin they shall call most devoted to Brahman and a sage. Thus [it is said].

The preceding human activities constitute the seed of that powerful person’s *sāhasa* (bold action); therefore, through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), it manifests in many forms such as *kṛṣṇa* and so forth—all of which consist of noble movement. First, for all inhabitants of the world, from the gods down to the animals, it exists because it proceeds by its own nature. Second, it consists of total renunciation for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the sacrifice. Third, it is approaching [the wife] only during the proper season (*ṛtu*), characterized by the upward flow of semen (*ūrdhvaretas*) and the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*). "Desire" (*kāma*) is the longing for sense objects. "Intention" (*āśaya*) is repeated cultivation of thought. "Affection" (*sneha*) is attachment to that very object. "The path" (*adhvanaḥ*) refers to that which is beyond the path of light (*arcirādi*) and is characterized by the three-quarters [of Brahman].
Viṣṇu [33.6]: This threefold gateway to hell, which leads to the ruin of the self—
namely desire, anger, and greed— one should abandon this triad.
Jābāla said:
One should abandon the fickleness of the senses as well as the reviling of Brahmins; one should also cast off deceit, envy, greed, and the impulses of anger for the sake of your strength.
Slander of others, delusions, begging for one's own sake,
idle quarreling, laziness, and likewise sexual intercourse.
Āpastamba [2.5.18]:
"By means of the mind, speech, the sense of smell, the eye, and the ear, one who avoids the outflows originating from the skin, the genitals, and the stomach becomes fit for immortality.
One should avoid the outflows originating from the skin, the genitals, and the stomach by means of the five senses; that is, one should refrain from them.
Manu [4.163]: One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, disparaging the deities, as well as hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness.

Hārīta says: Eating all kinds of forbidden food, consuming what is unfit for consumption, drinking what is unfit for drinking, officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, accepting gifts from the wicked, approaching the wives of others, seizing the property of others, and violence toward living beings—these are the bodily [transgressions]. Harshness, falsehood, quarreling, and the sale of the Vedas—these are the verbal [transgressions]. Causing pain to others, malice toward others, anger, greed, delusion, and egoism—these are the mental [transgressions]. These eighteen are the actions [that lead to rebirth]. "Consuming what is unfit for consumption" means eating the food of outcasts and the like. "Nairayāṇi" means causes for hell.

[387] Devala said: Now, therefore, we shall explain the faults of evil born of mind, speech, and body. Among these, delusion (*moha*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), greed (*lobha*), intoxication (*mada*), grief (*śoka*), the sense of "mine" (*mamatva*), egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), fear (*bhaya*), joy (*harṣa*), and arrogance (*modha*) and anxiety (*cintā*)—these twelve are mental.
And among them, threefold delusion is the source of all evils.
Ignorance, doubtful knowledge, and false knowledge—this is the triad.
Knowledge consists of discernment regarding all branches of learning, the independent investigation of meanings, and being invincible to faults; otherwise, it is ignorance.
In the oscillation between the non-beneficial and the beneficial, there arises doubt;
they call this "false knowledge," which perceives what is harmful as beneficial.
Unrighteousness arises from ignorance, and doubt arises from nescience;
from both together, the most wicked form of false knowledge is produced.
From ignorance comes the attainment of suffering, and from doubt it persists;
through false knowledge, the deluded one surely falls into the wombs of darkness.
All sense objects have been turned away by defects in dharma, just as the body [is turned away] from its qualities;
having heard of them in the heart, passion is the characteristic of one who is free from passion.
Due to lack of proximity, lack of knowledge, conceptualization, and self-conceit,
as well as from pleasure, passion arises in embodied beings toward sense objects;
[likewise, it arises] from knowledge, aversion, incapacity, affliction, and attachment to others.
Through separation, through desire, through grief, and indeed through dharma, one turns back.
If this passion of a person is turned back by causes such as aversion and the like, it arises again from attachment; it perishes only through knowledge.
An excessive attachment to enjoyments becomes a source of harm,
even when it involves merely a slight longing for the wives or the property of others.
Anger, intolerance, envy, malice, false reflection,
and that which deserves suffering— thus hatred is classified by the knowers of reality as being sixfold.
That which arises in the heart of a living being as a transformation,
consisting of the desire to do harm to another and accompanied by anger, is designated as "saroṣa" (with wrath).
Impelled by the very fault arising from defeat,
whatever hatred one feels upon seeing even a slight thing— that is the definition of intolerance (amarṣa).
But when one, out of hatred, does not rejoice upon seeing another's pure qualities that surpass one's own, that is declared to be *abhyasūyā* (envy).
He who constantly seeks to destroy the interests even of his friends—
those call him a wicked man of unfriendly mind, characterized by malice.
When one considers the faults of others to be malicious toward the virtuous,
and regards that [perception] as a false conceptualization, they say that it arises from the defect of mental disposition.
Reflection on evil deeds arising from hatred, greed,
and intention should be understood as resulting from past misdeeds and deserving of suffering.
Due to suffering and due to false frustration, this [suffering] becomes twofold;
it ceases through knowledge, through the passing of time, through dharma, and through joy.
Grasping at what is not reality, burning heat, trembling, confusion of knowledge, perspiration, eye disease, harshness, and labored breathing— these arise from the fault of hatred.
He who considers himself superior to all in every respect should be known as pride (māna), which is the cause of the ruin of one's desired goals.
The excellence of a man that arises from the conceit of self does not shine;
they say that begging is true excellence, for such excellence is free from humiliation.
The thirst that arises upon seeing or hearing of the wealth, enjoyments, and even the great prosperity of others for one's own sake— that indeed is greed.
From lack of greed and from fundamental reasoning, thirst is increased;
deluding one regarding very harmful things, greed cooks the wicked man.
There is no suffering equal to craving, and there is no happiness equal to renunciation;
therefore, a wise person should abandon craving, which is known as greed.
Even having obtained the entire earth, craving is indeed not appeased;
it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
They say that thirst is never beneficial, because it is painful, because it is finite, because it is impermanent,
because it brings no satisfaction, and because it leads to sorrow later on.
When one is oppressed by others through their own family status, prosperity, learning, wealth, power, and splendor, that is the characteristic of madness in this world.
The causes of the arrogance and intoxication of gods, asuras, and humans—those very beings perished through that same intoxication; therefore, intoxication should be abandoned by the wise.
Joy, the sight of sorrow, hypocrisy, arrogance, and pride— these and other such states are the conceptual variations born of intoxication (mada).
Suffering in the heart arising from aversion born of union with the undesirable, or from attachment born of union with the beloved, or from affliction— that is designated as sorrow (*śoka*).
All phenomena are impermanent, and thus sorrow does not exist therein;
or, if they were permanent, from what could sorrow arise?
For one established in *sattva*, or even one who is purely *tāmasa*, does not grieve in this way;
in brief, it is the *rājasa* person here who, through grief, incurs suffering.
He who, regarding himself as the owner, thinks "this is mine" with respect to his own things,
while being ignorant of impermanence— that, they know, is called the sense of "mine-ness."
That which proceeds toward actions involving cause and effect through the conceit "I am" is the definition of egoism (ahaṃkāra).
All embodied beings are oppressed by the notions of "I" and "mine" during their various engagements in saṃsāra; however, one who is liberated from these two is truly liberated.
When one hears of or sees something threatening to oneself present before one,
that agitation which arises in the heart is known as fear.
One should not fear as long as the danger has not arrived;
but having seen that the danger has arrived, one should act without fear.
"What is to be must indeed come to be; there is no bypassing of karma. For those who have thus seen reality, fear never arises at any time.
Upon seeing one’s own heart and the misfortunes of others,
the mental joy of a living being is designated as "delight" (harṣa).
When one reflects and perceives that all things are impermanent, momentary, and devoid of happiness, there is no occasion for joy.
Even neutrality is a fault when others encounter calamity;
how much more so is rejoicing with a foolish mind during their total destruction?
He who vainly contemplates various matters with his mind is said to engage in "futile reflection," which destroys both dharma and one's actions.
He who, out of greed, pursues enjoyments, power, wealth, and the like in vain,
destroys himself through futile thought, as well as his intellect and his actions.
Therefore, having abandoned far-reaching anxiety and the sorrow born of action,
one should undertake auspicious deeds in every way in order to attain wisdom.
The wise man, having uprooted those thoughts born of passion that are firmly established in the heart,
destroys them with the sword of knowledge of reality as an oblation.
One should contemplate with the mind the means for protecting oneself, the impermanence of the body, and what is beneficial for all living beings.
These mental states are defects, the twelve causes of inauspiciousness;
they are declared to be delusion and the rest, which delude gods, asuras, and humans.
Through union with that [mind], by guarding the mind, through devotion to knowledge and dharma,
and by abandoning vices and the like, human beings attain liberation from suffering.
Likewise: First, born of evil, there arises in the hearts of embodied beings from delusion a darkness that obscures the intellect on all sides and renders it incapable of illumination.
From delusion arises passion, and from passion hatred is born;
through these three, there thus comes to be evil consisting of body and speech.
Therefore, among all mental states, these three are the most serious;
to abandon all faults, one should first renounce these three.
Having described the faults of sin pertaining to speech, Devala further states regarding the persistence of such faults:

"There are four types of bodily sins: violence, misconduct, theft, and the corruption of wealth. The corruption of wealth consists of the destruction of what has been done and the ruin of property. Specifically, the burning of houses, fields, or crops, the breaking of embankments, and the destruction of one's livelihood constitute the destruction of what has been done. The ruin of property constitutes the corruption of wealth.
Having categorized these various types of offenses according to their specific characteristics, one should proceed to deal with them as previously described.
The remaining sins have been specifically declared.
Manu [4.162, 165–169]: One should not harm one's teacher, a reciter of the Veda, a father, a mother, a preceptor, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
A twice-born man who, desiring to kill, merely threatens a Brahmin or others,
shall wander in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [a being] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in evil wombs, devoid of higher rebirths.
By inflicting great suffering upon a compassionate Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting,
a man, through his lack of wisdom, attains immense misery after death.
For as many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth,
for that many years shall the one who shed that blood be devoured by those very beings in the world beyond.
Therefore, a wise man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.

Likewise, Manu (11.206) and Yama state: "But having merely threatened a Brāhmaṇa, one enters hell for a hundred years; but having struck him with the intent to kill, one enters hell for a thousand years."
Likewise, [11.207]:
"For as many particles of dust as the blood of a twice-born man takes up,
for that many thousands of years shall the one who caused it remain in hell."
"Non-birth" refers to births; "therein" means in the next world; "is eaten" means is consumed. Uśanas says: "One should not cause distress to a Brāhmaṇa."
Yama said: "That man who, having defeated a Brahmin in debate, experiences joy,
shall become a tree in a cremation ground, frequented by vultures and herons."
Hārīta says:
The gods, the worlds, as well as the Vedas, the cows, and likewise the sacrifices—
these are established most abundantly in Brāhmaṇas in all their respective places.
For these are honored by those who honor them, and they are hated by those who hate them;
they are indeed censured by those who censure them. Therefore, the brahmin is the presiding deity.
Furthermore, Hārīta says:
Fire situated nearby burns the body by its very heat;
likewise, a Brahmin may burn his own excellence, well-being, natural state, and fame through his wrath.
Fire burns what is near, but a twice-born man burns from afar;
therefore, one should honor him according to the rules, for he is indeed more intense than fire.
What is cut by a weapon heals; what is burned by fire heals;
but for one consumed by the anger of a Brahmin, no healing exists at all.
One should always feed the Brāhmaṇas and always honor the Brāhmaṇas;
through the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, one shall attain peace in every respect.
Just as a great ship launched upon the ocean swiftly carries those who are sinking across that difficult passage,
so too do the twice-born here, being joyful, [carry others] across in an instant.
They would rescue [others] even from a great calamity.
"One should honor" by means of prostration and so forth. Manu [4.164]:
"One should not inflict punishment upon another when angry; one should not strike him down."
Except for a son or a disciple, for the sake of instruction, one may strike them there.
"This" refers to the staff. "For the sake of correction" means for the purpose of instruction. "Therein" refers to the case of the son and the pupil. Yājñavalkya [1.155]:
One should not perform censure or beating; rather, one should strike the son and the pupil.
[Manu 4.141] One should not mock those who have missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those deficient in learning, those superior in age, those lacking beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.

Viṣṇu [71.1–3]: One should not show contempt for anyone, whether they have missing limbs or extra limbs. Nor should one mock those who are foolish or destitute. Likewise, one should not despise a woman. One should not hold those who are inferior in low esteem.
One should never, under any circumstances, treat with contempt a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are seen to be emaciated.
For these three, when treated with contempt, utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should not treat them with contempt with any effort.
One should not despise oneself because of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity, and one should not consider it unattainable.
Śaṅkha and Likhita: One should not treat the learned with disrespect. Baudhāyana [2.4.25–27]:
One should completely avoid wretchedness, deceit, and crookedness.
Furthermore, in this regard, they cite a verse from the dialogue between Uśanas and Vṛṣaparvan’s daughter:
"You are indeed the daughter of one who praises, begs, and accepts."
Then, while I was being praised, I gave without accepting anything in return.
Devala says:
One should not curse oneself; being free from disease, one should not sleep during the day;
one should not scratch the earth with one's nails, nor should one lie down with cattle at night.
One should not speak of a river while among rivers, nor of a mountain while among mountains;
likewise, while staying at sacred fords or shrines, one should not praise anything else.
One should not abandon a companion in matters of lodging or food;
one should follow gods, kings, and sages for at least seven steps.
A wise man should not revile or despise brahmins, kings, the learned, cows, or even children; he should honor them as if they were deities.
One should not plunge into water naked, nor should one step over fire with the feet;
one should not smear the limbs with oil that remains after anointing the head.
The word "not" (*na*) is to be supplied here. Viṣṇu [states]:
"One should not play with snakes nor with weapons."
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own orifices without a reason;
he should avoid touching all the hairs of the private parts as well.
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others.

Vasiṣṭha [6.33, 35, 41, 42]: One should not practice scratching the limbs with the fingernails, nor should one drink water from the hollowed palms. One should not learn the speech of barbarians. Furthermore, they cite this: One should not be fickle with one's hands and feet, nor should one be fickle with one's eyes.
Nor is one who is fickle in speech and limb within the sphere of the cultured.

Gautama [19–49–51]: One should not drag [anything] with the foot or the mind. One should not make the genitals, the belly, the hands, or the feet restless. One should not, without cause, perform cutting, piercing, scratching, rubbing, or the cracking of limbs.
"Avasphoṭana" refers to the cracking of the joints of the hands and other limbs.
Manu [4.63–64]: One should not engage in useless exertion, nor should one drink water with cupped hands;
one should not eat food placed in one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
One should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
one should not clap hands, nor shout, nor utter cries while overcome by passion.

“Clapping” (*āsphoṭana*) is the striking of the armpit with the hand; “roaring” (*kṣveḍana*) is the lion’s roar; “passionate” (*saṃrakta*) means exhilarated; “shrieking” (*virāva*) is a distorted sound. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One should not scratch the ground, nor strike it with one’s foot.”
Yama says: One should never sing, nor dance, nor play with dice;
one should not play musical instruments, nor ever shout.

[401] One should not snap one's fingers, nor run, nor act with excessive rashness. Hārīta says: One should not void urine or excrement on a path, nor cast down stones. One should avoid pulling out grains of rice, crushing clods of earth, scratching lines in the ground, and playing with fingernails or teeth as if on a lute. One should avoid displaying one's own wretchedness. Likewise, one should avoid wearing garlands or applying unguents, various negligent behaviors, and the consumption of intoxicants or white substances (such as opium).
"Niṣkṛṣaṇam" means removing the husks with the fingernails. "Avalopa" means pride or arrogance. Regarding Yama:
one should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one remain naked in a place.
One should never sleep naked, nor should one go to bed while still impure from food.
One should not walk away, nor recite [the Veda], nor likewise touch one's head; one should not refuse curd or jasmine flowers, nor oneself.
One should not remove a garland from another, nor should one wake one who is asleep.
The heat of the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided.
One should not clip one's nails or hair with the teeth, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.
One should not pick up a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless action, nor anything that results in unhappiness in the future.
The man who eats clods of earth, who cuts grass, who bites his nails, who is a slanderer, and who is impure— he quickly goes to destruction.
Regarding the continuation of the rule "one should avoid," Āpastamba [1.32.28] states:
"The cutting of grass, the crushing of clods of earth, spitting, and whatever else the learned (śiṣṭas) censure when done without cause.
"Without cause" means without a specific purpose, that is, by whim; the remainder of the sense is that "the learned avoid" these acts.
Furthermore, Āpastamba [2.12.12]:
One should not let one's two hands touch each other behind one's back.
Yājñavalkya [1.138]:
One should not play with dice, nor sleep with those who destroy dharma or those who are diseased;
one should avoid forbidden actions, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and crossing a river [by swimming].
[403] “Crossing a river” means crossing a river; the sense is that one should avoid doing so by means of one's arms.
Manu [4.74]: One should never play with dice, nor should one carry sandals oneself.
Likewise [4.57]:
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a sleeping person. One should not speak with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice uninvited.
Āpastamba [2.20.12–17]:

One should avoid washing one foot with the other, and likewise stepping upon it; as well as swinging the feet, placing the foot upon the knee, or scratching the nails with the nails; nor should one snap the fingers without cause, or whatever else is censured in this regard. "Swinging" means moving them here and there. "Placing upon" means resting [the foot] on top [of the knee].
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
"One should not wash one's feet with the foot; nor should one wipe them with *darbha* grass. Viṣṇu [71.37–39]:
One should not warm one's feet [over a fire]. One should not wipe them on *kuśa* grass. One should not wash one's feet in a bronze vessel. Yama says:
"One should not wash one's feet in bronze where food is also kept."
Gautama [9.12–13]:
One should not discharge urine, feces, or other impurities while looking toward the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, a deity, or cows; nor should one stretch out one's feet toward these deities.
Āpastamba [1.31.25].
One should not, within one's power, extend one's feet toward fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, or the door of a deity.
The word "feet" is to be understood as the subject.
— Hārīta.
One should not stretch out one's feet in the presence of gods, teachers, cows, or Brahmins.
Devala says: [One should avoid] sleeping, bathing, Vedic study, or using vehicles and carriages while impure.
And one should by no means go outside at all.
One should always avoid sleeping, studying, bathing, walking on a road, eating, and traveling during both twilights and at midday.
Yājñavalkya [1.155]:
One who has not washed after eating should not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food with his feet.
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
One should not step over fire, a cow, or a Brāhmaṇa with one’s foot.
Āpastamba [1.31.4–7]:

One who is impure should avoid uttering the names of deities; likewise, one should avoid harsh speech toward both deities and kings. One should avoid touching a Brāhmaṇa or a cow with the foot, as well as touching them with the hand without a specific reason.

The plural number in the phrase "of the deities" (*devatānām*) is used to denote a class. "Of both" refers to the deity and the king. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One who is impure shall not tend the fire; he shall not recite the names of the sages, ancestors, or deities; he shall not plunge into water that is knee-deep; he shall not drink water with his cupped hands; and he shall not hold water and fire together in one place.

“Ancestors” refers to those such as the Agniṣṭattas; “deities” refers to Viṣṇu and others. “On one side” means on one hand or similar limb. Vṛddha-Śātātapa states: “A Brāhmaṇa who is weak in knowledge [should eat] with the hand that is currently available.”
If one drinks water with the mouth, breathlessness will arise; it cannot be otherwise.
If a twice-born man drinks water that he has drawn up with his left hand,
Manu, the Lord of Creatures, has declared that it is equal to the drinking of liquor.
In the context of the term "unfit to be eaten," Vasiṣṭha [14.36] states:
"Water within a navigable river.
This means that water situated in a boat is not to be drunk.
Āpastamba [2.12.9–10]:
One should not hold fire and water simultaneously. One should also avoid the mixing together of different fires.
"Mixing" (*saṃnivāpa*) means contact.
Gautama [9.9–11]: One should not let water come into contact with impure substances; one should not drink from one's cupped hands; one should not stand [in water]. Hārīta.

One should not enter the water naked; one should not spit; one should not cross over it without having sipped water (ācamana); one should not drink water with cupped hands; one should not perform any ritual act with water that has not been drawn out; and one should not discharge semen, urine, or excrement into the water. Manu [4.56]:
"One should not discharge urine, excrement, or spittle into the water."
Whether it be smeared with impurity, or something else, or blood, or poisons.
[407] Āpastamba [1.30.22]: One should avoid spitting and acts of sexual intercourse in water. Yama:
One should not step across a flowing river, nor likewise over a blazing fire;
one should certainly not cut down a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), nor should one void excrement where the ground is dry.
Neither semen, nor poison, nor urine, nor blood;
neither bone, ashes, nor a skull; nor hair, nor snot, nor nails.
Manu [4.53–54]: One should not blow on the fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one’s feet over it.
One should not place it underneath, nor should one step over it;
one should not make it speak, nor should one cause injury to living beings.
Āpastamba [1.15.18–21]: One should not sit upon fire while impure. Others say [it should be at a distance] of one arrow-length. Nor should one blow upon it. Nor should one place it on a bed.
Regarding "at a distance of one arrow-length" and so forth, the phrase "blowing from a measured distance" is to be supplied [to each].
Paiṭhīnasi: One should not climb a tree that has not flowered. Devala: [same].
One who is impure should not first look [at the fire]; one should not rub one foot with the other;
one should not throw anything nakedly into the fire, but rather extinguish it with water.

One should not cause injury to the vital breaths of others by means of impure acts and the like; nor should one cause others to hear of the grief arising from the death of a friend, unless it be without malice.
One should not oppress friends through aggression or out of sheer folly;
for even a poor man endures the suffering caused by his friends out of a sense of courtesy.
Living beings must not be harmed, nor should one cause them to be killed through afflicted violence; one should not employ for sale anything that is unfit for trade or anything tainted by leprosy.
One who knows the true nature of Dharma should not kindle a fire with his breath,
nor should he point a weapon at a cow, a guru, a woman, or a child in vain.
One should not plow a sacred site, a water source, or the boundary line;
nor should one ever break a prior agreement that has been entered into.
Indeed, lack of trust becomes most sinful through the breach of agreements;
likewise, when a deposit or a sealed pledge has been received, one should restore it accordingly.
The Noble Ones declare that the removal [of merit] after having given is like the gateway to hell;
the most wicked man who would engage in sexual intercourse with those of animal birth [falls there].
Furthermore, by entering into improper wombs, he is born again among those of base birth;
one should not cause animals, fools, or birds to fight with one another.
One should not cause harm to others by means of water, windows, or other such devices;
nor, having caused artisans to perform their work, should one later deceive them.
One should provide them with food and wages in accordance with their work;
one should not invite them elsewhere, except from the house next door or the house beyond.
If a house is on fire, one should proceed with haste toward the water nearby.
In the evening and in the morning, one should not knock at the door of a house for the sake of alms.
A husband should not allow his daughter to dwell long in the house once she has attained her fruit [i.e., given birth].

“Defiled by malice” (*kliṣṭāghātam*) means preceded by much affliction for the sake of futile delusion. “Deposit” (*nikṣepa*) refers to property handed over openly. “Entrustment” (*upanidhi*) refers to that which is handed over covered with cloth or the like, its nature being undisclosed. “Water-pipe” (*jalāyana*) refers to a conduit for water and so forth. “Wind-pipe” (*vātāyana*) refers to a window. “Artisans” (*kārūn*) refers to laborers. “By the neighboring house and the adjoining house” (*prativeśmānuveśmābhyām*) is an indication of houses in close proximity. “For the sake of alms” (*bhikṣārtham*) means for the purpose of obtaining alms. “One should not strike against” (*nāvaghaṭṭayet*) means one should not obstruct it. The “owner” (*svāmin*) here refers to the father or others. “One who has obtained fruit” (*prāptaphalām*) means one fit for the fruits of pleasure and progeny.

Paiṭhīnasi: One should not stand while eating; one should not laugh or chatter; one should not step over fire; [one should not blow on it with the mouth]; one should not touch a blazing fire with both hands; and one should not bathe for a long time in water. Uśanas:

One should avoid crossing, wading through, climbing over, embracing, or conversing with full rivers, trees, hollows, crossroads, and the wives of others. "Full" (*pūra*) refers to a swollen flow of water. "Hollow" (*nikuṭa*) refers to a tree cavity. One should avoid crossing or wading through full rivers; one should avoid "climbing over" (*atirohaṇa*), meaning excessive treading upon, hollows and crossroads; and one should avoid embracing or conversing with the wives of others. These one should abandon. [411] Āpastamba [1.30.14].
And during the day, one should avoid covering the head, except when voiding urine or excrement. Gautama [9.36–37] states:
"One should not wander about during the day with the head covered; one may do so at night. Likewise, one should not fan oneself with a cloth."
[412] 31 Now, the avoidance of others' wives and so forth.
In this regard, Manu [4.134] states:
"There is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife."
Vyāsa says: One should always be devoted to one's own duties and devoted to one's own wife;
by serving the wives of others, there is rebirth in hell for those engaged in such acts.
Uśanas:
One should not approach the wife of another. Yama: [The same].

One should not have sexual intercourse with another's wife. Devala says: "Approaching those who should not be approached is a transgression. Regarding another's wife, however, those who should not be approached include a woman of a higher caste, one's own sister, one's daughter, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), a *caṇḍālī*, an outcaste woman, a female ascetic, and those of animal birth.
Violating even marriageable maidens is said to be a sin;
however, if one subsequently takes her, it may be considered a Gandharva marriage according to the agreement.
“Of those who are approachable” means those fit for marriage. “Corruption” refers to embracing, kissing, and so forth.
Yājñavalkya [1.160]:
One should avoid the beds, seats, gardens, houses, and vehicles of others.
One should not eat the food of one who has not maintained the sacred fires, unless there is an emergency.
“Ungiven” means not permitted.
Manu [4.202]: “His vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, and houses...”
One who enjoys things that have not been given shall incur a fourth part of the sin.
Thus ends the avoidance of others' wives and so forth.
Now, regarding the avoidance of intermixture, Bṛhaspati [Āpaddharma, 52] says:
"Having entered the womb of a Brahmin, one should avoid intermixture."
Human birth is superior in the world; the status of a Brahmin is superior even to that.

[Prāyaścitta 24–25] Sharing a bed or seat, sitting in the same row, mixing vessels or cooked food, officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching, marriage alliances, and likewise eating together.
The ninefold intermixture has been declared; one should not associate with the base, but rather with the superior or with equals.
"Yoni" here refers to a blood relationship. "Eating together" means eating from the same vessel.
Yama says: One should protect one's Brahminhood by avoiding association with those of different lineages.
From wicked legal proceedings and likewise from the seizure of wicked persons.
From impure actions and from association with the impure—
these causes leading to such association have been proclaimed by the virtuous.
Through association, through physical contact, through sharing a bed,
through eating together, through conversation, and through living together, evil is transmitted among men.
Likewise:
"Dvijas who are defiled by contact with vessels, by confusion of wombs,
or by confusion of food, indeed go to a degraded birth."
Likewise: "The womb of Brahman is difficult to attain through intermixture and not otherwise;
the state of Brahman is not easily obtained; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should be awakened [to this truth]."

“Corrupt persons” (*duṣṭāḥ*) refers to those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) and so forth. “Social interaction” (*vyavahāraḥ*) refers to such things as visiting each other’s homes. “From evil ones” (*aśubhebhyaḥ*) means from thieves and the like. “By impure things” (*aśubhaiḥ*) means by unclean substances such as blue or red dyes. “Those resulting from contact” (*saṃsargagāminaḥ*) refers to the sins that will be described which proceed through contact. “Connection” (*saṃbandhaḥ*) refers to matrimonial ties and the like. Hārīta says:
“From conversation, from the touch of the body, and even from the breath...”
But by sharing a single vehicle or a single seat, sin is transferred among men.
The impure may destroy the pure, but the pure shall purify the impure;
for the impure one, who is like darkness, becomes purified through dwelling with the pure.
Between those two, purity and impurity are traditionally held to be determined by whichever is more predominant here.
Baudhāyana [2.5.9]:
Those who mix with their teachers, those who mix with their pupils,
and those who mix even in matters of food alone, dwell for a long time in darkness.

Hārīta says: Some maintain that drinking-vessels, beds, and seats are not to be avoided, on account of their specific color, because we observe the mingling of the pure with the impure, and because of the possibility of the transmission of disease through contact with sin. Therefore, those who are purified separately are superior. When purification is otherwise impossible, they prescribe that one should cover [the object] and then use it. In the case of extreme contact, one must bathe with one's clothes on. For thus he says:
"One should employ a seat, a bed, or a drinking-vessel after having covered it."
One should not wear the sacred thread, sandals, or garment that have been worn by others.
The Brāhmaṇas do not even prescribe eating together with their own kin;
due to the risk of attachment and the fault of ritual actions, they likewise maintain other forms of purity separately.

From the specific nature of the substance, there is a distinction between the white and the soiled; a change in color is observed through contact. "In its own impossibility" means when one's own seat is unavailable. "Having covered with a pure [garment]" refers to a clean cloth or similar item. "The *brahmasūtra*" is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). One should never wear that which has been worn by another. However, shoes and garments, once washed, may be worn over [one's own]. This is because of the statement of Gautama: "when unable to wash them. "Eating together" means in a single vessel or in a row. "With one's own" means with one's kinsmen. "By association" means even with another who has committed a sinful act, since there may occasionally be an occasion for eating due to constraints or other such reasons.
Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 93, 96]:
Those who sit in a single row and do not touch one another,
having established a boundary with ashes— between them there shall be no confusion of status.
By fire, by ashes, and especially by water,
as well as by a door and by the path of a pillar— by these six, a row is divided.
Thus ends the avoidance of confusion.
Now, regarding those who should not be abandoned and those who may be abandoned, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The mother, the father, and the sapinda relatives, provided they are virtuous, are not to be abandoned; indeed, all [these] are not to be abandoned."
“Virtuous” means those distinguished by learning and conduct.
Devala says:
[One should not eat with] a father, a brother, a son, a daughter, a sister, or a daughter-in-law.
One should not, out of hatred or greed, abandon even one's own wife, provided she has not fallen from her status.
Indeed, the abandonment of one's mother is not taught in the scriptures under any circumstances;
whether she be outcasted or accused of a crime, a mother does not deserve to be abandoned.
Men who are elders by lineage, elders by knowledge, elders by age,
and elders by virtue should be honored according to the weight of their own respective qualities.
The term "not fallen" (*apatitān*) is a qualifier in every instance. Hārīta says:
"The father is the progenitor; by mortals, the teacher of one's own Vedic recitation (*chandas*) is called the *ācārya*."
Having encircled it, he produces it; or rather, the Adhvaryu places the fire.
Therefore, one should always honor these elders and not abandon them;
for by abandoning them, one does not attain the desired worlds.
In the case of impurity, however, there is abandonment [of the teacher] when he commits a mortal sin or officiates at a sacrifice for one unworthy of sacrificing;
this abandonment applies to the sub-teacher and the sacrificer, but the abandonment of the father is never prescribed.
Those who abandon their preceptor out of passion,
or those who treat him with contempt out of delusion— for them, no atonement is prescribed.

"In the *chandahs*," that is, in one's own Vedas; "impurity" here consists of performing sacrifices for those who are unworthy (*apātra*) or officiating at sacrifices for those who are forbidden (*ayājya*). The connection is that there is no abandonment [of the teacher] even when the officiant (*yājya*) is impure as described above. There is no abandonment of the father, even in the aforementioned cases of impurity. Viṣṇu states: "A wife, a disciple, and a son—even if they are involved in sinful acts—[are not to be abandoned]."
Having been censured, she should be abandoned; he who acts otherwise becomes fallen.

[420] Sacrificial priests (*ṛtvij*), teachers (*ācārya*), officiating priests (*yājaka*), and instructors (*adhyāpaka*) are to be avoided, except for the purpose of relinquishing them; one should speak of the fallen (*patita*) after having analyzed and explained their condition.
Āpastamba [1.21.5–6]:
"No social interaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) is permitted with those who are fallen, nor likewise with those who are outcaste (*apapātra*)."
“By those who have fallen from their vessels,” such as Śabaras and others.

A priest (*ṛtvij*) and a teacher (*ācārya*) are to be abandoned if they teach out of ignorance or if they serve one who has fallen from his caste; otherwise, one falls by abandoning them. According to some, one also falls by accepting him as a dependent. There is never a lack of maintenance for one's mother and father, but they shall not inherit the estate.

The term *ajñānādhyāpanāt* is a collective dvandva compound; the negative particle *nañ* is to be connected with it afterwards. Regarding *ajñānāt*: when a specific ritual act is performed out of ignorance—that is, by manifesting ignorance—the officiant (*ṛtvij*) or teacher (*ācārya*) who abandons such a person falls; so too does another who accepts him as a disciple. *Avṛttiḥ* means a lack of favorable conduct, that is to say, a lack of service. The phrase *dāyaṃ tu na bhajeran* implies "the sons shall not divide the inheritance. (Āpastamba 1.28.6–10).

One should not go to see an outcast teacher or a relative; nor should one enjoy any wealth from them. If they should happen to meet by chance, one may greet them and then pass by in silence. A mother may perform many duties for her son, and toward her one must always maintain service even if she has fallen [from her status]. However, there should be no sharing of religious rites with her.

“*Darśanārtham*”: that for which seeing is the purpose is so described. “*Putratvasya*”: for the sake of establishing sonship in one who has conceived a fetus, there is the union with the embryo. “*Vāpaḥ*”: the gathering together for religious duties such as the *śrāddha* ceremony. Vasiṣṭha [13.47]: A fallen father is not to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall [from her status] toward her son.
Baudhāyana [2.3.42–43]: No social intercourse with outcasts is permitted; however, one should support even an outcast mother, provided one does not converse with her.
Gautama [20.1–7]:

One should abandon a father who is a regicide, one who officiates at sacrifices for Śūdras, one who corrupts the Vedas, a killer of an embryo, or one who lives with outcastes (antyāvasāyins) or among outcastes. Having assembled his teachers of knowledge and his kin, they shall perform all the water-libations and funeral rites for him. They shall overturn his sacrificial vessel. A male slave or a laborer, having brought a vessel of impure matter from the refuse heap and filled it from a jar belonging to a female slave, shall stand facing south and overturn it with his foot while pronouncing the name, saying: "I perform this non-water libation. All of them, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītīna) and with their topknots loosened, shall undertake this. The teachers of knowledge and the kin shall look on, and after touching water, they enter the village.

"A sacrificer for a Śūdra" is one who performs a sacrifice after having obtained wealth from a Śūdra. "Defilers of the Vedas" are those who teach during times when study is prohibited. "By Antyāvasāyins" means by Caṇḍālas and others. "Co-residence with Antyāvasāyins" refers to sexual intercourse and so forth. "Of him"—meaning of that person who is to be abandoned—while he is still alive, "they should perform the funeral rites"; the word "sons and others" is to be supplied. "Having assembled" means having gathered together. "Water and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the performance of the *preta-śrāddha* is intended. "Inversion" means turning [the vessel] face down. "Refuse" is a heap of dust and other debris discarded by a broom; [he should be assigned] a slave or a laborer for that. "All" refers to the sons and others mentioned previously.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

In the presence of the relatives of that teacher who has fallen, been accused, or is of wicked nature, and who causes the ruin of his family, one should proclaim his fault and address him repeatedly, saying, "May you regain your proper state. If he should remain with such a disposition, then, taking a broken vessel filled with water, having performed the *apasavya* (leftward) rite, one should cast it toward the southern direction with the left foot. Having turned the vessel *apasavya* and offered the discarded water, they should perform the worldly purification rites. For one who has been excluded from the community (*apapātrita*), inheritance, the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the water libations cease. One should not engage in conversation, sit together, or conduct business with him.

“Accused” (*abhiśasta*) means one who, though not having actually committed a sin, is notorious as a sinner. “Constantly” (*satatam*) refers to one of evil mind whose intention is fixed upon sinful deeds. “Causing the ruin of the family” (*kulakṣayakara*) is by such acts as the deliberate avoidance of approaching one’s wife during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*). “State” (*avasthā*) refers to the state of purification. “One whose mind is not settled” (*avasthitamati*) is one whose mind is not resolved toward the state of purification mentioned by the kinsmen. “Water for casting off” (*apaviddhodaka*) is the water used for the rite of renunciation (*tyāga*). “Worldly purification” (*laukikaṃ śaucam*) consists of bathing, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth. Vasiṣṭha [15.12–16]:

Those who are defilers of the Vedas, sacrificers for Śūdras, or outcasts from the highest classes of society—for them, because of the confusion of vessels and the mixing of those worthy of receiving gifts (*pātra*) with those unworthy (*apātra*), one should take an incomplete vessel and, having spread out red *darbha* grass with their tips pointing toward the left, pour out a full vessel for him. His relatives, with disheveled hair, should touch the person pouring it out; then, having driven him away, they may settle him at will in their own houses. From that time forward, they shall not enforce the law against him. Those who follow his conduct, however, if they continue to enforce the law against him, [are themselves liable].

“The class of the highest caste” (*uttamavarṇavargaḥ*) refers to the group of Brāhmaṇas. “Incomplete” (*akṛtsnam*) means fragmentary. “Fallen” (*patitam*) means one who has been expelled. “A non-relative” (*bandhur asadṛśaḥ*) refers to a brother or other kin of a different caste (*asavarṇa*). “With their tips exposed” (*vyaktāgrāḥ*) means with the tips visible. “Red” (*lohitān*) refers to red ochre and similar substances. “Not full” (*apūrṇam*) means empty, as it may be. “At will” (*svairam*) means slowly. “They might fall into” (*āpadyeran*) means they would become degraded. “They should not perform the rites” (*na dharmayeyuḥ*) means they should not conduct the funeral ceremonies. Manu [11.182–185]: “The water-libation for an outcaste must be performed by the *sapiṇḍa* relatives outside [the village],” and so forth.
On a censurable day, in the evening, and in the presence of kinsmen, officiating priests, and teachers.
One should kick over a water-pot filled with water with the foot, as if for a dead person;
they should remain in attendance for a day and night, but there is no impurity for them together with their kinsmen.
They should desist from conversation and sitting together with him;
however, one may give him gifts and even a worldly vessel.
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as shall the wealth acquired by the eldest;
however, a younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the share of the eldest.
Manu and Vasiṣṭha state in the fourth [chapter]:
"But when the penance has been performed,
one should bathe in a sacred body of water and drink from a new jar full of water along with that very person."
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the funeral rites for the deceased as before.
In this very same manner, one should perform the ritual even for women who have not fallen from their status;
however, clothing and food should be given to them, and they should dwell near the house.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins and have not performed purification;
however, once they have completed their purification, one should never despise them.
[425] Regarding this section on those who have not fallen [from their status], Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

If he has fallen [from his status] after death and seeks purification, he should summon those very people, address the king, and proclaim their virtues; then, having filled a new vessel with curds, honey, ghee, water, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and having brought it adorned with perfumes and garlands, they should circumambulate it three times to the right. Then, at the conclusion of the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblations, the kinsmen and women should cause that vessel to flow away into the midst of the waters, saying, "May the inauspicious and ill-spoken words be pacified. Thereafter, having bathed, being pure and dressed in white garments, he should re-enter his home with the consent of his kinsmen. In the same manner, there is the abandonment of women who have become corrupt, and the readmission of those who were previously rejected.

“Āvāhana” is the performance of the rite together with kinsmen. “Pratyāpannaḥ” means one who has again attained purity. “Śuddhim anvicchet” means he desires social intercourse appropriate to his state of purification. “Śauddhikam” means that which effects purification. Having in some cases described the commencement of the penance and so forth, Yājñavalkya [3.211] states:
“When the water-jar has been discarded, standing in the midst of his kinsmen, he should give grass to the cows.”
For one who has been honored with cows, the first act of hospitality should indeed be to bestow more cows.
“Satkāraḥ” means the giving of gifts preceded by respect.
Vasiṣṭha [15.17] states that it is the restoration of those who have fallen but have performed their penance.
Moreover, they also cite this: "One who lifts up [the burden] first should go as if playing, as if laughing;
one who casts it down later should go as if grieving, as if weeping."

[426] Those who have killed their teacher, mother, or father, or who have committed a blameworthy act through negligence—these may undergo expiation. Having filled a golden vessel, even one made of clay, with water from the *pūrṇa* or *pavitra* rites, they should sprinkle him with the *āpohiṣṭhā* verses. For one thus consecrated, the entire restoration of status is explained by the same rite as that performed upon the birth of a son.

"Killers" (*hantāraḥ*) here also refers to those who cause suffering. "Blameless" (*apavācyāḥ*) means those whose sins have been removed. "Restoration" (*pratyāpattiḥ*) means the act of making oneself known again. Regarding the phrase "flowing from river water or from streams" (*pravṛttam nadījalāt sravantībhyo vā*), this is according to the statement of Gautama (GDh 20.10). "A vessel made of earth" (*māheyam*) means one made of clay. By the statement "explained by the birth of a son," it is meant that one should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*) such as the *jātakarman* and others. (Gautama 20.10–17).

If one who is purified by penance should become pure, they should fill a vessel made of *śatakumbha* (gold) with water from a most sacred pool or from flowing rivers, and then touch him with that water. Then they should give that vessel to him; having accepted it, he should mutter: "May heaven be peaceful, may earth be peaceful, may the atmosphere be peaceful and auspicious; I take unto myself that which is the radiant realm. With these *yajus* verses, with the *vāvamānī*, *taratsamandī*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns, he should offer clarified butter into the fire. Or he should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa, or a cow, and also to his teacher. But he for whom the penance ends only with death becomes pure upon dying; they should perform all the water-libations and funeral rites for him. This very same *śāntyudaka* (water of pacification) should be muttered in all cases of mortal sin.

[427] The section beginning with "peaceful" (*śānta*) and ending with "I accept" (*gṛhṇāmi*). "Yajus-formulas" refers to those recited according to the revealed texts (*śruti*). "With the *Pāvamānī* verses" means with the *Taratsamandī* hymns. The phrase "they should touch water" connects with what precedes. The gift of either a cow or gold to the Brāhmaṇa is optional; the same applies to the teacher (*ācārya*). Thus says Baudhāyana [2.1.36–37].

Now, if his kinsmen should pour out a vessel of water for him in the assembly, saying, "I am such-and-such a person," and when he has begun by saying, "Having consumed water, milk, ghee, honey, and salt," the Brahmins should say to him, "You have performed [the penance]. He replies, "Om. They should perform for him the *savanīya* rite that fulfills the performance [of penance]. "Fulfilling the performance" means having completed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). "Savana" refers to the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*); the *savanīya* rite is the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and others connected with that. Viṣṇu [54.32].

One should not associate with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed women, even if they are pure according to the Dharma.
One should not perform acts such as drinking water together with them in a group. Hārīta says:
"Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra..."
One should avoid from afar one who is devoid of good conduct and of evil behavior.

They say that a Śūdra who abides by his own station, maintains good conduct, and laments over his own duties is most meritorious; others—the three [higher] castes who have fallen from their conduct—are not so.

[428] "The wise praise good conduct alone in all undertakings; for those who abide by good conduct attain the highest worlds, just like the immortals. Thus it is said. One who is "established in his own station" is one who serves the twice-born. One who is "established in his own conduct" is one entitled to perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*). One who is "lamenting over his own duties" is one whose wealth has been exhausted through service to the twice-born.
Yama said: That Brahmin who follows this boundary of dharma established of old by the seers, rejoices both in this world and after death.
This is the path practiced by the cultured; for the uncultured, it is otherwise. Therefore, the cultured go to heaven, while the uncultured go to a downward state.
Gautama [9.37]:
"And one who is in a state of distress (*āpadkalpa*) should maintain that entire conduct even with the mind.

The meaning is that when one is unable to perform the practice together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), one should accomplish it together with those parts by means of mental meditation (*dhyāna*).
Thus end the [categories of] things to be abandoned and things not to be abandoned.
Now, regarding the repayment of debts:
on this matter, Baudhāyana [2.16.1–5] states that there is an instruction for one desiring offspring; the Aśvins said that the designation [of the sacrifice] is based on procreation.
Endowed with long life and austerity, devoted to the study of the Vedas and sacrifice,
and having conquered his senses, he should diligently procreate offspring within each of his own respective caste.
From birth, a Brahmin enters into a bond with three debts;
by discharging them, he becomes self-possessed and liberated from doubt regarding dharma.
Having honored the seers through Vedic study, Indra with the Soma sacrifice,
and his ancestors with offspring, he becomes free from debt and rejoices in heaven.

Furthermore, Baudhāyana [2.16.7–14] states: It is known from scripture—"When a Brāhmaṇa is born, he is born burdened with three debts: to the seers by means of the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny. Thus the Veda demonstrates this connection with debt. Debt is bondage; its release is liberation. Progeny is the drawing forth of the fruit, and the word "drawing forth" refers to the ancestors; thus one becomes possessed of progeny and is not cut off.
“One who possesses offspring conquers the inexhaustible world for as long as he is thus sustained by his offspring.
By procreating a virtuous son, one delivers oneself—
seven descendants, seven ancestors, and six others, making oneself the seventh.
But by obtaining a virtuous son, one is delivered from the fear of sin.

Since one obtains the fruit by producing the continuity of progeny, therefore one should diligently produce offspring through the conjunction of medicinal herbs and mantras. Its instruction is taught by way of a common scriptural tradition, because it yields fruit for all castes.

For the sake of attaining the fruit for oneself, it is understood that by procreating a son, one procreates oneself; as it is said: "The self, indeed, is called 'son'. Thus, the second self should be regarded as living. "He who procreates a son—therefore, the self must never be cast away in what is not a field (an improper womb). For if he procreates himself elsewhere, he becomes such [a person]. Therefore, from the very beginning, one should seek thus: through the instruction regarding a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*), one should procreate offspring in that union with the application of herbs and mantras. This instruction is taught for all castes by virtue of the commonality of the scriptural injunctions. "Because it is a fruit"—this is the instruction for one desiring offspring; the word "will be performed" is the ellipsis. "Procreation" (*prajananam*) means the production of offspring. "Renown" (*samākhyā*) is the glorification of the family line. "By longevity" (*āyuṣā*) means by long life. "By long [practice]" refers to the performance of duties such as the avoidance of neglecting the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyopāsanā*). "By austerity" (*tapasā*) means by religious observance (*niyama*). "Sacrifice" (*ijyā*) is a *yāga*. "Diligent" (*yuktaḥ*) means one who exerts effort. "One who has conquered the senses" (*jitendriyaḥ*) is one who avoids the wives of others and sexual intercourse at forbidden times. "Self-possessed" (*ātmavān*) means one whose soul is praised. "By resorting to dharma" means by resorting to dharma in the form of procreating sons and so forth. The mention of "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is because acts such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must necessarily be performed, just like the clearing of a debt. "Attraction of the fruit" (*phalānukarṣam*) refers to the recollection of fruits such as heaven which depend on offspring, and the fulfillment of the ancestors' rites; it is the continuation [of the lineage] in the form of sons. "And words" refers to the glorification of the ancestors and so forth, which depends upon offspring. "The Veda shows"—this is to be connected to each [term]. "Not destroyed" (*anutsannaḥ*): even though dead, one truly exists in the form of offspring. And thus it is said in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (1.5.5.6): "Through offspring you are born again; that, O mortal, is your immortality. "In what is not a field" (*akṣetre*) means in the wives of others and so forth. "Of the same caste" (*savarṇe*) means of the same class.
