"By instruction" (*upadeśena*) means by means of the *garbhādhāna* rite and others. Regarding that procreation of a son, there is the "scriptural instruction" (*upadeśaśruti*). "By the application of herbs" is stated generally and commonly for those of the same caste in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; the meaning is that it is taught and recited there. "By being fruitful, etc."—the words "of the herbs and mantras" are the ellipsis.
Viṣṇu and Vasiṣṭha [Vi 15.45; Vas 16.2]: A father pays off his debt through this son and attains immortality, provided he beholds the face of his living son once he is born.
Bhartṛyajña [interprets] "of one who is born" as "one capable of discharging his debts. "He offers together" (saṃnayati) means "he transfers.
Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:
"Having seen the face of a living son, a father is free from debt to the ancestors."
Having entrusted that [son] to him at that very moment, he attained heaven by virtue of that birth.
Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Paiṭhīnasi say:
"Wherever he may be born, a son brings joy to his father;
by offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), he indeed attains freedom from debt to the ancestors."

[432] “In whatever place,” even in another’s field, provided it is preceded by mutual agreement between the owner of the field and the owner of the seed. Hārīta says: “He whose son is pure, capable, righteous, and in the prime of life...”
And being restrained against his own faults, he delivers his ancestors.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha 120]: Since a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he should strive for his birth even by merely looking upon his face.
This is the fruit of merely producing a son. Hārīta says:
"The hell named Puṃs is proclaimed, as well as the hell Chinnatantra."
Because he indeed protects [them] there, therefore he is remembered as "putra" (son).
“Nairakaḥ” means one who goes to hell. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
“The Agnihotra, the three Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by hundreds of sacrificial fees...”
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of one who has fathered an eldest son.
"For one who is established in sons and grandsons, who has many offspring, who is living,
and whose Vedic study and sacrifices have not declined, heaven is within reach of his hand.
"Of one who has given birth to an eldest son" means at the time of the first son's birth.
Manu, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Viṣṇu, Vasiṣṭha, and Hārīta [state]:
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one enjoys them eternally;
and through the grandson of a son, one attains the realm of the Sun."
Baudhāyana says:
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a grandson, one ascends to the very vault of heaven."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The ancestors rejoice in a son who increases the lineage, who is devoted to the duties toward his father, and who is endowed with devotion to the gods and Brahmins."

“Increasing the lineage” means capable of procreating sons. “Endowed with gods and Brahmins” means devoted to the worship of gods and Brahmins. Vasiṣṭha [17.2–4]: “It is known that endless worlds belong to those who have sons; there is no world for one who has no son,” and also by the Vedic citation: “Through offspring, may I attain immortality from Agni. “May those without offspring be devourers” is a curse. Rākṣasas are of a predatory nature.
The essential meaning is that this must surely be a great misfortune, since the *rākṣasa* marriage is not permitted. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.88]:
A son should be procreated with effort by one who is childless, regardless of what kind he may be.
For the purpose of performing the rites of the funeral cake and water-libations, and for the proclamation of his name.
Ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons—
whether they be principal sons, daughters' sons, or others, regardless of their kind—
just as one who crosses water by means of a leaky boat obtains whatever merit [is possible].
One attains such a quality as one who crosses over the darkness by means of bad sons.
Bṛhaspati [Āpaddharma, 53]:
Just as a man drowning while crossing water with a bad boat sinks,
even so does a father sink into blind darkness because of wicked sons.
The essential meaning is that his son must certainly be instructed; likewise, from the Śatapatha-Śruti:
"They say that the world belongs to the instructed son; therefore, one instructs him. And from the Ādi-purāṇa:
Having seen the face of your grandson, why do you grieve?
For one who is immersed in the great cycle of existence, there is indeed no fear of hell.
Having discharged his debts to the great sages, the ancestors, and the gods in due order,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live established in equanimity.
One should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself;
reflecting alone, the brahmin attains the supreme good.

“Equanimity” (*mādhyasthyam*) means the renunciation of the sense of ownership (*mamatā*) regarding wealth, sons, and so forth. “Solitary” (*ekākī*) means without companions, such as fellow students and others. One should contemplate one’s own welfare, excluding conversation and the like; the meaning is that one should meditate upon the nature of Brahman as described in the Upaniṣads. Yama says: [One who has] abandoned and left behind the life of a householder, and is liberated from former kinsmen...
The gods know him as an elder who has conquered his senses and is free from greed.
[435] Manu [4.259–260]: This eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder has been declared.
And the ritual procedure for the vows of a Snātaka, which increases one's inner strength and is auspicious.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from all taint and is glorified in the world of Brahma.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
a Brāhmaṇa should dwell in his house during the second stage of life.
[4.1] Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, the twice-born man,
having taken a wife, shall dwell in the household during the second quarter of his life.

Thus, Medhātithi explains that this method applies to a householder who has discharged the three debts, who is capable of maintaining his family and so forth, who has entrusted the care of his wife and dependents to a capable son, and who has abandoned all sense of "mine-ness" by having performed the formal transfer of those responsibilities onto himself; such a person, being without a wife or having lost the sacred fires, ceases from rites requiring material substances like the *śrāddha*, and performs only the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), water libations (*udakatarpaṇa*), purification, and meditation on the Self. This is the manner [of life] for him.

Thus ends the section on the householder (*gṛhasthakāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsandhivigrahika*) to His Majesty the Great King, the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
